PREFACE THE BUSINESS GUIDE contains cold blooded busi- THE 

ness data, boiled down legal information, proven methods for making money and saving money and innumerable rules, formulæ, statistics, forms, diagrams, facts and figures for ready reference. 

Fundamentally, therefore, it is not a volume of romance or mystery, although where will you find more of romance or mystery than in a successful business career?

It is rather a book for occasional study and for convenient reference in the home, on the farm or at the office or factory.

In its forty years of service THE BUSINESS GUIDE 

has solved the business problems of millions of readers. 

Originally it was the crowning achievement of a poor orphaned immigrant who in an incredibly short time rose to a professorship in an American College and attained a high rank among successful business men. 

Today it is the product of many minds, well known attorneys, captains of Industry, statistical organizations, educational institutions and government bureaus.

Business and Legal Forms for Practical Use.

EXPLANATION 

BUSINESS man should know some law, not because he wants to be a lawyer, but because he must understand his relation to others in order to carry on his business intelligently. 

The following legal department has been prepared in simple form. The information is accurate, brief, and reliable. Its purpose is to prevent unnecessary suits and expensive litigation. It will settle disputes and end arguments. And in emergencies, when the loss of an hour or so a day may mean the loss of hundreds of dollars, it will enable the layman to draw up the required legal documents, quickly and correctly.

EXPLANATION OF TERMS 1. Definition of Terms.-Statute refers to the laws pass ed by Congress and the several State Legislatures. The term common law refers to that body of law and jurisprudence which was originated, developed, and formulated, and is administered, in England, and has been adopted among and by the United States. An action is a suit or case which one party brings against another in court. 

2. Common Law. In a large measure the common law establishes the rules and regulations under which we live. 

Legal decisions are precedents which must be followed in other cases of the same general nature. The lower courts must follow the findings of the higher courts; the State courts are bound to follow the decision of the Federal Courts; but the courts in one State are not bound by the decisions of a court in another State. Of course, the common law decision may be set aside by statute or modified when it no longer applies to present conditions. 

3. Law and Equity.-These two terms appear frequently in the following pages and are quite generally misunderstood. The word law signifies a rule of action, either written or unwritten. Equity rather looks to the substance than to the form. When an act is equitable it is just even though it has no foundation in the law. Formerly separate courts existed to try cases in equity. The modern tendency is to combine law and equity and to give judges the power to try both law and equity cases. (See legal remedies and equitable remedies.) 

4. Civil Law and Criminal Law.-The difference between civil and criminal law is not always understood. Criminal law may be defined as the law dealing with offenses against the people and is founded on the statutes. The acts that are crimes are clearly defined and the cases are prosecuted by public officers. Civil law takes in all law not penal in its nature. Wrongful acts may be subject to both criminal and civil actions. If a man steals a horse, he has committed a crime against the State, or public policy, and at the same time the person robbed has a civil action against him for the loss. (See Torts.) 

5. Classes of Courts.-There are three kinds of courts in

Louis A. Paeth MAKING A PLEA IN A KING'S COURT IN THE MIDDLE AGES.

EXPLANATION OF TERMS 

9 each of the States. The first are the courts which have jurisdiction over petty criminal offenses and in which minor suits are brought. Second, there are the courts in which more important suits are brought and in which decisions in the lower courts are reviewed. And finally, there is the 

Supreme Court, or court of last resort, which reviews the decisions of the lower courts. 

6. An example. Of course the judicial system varies widely in the different States. The Illinois law provides for 

Justice of the Peace Courts in which minor cases are tried. 

Next comes the County Court, one in each county. Then there is the Circuit Court comprised of three judges who can sit in any of the courts in their circuit. Following the Circuit 

Court comes the State Appellate Court, or Court of Appeals, and at the top the State Supreme Court. Besides these courts, the larger Counties have special courts to hear probate cases and the like. Cities with a populaton of 50,000 or more have municipal courts with jurisdiction over cases confined to the city, and the criminal courts establish branches called police courts. Many States have only two classes of courts, lower and higher. 

7. Federal Courts.-There are also three classes of Federal Courts. The lowest is called the District Court, taking its name from the fact that the country as a whole is divided into districts with one court for each district. Next is the Appellate Court to which appeals from the District Court are taken. And finally, there is the United States 

Supreme Court in which appeals may be sought from decisions of the Appellate Courts and from the Supreme Courts of the several States. After an application is made in proper form this court decides whether or not it will review the case. 

8. Basis of Appeals.-No court will review the decision of a lower court unless the application is founded on errors in the former proceedings. Thus the proof of wrongful admission of or refusal to admit evidence in the former trial would be sufficient to grant a rehearing. 

9. Evidence.-Evidence includes all means and ways by which the truth of an alleged fact is established or disproved. Legal evidence is direct testimony of a witness or written documents and records, which are competent, relevant, and material to the issues joined. Circumstantial evidence

is a chain of facts or circumstances, all tending, when connected up, to establish a logical inference or conclusion. 

10. The Reason for Laws.—In the beginning there was no law save that of brute strength or the survival of the fittest. A man had to protect his person and his property by force. Common dangers threatened and men banded themselves together, vesting all law making powers to the tribal chiefs. Gradually the evolution proceeded until today we have a system of laws of the people, for the people and by the people, making all men equal in their rights and duties.

1. Definition.-Adoption is making the child of another, one's own child as far as it is possible under the law. Any child whether its parents are living or not may be adopted. 

If the parents are living they lose all personal rights and ueben 

ROVER FRIENDLESS AND ALONE MY PAL, ORPHAN What

are relieved from all legal duties. The adopting parents acquire the right to the adopted child's custody, services, and earnings, and must support and educate him. 

2. Method of Adoption.-The formalities of adoption are different in most of the states, but application is usually made to the County Judge. The child cannot be adopted without the consent of the parents, but once given, the consent cannot be revoked. If the child is over 14 years of age his consent is also necessary. 

3. Inheritance in Cases of Adoption.-In most states an adopted child acquires all the legal rights of a natural child. 

He can also inherit from his natural parent and kindred exactly as though he had not been adopted. There are some exceptions to these rules. (See Parent and Child; Husband and Wife.)

1. Definition. An affidavit is an oath or affirmation made in writing, sworn to or affirmed, before an officer empowered to administer the same. Affidavits are not testimony in courts of law, because the makers are not cross-examined; but a false affiant may be punished for perjury. 

2. Form. The following is a common form, and with certain modifications can be made to apply to almost any case:

Common Form of Affidavit STATE OF ILLINOIS, Į COUNTY OF HENRY. 

88.

John Jones being duly sworn on his oath states that he is well acquainted with the handwriting of Daniel Seitz one of the subscribing witnesses to the deed hereto attached; that affiant has frequently seen him write and knows his signature; that he believes that the name of the said Daniel Seitz, signed in the said deed, is in the handwriting of the said Daniel Seitz, and further affiant says not. 19.... 

(Signed) JOHN JONES 

Subscribed and sworn to before me this 28th day of February, A. D.

AGENCY 

1. Definitions.-Agency is the relation between two or more persons by which one person (the agent) represents another (the principal) in the transaction of lawful acts or business. Agents are of two kinds, general and special. 

A General Agent is authorized to represent the principal in all of his business, or in all business of a particular kind just as the principal himself would do. A Special Agent is authorized to do a specific thing, to sell a farm, buy a house, or to transact some special business for the principal. 

2. Who May Act as Principal and Agent.-Any person who is able to act for himself, may act as principal. This excludes a lunatic, an infant, or an alien enemy, or any other person incapable of contracting. On the other hand any person who is competent to act in his own right, and who is of sound mind and understanding, may act as an agent. Husband and wife may act for each other, except where prevented by the statutes of the particular State. A person unable to contract on his own account, such as a person under age, may sometimes act as an agent. Anyone except a lunatic, imbecile, or infant of tender years may be an agent. Corporations often act for others.

AGENCY 

15 3. 

Authority, How Given.-The authority of an agent may be constituted in three ways: By deed under seal, by writing, or by mere word. Express authority is given to an agent by what is called a power of attorney. If the authority is to execute a writing, under seal and acknowledged, the power of attorney must be likewise under seal and acknowledged. An agent to sell land, or to do any important business, where he is required to make contracts, draw or sign notes, drafts or checks, should be appointed by "power of attorney." If an agency is proved without its extent being shown it will be presumed to be a general agency. The acts of a general agent will bind the principal, even though he had no authority to do them, provided he acts in the general scope of the business which he was authorized to transact. If a special agent exceeds his authority, the principal is not bound, but if a general agent exceeds his authority the principal is bound, provided the agent acted within the ordinary and usual scope of the business he was authorized to transact, and the party dealing with him did not know he was exceeding his authority. 

Agency may be implied from previous dealings and transactions between the parties. If the principal has held a person out as an agent he will be bound by his acts, even though as a matter of fact the agent had no authority to represent him. The acts or contracts of an agent made beyond the scope of his authority may be ratified by the principal and when so ratified are binding on the latter. 

4. Agent's Responsibility.—An agent concealing his principal is himself responsible, and if acting fraudulently or deceitfully is himself responsible to third parties. He cannot appoint a substitute or delegate his authority to another, without consent of his principal. If an agent embezzles his principal's property it may be reclaimed if it can be identified or distinctly traced. An agent employed to sell property cannot buy it himself, or if employed to purchase property, cannot buy from himself. 

5. Principal's Liability.-The principal is liable to the third person for the negligence or unskillfulness of the agent, when he is acting in the fulfillment of the agency business. 

The principal is liable for all acts of his agent within the scope of his agency, but money paid by an agent can be recovered by the principal, if it has been paid by mistake. 

The knowledge of the agent relating to the business of the

agency is binding upon the principal, and notice to an agent as to matters relating to the agency is notice to the principal. 

6. Authority May Be Revoked.-The authority of an agent may be terminated: First, by the express revocation thereof by the principal. Second, by renunciation of such power by the agent. Third, by the death of the principal, which also revokes the agency. Fourth, by the expiration of the time within which the agent was to perform the acts which were to be done by him, or by him having completed and fully performed the commission and closed the business which he was to transact. Fifth, by the sale of the subject matter of the agency. Sixth, by the insanity of either principal or agent. A revocation of authority takes effect, so far as the agent is concerned when he receives notice thereof; so far as the third persons are concerned when they receive notice of such revocation. Personal notice or its equivalent is required, and is sufficient to those who have dealt with the agent. Advertising the fact would be sufficient as to all others. Without a sufficient notice of the revocation, a contract made in good faith with the agent after revocation will bind the principal the same as before. 

7. Special Rules of Agency.-An agent cannot delegate his powers to another without the consent of the principal, unless the act to be done is a minor service, or one requiring no personal ability or skill. Both principal and agent are liable if the persons with whom the agent is transacting business do not know of the agency relationship. An agent can receive no personal profit from a transaction. 

8. Caution.-Persons dealing with agents who are strangers should be very careful to ascertain that the agent has authority to transact the business in hand. In all transactions in regard to real estate the authority of the agent should be in writing, signed by the owner of the property, in order to be binding upon him. In all cases of doubt as to the authority of an agent or the extent of his authority, it would be wise to require of the agent a written proof of his agency and the extent of his authority. 

9. Power of Attorney.-To delegate to an agent the power to sign notes, checks, and other legal documents, as well as to transact any business where such decuments are necessary, is called power of attorney—that is, the power

AGENCY 

17 to be attorney for you. Such power or authority should be given in writing. It should be witnessed and should state clearly what the attorney has power to do.

AGREEMENT TO PURCHASE LAND 1. Must be in Writing.-An agreement to purchase real estate must be in writing, and should be signed by both buyer and seller. The writing need not mention the amount to be paid for the land. It may be signed with a lead pencil or with a rubber stamp. The entire contract need not be on the same sheet of paper, as in cases where agreement to purchase land is completed through correspondence between the two parties. 

2. Exceptions.-There are some exceptions to this rule.

For instance if A sells a piece of property to B and without a written agreement allows B to take possession of the property, the courts will compel A to give B a deed to the property. In other words the law gives B an opportunity to prove that he is not a trespasser but the real owner of the land. 

3. A Common Misunderstanding.-It is quite generally believed that if a purchaser makes an oral agreement and pays part of the purchase price he can compel the seller to give him a deed to the real estate. This was formerly the rule but the courts abandoned it on account of too frequent frauds. The purchaser can compel the seller to return the advance money. 

4. Options. An option is a contract between two parties for the transfer of property or rights. For example A agrees to sell a piece of property to B at a certain price within a certain period of time, for which B gives A a valuable consideration. B must either exercise his option and purchase the property within the time limit, or forfeit his consideration. All options must be in writing. If no time limit is fixed in the agreement, the option must be exercised within a reasonable time. 

5. Tranferring of Title.-In most real estate contracts the seller agrees to furnish the buyer with a good or merchantable title. That is, he agrees to transfer the property by proper conveyance of a Warranty Deed which warrants the title in him and the buyer against any loss which might be occasioned by defects in the title. All wise purchasers will demand a contract that will require the seller to furnish and deliver a merchantable title. There are four systems used by which this is shown. First, the Abstract system; second, the Title Insurance or Guarantee Policy; third, Certificate

AGREEMENT TO PURCHASE LAND 

19 

of Title; and fourth, by the Public Registrar Certificate or 

Torrens system. 

6. The Abstract System is the one mainly used and is, in fact, in universal use, except in the Pacific Coast states and the cities of the country. An abstract is simply a history or pedigree of the title to the land. The public records are searched and the matters shown therein briefed. An abstract will show all transfers, mortgages, judgments, tax sales, liens of all kinds, court proceedings and everything in fact of record affecting the title to the property. These abstracts are prepared by private concerns or individuals known as abstract companies or abstracters. Getting an abstract, however, does not mean that the purchaser is getting a good title. The abstract is only intended to show the title as of record. To determine whether or not it is good, the purchaser should have the abstract examined by an attorney, competent to pass upon the law of real property. This examination by an attorney will reveal the validity or merchantability of the title. Whatever objections the examiner might find are usually capable of being corrected to his satisfaction without a great deal of delay or expense. This works no hardship on either party, because it is the accepted custom that the seller pays all of the expenses incidental to bringing the abstract down to date and getting the title acceptable to the purchaser's attorney. The purchaser pays the examination fee. The objections to this system are that every attorney who examines the abstract will probably find some objections, but these will have to be accepted as a part of the system, because each examiner has a right to his own personal opinion, as is human nature. 

7. Title Insurance or Guarantee Policy.-By this system the private title or trust company issues a policy guaranteeing the purchaser against any loss he might sustain by reason of any defect in the title, whether of record or otherwise existing, before or at the time of the issuance of the policy. 

This system is necessarily becoming more and more popular and in use in the cities because of the demand for facilities to expedite real estate transactions and also because of the protective feature. The formal abstract is not necessary; the purchaser merely makes application for the policy and the title company investigates the title and if reasonably safe issues the policy in a short time. An attorney's examination and opinion with the usual suggestions and requirements to

the title are eliminated. If rank defects are found so that the title company does not want to insure it, they can many times correct them or overcome them in some way, thereby making it possible to close an otherwise impossible deal. 

These title companies are safe, sound, financial institutions. 

8. Certificates of Title.-Certificates of title are simply a combination abstract and an attorney's opinion prepared in one act by a title company. The private company simply makes the statement that it has examined the title to a certain property and that the title is in whoever the name of the record owner might be, and if there are any defects in the title, mortgages or liens upon it or unpaid taxes, the certificate immediately enumerates them. The only advantages in a certificate of title over the abstract and attorney's system is that the preparation of a formal abstract with the additional consultation of the examining lawyer is unnecessary. The title company does both. 

9. Torrens System.-The Torrens System is a system comparable to public title companies. Under this system real estate is tranferred by certificate issued by the County Registrar. It is based upon a court decree which is supposed to define the title and adjudicate or guarantee it down to a certain point. Those depending upon it are supposed to be protected by a fund established from the fees of the offices. 

However, the system is not applicable to the title laws and property rights of our country; those administering the offices are usually political supports and the fund for protection and payment of losses is usually negligible. It is only used in a few places. It takes a long time to get a title originally registered and takes away the privilege of handling your real estate in privacy. (See Deeds).

AUCTIONEER 

1. Definition.-An auctioneer is a person employed to sell property to the highest bidder at public sale. 

2. Agent For Both Buyer and Seller.-An auctioneer is the exclusive agent of the owner until he accepts the purchaser's bid and knocks down the property to him. On accepting the bid the auctioneer becomes the agent of the purchaser also, and thus represents both parties. 

3. When is the Sale Complete.-A sale by auction is completed when the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer, or in any other customary manner. 

Until such announcement is made, the auctioneer may withdraw the property from sale unless the sale has been advertised to be without reserve. Any bidder may also withdraw his bid at any time before the fall of the hammer. 

4. Responsibility of Auctioneer.-Authority to sell prop erty does not imply power to sell at auction. Thus a purchaser buying goods from an auctioneer when he knows the auctioneer has no authority to sell them, acquires no title to the property thus purchased. The seller or owner is not bound by any statements by the auctioneer differing from those given to him. An auctioneer is supposed to accept the most favorable bid. He cannot, therefore, refuse to ac-

cept legitimate bids. He is justified in throwing out the bids of insane or drunken persons, minors, trustees of the property, or the bids of persons who refuse to comply with the terms of the sale. 

5. Things An Auctioneer Cannot Do.-An auctioneer is not allowed to assign his duties to another, except it be in the discharge of minor or incidental duties. He cannot act contrary to the wishes and instructions of the owner, in any matters relating to the details of the sale. He may not permit a bidder to withdraw his bid after its acceptance, without the consent of the owner. He cannot sell the property to himself, nor employ another to bid it in for him. He is not permitted to sell at private sale contrary to the owner's instructions. He should never conceal the name or identity of the owner, otherwise the bidder is not bound. 

AUTOMOBILE 1. The Right to Use the Highways.-The public has a right to use the public roads to travel and transport property. Drivers of automobiles have an equal right on the highways with other vehicles, but they do not have any greater right. Each has the same rights and the same restrictions. Again the courts hold that all travelers have an equal right to use the highways. Thus, a pedestrian has the same right as the driver of an automobile. The state cannot exclude non-residents from the public roads, nor place greater restrictions or burdens on non-resident motorists than those imposed on its own citizens. 

2. Parking. In the absence of city ordinance or statutory regulation an automobile may be left at the side of the road after shutting off the power and setting the brakes. 

3. License.-The several states issue licenses to the owners of automobiles, motorcycles and trucks permitting them to use the public highways. Most cities also require a municipal license. Such a license is neither a contract nor a tax. It is simply a privilege, and as such does not pass to a purchaser of the vehicle and may be revoked for any good reason. The driver of an unregistered car is a trespasser on the highway. 

4. The Law on Rented Machines. Suppose A rents his automobile to B for a certain consideration.

According to

AUTOMOBILE 

23 law A is not responsible for the negligent acts of B even if B is an unskilled driver. On the other hand if A knew when he rented the car that B was an immature child or of low mentality, or under the influence of alcohol, the courts would hold him responsible. If the owner lends his car with a chauffeur, he will be held liable for the negligent acts of the chauffeur. This does not apply if the car is loaned without the chauffeur. In case of damage to the rented car, the renter is liable only if it can be proved that he did not exercise ordinary prudence and care. In case of misuse the owner can bring action to repossess himself. Should the renter sell the car without the owner's authority, the owner can recover even from an innocent purchaser. The owner of an automobile is entitled to a fair compensation for its use, even if no definite sum is agreed upon, and he can collect a reasonable hire if his mcahine is used by another without his knowledge or consent. Criminal liability is attached to the unlawful use of another's automobile. 

5. The Speed of Automobiles along a public road is regulated by law. The State laws prescribe the maximum rates of speed for the business district, residence district and country. A municipality has the right to modify the speed laws in accordance with local requirements. The courts have recently held that any rate of speed which does not endanger the lives of the occupants of the car, or the lives and property of others, is a legal rate of speed. 

6. The Laws of the Road are intended to prevent collisions and accidents. 1. Vehicles are required to pass each other on the right. If, therefore, two automboiles collide in a street which is wide enough for safe passage, the driver on the wrong side of the road is responsible for the other driver's injury. Where there is no obstuction on the road a driver is permitted to pass on the left hand side. 

2. Each driver must pass on his own side of the center of the traveled road. This applies when the road is covered with snow, to side roads, and to roads under construction. 

3. It is the duty of every driver to exercise reasonable care in avoiding accidents or injuries to others. This rule applies just as strongly when the driver's machine is on the right side of the road. 4. At street intersections the rights of the travelers are equal but it is usually the custom to allow the right of way to the vehicle approaching from the right. 5. It is the duty of the driver to keep his car under

control at all times. When approaching corners, or when seeing that his machine is frightening a horse, the motorist must slow down, or if necessary stop his car. 6. If one wilfully or negligently drives a car on a street or road at an unlawful speed, thereby killing another, he may be guilty of homicide. 7. The driver of a car may be charged with carelessness if, without warning to others, he changes the course of his direction or backs his machine. A driver may not back his machine on a public road without looking backward. 

7.-The Fitness of the Driver.-The driver of an automobile must be physically and mentally fit. A man who is subject to fainting spells or epileptic attacks has no right to drive a car upon the public highway. The same rule applies to one with defective eyesight. Proper eyeglasses are held to restore the competency of the driver. It is a serious crime to drive an automobile while intoxicated, thereby endangering the lives of others. 

8. The Chauffeur's Liability.-As a general rule the own er is liable for the acts of his chauffeur, provided the chauffeur is acting within the scope of the owner's business. 

However, should the chauffeur use the car without the consent or knowledge of the owner, or should he be using it for his own business and with the owner's consent, the owner is not liable for the driver's acts. The same rule applies when the owner's son uses the parent's machine without his knowledge or consent. If the car is run with his knowledge by a member of his family, or for the convenience of other members of the family, the parent is liable for the negligent acts of the driver. Children under 15 are usually forbidden by the State law to drive an automobile. Under the statutory law the husband is not liable for the negligence of his wife while driving an automobile. 

9. License. Most states require a chauffeur to take out a license. Even though the license is defective it remains in force until revoked by the proper authority. Thus a chauffeur whose license is defective cannot be held a trespasser on the public highway. 

10. Minor.-The state statutes forbid minors to drive automobiles. The owner of a car, therefore, who allows a child to operate it, may be held responsible for accident or injury resulting from the child's negligence.

25 

11. The Chauffeur's Rights.-A chauffeur may recover damages from his employer for injury received while operating the car, provided that the employer has in some way contributed to the result. On the other hand if his injury was due to a defective part, he could not recover, unless it so happened that the employer knew of the defect and the chauffeur did not. If a chauffeur should be injured while riding in a car driven by the owner, the chauffeur could recover for injuries sustained due to the owner's negligence.

12. Workmen's Compensation Laws.-These laws provide that a chauffeur who is injured while running his car beyond the speed limit prescribed by statute, can recover nothing, and the statutes disregard the custom of other chauffeurs in this respect. It is generally customary for chauffeurs to travel at between twenty-five to thirty-five miles per hour on the boulevards in our larger cities, although the lawful rate of speed is not in excess of twenty miles per hour. A chauffeur injured under such circumstances cannot hold his employer. 

13. The Owner's Injury.-If the owner of a car be injured in any way through the wrongful acts or negligence of his chauffeur, the chauffeur may be held liable. 

14. Garage Keeper.-A garage keeper is a bailee for hire and therefore bound to exercise reasonable care for the property bailed. The owner of a car is not liable for the negligence of the garage keeper or his employees in the care and operation of his automobile. If a garage keeper

or his employee operate an automobile the garage keeper is liable for any damage done to the car or to third persons. 

A public garage, while not considered a public nuisance, is subject to public regulations as to location, odors, noise and fire hazards. A garage keeper has a lien for a reasonable compensation on an automobile for storage or repairs. He is not liable for fire damage to the automobile unless the fire is caused by his own negligence or that of his employees. He is liable for theft. 

15. Used Automobiles.-There are two points to keep in mind when purchasing a second hand machine. Such automobiles are usually sold “as is” and the motorist often finds fault when he finds the car is not in perfect running order. 

If the cylinders prove to be scored or the bearings loose the purchaser has no redress at law. The law presumes that if any warranty was made it would have been reduced to writing in the form of a contract. In the second place there are many instances of sharp practices among the dealers in used automobiles. Frequently the purchaser discovers to his sorrow that the car is stolen or that it is covered by a chattel mortgage. In every case a bill of sale should be demanded and the records searched for incumbrances. 

16. The Bill of Sale should be drawn in accordance with the laws of the State where the purchase is made. The following form will answer the purpose in most of the States: 

Bill of Sale 

"Know all men by these presents that I (here insert name and address of party selling the car) in the county of..... state of.. in consideration of (here insert amount of money to be paid party selling by party buying) dollars this day to me in hand paid, do hereby grant, sell, transfer and deliver unto the said (here insert name of party buying) the following goods and chattels to-wit: (Then insert name of automobile its model, the engine number and the car number, also the type of car, its color, together with any other information which will help to identify it); to have and to hold said goods and chattels to the said (name of purchaser), his executors, administrators and assigns to their use forever. "I hereby covenant with the said grantee that I am the lawful owner of the said goods and chattels; that they are free and clear from all incumbrances; that I have good right to sell the same and that I will warrant and defend the same against the lawful claims and demands of all persons. 27 17. In Case of Accidents.-Accidents will happen in spite of the most careful driving. If you chance to be mixed up in one here are a few things to remember: a. Do not drive away without reporting the facts to the police or nearest police station, or without giving your name, address and license number to the other party involved. Such action on your part would constitute a felony, punishable by fine or imprisonment. b. Be sure to get the name and address of the other party, or if he drives away, his license number. c. Get the names and addresses of all persons who witnessed the accident, or saw the results of it, including all injured persons. d. Try to visualize just how it happened, remember your own position and that of the other party, both before and after the accident, and note carefully the wheel marks on the road or pavement. e. Be calm and courteous. Do not admit that you are in the wrong or accuse the other party. f. Do not make immediate settlement or offer to do so, nor incur any expense except for necessary medical relief.

Where the word "reciprocal" appears as for instance after Massachusetts, it means that whatever laws are applied to the citizens of Massachusetts when visiting the state of the visiting motorist, apply to such motorist when in Massachusetts. For example the New Jersey law allows a visiting motorist to stay only fifteen days on the license of his home state. Thus, a car carrying a New Jersey license could stay in Massachusetts only fifteen days. On the other hand an automobile bearing a Pennsylvania license could stay indefinitely in Massachusetts.

BAILMENT 

1. Definitions.-Bail is the security for releasing a person from custody. A Bailment is a delivery of a thing in trust for some special object or purpose. A Bailor is one who makes a bailment or delivers goods to a bailee. A 

Bailee is a person who receives goods of another to hold according to the purpose of delivery. 

2. Bail means securities who bind themselves either to satisfy the plaintiff, his debt and costs, or to surrender the de-

BAILMENT 

29 fendant into custody, provided judgment is rendered against him in the action. The above definition applies to civil action. In criminal cases bail means the sureties who bind themselves to have the prisoner present in court when required for trial. In ordinary parlance the word bail is used as synonymous with the word surety and practically means the same thing. We shall treat the subject in its relation to civil matters under the law of suretyship. In criminal matters, the subject not being germain to the purpose of this book, it is not further discussed. 

3. Bailor and Bailee.-To create this relation the property must be delivered to the bailee. Thus if A takes his car to a public garage to remain over night, the garage owner becomes a bailee for hire. The contract of bailment also exists when a man takes a suit of clothes to a tailor shop to be altered, or when a farmer takes a load of oats to a mill to be ground. If, however, the goods are delivered to another to be sold or exchanged, the contractual relationship ceases and the person to whom the goods were delivered becomes the debtor of the owner. 

4. The Law on Lost Property.-In point of law, the finder of lost property is entitled to keep it until the owner is found. To attempt to keep it when the owner is known, or where there are means of discovering him, is construed as larceny. The law usually provides the necessary steps to be taken in the case of lost property. The finder must make an honest effort to locate the owner. Failing in this he may retain the property and maintain his rights as against all others. Should the true owner appear, the finder has no lien on the property unless a reward has been offered for its return. 

5. The finder does not always take title to the article found. The article must actually have been lost, not merely laid down or aside voluntarily, and forgotten. Thus, if a woman lay down a package in a department store, the owner of the store is the proper custodian, rather than the finder. 

6. The Bailee's Responsibility.-A bailee cannot as a rule limit his liability by agreement. He becomes the custodian of the goods and is required to exert reasonable care against accident or loss. His liability is limited only as to loss resulting from the nature of the goods stored. For example if a truck load of fruit arrives at a cold storage plant, the owner is not responsible for any loss due to the condition

of the fruit when it arrived. On the other hand if an em、 ployee of the storage company negligently allows the goods to spoil, the owner of the fruit can recover from the storage company. 

7. Suppose your bank grants you the privilege of keeping a strong box in the bank building without making any charge therefor; is the bank responsible for the loss? The bank, of course, is not bound to exercise as much care as a regular safety deposit company, but it is required to take reasonable precaution, as much care as it uses to protect its own property. Suppose the cashier steals the box, who is responsible? The bank employed the cashier to carry on the business of banking, not to steal. If, therefore, the bank had exercised reasonable care, and if the cashier was a long trusted employee against whom there was no cause for suspicion, the bank would not be responsible for the loss to any greater extent than if the box was stolen by a common burglar. 

8. The Bailee's Duty.-The bailee is usually a keeper only. However, if he is keeping live stock, he must supply the food necessary to the animal's good condition. Milch cows must be properly milked and in case of sickness animals must be given proper medical care and attention. In every case the bailee is required to exercise reasonable care for the goods in the bailment.

BANKRUPTCY 

1. A National Bankruptcy Act was passed by Congress and went into force July 1, 1898, which virtually supersedes and does away with all state insolvency laws and proceedings. 

2. Courts. The courts having jurisdiction in bankruptcy cases are the District Courts of the United States, in the several States and Territories, and the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia. 

3. Bankrupts.-Bankrupts are of two kinds, voluntary and involuntary. Involuntary bankrupts are those who are declared bankrupts by the proper courts on petition of creditors and who have committed one or more of the acts of bankruptcy hereinafter specified. Voluntary bankrupts are

BANKRUPTCY 

31 those who are declared to be bankrupts on their own motion or petition. Any person who owes debts, except a corporation, may become a voluntary bankrupt. Any person, except a wage-earner or farm- er, any incorporated company or any corporation owing debts to the amount of One

Thousand Dollars or over, may be declared an involuntary bankrupt. 

4. What Are Acts of Bankruptcy?-The 

National Bankrupt

Law defines various acts that constitute an act of bankruptcy. 

They are five in number, namely:

BANKRUPT 

a. Admitting in writing of a person's inability to pay his debts. This may be done by a corporation through its regularly constituted officer. b. Fraudulently conveying, transferring, concealing, or removing property with the intention of hindering, delaying or defrauding creditors. The intention to hinder, delay or defraud is a question of fact, to be decided by judicial inquiry. Thus, if a man signs over his property. to his wife in order to avoid payment of his debts, the court may construe this as an act of bankruptcy. However, if the transfer was made when the owner was free from debt, the property cannot be impeached by subsequent creditors. The transfers of property covered by the act are those which the common law regards as fraudulent. c. Transferring property when a person is already insolvent constitutes an act of bankruptcy. d. A general assignment for the benefit of creditors is an act of bankruptcy. In the same way a general assignment for the benefit of creditors made

by the majority of the board of directors and of the stockholders constitutes an act of bankruptcy for a corporation. A petition for the appointment of a receiver of a corporation under the state statutes is NOT an assignment for the benefit of creditors and is, therefore, not an act of bankruptcy. e. Suffering a creditor to obtain a preference when the debtor is insolvent constitutes an act of bankruptcy. This includes the transfer of property and the payment of money within four months of the time of filing the petition. Like a fraudulent transfer, the intent to prefer one creditor as against another must be proved, although in many cases it is so apparent as to be presumed. 

5. Filing a Voluntary Petition.-A voluntary petitioner should file his petition in the court of bankruptcy in the judicial district where he has principally resided for the preceding six months. When there is no estate and no claim has been proved and no trustee has been appointed, a bankrupt may withdraw his petition on paying the costs and expenses. The petition must be accompanied by a schedule of the petitioner's property, showing its kind and amount, location, money value, and a list of his creditors and their residences when known, the amount due to them, the security they have, and a claim to legal exemptions, if any. After filing a voluntary petition the judge makes an adjudication. He may do this ex parte, that is without notice to creditors. 

6. Involuntary Petition.-A petition may be filed against a person who is insolvent and has committed an act of bankruptcy within four months after such action. Three or more creditors having bona fide claims of $500.00 or more in excess of securities held against the debtor may file an involuntary petition in bankruptcy, or if there are less than twelve creditors then any one creditor may file the petition provided his claim amounts to more than $500.00 Creditors whose claims are prior or secured are not considered in involuntary bankruptcy proceedings. The petition must state the names and addresses of the creditors and the bankrupt, his place of business, the nature of it, his act of bankruptcy, that it occurred within four months of the filing of the petition, and that the amount of the claim against him is in ex-

BANKRUPTCY 

33 cess of $500.00. This petition must be duly signed and verified. It may be changed or amended for good cause. 

7. Filing the Answer.-The bankrupt is then subpoenaed to appear before the court to file his answer to the petition. 

In the meantime, his property may be seized if it can be proved that he is neglecting it or allowing it to decrease in value. Within ten days after he has been declared a bankrupt he must also file with the court a schedule of his property with a list of his creditors, the amounts due them and the security held by them. 

8. Meeting of Creditors.-After the party has been adjudged a bankrupt, a meeting of all creditors must be called not less than ten days nor more than thirty days after such adjudication, at the county seat of the county where the bankrupt has his principal place of business or resides. 

At the first meeting of the creditors, the referee presides, allows or disallows claims of creditors, and may publicly examine the bankrupt. At this meeting the trustee is appointed. All claims must be presented under oath in writing, setting forth his claim to the referee. Subsequent meetings may be held at any time. 

9. Who May Vote.-Only creditors who own provable claims may vote at a creditor's meeting. The membership is usually decided by the referee at the first meeting. An agent, attorney, or proxy with proper credentials may represent a creditor at a creditor's meeting. A ceditor of one of the individual members of a bankrupt partnership cannot vote in a creditor's meeting. A creditor with a secured claim can vote only on the unsecured part thereof. 

10. Proving Claims.-The next step is the proving and allowing of claims. Bankrupts are allowed the same exemptions as against executions and attachments. Any debt recoverable at law or in equity may be proved. A contingent liability is not provable. 

11. Officers in Bankruptcy.-The principal officers in bankruptcy proceedings are the referee and trustee. The referees are appointed by the District Judge, hold their terms for two years, and are practically assistant judges to the court, and have general charge of bankruptcy proceedings. Their number is determined by the amount of business, and is largely discretionary with the United States District Judge. Their fee is Ten Dollars, which must be paid when the proceedings are commenced. The trustee is 3

appointed by the creditors at their first meeting after the person has been declared a bankrupt, and their duties are largely the same as those of receivers or assignees in insolvency proceedings. The trustee represents the bankrupt debtor and the creditors. His duty is to gather together all the debtor's property and to dispose of it for the best interests of the creditors. He can disburse money only by check or draft and must give a detailed accounting at the final creditor's meeting. Both referees and trustees are required to give bond. 

12. Discharge in Bankruptcy.-After one month and within a year of the adjudication of bankruptcy, the bankrupt may apply for discharge. Creditors are given ten days notice to make objections and then the court considers the application and acts upon it. Discharges in bankruptcy, which protect persons from all debts except those hereinafter mentioned, may be secured on petition to the proper court after the expiration of one month and within twelve months after being adjudged a bankrupt. Such discharge releases a bankrupt from all of his debts, except taxes, judgments for fraud, debts not scheduled, debts created by embezzlement, misappropriation or defalcation. 

13.-Penalty. If a bankrupt be convicted of fraudulently concealing any property belonging to his estate as a bankrupt, or if he make a false oath in a bankruptcy proceeding, or enter a false claim against his estate, he is liable to imprisonment for two years or less. 

14. Compositions.-After a bankrupt has filed the schedule of his property and list of his creditors and has been examined in open court or at a meeting of creditors, he may, if he desires, offer terms of composition. That is, he offers to make immediate payment of a certain proportion of each claim provided the creditor will release him from the balance. This is, of course, precisely what happens by operation of law if the bankruptcy proceeding is carried to a conclusion, but a composition is often more desirable because it can be carried out at once, thus dispensing with a good many of the costs of longer proceedings, and preserving the estate in cases where the property is of a nature that will deteriorate or accumulate expense during a delay. 

Then, too, if the composition is confirmed by the court the debtor is spared some of the ignominy of having gone through bankruptcy and received a discharge. Before being

BENEFICIAL ASSOCIATIONS 

35 filed in court the composition must have been accepted in writing by a majority in number of all creditors whose claims have been allowed, which number must also hold a majority in amount of such claims. When the application for confirmation of the composition is filed in court the money necessary to carry the composition into effect, together with that necessary to pay all debts which have priority, and to pay the costs of the proceedings which have already taken place must be deposited in such place as shall be designated by and subject to the order of the judge. If the judge is then satisfied at a hearing that the composition is for the best interest of the creditors and offered by the bankrupt in good faith, he will confirm it and dismiss the case after each creditor has received his share of the money set aside by the bankrupt as a consideration for the composition. The confirmation of a composition has the same effect as a discharge in that it wipes out all debts of the bankrupt that would be wiped out by a discharge in regular form. In case there is fraud in procuring a compositon, the judge may set it aside upon application of parties in interest filed within six months after the confirmation. If confirmation is refused, or the composition later set aside, the bankruptcy proceedings continue in the manner specified by statute.

BENEFICIAL ASSOCIATIONS 

1. Definition.-A beneficial association is an association of individuals for mutual benefit. Sometimes they are business organizations, again purely social. Usually they are both. Fraternal societies, fraternal insurance lodges, trade-unions, churches, and many other religious, social and charitable institutions might be mentioned as examples of beneficial associations. 

2. A Law Unto Themselves.-The members of a benefi cial association agree among themselves to adopt certain laws by which they are bound. Thus, they can do certain things and incur specified liabilities so long as they are not contrary to the civil laws. In this they have much the same powers and privileges as a corporation.

3. Personal Liability.-Has a beneficial association the right to sue and be sued? Are the members liable for the debts of the association? The law is not very definite on these questions. It differs in the several states, and even when it is clear, the law does not cover all cases. The 

Supreme Court of New York has held that the members of an unincorporated beneficial association were partners in the association, and liable to its creditors by common law principles. 

4. A Church Quarrel.-Suppose, as sometimes happens, the members of a church split off into two factions. Which is entitled to the property? The courts have held that the faction adhering to the laws and customs of the general association is entitled to the property, even though such faction be a minority. 

5. Beneficial Associations and Taxes.-Purely charitable associations are not taxed as heavily as ordinary commercial associations. The question then arises: Are benefit societies charities? The courts hold that an association promising to pay a fixed sum as a benefit during a member's illness is not a charitable society, and therefore not exempt from taxation. The test is to be found in the objects of the institution. Masonic lodges are regarded as charitable institutions. 

6. The Powers of the Association.-If the society requires a ceremony of initiation, the mere election of a member does not entitle him to the benefits of the society without such initiation. A benefit society may at any time change its rules as to the payment of dues or the payment of benefits to sick members. Every society or association has the power to expel members unless it is organized purely for gain, and provided that the power is exercised in good faith and for good cause. The following charges are not sufficient to justify expulsion or suspension from a beneficial association: a. Slander against the society. b. The illegal drawing of benefits. c. Defrauding the society of a small sum of money. d. Conduct unbecoming a gentleman. e. Speaking ill of a member, etc. 

7. Failure to Pay Benefits.-Suppose a member make application for a promised sick benefit and his application is refused. Can he hold the members of the society liable?

BONDS 

37 The applicant should have every right to prove his case but he cannot hold the members of the association personally liable. In the same way an agreement to refer future controversies to arbitration cannot be enforced, as it would deprive a member of his rights under the law. 

BONDS 

1. A bond is defined to be an obligation in writing under seal. It is a form of contract which is almost infinite in variety. The parties to the bond are the obligor and the obligee, the former being the one who makes the promise and the latter the person to whom the promise is made. 

2. A simple bond is an instrument for the payment of money at a certain time, and generally bears interest at the rate specified in the bond. Nearly all corporate and municipal bonds are of this character and contain no condition except for the payment of the amount of the bond at a certain time and place with a certain specified rate of interest. 

Frequently interest coupons are attached to the original bond providing for the payments of the several installments of interest as they come due.

The following is the form commonly in use for such bonds:

2. Bonds of Public Officials conditioned for the faithful performance of certain things are almost of infinite variety and in common use. All State, county, town and city officers having in their hands moneys or funds of any character belonging to said corporation are required to give bonds for the proper performance of the duties of their office. 

The following form of a bond of city treasurer can be used with few slight changes for almost any office: 

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, That we, John Jones, Henry Smith, and Charles Marshall of the City of Naperville, County of Du Page, and State of Illinois, are held and firmly bound unto the City of Naperville in the penal sum of Twenty Thousand ($20,000) Dollars, for the payment of which, well and truly to be made, we bind ourselves, our heirs, executors, and administrators jointly and firmly by these presents. 

Witness our hands and seals this 14th day of July. 19....

The condition of the above obligation is such that whereas the above bounden John Jones has been duly elected to the office of City Treasurer of the City of Naperville, Now if the said John Jones shall faithfully perform all the duties of said office and shall account for and pay over all moneys that may come into his hands as such Treasurer, according to law, and the ordinances of said City and the order and direction of the city council of said City, then this obligation to be void, otherwise to remain in full force and effect. 

JOHN JONES, HENRY SMITH, CHARLES MARSHALL. 

(Seal.) (Seal.) (Seal.)

5. Executor's Bond.-Executors, administrators, guardians and conservators are required to enter into bonds to be approved by the proper court before they are allowed to enter upon their duties as such. The forms for such bonds, however, vary in the different States. 

BROKER 

1. Definitions.-A Broker is a person who transacts business for another, commonly in stocks, bills, notes, shipping, insurance, real estate, pawned goods, merchandise, etc., using the name of the principal. His sales are usually private. 

Brokerage is the fee charged for transacting business by a broker. 

2. Why Brokers Are Employed.-Brokers are often employed to transact business or to negotiate bargains between different individuals. Their attention being given to one class of business, they acquire a knowedge and skill that an average merchant does not possess. It is often advantageous for large firms to employ brokers to buy their raw material. In our large cities brokers in anything and every-

thing that is bought and sold in large quantities are extensively employed. The business of brokerage is regulated largely by the customs of the trade. 

INFORMATON A TYPICAL BROKER'S OFFICE. 

3. A Broker's Liability.-A Broker usually has no special property in the goods he sells. If he does not disclose the principal's name he is liable like other agents. He must serve faithfully and cannot act for both parties in the same transaction without the consent and knowledge of both. 

Neither can he delegate his powers without the principal's assent. He is bound to obey the express instructions of his principal, and to keep accurate accounts of his transactions. 

4. A Broker's Compensation.-Usually a broker's com pensation is a commission or percentage of the value of the thing sold or exchanged. If the amount of the compensation is not fixed, the custom of the trade rules. A broker is entitled to a reasonable compensation for his services. 

5. A Real Estate Broker must act for his principal alone. 

He is employed to negotiate sales and exchanges of land, and often such additional duties as renting real estate, collecting rents, and procuring loans. To gain his commission on the sale he must produce a customer who is ready, able and willing to accept and live up to the terms of the sale.

CARRIERS 

41 A property owner cannot avoid paying the commission or brokerage by selling the property himself, or at a lower price than he listed with the broker. 

6. Pawn Brokers.-The business of a pawn broker, the rate of interest he may charge, and the sale of pawned goods are usually regulated by law. A license is usually required and the business is always subject to regulation and control. Suppose A takes a watch to a pawnbroker who advances him $20.00. A, or his assignee or the purchaser of the pawn ticket may redeem it within the fixed time, or even beyond that time, if the pawn broker has not exercised his right to sell the watch. Thus a pawner has the right to assign or sell his interest in the watch. If A fails to redeem the watch, the pawnbroker can usually hold him for any deficiency after the watch is sold. In like manner, if A gives the watch to B to sell, who instead of selling it pawns it, the pawnbroker is protected in taking it as security for a loan. (See Agency.)

CARRIERS 

1. Definitions.-A carrier is a person or company that undertakes, or whose business it is to carry persons or merchandise for hire. Carriers are of two kinds, private and public. A Private Carrier is one who carries only occasionally, and not as a public business. Such a carrier need not serve all who wish to employ him, but is liable for negligence in transporting the goods he accepts. A Public or Common Carrier is one whose regular business it is to carry goods or passengers from place to place for all persons who elect to employ and pay him. 

2. Examples.-A private carrier is usually an individual who carries merchandise from one point to another as a favor to a friend or for a consideration either orally or in writing. He is bound to exercise such care of the property as a man of ordinary intelligence would of his own property. 

His liability is less if he acts without compensation. Examples of common carriers are railroad companies, steam ship companies, street car companies, taxi cab companies, truckmen, wagoners, teamsters, express companies, and porters who hold themselves out to carry goods or passengers from one country to another, from one portion of the country to

another, from one town to another, or from one place in the same town to another, for all persons who offer to employ them. 

3. Responsibility.-Common Carriers are responsible for all loss and damage caused by transportation from whatever cause, except the act of God and public enemy, and they are bound to carry all goods which are offered them, and if they refuse without just excuse they are liable to an action. 

4. Act of God is held to extend only to such inevitable accidents as occur without the intervention of man's agency. 

The carrier is not responsible for losses occurring from natural causes, such as frosts, fermentation or natural decay of perishable articles, or the necessary and natural wear in the course of transportation, provided he exercises all reasonable care to have the loss or deterioration as little as practical. 

5. Loss by Fire. The carrier is liable for any and all loss occasioned by accidental fire. 

6. Perishable Goods.-Carriers are not responsible for loss to fruits that decay in their possession or goods shipped in defective boxes, such as glassware not properly packed and other articles that are easily broken. Goods must be properly packed in order to make the carrier responsible. 

7. Bill of Lading.-Bill of lading is the receipt given by the Common Carrier to the owner of the goods desiring to have the same shipped and should contain a description of the quantity, the marks on the merchandise, the name of the shipper, or the person sending the goods, and the consignee, the name of the person to whom the goods are shipped, place of departure and place of discharge of the goods and the price of freight, and also weight of the separate packages and the number of the car in which the same were shipped. 

8. Equal Liability.—Railroad Companies and other car riers who allow express companies to carry parcels and packages on their cars or other vehicles are liable as the Common Carriers for all damages which occur, without regard to the contract between them and such express company. On July 1, 1918, the government took over the control of the principal express companies, operating them as one unit under the name of the American Railway Express Company. The government supervision is now at an end,

CARRIERS 

43 but the individual companies still act as one unit under the same name. 

9. Baggage. In the transportation of the baggage of passengers the liability of the carrier for loss to the same is the same as in case of transportation of goods for hire, and in case of loss the carrier must make it good. 

10. When Liability Begins and Ends.-The responsibility of the Common Carrier begins upon the delivery of the goods for immediate transportation. A delivery at the usual place of receiving freight or to the employes of the company in the usual course of business is sufficient. The responsibility of the carrier terminates after the arrival of the goods at their destination and sufficient time has elapsed thereafter for the owner to have received them during business hours. 

After the expiration of such time the responsibility of the carrier is simply that of a warehouse man and he is only required to keep the goods with ordinary care. 

11. Limitation of Liability.-A carrier can limit his liability by contract, unless forbidden by statute. Thus a bill of lading given as a receipt for a freight or express shipment, or a receipt given a passenger limiting the amount of the carrier's liability on his baggage is considered binding by the courts, and relieves the carrier of additional liability. 

The general rule is that a carrier may relieve himself from all liability except from his own negligence. 

12. The Passenger's Rights.-The law compels carriers to carry all passengers who pay the required fare, and who are in a sufficiently intelligent condition to travel. The carrier must exercise great care in transporting passengers and is liable for damages should injury occur due to the carrier's negligence. If the passenger was himself negligent and contributed to his own injury, he cannot as a rule hold the carrier liable. Although a sleeping car company is not a common carrier, it is liable for negligence in protecting the passengers from theft. 

13. Different Lines.-Where goods are shipped to points beyond the line of the carrier to whom they are first delivered, such carrier is not responsible beyond his own portion of the route unless he gives bills of lading for the entire route and the contract contemplates the transportation and delivery of the goods at their destination. 

14. Demurrage is the penalty exacted by transportation companies for not unloading goods from their cars within

the time fixed by the rules of the companies. The rules of a large number of railroad companies require that the car be unloaded within twenty-four hours after its arrival at the destination and a fixed rate of demurrage for each twenty-four hours of delay after the expiration of the usual time for unloading is imposed on the persons to whom goods are shipped. In practice companies are not very strict in enforcing this penalty, unless they are unable to meet the demand for cars. 

15. A Public Officer in performing his duty is exempt from all liability. In like manner the U. S. Government acting as a common carrier of the mails cannot be held liable. 

16. The Carrier's Rights.-The carrier is entitled to a reasonable compensation for his services, and may demand payment in advance. The shipper is liable for freight, unless the carrier agrees to look exclusively to some other party; or after delivery, the carrier may recover the amount of freight from the consignee. But freight may be collected only for the goods actually delivered, unless the delivery be prevented by the owner, or it be agreed that freight shall be payable regardless of losses by the way. The carrier also has a lien on the goods for his freight and advances on such goods, and may refuse to deliver until such charges be paid. 

This lien has priority over the vendor's right of stoppage in transit, and the claims of the general creditors of the owner on consignee. A carrier by water also has a lien for salvage, and for customs duties advanced on imported goods. 

17. Telegraph and Telephone Companies are not common carriers and may therefore establish reasonable regulation for the transmission of messages. Like common carriers, however, they are required to serve all who apply and offer to pay the charges and are liable for damages when messages are not sent promptly and accurately.

CHATTEL MORTGAGE 

45 

CHATTEL MORTGAGE 

1. Definition.-A chattel mortgage is a conveyance of personal property to secure the payment of a debt. It is a pledge that the debt will be paid. Any personal property that may be sold may be mortgaged such as live stock, machinery, farm implements, life insurance policies, corporation stock, wages, crops, premiums, profits and many other things. The mortgagor is the person who conveys the property. The mortgagee is the person to whom the transfer is made. 

2.-Form of Mortgage.-The usual form of a chattel mortgage is a bill of sale with the conditional clause stating the terms of the loan, and that on the mortgagor's failure to pay, the mortgagee may take possession of the property. 

Any person competent to make a contract, or his agent, may make a chattel mortgage. Partners or joint tenants may mortgage jointly on their individual interests. A corporation may also mortgage its personal property. 

3. Chattel mortgages are usually given to secure notes of the mortgagor in the same way in which real estate mortgages are given to secure notes of the mortgagees. 

Greater strictness, however, is required in the acknowledgment, docketing, and recording of chattel mortgages than in the case of real estate mortgages. A chattel mortgage must be acknowledged before a justice of the peace, or before the county judge of the county, in which the mortgagor resides; in South Dakota they are not acknowledged, but require two witnesses. 

4.-Describing the Property. The property mortgaged must be described clearly enough to enable third persons to identify it, but this is determined largely by the nature of the chattels. Animals are usually described by weight, age, sex, color, height, breed and location. "All" articles in a stated place is generally a valid description. 

5. Foreclosure.-When the mortgagor fails to pay his debt, the right of the mortgagees to proceed in taking the property is regulated by law. In most chattel mortgages a clause is included permitting the mortgagee to seize and sell the property should the mortgagor fail to make payment. Unless the property is so taken, it can be taken by other creditors.

General Principles.-Chattel mortgages may in most 

States not run longer than one year. To sell property covered by a chattel mortgage is a criminal offense. A chattel mortgage given on personal property which is left in possession of mortgagor is prima facie void as to creditors of mortgagor. To render it valid it must contain permission by mortgagee that mortgagor may retain possession of the chattels, and that mortgagee may take possession of them whenever he feels himself insecure for any reason. Recent statutes provide that notes secured by chattel mortgages must show on their face that they are secured by chattel mortgages, or they are absolutely void. Any defense which the maker of the note secured by chattel mortgage could make against the original payee is good against the note in the hands of an indorsee, even though indorsed before maturity. Chattel mortgages on household goods must be signed by the wife of the mortgagor and can only be foreclosed by a court proceeding. (See Mortgage.)

CITIZENSHIP 

1. Definition.-A Citizen is a member of a state or nation who enjoys political rights and is entitled to public protection. Citizenship, therefore, carries with it the duty of allegiance to the government and the right of protection from it. 

2. General Principles.-A person residing in any of the several states owes an allegiance both to the United States and to the State, and may demand protection from each government. A resident of the District of Columbia or 

Alaska is a citizen of the United States only. A citizen's ordinary rights are protected by the state government. 

All persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens of the United States. Formerly a woman took the citizenship of her husband upon marriage. Now marriage does not affect the citizenship of the wife unless her husband is ineligible for naturalization. Neither does naturalization of the husband operate to confer citizenship upon the wife.
