The year 1920 brought the passage of the nineteenth amendment to the constitution of the United States granting women complete suffrage in all the states.

3. Naturalization.-Aliens may acquire American citizen ship by becoming naturalized. This requires, first, a continuous residence in the United States for five years, second, one year's residence in the State, and third, that the alien must have appeared in court at least two years before and then and there declared his intention to become a citizen. and renounced allegiance to his former sovereign. He must prove his residence and his good character, and must take an oath to support and defend the constitution and laws of the United States and renounce allegiance to any foreign prince. Thus naturalization confers American citizenship on his minor children if they reside in the United States. 

4. Alien's Rights.-Aliens have the right to hold and transfer title to real estate. At common law they are entitled to purchase, own, and sell personal property, engage in business and to make contracts or wills. In return they must obey the laws and the courts of the land in which they reside. Anarchists, polygamists, diseased or criminal immigrants, and Chinese laborers have been excluded from the United States. 

5. Fees. It costs an alien $5.00 to become a Naturalized 

American citizen, $1.00 for declaring intention, $2.00 for filing the application for citizenship, and $2.00 for entering the order and issuing certificate of citizenship. During the world war all foreign born members of the army or navy were granted complete citizenship immediately after enlistment. Thousands took advantage of this simple, speedy, and inexpensive method of acquiring citizenship. 

COMMERCIAL PAPER 

1. Definitions.-The term "commercial paper" covers all papers used in the course of trade. Negotiable paper is paper that can be sold or transferred. A negotiable instrument is any paper that may be transferred by assignment, indorsement, or delivery. The person who promises to pay is called the maker, and the one to whom he promises is called the payee. 

2. Kinds of Negotiable Paper.-Almost every written contract or agreement to pay money is negotiable, in the sense that the owner can sell it to a third person who can

COMMERCIAL PAPER 

51 enforce it from the maker. However, in the strictest sense of the word there are only three forms of negotiable paper, namely checks, notes, and bills of exchange or drafts. 

3. Form of Negotiable Instruments.-The law does not require negotiable instruments to be in any prescribed form. 

However, certain things are necessary in all checks, notes or bills of exchange to make them negotiable: a. They must be in writing, on any kind of paper and in pen, pencil or type. b. They must be signed. c. They must be payable on demand or at a fixed time. d. They should be made payable to bearer or to order. e. The name of the place and State should be written on the note. It is as important as the date. f. The amount must be specified and certain. g. It must be an unconditional promise to pay in money. h. There must be no apparent alterations, erasures or additions. i. The time of payment must not have passed. 

4. Consideration.-While it is not always necessary to express any consideration in negotiable paper, it is safer to do so. 

In the hands of an innocent third party, the law assumes a valuable consideration. The words "for value received" usually appear on promissory notes. 

5. Protest.-A protest of a note, check or draft is a formal statement by a notary public that the paper was presented for payment and was refused. The costs are added to the instrument. 

6. Negotiability. The words "or bearer," or "or order” render a paper negotiable. Any person capable of making a contract is capable of making a negotiable instrument. 

A paper which passes into the hands of an innocent third party carries a good title provided: (a) The paper is negotiable, (b) it was made in good faith and for valuable consideration; (c) the purchaser was not aware of any legal or equitable defense.

A. Notes 

1. Definitions. A note is a simple written promise to pay a certain sum at a certain time, or on demand or "at sight" to a person named therein. An individual promissory

note is a note in which one party promises to pay another a certain sum of money at a specified time. A joint promissory note is the same as an individual note except that it is signed by two or more parties, all of whom are liable jointly but not severally. In a joint and several promissory note two or more parties severally and separately agree to pay a certain sum at a specified time, and each signer is responsible for the whole amount. 

2. Transferring Notes.—The following rules govern the transferring of notes: a. Paper payable to bearer is transferred by delivery, payable to order by indorsement. b. An endorser is a person who writes his name on the back of it. c. Indorsement in blank is writing only the name without the words, "pay to the order of." d. The indorser is liable for its payment if the maker fails to meet it. e. An indorser who is compelled to pay a note has a just claim against the maker and against each indorser whose name appears above his own. f. An indorser to whose order a note is drawn or indorsed, can transfer it without becoming liable for its payment by writing the words "without recourse" over his signature on the back. 

3. Collecting Notes.

a. A note destroyed by fire can be collected by proof of loss. b. Money paid under mistake must be refunded. c. If no time is specified the note is payable on demand. d. The day of maturity is the day on which a note becomes legally due. In some states three days, called days of grace, are allowed after the expiration of the time given in the note before it becomes legally due. (See Interest Laws and Statute of Limitation.) e. In finding the day of maturity actual days must be counted if the note is drawn days after date, but months are counted when the note is drawn months after date. f. Negotiable paper payable to bearer or, indorsed in blank, which has been lost or stolen, cannot be collected by the finder or thief, but a holder who inno-

COMMERCIAL PAPER 

53 cently receives it in good faith before maturity for value, can hold it against the owner's claims. g. A note made in one State, payable in another, must be governed by the laws of that State in which it is to be paid. h. Demand for payment of a note must be made upon the day of maturity and at the place named. If no place is specified then it is payable at the maker's place of business or at his residence. If it falls due on Sunday, demand must be made the day previous. 

In most of the States where note falls due on Sunday or legal holiday, by statute the maker is given until the following day to pay the same. i. An extention of the time of a note by the holder, releases sureties and indorsers, unless consent to such extension has been given by the indorsers or sureties. j. Upon presentment for payment and refusal by the maker at maturity, in order to hold the indorser, suit should be immediately instituted upon the note against the maker, and notice of default should be given to the indorser, and in some States the note should be protested by a notary public. 

4. Payment of Notes.-All the parties who have endors ed a note are liable for the amount, but only one satisfaction can be recovered. Payments made to apply on a note should always be endorsed on the back thereof. In many cases payment is defeated and the notes become void especially when held by the original payee. Such are: a. A note given by one who is not of age, unless the minor ratifies it after becoming of age. b. A note made by an intoxicated person. c. A note given by one who cannot write and not witnessed to at the time. d. A note obtained by duress, in case of compulsion, by fear of illegal imprisonment or by threats that would lead an ordinary person to fear injury to his person, his reputation or his property. e. Obtained by fraud or by finding. In these cases the original parties can not collect anything. f. A note that has been stolen cannot be collected by

the party that committed the theft, but if an innocent person buys the note for a consideration, he can collect it. g. A note given for illegal consideration is illegal everywhere. h. One who receives a note knowing it to have defects, gets no better right to collect it, than the one from whom he received it had. i. If a person at the time of taking a note has notice that it is void through fraud, or upon any legal grounds, he cannot collect it.

B. Checks 

5. Definitions.-A check is a bill drawn upon a bank, payable on demand. The person who writes the check is the drawer, the bank on whom the check is drawn is called the drawee, the person to whom the check is made payable is called the payee. 

6. Signature.-A check must be properly signed. This is not a valid signature:

J. L. NICHOLS & CO. 

By Treasurer 

It should be: or 

JOHN JONES By Agent or 

JOHN JONES By J. Keeler, Agent. 

J. L. NICHOLS & CO. 

By F. A. Lueben, Treasurer. 

7. Presentation.-A check must be presented for payment within a reasonable time after its issue, or the drawer will be discharged from liability thereon to the extent of the loss caused by the delay; and it is generally held that one day after the receipt of the check is a reasonable time to present or forward the same for presentation. 

8. The Agreement to Pay is between the bank and the depositor. For this reason a check, of itself, does not operate as an assignment of any part of the funds to the credit

COMMERCIAL PAPER 

57 of the drawer with the bank. Consequently, should the bank refuse to pay the check the holder cannot bring action against the bank, unless or until the bank has accepted or certified the check. On the other hand, if the bank fails to fulfill its contract with the depositor he has a just cause for action against the bank. Should the bank refuse to honor a customer's check owing to an employee's mistake in bookkeeping, the bank could be held responsible for any loss resulting therefrom. 

9. Certifying a Check.-A certification of a check by the bank is equivalent to an acceptance, and discharges the drawer and all the endorsers preceding the holder who secures the certification. When a check is presented to a bank for this purpose, the bank charges the drawer's account with the amount, so that as far as the drawer and the bank are concerned the check has actually been paid. 

Thus if a certified check is not presented at his bank for payment and is returned to the drawer, it should not be destroyed but redeposited as cash. 

10. Stopping Payment.-The drawer of the check may order the bank to stop payment on a certain check before it is presented. The bank is required to follow out these instructions to the letter and is liable for any loss resulting from failure to do so.

59 "raised," the bank is liable for any improper payment. The drawer of the check must also use every precaution to prevent alterations. He should write in a way to avoid confusing the banker who is supposed to pay the check. 

Carelessness on the part of the drawer will relieve the banker of any liability. Another rule applies when checks have been altered or raised. The depositor must within a reasonable time after the return of his bank book, demand immediate correction if payments have been incorrectly made. 

12. Vital Points on Checks.-A check is not due until presented. It is negotiable. It has no days of grace. Giving a check is no payment of an indebtedness, unless the check is paid. The death of the maker of the check before presentment to the bank renders the check null and void. 

The amount of the check should always be written out in words. Every holder of a check is liable to a subsequent holder only for the time for which he would be held, if originally liable. It is the safest rule always to act with diligence in presenting checks for payment. If a raised check is paid by the bank, it can only charge the depositor the amount for which he drew, unless the raising of the check was made possible by the carelessness of the maker. In that case the maker would be responsible for the loss.

If you have money in a bank and you wish to draw out a certain sum, write "Pay to myself," instead of writing your name in the body of the check, and then sign it. Banks of this country do not cash a check drawn payable to order unless the person presenting the check is known to the bank. 

If you write a check for a stranger who needs identification at your bank, have him indorse the check in your presence and under his indorsement write "Indorsement above guaranteed," signing your name. He can then cash the check without further identification by signing his name again in the presence of the banker. Another method is to write "Pay to Cash." Do not draw a check unless you have the money on deposit or in your possession to deposit. Do not presume on the generosity of your bank by drawing a sum larger than your balance.

C. Drafts 

13. Definition.-A draft is a written order by one person on another for the payment of a specified sum of money. 

The one who writes the draft is called the drawer, and the one on whom it is written, the drawee, and the one to whom it is to be paid, the payee. 

14. Kinds of Drafts.-Drafts may be made payable at sight, on demand or at a certain time after date, or after sight. A sight draft or demand draft is drawn on one person against another payable when presented. Time drafts

15. Acceptance.-Sight and on demand drafts are presented for payment only. Time drafts require acceptance by the party against whom they are drawn. The usual method of acceptance is to write across the face of the draft in red ink the word "accepted," followed by the date and the signature. Should the person on whom the draft is drawn die before it was accepted, it should be prescribed to his legal representative for acceptance. 

16. General Principles:

a. When either acceptance or payment is refused, the draft may be protested like any other note or check. b. Drafts are negotiable both before and after acceptance. c. When buying a draft at a bank it is safest to have the draft made payable to yourself and then indorse it over to whomever it is to be made payable. d. Any material alteration of a draft after it has been drawn or accepted makes it valueless.

D. Indorsements 

17. Definition. An indorsement is a writing on the back of a negotiable instrument for the purpose of transferring the title or ownership from one person to another. The writing may be in pen or pencil upon any part of the instrument or upon a paper attached thereto. It consists ordinarily of the payee's signature and that of other holders. When money is received on a bill or note, the amount is written on the back thereof and this is also called an indorsement. 

18. How to Endorse.-Write across the back of the paper 

(not lengthwise) near the left end. Always endorse check or note exactly as your name appears on the face. 

If the check is payable to F. Black, do not write Frank

Black. If your name is misspelled, indorse first as it appers on the face and then write your correct signature underneath. Do not write any unnecessary information on the back of your check. A story is told of a woman who received a check from her husband, and when cashing it wrote "Your loving wife" above her name on the check. 

19. Kinds of Endorsements.-The same rules govern in-

Such a note or check is negotiable without further indorsement.

E. Orders 

An order is a written request to deliver money or goods to a person named, or to his order, or to bearer, the same to be charged to the person signing the request. 

Orders are negotiable, but the person on whom they are drawn is not under obligation to pay them unless they have been accepted, for an order partakes of the nature of a draft. $54.00.

F. How to Write all Kinds of Due Bills 

A due-bill is not generally payable to order, nor is it assignable by mere indorsement. It is simply the acknowledgment of a debt; yet it may be transferred. It may be payable in money or in merchandise. 

Due-bills do not draw interest, unless so specified. $125.00.

F. How to Write All Kinds of Receipts 

20. A receipt is an acknowledgment in writing that a certain sum of money or thing has been received by the party giving and signing the same. 

21. A complete receipt requires the following statements:

That a payment has been received; the date of the payment; the amount of article received; from whom received, and if for another, on whose behalf payment is made; to what debt or purpose it is to be applied; by whom received, and if for another, on whose behalf it was received. 

22. If the giving and receiving of receipts were more strictly held to in the transactions of the various kinds of business, less trouble, fewer law-suits, and the saving of thousands of dollars would be the result.

COMMERCIAL PAPER 

69 23. If payment is made upon account, upon a special debt, or in full, it should be so stated in the receipt. 

24. When an agent signs a receipt, he should sign his principal's name and then write his name underneath as agent. 

25. It is not necessary to take a receipt on paying a note, draft, or other instrument indorsed by the payee, because the instrument itself becomes a receipt. 

26. If a receipt is obtained through fraud, or given under error or mistake, it is void. $250.00.

Receipt for Payment on Account.

COMMON LAW TRUSTS 

1. Definition.—A common law trust company is a form of business organization founded on the common law right of contract. It is not created by statute, nor does it depend upon any specific enactment for its validity. These organizations are commonly called "Massachusetts Trusts," "Express Trusts," or "Business Trusts." 

2. Origin. The modern common law trust company must not be confused with "Trusts" or "Trust Companies." Certain large organizations are loosely called "Trusts," for example, "The Tobacco Trust," "The Steel Trust," etc. On the other hand many financial institutions handling estates and other probate matters are known as "Trust Companies. 

The Common Law Trust Company is simply another kind of business organization developed out of the common law trust relation, by which one person called the trustor could convey property to another person called the trustee, such property to be held, used and managed for the benefit of third persons. 

3. Formation.-In forming a common law trust company the first step is to draw up the Declaration of Trust. This is in reality a contract between the trustors and the trustees, and takes the place of a charter in a corporation, or articles of co-partnership in a partnership agreement. It states the purposes of the trust, the period of its existence, the number and names of the trutees, the manner of choosing new trustees, etc. This declaration of trust also creates the 

Trust Fund or "capital" of the company, and conveys the property to the trustees, subject, of course, to the terms of

COMMON LAW TRUSTS 

71 the agreement. The trustors receive "certificates of interest," very much like the certificates of stock which are issued by a corporation. 

4. Recording.-The Declaration of Trust must be recorded in the Recorder's office of the County where the company was organized. 

5. Cost of Organization.-There are no charter fees, franchise taxes, or capital stock taxes to pay such as are always required from corporations. Fifty or seventy-five dollars will cover the entire cost of preparing and recording the declaration of trust, drawing up the by-laws, and the purchasing of minute book, book of blank certificates, and official seal. There are a number of firms who make a specialty of organizing Common Law Trust Companies. 

6. Compared With Corporations.-The advocates of the 

Common Law Trust Co. as a business organization claim that it has all the advantages of the other forms without any of their disadvantages. In the first place the Trust 

Company is much like a corporation in that the trustees control the business for a term of office, just as the directors of a corporation do. Secondly, the Trust Company may buy and sell, trade, manufacture and transport merchandise, may sue and be sued, under its trust name, exactly the same as a corporation. In the third place a common law trust company may do business anywhere, while a corporation being created by state law, is required to register and pay non-residence fees when doing business outside the parent state. Fourthly, the state laws regulate the nature of the business in which a corporation may engage, whereas, a common law trust company may be organized for any purpose for which it would be lawful to make a contract. And, finally, the common law trusts are not subject to any of the excise or franchise taxes that are levied against corporations. They pay only such taxes as would be levied against an individual. 

7. Compared to Partnerships. In a partnership each general partner has an equal share in the management of partnership affairs. In the Common Law Trust Company the holders of the interest shares have no voice whatever in the management. The trustees must have the legal title to all the property and the sole control of the business during their term of office. If this rule is ignored the courts will consider the trust as nothing more than a partnership.

Again, the death or resignation of a general partner, automatically dissolves the partnership agreement, requiring the settling up of all partnership affairs, and often greatly inconveniencing the remaining partners. In a common law trust company this is all done away with, as the removal of one of the interested parties has no effect whatever upon the organization. Beneficial shares may in fact be sold or transferred just like stock in a corporation or like any other personal property. These are the two principal ways in which a common law trust company differs from, and is an improvement upon, the partnership. 

8. Disadvantages. The most unsatisfactory thing about a partnership is that each general partner is personally liable for the debts of the firm. Stockholders, on the other hand, are not liable for the debts of the corporation. Now if the holders of the interest shares in a common law trust company were equally free from personal liability, this would indeed be the ideal form of business organization. 

But, unfortunately, this is not the case. The trustees are liable for the debts of the company. Of course, the money comes out of the trust fund, but if there does not happen to be sufficient funds in the trust fund, then the individual members are held liable, unless there happens to be a specific agreement with each creditor. The making of such agreements, however, would be a great handicap in the conduct of the business. 

9. The Best Form.-In studying the various forms of business organization it will be seen that there are advantages and disadvantages in each one. Just which form is the best to adopt will depend to a large extent upon the nature of the business in which it is desired to engage. 

CONTRACTS 

1. Definitions.-A contract is a mutual agreement between two competent parties for a valuable consideration to do or not to do a particular thing. A Simple Contract may or may not be in writing but requires no seal. A Specialty is a contract in writing which does require a seal to the signatures. An Executed Contract is completed, an Executory Contract is one to be executed or completed. An Express Contract is a contract actually made between two or

CONTRACTS 

73 more parties; An implied Contract, as the name suggests, is one in which some of the provisions must be implied from previous agreements or from existing customs. 

2. Requirements.-A contract must have: 

a. Two or more parties, b. Subject matter, c. Seal or consideration, and d. Assent of the parties. There cannot be a contract when any of these are wanting.

How to Write a Contract 3. The parties to a contract are taken in the order in which they are written and referred to as "the party of the first part," "the party of the second part," without repeating their names. It matters not which name is written first. 

4. After writing the date, names of the parties and their places of residence, state fully all that the first party agrees to do, and then state all that the second party agrees to do. 

5. Next state the penalties of forfeitures in case either party does not faithfully and fully perform, or offer to perform, his part of the agreement. 

6. Finally, the closing clause, the signatures and seals, the 

LOLLIS 

Paeth

A VERBAL CONTRACT BETWEEN FRIENDS

signatures of witnesses are written. (A seal is simply the mark of a pen around the word "seal," written after the signature.) 

7. No particular form of legal language is necessary. 

Use your own words and state in a plain way just what you want done. Any one who can write a letter and express his desire in an intelligent manner can write a contract. 

8. Errors in grammar or spelling do not affect the legality of the agreement. 

9. If the language should be obscure on certain points, the "court" will always interpret the intent of the parties, when they entered into the agreement, provided the intent can be gathered from the terms of the instrument itself. 

10. When an agreement is written it must all be in writing. It cannot be partly written and partly oral. 

The Vital Part of a Contract-Consideration 

11. Definition.-A consideration is the thing which induces parties to make a contract. It is the substantial cause or reason moving parties to enter into an agreement. 12.

A Sufficient Consideration. The law does not require that the consideration should be a good or bad bargain. As long as something is done or suffered by either party the consideration is good. The smallest consideration is sufficient to make it legal. The value of the consideration is unimportant. For instance: $10,000 worth of property can be sold for $1. 

13. Promise of Marriage.-If a man promises a woman any certain sum of money if she would agree to marry him, he can be made to fulfill his promise, and then the court will hold that the promise of marriage was a sufficient consideration for the money. Marriage contracts may be entered into under age. 

14. A Valuable Consideration.-A valuable consideration is one which is equal to money or may be changed into money. 

15. A Good Consideration.-A good consideration is one which is based upon love, gratitude or esteem, or blood relationship. But in order to make a good consideration legal, the agreement has to be performed by one or both parties. 

For instance: If a man should promise to give a lady $500 because he loved her, it could not be collected, but if the

CONTRACTS 

75 money was once paid to the woman it could not be recovered.

16. Gratuitous Consideration.-A gratuitous consideration is a consideration where something is done or money promised on account of some affection or charity, and like a good consideration the act must be performed in order to hold the party. For instance: If a father gives his son a note on account of his affection for him, the son cannot force the father to pay it; so also if a person subscribes for a church or charitable society he cannot be compelled to pay it, unless the church or charitable society can show that it depended upon that money when it entered upon some contract, or assumed some obligation on account of it. 

17. Immoral Consideration.-All considerations which are immoral are consequently illegal. 

18. Impossible Consideration.-If a man should promise to cross the ocean in one day, or walk from Philadelphia to

New York in two hours the consideration is illegal and void. 

The Law Governing All Kinds of Contracts 

19. An alteration of a contract in a material part, after its execution, renders it void. 

20. A contract made by a minor, a lunatic, or an idiot is not binding upon him, yet he can hold the party with whom he contracts, to all the conditions of the contract. 

21. A frauduent contract may be binding on the party guilty of fraud, although not laying any obligation on the part of the party acting in good faith. 

22. A contract for the sale or purchase of personal property over a certain amount-ranging from $30 to $100 in the different States-must be in writing. 

23. A contract which cannot be performed within a year must be in writing. 

24. If no time of payment is stated in the contract, payment must be made on the delivery of the goods. 

25. A contract totally restraining the exercise of a man's trade or profession is void, but one restraining him in any particular place is not void. 

26. An offer or proposal, which includes the essential parts of a contract, becomes a contract as soon as accepted. 

Generally the acceptance must be at the time of receiving

the offer. The offer may be withdrawn at any time before it has been accepted. Offers may be made and accepted within a reasonable time by word of mouth, telephone, telegraph, or mail. 

27. A contract required by law to be in writing cannot be dissolved by verbal agreement. 

Babylon Clay Tablet Contract. (The Outer Case Has Been Broken Away Showing the Inner Repetition.) 

28. A contract cannot be rescinded except by consent of both parties. 

29. An oral contract must be proved by evidence. 

30. A contract binding in the place where it is made is binding everywhere. 

31. Each party to an agreement or contract should retain a copy. 

32. While signatures or contracts written with a pencil are good in law, it is always safer to write them in ink. 

Contracts That Are Not Lawful 

33. A contract to commit a breach of peace. 

34. Contracts made on Sunday, are, in most of the States, now held to be legal and binding. 

35. An agreement for immoral purposes. 

36. All agreements in which there is a fraud. 

37. An agreement made by threats or violence. 

38. Wagers or bets cannot be collected by law. 

39. More than legal interest cannot be collected. 

40. If any part of a contract is illegal, the whole is illegal. 

41. A contract with an intoxicated person, lunatic, or minor. 

42. A contract in violation of a statute in the State in which it is made. 

43. An agreement to prevent competition on a sale under an execution. 

44. An agreement to prohibit the carrying on of a trade throughout the State. 

45. A contract impossible in its nature; such as crossing the ocean in one day, is void.

CONTRACTS 

77 46. Where consent to an agreement is given by mistake, it cannot become a contract. 

47. The right to vote or hold office, etc., cannot be sold by contract. 

48. Contract without a consideration; such as a promise to make a gift, cannot be enforced. 

49. Two or more persons cannot intentionally make a contract to the injury of a third person. 

50. Contracts for concealing felony or violating public trust, for bribery and extortion, are prohibited. 

51. Useless things cannot become the subject of a contract; such as agreeing not to go out of the house for a month. 

52. Money borrowed for the purpose of betting, the lender knowing it to be for that purpose, cannot be collected. 

53. A verbal release without payment or satisfaction for the debt is not good. Release must be under seal. 

54. If there are two parts to a contract, the one conflicting with the other, the first part holds good in preference to the last. 

55. Contracts in which there is misrepresentation or concealment of material facts cannot be enforced. It is fraud to conceal a fraud. 

56. If a thing contracted for was not in existence at the time of making the contract, such as buying a horse and not knowing that he was dead at the time, the contract is not good. 

57. If a person agrees to serve as a laborer or clerk, he cannot be compelled to fulfill his agreement; damages, however, can be recovered for a failure to perform. 

58. An agreement with a thief to drop a criminal prosecution, by his bringing back the goods and paying all damages, is not good, and will be no bar to a future prosecution. 

59. Guardians, Trustees, Executors, Administrators or

Attorneys cannot take advantage of those for whom they act by becoming parties to contracts in which their wards are interested. 

60. Quasi Contracts.-A quasi contract may be defined as almost a contract or partly a contract. It is a legal obligation resulting from some direct or indirect benefit accruing

888 

to one party from the other without his assent. The law compels him to pay. For example: a. One who has reason to believe that payment for goods tendered is expected, must not accept them unless he intends to pay for them. b. A man employed under the promise of good wages or division of profits is entited to fair treatment, even though such a contract is no contract at all. c. Money paid on an illegal contract or on one which is void because of non-existence of the property, may be recovered. d. If an express company deliver valuable goods to the wrong party, the company can recover from the person who wrongfully accepted them. e. pays his 

If, on account of a mistake a man grocery bill twice for the same month, he can recover. f. Action to recover can be brought against a man who sells property not his own, or which proves to be worthless. g. All these questions hinge on the presence or lack of consideration in the agreement. h. A liability of this kind cannot be imposed upon a person without his act or consent. 

61. Statute of Frauds.-In every state there is a statute called the statute of frauds which provides that certain contracts must be in writing to bind the parties: Thus:a. All agreements for the sale of real estate are void unless they are in writing. b. A contract for the sale of goods exceeding the sum of from $30.00 up to $100.00 according to the several states, must be in writing or else there must be actual delivery and acceptance of the goods. c. A contract must be in writing to charge the defendant upon any special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person. d. A written contract is necessary to charge any person upon any agreement made upon consideration of marriage, or upon any agreement that is not to be performed within the space of one year from the making thereof.

CONTRACTS 

79 What actually constitutes delivery and acceptance is a question of fact and depends on the intention of the parties. 

Damages For Violation of Contract 

62. A statute which provides no penalties for the lawbreaker is merely the expression of a wish, or the giving of advice. Similarly the contract must be binding on both parties. This element of mutual obligation is the very essence of a contract. 

63. Where no actual loss has been sustained by the violation of a contract, the plaintiff is entitled to nominal damages only. Thus, A contracted to drill a well for B and to complete same within a specified time or forfeit $1000.00. 

The courts will not compel A to pay the $1000.00 damages unless his failure to complete the well has actually meant a loss of $1000.00 to B. 

64. Actual expenditures under the contract may be recovered. 

65. Expected profits or speculations in real property cannot be recovered in case of a violation of contract. 

66. Failure to convey real estate or deliver personal property according to agreement entitles the plaintiff to recover damages or to sue for specific performance of the contract. 

67. In loss of goods by common carrier the plaintiff is entitled to the value of the goods where they were to be delivered, less the freight on such goods. 

68. If a party contracts to employ another for a certain time, at a specified compensation, and discharges him, without cause, before the expiration of the time, the plaintiff can obtain judgment for the full amount of wages for the whole time, provided he is unable to secure employment in the same line of work, after making an earnest effort to do So. Should he obtain work at a lower wage he can collect the difference. 69.

To prevent lawsuits and disputes the amount of damages for the violation of contracts is sometimes fixed by inserting in the contract the following clause: 

AND IT IS FURTHER AGREED that the party that shall fail to perform this agreement on his part shall pay to the other the full sum of (here state amount), as liquidated, fixed, and settled charges.

70. The general rule is that the courts seek to do justice between the parties.

COPYRIGHT 

1. Definition.-Congress has defined copyright as the liberty of printing, publishing, compiling, executing and vending any original book, map, chart, dramatic or musical composition, engraving, print, photographs, or negative thereof, or of a painting, drawing, chromo, statue, or statuary, and of models or designs intended to be perfected as works of art. 

2. Application.-Persons seeking registration of any work must specify to which of the following classes the work belongs: (a) Books, (b) periodicals, (c) lectures, sermons, addresses prepared for oral delivery, (d) dramatic compositions, (e) musical compositions, (f) maps, (g) works of art, models, or designs, (h) reproduction of a work of art, (i) drawing of plastic works of a scientific nature, (j) photographs, (k) prints and pictorial illustrations, (1) motion picture photo plays, (m) motion pictures other than photo plays. 

3. Protection.-The copyright of an article or publica tion gives the owner of it the exclusive right to print, translate, reproduce, or dramatize it. Thus if a book is copyrighted it cannot be copied or quoted in any other publication without the consent of the holder of the copyright. 

4. How to Obtain a Copyright for a Book or Magazine.

a. Publish the work with the copyright notice.

b. Send to "The Copyright Office, Library of Congress, 

Washington, D. C.," two copies of the best edition of the work with an application for registration, and the statutory fee of $1.00. c. Make affidavit that the typesetting, printing, and binding have been performed in the United States. (See form at end of chapter.) 

5. How to Obtain Copyright for Other Articles.-Differ ent rules apply for works not reproduced in copies for sale. 

The fee is $1.00 and application must be made in the regular way. Applicant must send:a. In the case of lectures, or dramatic or musical composition, one complete manuscript or typewritten copy of the work. b. In the case of photographs not intended for general circulation, one photographic print.

c. In the case of works of art, the photograph or other identifying reproduction of the work. d. In the case of motion picture photoplays, a title and description with one print taken from each scene or act e. In the case of motion pictures other than photoplays, a title and description with not less than two prints taken from different sections of a complete motion picture.

Upon publication of any of the above, a second deposit of printed copies for registration and the payment of another fee are required. 

6. Notice of Copyright.-The notice of copyright consists of the word "copyright" (or Copr.) with the name of the proprietor and the year in which the copyright was secured. 

In the case of books this notice should appear on the title page, or the page immediately following. In the case of pictures, maps, photographs and the like, the notice may consist of the letter C enclosed in a circle, thus (C), accompanied by the initials, monogram, mark, or symbol of the owner. 

7. How Long is a Copyright Good.-A copyright is good for 28 years from date of publication. Within one year preceding the expiration of the term, the author, or his heirs or executors may secure a renewal of the copyright for another 28 years. In the case of composite works, if the proprietor secured the original copyright, he may also secure the renewal. 

8. Assignments.-A copyright may be assigned by any instrument in writing, but such assignment to be valid must be recorded in the copyright office within three months after its execution in the United States or within six months after its execution outside the United States. Every assignment of copyright executed in a foreign country must be acknowledged before a consular officer of the United States. 

9. Infringement.-Any person who wilfully and for profit infringes any copyright or assists in such infringement is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by imprisonment for not exceeding one year, or by a fine of not less than $100 or more than $1000, or both. In addition the owner of the copyright has both a legal and an equitable remedy in that:-

COPYRIGHT 

85 a. He can compel the wrongdoer to pay the damages sustained and any profits he may have made from the infringement. b. He can get out an injunction restraining the wrongdoer from infringing the copyright. 

10. Foreign Copyrights.-Registration in the Copyright 

Office of the United States does not insure protection in European countries, because the United States is not a member of the International Copyright Union. In order to secure copyright abroad it is necessary to comply with the law and administrative regulations of the country in which such protection is desired. As the requirements vary the practical course for one wishing such protection is to secure the services of a publisher or agent in such country to transact his copyright business.

Upon obtaining valid copyright in one of the countries belonging to the International Copyright Union, such as Great Britain or France, copyright is also secured in the other countries belonging to the Union, 11. Fees.-The fee for copyrighting any work is $1.00 which includes a certificate of registration under seal. Each additional certificate or copy under seal costs fifty cents.

The fee for renewal of copyright is fifty cents. The fee for photographs is fifty cents if a certificate is not requested.

For recording and certifying an assignment of a copyright, or for a certified copy of an assignment, the fee is $1.00 if the instrument is not over 300 words; $2.00 between 300 and 1000 words; and $1.00 extra for each additional 1000 words and fractions thereof over 300 words. Only one fee is charged when more than one volume of the same book is deposited in the copyright office at the same time.

POWER STEEL GAS CORPORATIONS 

1. Definition.-A corporation is a body created by law, composed of individuals, united under a common name, and having succession while it shall exist. It is the creature of the law, and derives all its powers and capacities from the law of its creation. known as 

2. Kinds of Corporations.-Corporations 

Business Corporations are the most common. Railroad corporations, and other public service corporations, though performing a public service are nevertheless Private Corporations. Then there are Religions, Charitable and Beneficial 

Corporations, usually organized for beneficial purposes, not for profit. Quasi Corporations, such as school districts, resemble corporations in some ways. They can own and manage real estate, make contracts, sue and be sued like any other corporation. A Close Corporation is one where the capital stock or ownership is confined to one family or distinct group of individuals.

CORPORATIONS 

87 

3. Formation of Corporation.-First, write the Secretary of 

State in your State for a copy of the corporation laws, and full information. Second, file with the Secretary of State a statement giving name, object, amount of capital stock, location of office, and duration. Third, as soon as a license is issued, and the stock subscribed for, hold a meeting and elect directors. State laws vary but usually three or more individuals may form a corporation. Charters are granted for a limited number of years. Corporations created in one 

State may transact any lawful business in another state, and they can acquire and transfer property as individuals. They are called foreign corporations. 

4. Life of a Corporation.-A corporation exists to the end of its charter unless it fails or is discontinued for other good reasons. The stockholder's rights pass from one to another by sale or by inheritance. Should one stockholder acquire all of the issued stock, the corporation would cease to exist after a limited time, and would be regarded as an individual. 

5. Capital Stock,-Corporations have assets composed of money, real estate, buildings, machinery, patents, copyrights, etc. The capital is paid in by members. Capital stock is divided into parts called shares, and the owners of the shares are called stockholders. By this method of promotion the necessary money for the enterprise may be collected from many different sources, and unlike a partnership the individual stockholders are not personally liable for the debts of the corporation. In large measure these facts account for the great popularity of the corporate form of organization. Corporations may increase or decrease the amount of their capital stock, provided the change is made in good faith, without intent to defraud. 

6. Who May Subscribe For Stock.-Anyone capable of making a contract may subscribe for the stock of a corporation. Minors are excluded, as well as married women in some states. However, there is no law to prevent subscription for stock by a friend and later making an ordinary transfer. Where fictitious subscriptions are used to induce others to buy, the purchaser may refuse to pay his subscription. If already paid for he may recover the money, or he may keep the stock and sue for damages. 

7. The Stock Certificate is a written statement of the number and par value of the shares to which the holder is

entitled. In other words, it is the evidence of ownership. 

A stockholder may prove ownership even though a certificate has never been issued him. When the capital stock of a corporation is increased each shareholder usually has the right to purchase his proportion of the new stock. 

8. Preferred Stock. This kind of stock takes preference over the ordinary or common stock of a corporation, and the holders are entitled to a stated per cent, annually out of the net earning before a dividend can be declared on the common stock. Preference rather than actual payment is guaranteed. Preferred stocks are generally the result of reorganization, although sometimes issued in payment of floating or unsecured debts. Preferred shareholders are not liable for the debts of the corporation. They usually have the right to vote at any stockholder's meeting. 

9. Common Stock is the ordinary stock of a corporation. 

The holders are entitled to all the rights incident to their ownership. 

10. Transfer of Stock.-This is provided for by statute. 

Usually the seller must assign the certificate to the transferree, execute a power of attorney and deliver the certificate to the company for registration. The transfer agent then issues a new certificate to the purchaser. 

11. A Subscription For Stock is a Contract and must be in writing. An agent cannot refuse to receive a subscription from a competent person, neither can he release a subscriber or alter the terms of the contract. The subscriber must inform himself as to his obligations and cannot evade payment unless he can prove fraud. 

12. A Corporate Lien.--A corporation cannot secure a lien on a shareholder's stock to cover the owner's personal indebtedness. The National Banking Law prohibits this, yet a bank may hold out a shareholder's dividend to apply on his indebtedness at the bank. 

13. The Shareholder's Liability.-As stated previously a corporation differs from a partnership in that the shareholders in a corporation are liable only for the amount of stock they own. Each member of a partnership is liable for all the debts of the concern. However, in the case of 

National Banks the shareholders are liable for the amount or just double the amount of their holdings in case the bank fails and that much money is required to pay the debts. A large surplus earned or paid in advance has no effect on this

CORPORATIONS 

89 fundamental liability. The amount of stockholder's liability is fixed by statute in the several states. A stockholder in any corporation is liable for the full amount of his stock, whether paid in full or not. 

14. Receivership.-When a corporation fails a receiver is appointed by the court to settle up its affairs. The receiver has the power to convert the property into cash, levy and collect assessments from the shareholders, where authorized by law, and pay dividends to the creditors, as in the case of bankruptcy proceedings. The receiver may be an individual, a group of individuals, or a trust company. 

15.-Management.-The power of a corporation rests in its members or individual stockholders-except as restricted or limited by law. Unless the charter or state laws alter the case the majority rules, that is a shareholder has as many votes as he owns shares in the corporation. The right to vote in a stockholder's meeting is determined by the stock record as the ownership appears on the date of the meeting. A stockholder has the right to vote even if no certificate has been issued to him. He may vote in person or by proxy. An executor or trustee may vote the stock of his testator. 

16. Meetings.-The statutes usually prescribe the manner in which meetings are to be called. In accordance with these statutes, the constitution or by-laws fix the time and place of meetings. Should the proper officer fail to call a meeting at the required time, the meeting may be lawfully held later, and if he refuse to issue the proper notice, he may be compelled to do so by mandamus proceedings. 

Regular Meetings are held in the manner set forth by the charter or by-laws, and the object need not be stated in the call. On the other hand, special meetings may be called at any time on proper authority, but the notice must state the object of the meeting and no other business may be there transacted. Any authorized meeting may be adjourned from time to time or from day to day, and the adjournments must be considered as the same meeting. Even if a meeting is illegally called it becomes a valid meeting by ratification of the proper official or by the shareholders. 

Notice of meeting is sent to whoever has the right to vote the stock, regardless of the rights of any pledger or pledgee. 

17. Directors.-Active management of a corporation is vested in certain trustees or directors. Trustees are used

in many savings Banks having the power to fill vacancies among their number. Most corporations delegate managerial powers to directors who are either elected by a majority vote of the shareholders, or by a cumulative system of voting when such system is used. The directors must be shareholders. Their powers are established by charter or statute, custom or by-laws. As a rule they have general supervision over the business of the corporation. Their authority may be delegated to committees, corporate officials, or to individuals. Thus the President, the Secretary, the Treasurer, and other officers and committees of the corporation are chosen by the Board of Directors to act in the capacity of agents, in administering its affairs. A director may not act for the corporation individually, but his unauthorized acts would bind the corporation if subsequently ratified. He cannot be expelled from the board unless fraud can be proved. A director may not act both for the corporation and for himself. Unless otherwise provided directors are not entitled to compensation for their services; but where a director is employed to perform duties which do not pertain to his office as a director, he is entitled to a fair compensation. 

18. The Director's Liability.-The directors of a company are liable to the company and to shareholders and outsiders for negligence, fraud, or for acts committed in excess of their authority. These are questions of fact to be determined by the courts. The directors of a corporation are personally liable for its debts if it can be proved that they incurred the obligations knowing that the corporation was insolvent. They have been held personally, jointly and severally liable as partners for debts of the corporation contracted in the State in which the company was found to have been doing business without having taken out a license. 

19. The Officers of a corporation are usually the President, Vice President, Secretary, and Treasurer chosen by and from the Board of Directors. The ordinary rules of agency govern their powers and duties.

The President is the chief executive officer and chairman of the Board of Directors. 

The Vice President takes over the duties of the President when for any reason the latter is unable to perform them. 

Quite frequently there are numerous vice presidents assigned to different duties.

CORPORATIONS 

91 The Secretary is the keeper of the records and the chief clerk of the corporation. He usually has the custody of the corporate seal.

The Treasurer has charge of the corporation's finances. 

He is usually under bond for the faithful performance of his duties. 

20. Dividends.-A dividend is a payment to the shareholders out of the net profits of the corporation. It may be in actual cash, in property or in additional stock. When stock is selling on the exchange above par, corporations sometimes grant shareholders the right to purchase additional stock at par instead of declaring a cash or stock dividend. The law will not permit the payment of dividends out of capital or from borrowed money, and the directors would be liable for such a fraudulent payment. Furthermore, illegally paid dividends may be recovered for the benefit of creditors. The net profit of a corporation is an asset, and not secure against creditors unless or until the money has been declared as a dividend. When the dividend has been legally declared payable, no action can be brought by creditors. The directors must act in good faith, but they cannot be compelled to pay dividends. The courts hold that dividends must be general on all the stock so that each shareholder will receive his just share, and that the dividend shall be paid to the owner as determined by the books of the company. According to income tax rulings, a dividend in cash is considered as income, one in stock as capital. 

21. Liabilities of a Corporation.-Through its agents or servants a corporation can be guilty of slander, libel, false representation, trespass, negligence, etc., exactly like an individual, and can be sued accordingly. 

22. The Shareholders Rights. A shareholder has the right to inspect the company's books at the proper time and for any reasonable purpose. Furthermore, he may employ an expert accountant to go thru the records if he has any reason to believe that the affairs of the company are not being handled properly. 

23. Trusts.-A trust is a consolidation, pool or combine of two or more competing concerns, which establishes a limited monopoly in any industry or group of industries. The name originated from the fact that details and arrangements of the combination were in the hands of trustees. Large trusts today, such as the Standard Oil Company, the United

States Steel Company, etc., have adopted the method of incorporating a company either to purchase the property and business of all the firms to be united, or to purchase and hold the stock of all the subsidiary companies, thus controlling the business of them all. This plan has to a large extent nullified the effectiveness of the Federal Anti Trust Law. A company organized for the single purpose of holding the stocks of other corporations and thus controlling them is called a holding corporation. 

24. Domestic vs. Interstate Business.-What constitutes doing business within a state is a delicate legal point. A 

Wisconsin corporation was refused the right to collect a large debt owed to it by a Michigan customer, simply because before selling the merchandise, the company had failed to qualify itself to do business in Michigan. Certain states require outside corporations to qualify and pay a license fee before they can transact domestic business within their borders. Similar rulings and an ever increasing code of laws make it necessary for all corporations to walk carefully, and consult expert legal advice before planning "turn-over sales," and other schemes which can be classed as domestic business.

CRIMINAL LAW AND PROCEDURE 

An 1. Definition.-A crime is an act in violation of some existing prohibitory statute and the common morality of the country. It is a wrong committed against the State. individual, therefore, cannot compromise a criminal wrong, for crime is a matter for the State to settle. 

2. Burden of Proof.-The burden of proof is upon the 

State. In other words a person accused of a crime is presumed innocent until the contrary is proved to the satisfaction of the jury. The verdict must be unanimous to convict. 

If any doubt remains in the minds of the jury, after hearing

all the evidence, it is their duty to acquit, and once acquitted, a prisoner cannot be brought to trial a second time for the same offense. 

Lous A Paeth THE BAR OF JUSTICE. 

3. Defenses.-The law takes into consideration two defenses, that of insanity, and self defense. A person who cannot distinguish right and wrong is insane and not held responsible for his acts, but the insanity must be proved. 

Again, a person may defend his person, family, or property and may use such force as is necessary. Intoxication, momentary insanity, and ignorance of the law are not looked upon with favor by the courts as defenses for crime. 

4. Confession.-A legal confession must be voluntary and free from all compulsion, either physical or mental. Third degree methods are unlawful and a confession procured by the use of threats or violence has no standing in court. 

5. Trial By Jury.-A person accused of a crime is guaranteed the right to a fair and impartial trial by a jury of twelve men, and to be represented by a competent lawyer. 

The trial must occur in the county where the crime was committed unless a "change of venue" is granted in cases where it can be proved that on account of prejudice the accused could not there receive a fair trial.

CRIMINAL LAW AND PROCEDURE 

97 

6. Habeas Corpus.-A writ of habeas corpus is issued by the court to prevent people from being unlawfully deprived of their liberty. The prisoner is released unless cause can be shown for his detention. This is a fundamental right of the Constitution. 

7. Criminal Procedure.-The first step in criminal procedure is the issuing of a warrant by a Justice of the Peace or judicial officer. When arrested the accused is either placed in custody or if he can furnish a satisfactory bond he is released on bail awaiting trial. If the offense is a misdemeanor the case is tried and settled before the Justice, if it is a felony, the Justice holds a preliminary trial, certifying the findings to the Grand Jury. Acting in an investigating capacity the Grand Jury may indict the accused and the case is tried on its merits in the regular criminal court, or it may be dropped on account of insufficient evidence. 

Criminal Law in Brief 

8. Adultery.-It is a crime for any unmarried man and woman to openly live together as man and wife. 

9. Accessory to the Crime.-Any person acting or assisting another to commit or abett a crime or to escape from the scene of the crime is equally guilty with the principal. 

10. Assault and Battery.-A person who threatens or attempts to strike another person is guilty of assault, even though not followed by actual battery. A successful assault becomes a battery when the injury is actually done. 

The slightest unlawful touching may be a battery. 

11. Bribery consists in the offering or giving of money or other valuable consideration to a public officer or one performing a public duty, as an inducement for him to commit an unlawful act. The giver and the receiver of the bribe are equally guilty. 

12. Blasphemy. The use of blasphemous language, defaming or defiling God or religion is a misdemeanor. 

13. Bigamy.—A person having more than one husband or wife is guilty of a crime. 

14. Burglary consists in the unlawful breaking or entering into the building of another with the intent to commit a crime. 

15. Bail means the sureties who bind themselves to have the accused present in court when required for trial.

16. Contempt of Court.-Any attempt to obstruct justice or to injure the dignity of the court is punishable by the action of the court, and is not subject to appeal. 

17. Conspiracy.-When two or more persons get together and agree to do an unlawful act, the agreement is called a conspiracy. 

18. Embezzlement is the wrongful appropriation and use of a person's property which has voluntarily been turned over to another person for some lawful use. 

19. Extortion is the asking and accepting of unlawful fees by a public officer. 

20. False Pretense.-It is a criminal offense to obtain money or other thing of value by the false or fraudulent representation of a past or existing fact. 

21. Fighting.-Affray or fighting is defined as the act of two or more persons fighting in a public place. 

22. Fornication.-When an unmarried person has illicit intercourse with a married person, he is guilty of fornication. 

23. Forgery is the false making or the material alteration of a written instrument, contract or legal paper. 

24. Homocide is the unlawful taking of a human life. 

There are four degrees of homocide. First and second degree murder, and voluntary and involuntary manslaughter. Voluntary Involuntary

TWO KINDS OF EMPLOYMENT.

CRIMINAL LAW AND PROCEDURE 

99 

25. Infanticide is the murder of an infant born alive. A person causing or assisting in the miscarriage of a pregnant woman is guilty of abortion. The killing of an unborn infant is murder. 

26. Larceny is the unlawful appropriation and use of a person's property. It differs from embezzlement in that the original taking is unlawful. Petit larceny is a misdemeanor, grand larceny a felony. 

27. Manslaughter is the unlawful killing of a human being without malice or premeditation. 

28. Mayhem is the act of maiming, disfiguring, or cutting away any part of the human body. 

29. Murder is the unlawful taking of a human life with malice and premeditation. 

30. Malicious Mischief is a crime which consists of the wilful and intentional injury of another's property. 

31. Offenses on the high seas are tried by the country under whose flag the ship is sailing. 

32. Perjury is the false swearing of a witness under oath. A person inducing a witness to perjure himself is equally guilty. 

33. Profanity.-The use of profane or insulting language in the presence of women or in public is a misdemeanor. 

34. Prohibition Laws.-It is a crime and a violation of the constitution of the United States to manufacture, sell, have for sale, or be in possession of liquor containing more than one-half of one per cent of alcohol. It is also unlawful to have in your possession any part of a still or distilling apparatus. 

35. Rape. It is a felony to have sexual knowledge of a girl or woman without her consent. Some states exact the death penalty. 

36. Riots.-A riot is an unlawful assembly of persons bent on carrying out certain unlawful ends. 

37. Robbery is larceny or stealing property from another by force and intimidation. It is a felony punishable by death in some states. 

38. Seduction.-To have intercourse with a girl through false promises of marriage is a crime. 

39. Stolen Property.-It is larceny to buy, receive, or conceal stolen property with the intent not to return it to the rightful owner. In buying property demand proof of the ownership.

40. Treason.-It is treason to make war against, or to assist the enemies of, the existing government. It is punishable by death. A foreigner, owing no allegiance to the government cannot be guilty of treason. 

41. Unlawful Assembly.-It is a criminal offense for two or more persons to assemble in contemplation of some unlawful act.

DEEDS 

1. Definitions.-A deed is a written agreement under seal for conveying real estate. There are three kinds of deeds: warranty deeds, indentures, and quit claim deeds.

Any person of legal age, competent to transact business and owning real estate, may convey it by deed. The seller is called the grantor, the buyer the grantee. 

2. A Warranty Deed is one in which the seller or grantor, as he is called, warrants the title to be good, and agrees to defend the same against all parties. Such a deed usually provides, a, that the seller has a right to convey the real estate; b, that he is the owner of the land mentioned in the deed; c, that the land is free and clear from all former and other grants, bargains, sales, liens, taxes, assessments and encumbrances of any kind; d, and that the purchaser will have the quiet enjoyment of the real estate. If it afterwards develops that the grantor did not have the right to sell or if the grantee discovers an encumbrance on the land, or if he has any trouble about the title, the purchaser has a good action against the seller. 

3. An Indenture is another form of deed used in selling land. It is signed by all the parties and contains the same warranties as are found in a warranty deed. The word indenture comes down to us from old English Law. In those days a deed was drawn up and signed by all the parties, and was then torn in half, one part going to the grantor, the other to the grantee. In order to establish title to the land the two parts or indentures had to match. As a matter of fact almost all deeds today start out with this form: THIS

INDENTURE WITNESSETH. 

4. A Quit Claim Deed releases only what interest the grantor may have in the property. This form of deed is

DEEDS 

101 given by the holder of a mortgage when it is paid or discharged, or by one whose title to the real estate is defective. 

In the latter case the seller conveys only whatever interest he may have. A quit claim deed contains no warrants. 

Paeth SIGNING THE DEED 5. General Principles.

a.

Deeds must be written or printed on paper or parchment. 

b. The names of the parties and places of residence are written first. c. The property must be fully described. The description should be by bounds, or by divisions of United States surveys, or by subdivisions into blocks and lots, as shown on the records. d. The deed must express a consideration, also a covenant to "warrant and defend," and be signed and sealed by the grantor or grantors. A deed without consideration is void.

e. Numbers should always be written in words folowed by figures in parentheses thus, Two Hundred Dollars ($200.00.) f. If the grantor is married both he and his wife should join in the grant and in the execution of the deed, signing and acknowledging. g. The acknowledgment of a deed can be made only before certain persons authorized to take the same, such as justices of the peace, notaries, masters in chancery, judges and clerks of the courts, commissioners of deeds, etc. h. The deed takes effect upon its delivery to the person authorized to receive it, and should be recorded at once. i. After the acknowledgment of a deed the parties have no right to make the slightest alteration. j. Never purchase real estate without a careful examination of the title, either by yourself or a trusted attorney. k. Always procure an abstract of title before advancing money or signing contract for purchase of land or lots. 

1. A deed in which a mistake has been made can be corrected in all cases of fraud or accident. m. In investigating the title to real estate, the attorney is bound to make a careful examination of the records and to report the facts, and is liable for any injury resulting from his negligence. n. The deed of a corporation must be signed by an agent or attorney and should be carefully executed. o. The execution of a deed is generally attested by witnesses. p. To have full effect a deed should be acknowledged and recorded. q. It is considered recorded as soon as it reaches the recording officer, who generally notes upon it the day, hour, and minute when it was received. r. If the land is a gift and no price is paid for it, it is customary to insert "in consideration of one dollar paid me, the receipt of which I acknowledge." (See "Agreement to Purchase Land.")

DOWER .L. S. 

1. Definitions.-Dower is the provision which the law provides for the support of a widow out of her deceased husband's estate. Unless modified by statute this interest consists of the use of one-third of her husband's land after his death. During the husband's life, the law protects the wife's interest by prohibiting the sale of real estate unless she joins with him in signing the deed. The interest which a husband acquires in the land belonging to his wife after her death is called curtesy. 

2. General Principles.-a. The dower right is regulated by widely differing statutes in the several states. b. If the land is subject to a mortgage or a lien of any kind, the wife cannot get possession until the encumbrance has been removed. c. A woman may revoke her dower right by signing with her husband a deed for the conveyance of the real estate. d. A husband can will his wife a certain amount in place of her dower, but the wife can claim the dower if she prefers it. e. The widow is usually entitled to administer. f. Dower does not exist in crops or trees, but does exist in mines and quarries. g. The widow of a partner is entitled to her dower in partnership land after the payment of all debts and a settlement made between the partners. h. A legal marriage is necessary to sustain a dower estate. absolute divorce or legal separation divests the wife of her dower. i. Dower may be barred by a marriage settlement or agreement made before marriage. j. Dower is assigned to the widow either by direction of the court or by agreement.

DRUNKENNESS 

1. Both the civil and the criminal courts are frequently compelled to rule on cases in which one of the parties was intoxicated. This in spite of the Volstead Act. 

2. In Civil Law the courts have recognized cases in which intoxication was an excuse for repudiating a contract. The mental condition must be taken into consideration especially where a man has become utterly incompetent or insane as a result of his intemperate habits. As we have seen before, such a man cannot make a contract. If one is visibly intoxicated the contract could be declared void on the ground that the other party must have realized his condition. The element of fraud enters still more strongly if one party deliberately induced the condition of the other. However, if the intoxicated party ratifies the agreement when sober or fails to repudiate it, he would be legally bound by it. 

3. In Criminal Cases the courts hold that one who voluntarily becomes intoxicated, cannot claim his intoxication as an excuse for his criminal acts. Yet in all such cases the facts must show that there was deliberate intent to commit the crime before there can be any conviction. This aspect has been brought up in many cases where the defendant was so drunk that he entered the wrong house, or carried off the property of others, or slandered the reputation of another. 

4. General Principles.—(a) It is the duty of those who come in contact with an intoxicated person to take his condition into consideration. (b) A sober party must exercise a reasonable degree of care to avoid injury to a drunken individual. (c) A railroad company is likewise bound to take into account the helpless condition of its passenger, and to exercise reasonable care in keeping him out of danger. (d) 

Drunkenness is not a legal excuse, but sometimes it is evidence of the absence of malice.

EMPLOYER AND EMPLOYEE 

1. Explanation.-The term employee refers to a person who is hired by a contract of service to perform certain duties under the direction of another person called the employer. 

2. Kinds of Con tracts. There are two general em ployment contracts. 

1st.-Contracts to do some particular thing such as to buy and sell stocks or provisions, to perform a surgical operation, or collect accounts. 2nd.

Contracts to do whatever the employer may direct. 

Farm hands domestic servants, and clerks belong to this class. 

3. Compensation. 

-If no agreement has been made before, the employee can claim the price usually paid for such service. If the employee leaves because of insufficient food, ill-treatment or disabling sick- Roeth

A LOAFER'S HEIRS NEVER HAVE TO CONTEST A WILL. 

ness, he is entitled to pay for the time he worked. 

4. Duties of Employee.-The employee should faithfully perform the services for which he contracted for the entire term or period of service. If he leaves before expiration of time, he can claim no pay for the work done. This is a general rule of law, but some able judges have decided that even in this case the employee is entitled to pay for work

EMPLOYER AND EMPLOYEE 

107 done less what the employer lost by necessity of paying higher wages, or what he lost by the employee's failing to perform his contract. The employee is bound to take reasonable care of the property in his care, and is liable for any loss or injury to it when due to his negligence. 

5. Discharge.-An employee may be discharged at the end of his contract without any cause or previous notice. If he is discharged without good cause and before the termination of his agreement, he is entitled to pay for the whole period provided that he has first made an earnest attempt to secure other employment in the same kind of work. If he gets work at lower wages he is entitled to the difference. 

If his pay is equal or higher than the former rate, he can not collect. If, however, the discharge is on account of incapacity, dishonesty, or misconduct, he is not entitled to any pay for the unexpired period. Frequently a person is hired for a month or for a year, at the termination of which the work continues. The law presumes a new contract on the same terms. 

6. Law of Kindness.-A kind and pleasant treatment on the part of the employer, even an expression of appreciation of work well done, goes far, very far, in making the employee worthy and competent. Harsh means and manners have often discouraged those who would by kind treatment have become efficient and competent in their work. In all cases of disagreement a friendly settlement is far better in every way than a resort to the law. 

7. Liability of Employer.-An employer's liability is of two kinds: 1st, liability for the acts of his employees, and 

2nd, liability for the injury or death of his employees. 

8. Liability For Acts of Employees.-The employer is liable for the wrongful acts of his employee producing injury to others, provided the acts are done in the course of the ordinary employment. Thus a railroad company is liable to passengers for negligence of conductors and engineers while running trains on the road. 

9. Workmen's Compensation.-In most of the states the liability of the employer for the safety of his workmen is determined by the general law of negligence. In other words, if a workman's negligence contributed to his injury, the employer is not liable unless it can be shown that the accident was partly his fault or the fault of a fellow servant.

10. Who is Entitled to Compensation.-Any person em ployed by a contract of service who is under the control of the employer while at work at the machine or other thing from which the injury arose is entitled to compensation. 

Previous physical condition is not considered in determining the amount. workmen's compensation

11. Who is Excluded. The acts differ in the several states. persons employed by the United gaged in Inter-State Commerce. While it is difficult to state a general rule, the following are excluded from the benefits in most states, in others the compensation is op tional: 

a. Minors and apprentices. b. Farm laborers. c. Domestic servants. d. Casual employees. e. Independent contractors. 

f. Public officers. 

12. Dependents.-The law also provides that the compensation be paid to dependents in case of death. Payments may be made to actual dependents or to partial dependents in accordance with the degree of dependency, but they cannot be made to those who do not belong in classes of relatives defined in the statutes. These include widows, children, step-children, illegitimate children, adopted children or a dependent parent. 

13. Payments.-The compensation acts provide for pay ments to the injured or his dependents in case of partial incapacity, permanent incapacity, or death, in amounts depending on the earning power of the injured at the time of the accident. Maximum and minimum amounts are usually specified. 

14. Insurance.-The compensation laws are rigidly enforced, and to protect themselves, employers quite generally take out liability insurance on the life and health of each employee. Then when an accident occurs, the Insurance Company assumes all liability and relieves the employer of any claims which might be made under the workmen's compensation law. This method of limiting liability is provided for in the laws of all the states.

EMPLOYER AND EMPLOYEE 

109 The cost of such insurance is based on the size of the payroll and the nature of the employment. It ranges from a purely nominal figure for office work to a rather high rate for the more hazardous occupations. 

15. Variations.-It would be impossible in a work like THE 

BUSINESS GUIDE to attempt an explanation of the Work men's Compensation laws in the different states.

For ex- ample, the law in California fills twenty-one pages larger than those in this book, is in fine print, and is very technical. 

A digest of the Illinois law covers fifty-six large pages. In some states deductions are made for contributory negligence, and in others awards are fixed for specific injuries, and in about every state there can be found numerous variations. 

In fact, there are so many differences and circumstances which act to modify the prescribed payments that no one table or group of tables could tell the story at a glance. 

16. Sources of Information.-Copies of the compensation and liability statutes may always be secured free of charge by writing to the Secretary of State for the State in question. He should be addressed at the State Capitol. Owing to the technical nature of the subject, however, it is always a good plan to ask your insurance adviser to explain your duties and obligations under the law. He is in a position to know the facts and to provide the protection you need.
