EXPLANATION 

HE success or failure of a work of reference depends upon its practical value....what it is worth in dollars and cents. This department of the Business 

Guide sets forth the various ways in which modern men and women are being swindled, exposes the amazing carelessness and ignorance which makes these losses possible, and presents tested and approved plans for making more money, and saving more money. On these three points its claims of practical value are based. 

SAVIN

HOW TO DETECT COUNTERFEIT MONEY 

1. Definitions.-A counterfeit is a fac-simile of the genuine, or made as nearly like it as possible. A spurious note is different in design from the genuine and is calculated to pass where the genuine is not known. An altered note is one altered from a lower to a higher denomination. Piecing is done by making ten notes or bills out of nine by cutting a counterfeit note into ten pieces.

THE DAILY PRE99 GIGANTIC SWIND 

2. 

Circulation.-Counter feiting has its good and bad seasons. During the war the high price of metals prohibited the manufacture of spurious coins. High wages in war time industries lessened the incentive. Now, as we are returning to normal conditions there has appeared what is known as a "normal circulation." 

3. Uncle Sam and the 

Counterfeiter. It is doubtful if many people realize that Uncle Sam has always been the counterfeiter's best friend and ally. For example there were in all fiftyfour different designs of various denominations in the old paper currency. Naturally this made counterfeiting easy. 

In the new small currency treasury officials have wisely reduced the variety and placed a distinctive portrait on each. 

Had they gone a step farther and adopted a distinctive color for each denomination they would have practically wiped out the counterfeiter's trade. 

Bills of eleven denominations have been issued as follows: Washington Jefferson $ 1.00 $ 2.00

Franklin 

McKinley Lincoln ..$ 5.00 Cleveland Hamilton $10.00 Madison Jackson $20.00 Chase Grant... $50.00 205 ..$ 100.00 $ 500.00 $ 1,000.00 $ 5,000.00 ..$10,000.00

How to Detect Counterfeit Bills 

4. Silk Threads.-There were two groups of silk threads running up and down in the old bills, one on the right side, the other on the left. In the new small currency tiny red and blue threads are quite generally distributed. As a sure test, hold the bill up to the light. No counterfeiter has ever been very successful in putting in the silk threads and imitating the genuine bills in this respect. 

5. Portraits.-See that the portraits are good, and notice that the pupil and the white of the eye show distinctly. 

Then see that the sky and water are clearly transparent.

In counterfeit notes the pictures are always poor and the sky, water, etc., look scratchy and irregular. 

6. Ink. The ink used in genuine notes is very difficult to imitate. It gives a clear, glossy expression, while counterfeiter's ink looks dull, smutty, and muddy. 

7. Paper. The pa per of a counterfeit is always of an inferior quality, while the government has the best and most perfect system of manufacturing the highest grade of paper. Rul- 

8. Medallion ings. Examine the medallion rulings and circular ornaments around the figures irst National Bank

COUNT WITH 

with a microscope, and see if they are regular and in all parts mathematically exact. This is done by a machine that costs from $75,000 to $150,000, and consequently is beyond the reach of counterfeiters. Engravings by hand can never imitate this work. These medallion lines or rulings can be traced by means of a line through the figures, never breaking or losing itself in another line. In counterfeit it is always broken and irregular. 

9. Altered Notes.-Notes are altered by raising the denomination by taking out the genuine with acid and printing in a higher denomination with a counterfeit die. They

HOW TO DETECT COUNTERFEIT MONEY 207 

can be easily detected by the stain which the acid produces when the figures are taken out. 

10. The Pasting Process.-Bank notes that have been altered by what is called the "pasting process" can be detected by holding them to the light. The parts pasted on will then be easily discovered. If any alteration has been made by substituting letters or figures for others that have been erased, the denomination in the center of the note, if carefully examined, letter by letter, will be found to be blurred and improperly formed, and the parallel lines irregular and imperfect. 

11. Put the Counterfeiter Out of Business.-The new paper currency is 2x6 inches. The portrait of a noted 

American will identify the denomination and make counterfeiting more difficult. In most cases a spurious note is easily recognized. It looks different. It feels different. Learn to identify the new bills by the portraits they bear, especially the $10,000.00 variety, and help to put the counterfeiter out of business. Remember too that no bill bearing the portrait of either Washington or Jefferson is worth more than $2.00. 

Rules for Detecting Counterfeit Coins 

12. Sound.-A counterfeit coin may sometimes be detected by its dull sound when thrown upon a counter. Some fake coins ring true but are so brittle that they are easily broken. 

13. Size and Weight are additional tests. A suspicious looking coin should be compared with a genuine one. 

14. Touch.-All counterfeit coins have a greasy feel when rubbed between the finger and thumb. 

15. The Acid Test consists in using a strong solution of nitric acid (6½ parts) muriatic acid (4 part) and water (5 parts). When applied to a scratch on the edge of a spurious coin the color will instantly change. If the acid has no effect the coin is genuine. 

16. Milling.-The edges of counterfeit coins are usually imperfect. 

17. Sweating, Plugging and Filling are methods used to debase coins, and the simplest tests are peculiarities in size, weight and appearance.

PARTH  

1. Swindlers have been with us since the beginning of the world. There has always been someone willing to take advantage of carelessness and ignorance and there always will be. We laugh at the victim of the old fashioned con game and gold brick artists, yet the same schemes, brightened up a little in new clothes are being worked just as successfully today. 

2. Three Practical Rules to Remember:

a. Never sign a paper of any kind for a stranger, unless he can prove that his business is legitimate and that he is acting within the limits of his authority. b. Never try to beat a swindler or a sharper at his own game. c. Sign no paper without reading it and understanding it. 

3. The Swindling Note.-There is a fundamental rule of law which provides that even a fraudulent note is good if it is in the hands of an innocent third party. Thus if A gets B to sign a paper which afterwards turns out to be a promissory note, B can be forced to pay the note to an innocent purchaser. Here is an example of a swindling note:- 208

Naperville, Ills., Oct. 20, 1923.

One year after date, I promise to pay Fred J. Davis or bearer Ten Dollars, when I sell by order Four Hundred and Seventy five Dollars ($475.00) worth of Victory Radio Outfits for value received, at ten per cent. per annum. 

Said ten dollars when due is payable at Naperville, Illinois. 

Witness: M. J. Moyer. 

C. E. Selby,

Agent for Fred J. Davis. 

Mr. C. E. Selby signed this contract thinking that he was securing the agency for Victory 

Radio Sets. He merely agreed to pay Fred Da vis the sum of $10.00 after he had sold a certain number of the outfits. He didn't read the paper carefully enough to notice that these last five or six words in each line could be torn off and destroyed in this manner: bearer Ten Dollars, when I sell by worth of Victory Radio Outfits 

Said ten dollars when due is

Agent for Fred J. Davis. 

leaving a perfectly good promissory note for $475.00:- 

One year after date, I promise to pay Fred J. Davis or order Four Hundred and Seventy-five Dollars ($475.00) for value received, at ten per cent. per annum. payable at Naperville, Illinois.

Witness: M. J. Moyer. 

C. E. Selby,

This note when sold at a bank becomes the property of a third and innocent party, and at the end of the year Mr. 

Selby is obliged to pay it. 

NEVER SIGN A PAPER FOR A STRANGER 

4. Counterfeit Money Swindle.-This is a shrewd method of blackmailing and is worked as follows: The swindlers arouse the interest of their intended victim by stories of the fabulous fortunes to be made by passing counterfeit money. 

To convince him they give him a genuine bill which, of course, is easily passed. He is persuaded to sign a document admitting him into a secret society, membership in which entitles him to receive an unlimited amount of the counterfeit bills at a trifling cost. As soon as his signature is secured, a hitherto unknown member of the gang represents himself as an officer of the United States, produces the damaging document, and pretends to place him under arrest. The victim is usually glad to pay from $100.00 to $2000.00 rather than suffer the disgrace of arrest and the humility of having his predicament made known. 

5. The Barb-Wire Swindle.-The "Wire Fence Man" is a new swindler working the farmers. The scheme is a shrewd one and is executed as follows: A nicely dressed man, very pleasant in his manner, meets the farmer in his field or at his home, and desires the privilege of exhibiting his wire fence stretcher machine, for which privilege he will build

the farmer thirty or forty rods of good fence for exhibition All the agent asks is board while he is at work on the fence, with the understanding that the farmer is to go after the ma. chine at the nearest depot and pay the charges, not to exceed $3 for the fence, all set up where he wants it. In order to have everything understood, and as a warrant of the farmer's good intentions, he requires him to sign a written order on a postal card, which he mails (as he says) to his partner, which proves to be a written contract for the machine, price $200 (worth less than $25). After the machine comes, a new man turns up with the postal order for the machine and requires the payment of $200 as per agreement on the card. He claims to be an attorney for the company and threatens to sue in the highest courts until he secures the payment of the order. 

6. Similar Swindles.-An affable stranger may offer you big commissions if you will sell some farm machinery he stores in your barn. He may offer to erect a patent fence or a windmill or a lightning rod at a ridiculously low price, provided you will agree to act as his agent. Merely as a matter of business (?) and just to have everything understood (?) you are requested to sign a lengthy agreement, specifying the terms under which the agency is to be carried on. If you read and understood a document of this kind you would never sign it, but many are led on by the certainty of future profits. At the end of thirty days you discover to your astonishment that the contract has been altered in such a way that you are legally bound to pay an exhorbitant price.

7. Warning.—It is always a simple matter to find out something about the character of the people with whom you are doing business. Before you make a contract of any kind with a strange firm, consult Dun or Bradstreet, or ask your banker to make an investigation for you. 

8. Fakers. Any large gathering of people is a Mecca for fakers and gamblers of all kinds. The three card monte trick and the shell game are the oldest and of course the best known. The players are slight of hand performers and it is impossible to beat a gambler of this type at his own game. In auction sales of cheap jewelry, the auctioneer openly stuffs a $20.00 bill into a dollar watch and sells it (at a sacrifice) for $10.00. The trusting purchaser discovers to his sorrow that his eyes had deceived him. In other games the faker has a box filled with envelopes, each envelope containing a number to correspond with numbers in a show case. The hopeful purchaser pays his dollar and selects an envelope. Most of the envelopes contain but one number which entitles the holder to one of the brass or silver washed prizes, worth but two or three cents each. But if a winning number is actually drawn, the envelope will contain two numbers, and it is hardly necessary to state that the unlucky number is the one shown. 

9. Cappers. In all these games, cappers are very extensively employed. A capper is a green, ignorant appearing man who wins large sums of money, or valuable prizes to draw others into the game. He buys a watch and shows the customers the $20.00 bill it contained. He never pulls an unlucky number. He is there to show you how easy it is to win, but you have only yourself to blame if you take his word for it and find out for yourself how easy it is to lose. 

10. The Matrimonial Agency.-There is a certain type of publication whose pages are literally cluttered up with fake matrimonial advertisements. Here is an explanation of their methods. The inspired proprietor makes the necessary arrangements with a young woman, and places a sum of money to her credit in the bank. He then inserts the following advertisement in every paper willing to accept it:- 

Beautiful young widow having $3000.00 cash would remarry. Only those who are qualified to handle finances successfully need apply. 

The Cupid Matrimonial Agency.

It is needless to say that countless men and boys are ready and willing to assume the role of husband and protector to this charming widow, and to invest her surplus funds. Each applicant receives a letter to the effect that the widow is very much pleased with his qualifications. He is urged to write again enclosing $2.00 for a photograph and to cover the fee of the agency. Once the fee has been received the widow writes regretting that she has changed her mind and decided to marry the man from Oshkosh. 

11. The Marriage Certificate Swindle.-This scheme is founded on the theory that all the world loves a lover. The scheme is simple but profitable. A man and woman hurriedly drive up to a farmer's house in search of a minister. 

From their flurried manner and their coy looks it is evident that they are eloping, but as there is no preacher within five miles, they are up against it. Just at this point the elopers' partner drives slowly by dressed as a country preacher. He is persuaded to marry the couple, the farmer and his wife sign as witnesses without reading the document, and at the end of thirty days are called upon by their bank to pay a note for $500.00. 

12. The Marked Bill Swindle. The swindler purchases a small item in the store of his intended victim, first carefully noting the number of the $10.00 bill he tenders in payment. 

A few minutes later his partner enters the store and makes a similar purchase laying down a one dollar bill. He picks up the change, counts it, starts for the door, then hesitates and asks: Didn't I give you a $10.00 bill? The storekeeper is quite positive. So is the purchaser. He remembers the bill because it was a nice new one and he even remembers the number of it. By this time an interested crowd has gathered around. When the bill is actually found in the merchant's cash register, there is nothing for him to do but give up nine of his hard earned dollars, thus doubling the working capital of the swindlers. 

13. Street Workers.-The means by which the street faker gathers in his unearned increment of dollars are many and varied. He may offer you Whosus' Bitters, a guaranteed cure for rheumatism, lumbago, eczema, cancer, headaches, liver trouble, impotence, constipation, summer complaint, tuberculosis and mumps, all for the sum of sixty-nine cents.

Probably it is distilled water with a little something added

to give it color and odor. Or he may have the most sensational article ever offered the public in a combination egg beater, monkey wrench, tire tool, jack knife, nail file, meat grinder and potato masher all for the insignificant sum of fifty cents. Before you realize how badly you have been taken in he is gone forever. 

14. The Fake Detective Swindle.-O'Henry tells of a crooked mayor who was beaten at his own game.

He re- fused to grant a license to a medicine show because he himself had a monopoly on the local medical business. The swindler's partner represented himself to be a detective and conspired with the mayor to get the goods on the medicine man. The mayor feigned illness and called in the medicine man to effect a cure. After the treatment he paid the bill with marked money, the detective stepped in, placed him under arrest, seized the money and retained it for evidence. 

Some days later the mayor suddenly came to the conclusion that he had been swindled. Both doctor and detective had gone. 

15. Beggars.-"For more than twenty years I have been in daily contact with beggars on the streets of greater New 

York. I have arrested, investigated, and talked with thousands of mendicants. Looking back on it all I must confess that I have yet to uncover a single deserving case." This is the extraordinary statement of John D. Godfrey, Mendicant officer for the Brooklyn Bureau of Charities.-American

Magazine October, 1922. 

16. The Profits of Begging are simply amazing. A capable beggar takes in from $15.00 to $100.00 a day and rarely devotes over three or four hours to his work. Think of that when next you are tempted to toss a coin to some deserving cripple. If he were an able bodied man in real hard luck he would patronize the bread lines or find opportunity to work for his meals. If he is disabled there are charity organizations in every city willing to take care of him, provide an artificial limb, teach him to use it, and find employment for him. If a man is out on the street asking for alms, he is there because it is the easiest way in the world to make his living. 

17. Kind of Beggars.-A "panhandler" is a poorly dressed individual who walks along beside you on the street telling a hard luck story and asking for a dime to get a cup of

coffee, or a sandwich. A "tramp" uses the same tactics in the country districts. A "flopper" is a beggar who has lost the use of one or both legs. A "throwout is one who fakes paralysis. A "high heeler" is a woman who wears an ugly HHHHHH 

THERE ARE THOUSANDS OF ROBBERS WHO NEVER USE A JIMMY OR BLACK JACK. 

brace on her foot giving her the appearance and the gait of a cripple. A "blackhood" is an old lady who sits on a camp stool with a crying baby in her lap and a tin cup in her hand. 

A "fit thrower" pretends to have fits or to faint from hunger. 

18. Publishing Fakes.-The number of people who have literary aspirations is astonishingly large. Certain firms

and individuals who have discovered this human trait have found a way to cash in on it. They run an advertisement something like this: 

BIG MONEY IN WRITING photoplays, stories, poems, songs. Send today for free Writer's Text

Book, full of helpful advice how to write and where to sell.

If you believe that you have latent talent of this kind you will answer this little ad and in the course of a few days you will get a book of instructions telling you how to make your fortune in literary circles. In the course of time you write a story or a song, or a photoplay and submit it to the publishers for free examination and criticism. Back comes a form letter, mind you, to the effect that there are great possibilities for your story or song or photoplay and that if you will send a certain sum of money, your work will be published at once or sold on a commission basis to some publisher or producer. Exactly the same letter is sent out no matter how good or how bad the work may be. The fees range from $10.00 up to $75.00 for typing and correcting the manuscript, or writing the music for a song, or selling the production to a publisher, whatever the agreement may be. Nothing is guaranteed in the contract, but the writer is led on by the hope of fabulous profits. Beware of these promoters. They will get your money and you will get nothing in return but experience. 

19. Wild Cat Stocks.-The Federal Trade Commission es timates that a billion and a half dollars are stolen every year from the investing public by so-called financiers. Think of it, a billion and a half dollars in worthless securities. In this way enough money is lost annually to pay off the National debt in a very few years, both principal and interest. This same amount of money turned into legitimate trade channels would make business boom in the United States, create new wealth and open up jobs for workmen. 

When you stop to think that in addition to the loss on these crooked schemes, the investing public throws away every year a still larger sum on oil, mining and promotion stock of various kinds which are perfectly legal, you begin to get an idea of the tremendous profits in this business. Don't be satisfied to think twice before you act. Think two hundred times and investigate every angle of the scheme and

the men behind it before you invest. The promoters have everything to gain and nothing to lose. You have everything to lose and nothing to gain in a fraudulent or speculative venture. 

20. Mail Order Swindles.-"We start you in the mail order business" is a familiar display head in many advertisements. 

Answer the advertisement and you discover with delight that here at last is an honest man who is going to make you rich. All you have to do is send him $25.00, $50.00 or $100.00 for certain schemes, formulae, mailing lists, stock in trade and full instructions for making a fortune in the mail order business. But once you part with your money you receive a shoddy assortment of merchandise and a worn out or fake trade secret, and you can repent of your folly at leisure. Mail order employment bureaus come in the same class. Suppose you are out of a job and an out of town agency sends you a letter listing hundreds of attractive positions they have open. "Send us $1.00 now" they say, "and the balance after you go to work." Wouldn't you be tempted to take a chance on a fair and square offer of that kind? Don't be deceived. The first dollar is all the agency wants. You will never be bothered about making the other payments because if you get a job it will be the result of your own efforts. 

21. Fake Wholesale Grocers.-Certain mail order grocers have recently made huge fortunes hoodwinking the public. 

They advertise sugar, flour, soap and other staples at greatly reduced prices, but in order to make this tremendous saving it is necessary for you to purchase the whole list of goods advertised. Thus, to save three or four cents on a pound of sugar or a cake of soap you must pay ridiculously high prices for a new brand of extracts, baking powders and spices. When you open up the package you find the cheap staples all right unless the supply is temporarily exhausted, but you also discover that you have paid out four or five times as much money as the shipment is worth. 

22. Medical Swindles.-The American public spends about one hundred million dollars annually for patent medicine. 

That statement sums up one of the most gigantic swindles ever attempted upon an intelligent public. The American 

Medical Association has published a book in which they take up each nationally advertised nostrum in order. Catarrh

remedies which contain dangerous drugs, soothing syrups which injure the health of infants, laxatives which enslave the user, headache powders which endanger life, mineral waters which are mineral in name only, dangerous home remedies for the treatment of venereal diseases, and tonics which develop a craving for alcoholic stimulant, and hundreds of similar remedies were exposed in this book. It showed that the average alcoholic content is about 25% in these remedies and that poor health and death itself were their inevitable result. It proved that half of the printed testimonials were paid for, that many were faked, and that the others were written by people willing to sign anything to get their names in print. As an example we cite the case of a man in Indiana who died of kidney trouble. Over a year after his death the manufacturer of a certain kidney medicine was using his picture and testimonial in all his advertising. In spite of these and countless other warnings the patent medicine business is growing day by day, and year by year. From the other side of the fence there is often voiced a criticism of the whole medical profession. 

Oculists who prescribe glasses when none are necessary, surgeons who resort to the knife on the slightest provocation, and practitioners who accept large fees for curing imaginary ailments are largely responsible for this feeling. 

There are unscrupulous individuals in every line of endeavor and it pays to be on the watch for them. 

23. Wanted New Faces for the Movies is an advertisement that has brought home thousands of unearned dollars to unscrupulous promoters. All you have to do to get into the movies is to send on $5.00 or $10.00. Your photograph is then printed in a portfolio or magazine which is supposed to circulate exclusively among motion picture directors who are always on the lookout for new faces. "It is fascinating work; the pay is big; and no experience or training is necessary," so reads the propaganda. "All we ask is one-half of your first week's salary of $500.00 or $1000.00." Sounds attractive, doesn't it, and yet all the advertiser ever hopes or expects to get is the original payment. 

24. One Sided Contracts. It is a regrettable fact, but none the less true, that numerous firms are making money through the use of an unfair or one sided contract. Let us see how they operate. Here, for example, is a New

York manufacturer (so called) who sells his product on the

exclusive territory plan, assigning certain large districts or territories to individual salesmen. He requires the salesman to guarantee a certain volume of business and to put up a substantial deposit in cash to bind the agreement. The product not being readily salable, the salesman falls down on his contract and forfeits the deposit. The manufacturer then hunts up another representative with some ready cash and resells the rights. Or again we find certain agency houses which guarantee that the salesman's commission over a period of months will equal a specified sum of money. 

A complete settlement and payment of any deficiency is to be made at the expiration of the contract. In the meantime the salesman is allowed a liberal commission but is required to pay cash for all goods ordered. A few weeks before the time is up the saleman's record is checked up. If he has not been making good on his agreement he is suddenly ordered over into California or up into Maine to finish his work. In indignation he gets out his contract and discovers to his chagrin that he must either travel a long distance at his own expense or violate the terms of his agreement. Similar one sided contracts are drawn up and signed every day. 

25. Correspondence Schools.-A vast amount of good has been accomplished by the correspondence schools in this country. Young men and women who were denied the privileges of college training have been able to get a liberal education or prepare for a better position by courses of home study. However, even this field is not safe from the swindler. He has organized fake detective schools, schools of science, literature, art, salesmanship, and courses of special instruction covering every phase of human endeavor. 

Earn while you learn is the great slogan. They have been exposed time and time again, but they still continue to get the money without giving any real value in return. A young man who wants to take up a course of mail instruction ought to make a careful investigation of the school and to be sure that he will get his money's worth. The tuition in a reliable school is frequently lower than that of its unworthy competitor. 

26. Home Work.-A great many people have a desire to increase their earnings by doing work at home after business hours. This is particularly true of women whose husbands are not able to earn enough to provide the luxuries of life. Knowing this to be the case the swindlers are al-

ways ready to help. For the small sum of $1.00 one man offers to send a list of reliable (?) firms who pay well for home work, such as addressing envelopes, sewing, fancy work, mailing circulars, etc. He is in the same class with the mail order employment bureau. All he wants is the dollar. Another sells an outfit for $5.00 which is supposed to enable you to do certain ornamental decoration on pillow tops, tidies, and pin cushions, and he assures you that your output will always be in demand at high prices. And still another persuades you to part with fifty or a hundred dollars for a knitting or weaving machine, which you are led to believe will pay for itself in thirty days and then provide you with a big income for the rest of your life. It is only after the money is hopelessly gone that you discover how worthless the machine really is and how slim your chances are of ever making any money with it. These sharks prey on the unsuspecting public, on women and children who can little afford to lose their hard earned cash. Boys and girls sell countless packages of worthless stick pins, washing powders, or post cards and receive in return a shoddy premium of little if any real value. Beware of these new schemes where science is baffled and thousands are growing rich over night. Invariably there is an unsuspected joker in the deck, and inevitably there is some cash to pay out first. 

27. Gasoline Pumps.-In some States the gasoline pumping stations are subject to state inspection. In others your chances of getting fair measure are about one in ten. Out of 

187 pumps inspected in a western city only five were found to be correct. Fifteen gave extra measure and 171 were condemned. Whether this situation is due more to carelessness than to deliberate intent is a question, but it is just another indication of the losses which confront us on every side. 

28. One Born Every Minute. And so we might go down the list. Yesterday we had the pocket size gold brick, the shell game and the lost gold mine; today we have the fake income tax collectors, the crooked lobbyists and the salesmen who sell us worthless land and stock; and tomorrow we shall see the same old gags worked in the same old way, on the same old gullible public. The newspapers inform us that just recently a gentleman from Iowa paid $2100 for a half interest in the Washington Monument that

someone else paid a few hundred for the Grant Park Monument in Chicago, and that the riparian rights for all of San Francisco Bay were sacrificed at $4500.00. People are looking for easy money, and their free and easy manner of hunting for it, makes easy marks out of them. 

29. Who is to Blame?-Are not the newspapers and magazines who print the fraudulent advertisements largely to blame for the sorrow and the heartaches which follow in the path of the swindler? Are they not in effect partners in the Crime? A publisher who does not take the trouble to look up the record of his advertisers or who is unwilling to stand behind everything sold thru his columns is violating his duty to his readers. Here surely we can place a part of the responsibility. Much of it must be laid at the door of ignorance as manifested by an unwarranted confidence in the sincerity and honesty of the whole human race. 

And finally, let us not overlook the great underlying principle in practically every big swindling scheme, namely the desire to get something for nothing. The most successful swindler swindles his victim by first arousing in the mind of that victim a desire to swindle someone else. 

30. Useless Warnings.—In bringing this chapter to a close let us call your attention to an amusing incident which occurred recently in a small western community. The local 

Banker received a circular describing a plainly fraudulent undertaking and seeking to enlist subscriptions for the capital stock. In the belief that he could do a real service to his patrons he posted up the circular in the Bank window and in his own handwriting wrote on the margin "This is a good example of a fraudulent stock selling scheme" and signed his name. Soon a crowd gathered at the window, men, women, and children rushed into the bank offering to draw out their savings and purchase stock in the new company, and the Banker was compelled at last to take down the circular in self defense. His warning was futile. Perhaps ours will be as well. But we have done our best to show the folly of trying to beat a swindler at his own game, of signing a paper for a stranger or of signing anything without reading it and understanding it.

RECEIVING TELLER 1. Explanation. - Under a Banking Sys tem in the United 

States where hundreds of millions of dollars change hands every day, it is only natural that huge losses occur. 

Some of them are direct-actual monetary losses in dollars and cents. Others are indirect resulting in the loss of reputation, the lowering of credit standings, or the inability to grasp an opportunity when it presents itself. All of them could be prevented. 

2. The Banker's Loss.-On account of the carelessness, ignorance, or incivility of its officers, a bank may lose friends and customers. Every bank has its overdrafts. 

Every bank has its past due paper. Every bank has a certain amount of real or personal property it has been compelled to accept in lieu of cash. But it is not of these losses we would deal. They are the inevitable result of circum, stances-bad management, poor judgment or dishonesty on the part of someone in the institution. The losses that count are the ones which affect you and I as plain citizens in our every day transactions with banks and bankers. 

3. The Cause of Bank Losses.-These losses are of two kinds: those due to our carelessness and those resulting from our ignorance of ordinary banking laws and customs. 

If every individual was as careful about money matters as he should be, and if he knew and understood the fundamental principles of money and banking, this chapter could remain unwritten. 

4. Losses Due to Carelessness.-Let us consider first of all the careless things people do in connection with their banking business. How do they write checks, how do they endorse them? How do they handle cancelled vouchers? What about overdrafts? Why is it that some people have no bank

account whatever? These and countless other questions must be considered if we are to avoid an apalling yet wholly unnecessary loss. The following illustrations bring out the points we wish to emphasize. 

5. Carelessness in Writing Checks.-Every banker knows that at least 50% of the checks passing through his hands could be raised or altered by the clumsiest amateur. The only reason that more of them are not changed is because there are not more dishonest people in the world. Millions of checks are written every year which could be changed as easily as a fourteen year old boy could raise the following check from $10.00 to $110.00, by placing the figure 1 before the 10 and writing the words "One Hundred" in front of "Ten."

6. Carelessness Costs Millions.-The annual loss through forgery and check raising is over fifty million dollars in the 

United States alone. Six years ago the loss was only twentyfive millions. This staggering increase is due to the con-

constantly growing use of the check and to the increasing skill and audacity of the crooks. 

7. Liability. Many persons believe that after making out a check payable to a firm or individual, writing in the amount and affixing the signature, that their responsibility ceases. But, sad to relate, such is not the law. One of the decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States reads: "Your bank is responsible for the signature on your check, but not for what is written in the body of the check, and money paid in good faith and without negligence on an altered check, cannot be recovered by the maker thereof." 

Espey vs Cinni Bank, 18 Wall, U. S. 118.

8. Blank Checks.-It would be an insult to a man's intelligence if you suggested that he sign his name to a check without filling in the amount or the payee's name, and hand It to a stranger. And yet, that's exactly what the average man is doing today when he sends his unprotected check through the United States Mails. The mails have been robbed. Almost any daily newspaper will verify that statement. Unfortunately there are dishonest employees who have been found guilty of stealing letters from the incoming or outgoing mail. And in robbing the mails, the modern thief would rather find one unprotected check, than several hundred dollars in currency. Why? Because the check's

value is limited only by the present worth of the signer.

Think of it! WHEN YOU WRITE AN ORDINARY CHECK YOU RUN THE RISK OF LOSING EVERY DOL- LAR YOU OWN. 

9. The Crook's Methods.-There are several methods by which a dishonest man can manipulate your check to his personal advantage. In the first place there are the simple pen changes which are illustrated on page 284. These are only a few of the many combinations that can be made by a careful study of the handwriting. For example, one to eight-one to eighty-one hundred to eight hundred -one thousand to eight thousand, etc. The employees of your bank are not mind readers and will consequently pay the check if there is no evidence of fraud. 10. The Acid Method.-It is a comparatively simple matter to apply an acid and wipe off every written word or figure except the signature on a common white check. This acid is worth about 25 cents per bottle and may be found on any bookkeeper's desk. On colored checks the fine lines of the signature are covered up until after the acid bath leaving the check perfectly white. Any convenient name and amount may then be written in. Even when safety paper (so called) is used, checks are altered every day. The professional check raiser has considerable knowledge of chemicals enabling him to alter checks, drafts, letters of credit and registered bonds. He is also something of an artist. For instance, if the payee's name on a safety check is to be changed, he delicately traces out the name with his 15

11. Changing the Payee's Name. The largest percentage of loss from altered checks occurs from changing the payee's name. Large checks are seldom raised, but the payee's name is changed to "bearer” or “cash.” Many names permit of changing by adding a letter or a syllable, or a few pen strokes. Thus, F. C. Ahrens is changed to F. C Ahrenson by simply adding the letters "on," and "The Fair has frequently been changed to Theo. Fairfax" by a very simple addition. 

12. History of Check Protectors.-The first mechanical device for protecting the amount of checks was one which crimped the paper over the numerical amount of the check. 

This was followed by a machine which punched the numerical amount of the check through the paper. Next came the machine stamping the words "Not over $000 dollars.". Check protecting manufacturers then produced a great variety of machines which wrote or stamped the amount in words in colored ink, as well as machines which stamped the amount in numerals. Such machines were generally accepted as insurance against alteration, and are still so considered by many people. 

13. A Game of Put and Take.-Step by step the cunning skill of the crook has kept pace with the inventive genius of the manufacturer. He soon learned that it was a simple matter to iron out the crimped surface of the check and to paste little discs of paper or apply tinted chalk when the check was perforated. In the case of machines which stamped the words "Not more than $000" in indelible ink he discovered a means of erasing the indelible ink and stamping in a greater amount by the aid of a similar device. 

With the invention of an instrument which broke up and disturbed the surface of the paper the criminal was forced to seek another method of fraud and he found it in the practice of changing the payee's name to bearer or to cash. 

Because of the fact that these check protectors do not permit of writing a large amount, the professional also devised the scheme of taking a small check reading

THIRTY-FOUR DOLLARS FIFTY CENTS 

and writing a larger amount above these words on a similar machine so that the check reads

ONE THOUSAND NINE HUNDRED AND THIRTY-FOUR DOLLARS FIFTY CENTS 

The paying teller can see at a glance that it would be impossible to write the whole amount on one line so he pays the check without questioning it. 

14. Protecting the Payee's Name.-The modern check pro tector accomplishes three things. First, it macerates the amount line and prints the amount in indelible ink into this broken paper surface. In the second place, it prints the words at such an angle that the very largest amounts can all be written on one line and in the proper place. And finally, it so macerates the payee's name when once written that it has never been successfully altered. Practically all of the earlier mechanisms eliminated the dishonest office man and the unskilled check alterer, but the professional was not discommoded. He found ready means of overcoming every barrier to his success, and his profits grew larger year by year. 

But the contest between inventor and criminal seems finally to have been decided in favor of the inventor, and for the present, at least, the man who uses the best protective device is comparatively safe. 

15. A Warning.-There remains only the necessity of bringing to the attention of the general public the ever present danger of sending out unprotected checks. Great and small, rich or poor, the liability is the same, and the rich man can better afford to suffer the consequences than his less fortunate brother. If thru your carelessness a crook raises your check and cashes it, you are liable for the increased amount even though that sum is a hundred times greater than your bank balance. And carelessness has been defined by the courts as the failure to take all reasonable precautions. 

16. Writing Checks in Pencil.-Checks written in pencil are perfectly good, but they are nevertheless a source of great danger. Some years ago a wealthy cattle buyer made a practice of going through the country handing out penciled checks in payment of his purchases. On one occasion he gave a farmer a $10.00 check in exchange for a calf. The

17. Rules for Writing Checks.

a. A check should be made payable "to the order of" a specific person, never to bearer. b. Write figures plainly with ink, never with pencil.

Don't make it necessary for your banker to pay every check on suspicion. c. Be sure that the amount in figures corresponds with the written amount. The bank will always pay the written amount. d. Write the amount of the check as far to the left as possible so that no additional words or figures can be inserted. e. Fill in the space remaining with a heavy black line so that nothing can be added. f. Exercise the utmost care in writing and handing out checks. The person who carelessly draws a check must stand any loss which may occur through its alteration. g. Remember that a check is your order to the bank 

TO PAY OUT MONEY, and that it is necessary for the bank to know WITHOUT QUESTION 

when, to whom, and how much it shall pay. h. Use the best known mechanical methods of protecting your check against alteration. 

18. Carelessness in Endorsing Checks.-The habit of en dorsing checks in blank should be discouraged for more than one reason. If you endorse a check by simply signing your name across the back of it, that endorsement has the effect of making the check payable to any holder, or to bearer. If it is lost or stolen it is as valuable to the finder or thief as the actual currency would be. Many business men make a practice of endorsing their checks in blank and carrying them to the bank for deposit. Suppose there is a hold-up or that in the excitement of an accident or a fire on the way to the bank, the checks disappear. The unfortunate owner has about one chance in ten of getting the money back.

Again, by endorsing a check you vouch for its genuineness in every respect. Thus, if you endorse in

blank and permit the check to come into the hands of a forger who afterwards raises the amount, you have made yourself liable for the larger amount. Always endorse a check payable to some specific person or firm. If the checks are intended for deposit, write across the back the words: "For Deposit in First National Bank" or "For Deposit 

Only" and sign your name. (For other forms of endorsement see Section 2 under Commercial Paper.) 

Lavis THE FIRST PASS BOOK. 

19. Carelessness in Keeping Records.-When a man put money in an English Bank three hundred years ago, his deposit was recorded by notches in a stick, which was then split, the bank keeping one part, the depositor the other. 

Before he could withdraw the money the two halves had to be matched together. When a man puts money into a bank today his deposits and withdrawals are all carefully recorded by an efficient system of modern bookkeeping. However, the individual does not always exercise the same great care in keeping his own accounts. As a result he allows his account to be overdrawn, injuring his credit with the bank, or he issues checks when he has no money in the bank thus lowering his credit standing with his creditors. One check coming back marked "Not sufficient funds" will do more damage to a man's credit than a dozen past due accounts,

and may destroy a commercial reputation it has taken years to establish. 

20. How to Check Your Bank Balance.-Call at the bank for your statement and vouchers every month. Check the bank statement with your own check book in order to avoid errors, detect strange checks, and to save confusion and loss of time. a. Always keep a correct record, on the stubs of your check book, of all deposits and checks. b. See that you receive all checks charged to you on the bank statement, and arrange them in order. c. Check off stubs for all checks returned with your statement, also verify deposits shown in your pass book with those shown on the statement. d. To the balance shown on the last stub used on which this statement is balanced, ADD the amounts of all checks shown on the unchecked stubs, that is the amount of outstanding or unpaid checks. e. The total should agree with the balance shown by the bank. Report any differences immediately. 

21. Losses Due to Ignorance.-Let us next take up the class of losses which are the direct result of ignorance.

What are some of the common mistakes people make in their banking business because they don't know any better? 

22. Ignorance of the Value of a Bank Account.-Although the number of bank accounts in the United States averages better than one for every person in the country yet there are thousands of people who do not take advantage of the convenience and safety which banks offer for the handling of money. There are four distinct ways in which the man who has no bank account is likely to lose. In the first place, when a check, a pass book, a certificate of deposit, or a bank draft is lost or stolen the owner has some chance to recover, but when the cash is gone, it is usually gone forever. Secondly, the lack of a bank account naturally leads to a lack of credit. The man without enough money to warrant a bank account has a decided limit placed on his buying power. Thirdly, the man who has no banking acquaintance is always subject to inconvenience and delay when he wishes to cash a check or a bank draft sent to him from another person. And in the last place it very often happens

that a young man going into business is denied the financial help he needs from the bank for the single reason that he is unable to show any satisfactory savings balance or other visible evidence of his character and habits. Thus the man who has no bank account runs the grave risk of losing money, credit, time, and opportunity. 

23. Failure to Cash Checks Promptly. The holder of a check should present it for payment within a reasonable time after he receives it. He may keep it as long as he pleases but if in the meantime the bank fails, he cannot demand payment again from the maker. The law provides that the check should be presented at the bank for payment or forwarded by mail for collection on the same day it is received or not later than the day following. Again a man's death automatically stops payment on all his outstanding checks. In other words, if a man dies before you have deposited his check, the bank will refuse to cash it and you will be obliged to wait for your money until his estate is settled. It is a matter of safety, therefore, to deposit all checks, or enter them for collection without any unreasonable delay. 

24. The Danger of Joint Accounts.-It is sometimes desirable for two persons to deposit money in their joint names, payable to either or both signatures. A joint account of man and wife subject to withdrawals by either during their lifetime, and by the survivor in event of the death of the other, is often a very wise arrangement. But in those states having an inheritance tax it may not be generally known that if one party to a joint account dies, the other is not permitted to draw out the money until the State Treasurer or other authority has been notified of the death, and given his consent to the withdrawal. The same laws govern the actions of a Bank or Trust Company having in its possession a safety deposit box of a deceased person. 

This box may not be removed or opened by friends or relatives until the proper State official has checked its contents and given his release. Thus it frequently happens that at a time when ready funds are most needed the cumbersome processes of the law step in and cause uncertainty and delay. 

25. The Liability of Shareholders.-The shareholders of most corporations are liable only for the amount they have contributed or subscribed. National Bank shareholders are

liable for another sum, equal to the par value of their stock, provided as much may be needed to pay the bank's debts in case of failure. Thus if the First National Bank fails and you own $1000.00 worth of its stock, you might lose the first thousand and be required to pay another thousand. The owners of bank stock do not always realize the extent of their personal liability, and the point is brought out here to show how easily and in how many unexpected ways a man can lose money because of his ignorance of the law. 

26. The Functions of a Bank.—To many individuals a bank is nothing more than an elaborately furnished building with a lot of dignified individuals sitting around at mahogany desks, trying to look wise, and an immense safety vault filled with gold and currency. To many others a bank is merely a convenient place in which to get a check cashed. 

Few really understand the internal organization of a bank, or know its real functions. As a result of this lack of understanding the Banks are unable to perform the services they otherwise might. Here briefly are the real functions of a bank: a. To provide a safe place for the custody of money and other valuables. b. To loan money for legitimate business purposes. c. To issue money (In case of National Banks). d. To facilitate the transmission of funds by drafts, or bills of exchange. e. To encourage thrift. f. To act in an advisory capacity with its patrons on all matters of an economic or financial nature. 

27. How a Banker Makes His Money.-A Banker primarily is a dealer in money. He borrows of one party and lends to another. The difference between the terms at which he borrows and those at which he lends, forms the source of his profit. By this means he draws into active operation those small sums of money which were previously unproductive in the hands of private individuals, and at the same time furnishes accommodation to those in need of additional capital for carrying on their commercial transactions. 

Anything that the banker can do to encourage thrift and improve methods of business among his customers, automatically increases his deposits and swells his profits. In banking, therefore, as in any other business, real service means suc-

cess, not only for the bank individually, but for the community it serves. 

28. What a Bank

Means to You.-A 

bank, therefore, means a place where you can leave your money in safety; a place in which to borrow money if you need it for some legitimate purpose; a place where you can purchase a draft or bill of exchange that will be legal tender in every country in the

BANK 

world; a place to learn the advantages of saving; and a friendly place to turn to when you are in need of information, advice, or assistance in your personal or business affairs. 

29. What the Federal Reserve Bank Means to You.-The framers of the Federal Reserve Act had three main purposes in view. They wanted, first, to prevent panics, second, to expand commercial credits, and third, to economize on the use of gold in bank reserves. In order to accomplish these ends the Federal Reserve System was established, not primarily a lot of banks, but a new banking machine supported by all the resources of the existing banks. The Federal Re. serve banks draw their capital from the established National and State Banks, and, through co-operative banking, put them in a better position to discharge their duties to business. While the Reserve banks are subject to government supervision, they are not in any sense government institutions. They are privately owned banks. Their stock is all owned by member banks. 

30. To Prevent Panics.-The panic of 1907 witnessed the complete breakdown of our money system. Cash was at a premium, banks stopped paying out money, and clearing house certificates were issued instead of currency. In the new federal reserve system it was planned to prevent any such money famine by the issue of bank notes based on

commercial paper, with 40% of gold reserve held against the notes by the issuing bank. These notes when presented at any other Federal Reserve Bank must be at once forwarded to the issuing bank for redemption, thus assuring the retirement of the notes when they are no longer needed. 

Provision is also made for the ultimate retirement of both United States' notes and National bank notes, and to give the country a currency composed of gold and reserve notes with silver certificates for small bills. 

31. To Expand Commercial Credits.-The rediscounting of commercial paper had been almost unknown in this country prior to the establishment of the federal reserve system. 

As a result credits arising from commercial paper stayed at the bank where the original credit was given instead of flowing from bank to bank according to the requirements and conditions in different sections of the country. The new law permits reserve banks to rediscount certain commercial notes, and also certain acceptances which are based on exportation or importation of merchandise. This rediscount feature means more to the ordinary mortal than all the others. Simply, rediscount means that when your local banker, with $200,000 deposits, has loaned out $160,000 on commercial paper (notes of your dry goods merchants, grocerymen, druggists, or farmers) he is no longer at the end of his rope. If some unforseen circumstance stampedes Tom, Dick and Harry, and the rest of the depositors into demanding their money at once, instead of closing the bank and going into the hands of a receiver as banks used to do before the establishment of the reserve system, your Banker endorses the $160,000 in notes and sends them to the regional reserve bank, which rediscounts the paper and sends back the cash. On the other hand, if business is good in your city and the manufacturers, merchants and farmers require additional capital to take advantage of the conditions your banker may rediscount the $160,000 in notes at the Federal Reserve Bank as before and loan the money out again. Thus a simple, sound, safe, and best of all an elastic system of credits is made possible. The credit facilities of your local bank are practically doubled and you personally have two chances to borrow money for legitimate purposes where formerly you had but one. 

32. What Paper May Be Rediscounted.-It is interesting to note that the main idea in the minds of the framers of

the Federal Reserve System was to hit the so-called "money trust" of the country. Wall Street was blamed for all the panics and for the fact that the credit system of the country could not supply enough funds for ordinary business development. The Federal Reserve Act not only broke the financial backbone of the money trust, but it went still further. It completely divorced investment banking from commercial banking. Notes secured by stocks or bonds as collateral, no matter how strong the market demand for such securities may be, cannot be rediscounted by a Federal

Reserve Bank. Notes secured by obligations of the United 

States are the only exceptions to this rule. Stock market fluctuations have thereby been prevented from having any effect on commercial business. All other commercial notes, drafts, bills of exchange, or acceptances bearing the indorsement of a member bank may be rediscounted with certain limitations. To prevent over-expansion or inflation of credit the Federal Reserve Board is authorized to define the character of bills eligible for discount, to limit and regulate the amounts and to fix the rates of discount. 

33. Less Gold For Bank Reserves.-The third purpose of the act was to economize on the use of gold for bank re serves. The Bank and Government vaults of the United 

States contained by far the greatest amount of gold ever accumulated by any nation-an amount larger than was necessary for the maintenance of sound credit. These big reserves were necessary because of the lack of unity in our banking system. In theory, each bank was supposed to keep enough gold on hand for its own emergencies. In practice this theory broke down time after time and it was only the voluntary co-operation among banks that saved our credit structure. Bankers soon learned that is was better business to assist a weak institution than it was to permit that bank to fail and drag others with it. The Federal reserve system has turned these voluntary and haphazard methods into regulated and systematic co-operation under the control of the Federal Reserve Board. Thus we have a unified system instead of a system composed of thousands of separate banks, each solely dependent on its own resources. Under such a system a much smaller gold reserve will serve as a solid foundation for the credit structure.

34. Limitations of the System.-The remark is often made that the Federal Reserve System is a cure for all business and financial troubles. It is not. Like every other man-made institution it has its limitations. Simply because it brought us safely through the trying times of the war and of the adjustment period afterwards, there is no good reason to suppose that it can build its superstructure on thin air. It can utilize and liquidate our inactive re- 

It can give to us the full benefit of our assets. 

But underneath it all there must be a foundation of honesty, virtue and sound business principles. sources. 

35. What the Federal Farm Loan System Means to You.- 

If you are a farmer or prospective farmer the Federal Farm Loan System means that a. You can borrow money for agricultural purposes up to 50% of the appraised value of your land and 20% of the value of the permanent improvements, provided that the amount is not less than $100.00 nor more than $25,000.00. b. You get your money at a lower rate of interest than would be probable through any other organization, especially in a new country where investment funds are scarce. c. The length of term and the optional privilege of payment, in part or in full, after five years, are unequaled by any other loaning agency. d. It gives you the privilege of spreading your payments over a period of 40 years in small installments. e. It enables you to pay off your loan according to your earning power. f. You are required to use the money you borrow for productive agricultural purposes. 

If you are an investor, the Farm Loan System means that: a. You can buy bonds which are in reality first mort, gages against the farms of the United States, every dollar borrowed representing $2.00 worth of land. b. These bonds are tax exempt, that is, you will not have income taxes, or state, county, or municipal taxes to pay on them.

If you are just an ordinary citizen, the Farm Loan System means, that: a. The cost of living will come down as a result of the establishment of more farms and of better farming methods. b. The wasteful and inefficient system of farm tenantry will give way to one of economical and intelligent ownership. c. That where our farmers formerly paid 9% annually on a volume of four billion dollars, they now pay but 5%. This alone is an actual saving of $160,000.000 not only to the farmers but to the country as a whole. 

Revolutionary? Yes. Socialistic? Yes. But it puts the interests of the majority above the interests of the few. It upsets all the dope in financial struggles but it writes "victory" on humanity's side. 

36. What Does a Bank Statement Mean to You?-Many people who have no knowledge of accounting, feel that they can not understand a bank statement, and therefore pay no attention to it. This is a mistake. Every person who has money on deposit, either in a savings or checking account ought to know the condition of his bank, and how its condition compares with that of other banks. Below is a simple statement of a moderate sized national bank, together with an analysis of the various items:-

37. Resources.-By resources is meant what the banks own. Let us consider each resource as it appears:- 

Cash on Hand and Due From Banks.—This item repre sents the actual cash on hand in the bank, the money which the bank has on deposit with the Federal Reserve or correspondent banks, and checks deposited for collection which are drawn on other banks. Banks usually keep a considerable sum on deposit with other banks, in order that they may draw drafts against that money, when necessary. 

Loans and Discounts.-This represents the value of the promissory notes of the firms or individuals who have borrowed money from the bank. The interest from the loans constitutes the main source of the bank's income. When you apply for a loan your request is passed on by the officers of the bank or a discount committee appointed for that purpose, whose business it is to see that the bank is properly safeguarded in giving you the money.

U. S. Bonds to Secure Circulation.-National Banks have the privilege of issuing their own National Bank notes, but in order to do so they must buy and deposit with the Treasurer of the United States an equal amount of United States' Bonds to secure payment of the notes. This amount may not exceed the capital of the bank. 

Redemption Fund.-This is a fund equal to 5% of a National Bank's outstanding bank notes which must be deposited with the Treasurer of the United States to redeem those notes which have become unfit for circulation. When notes are sent to the Treasury for redemption they are charged to this account.

Bonds and Other Securities.-This sum represents the value of such bonds or other securities as the bank has in- 16

vested in. High grade bonds make a very desirable investment for surplus funds because of their safety and because they can be sold advantageously on short notice, at a price quoted every day.

Banking House.-Under this head there is included the cost of the ground, building, furniture and fixtures used by the bank in carrying on its transactions. This is valuable property owned by the bank. 

Stock in Federal Reserve Bank.-All member banks in the Federal Reserve System must own a block of stock in their district reserve bank, equal to 6% of their combined capital and surplus. Up to the present time the Reserve banks have found it necessary to call only 3% of the requirement. 

38. Liabilities.-By liabilities we mean the things that the bank owes. Every dollar paid into the bank immediately becomes a liability. The earnings belong to the stockholders, hence are liabilities. A deposit of money is recorded as a resource, but it really belongs to the depositor and must be included among the liabilities. In this particular statement the liabilities are shown under seven different headings:

ors.

Capital Stock.-When a bank is organized the stockholders pay in a certain amount of money to protect the deposit- This is called the capital or the capital stock of the bank. It is shown as a liability, because the bank is indebted to the stockholders for what money they pay in. In other words, the stockholders are the owners of the bank. 

If, however, the bank goes broke or is unable to pay its depositors, the capital may be used. In addition the stockholders in National Banks and in some state banks are personally liable for an equal amount, if it is needed to pay the debts.

Surplus. A national bank is required by law to accumulate from its profits a fund which will equal 20% of its capital. This is called the surplus fund. Many banks of course accumulate a fund much larger than 20% of their capital. The surplus is also a liability because it belongs to the shareholders, but it remains in the bank as part of the working capital.

Undivided Profits.-The undivided profits account represents earnings which have neither been added to the surplus nor paid out in dividends. The size of this account varies

with the earnings and when it is large enough, it is transferred to the surplus account. A well managed bank never pays out all its profits in dividends. 

Demand and Time Deposits.-Money deposited with a bank in a checking account is a demand deposit. The savings accounts on which interest is paid are time deposits. 

The bank owes its patrons for all these deposits and must be prepared to meet their demands.

Rediscounts and Loans From Other Banks.—It frequently happens that a bank must borrow money from other banks in order to accommodate its customers. This is done by putting up good security as collateral for the loan, or in the case of a member bank in the Federal Reserve System, by rediscounting commercial paper as explained above. These loans being debts owed by the bank must be shown as direct or contingent liabilities.

Reserve for Taxes and Interest.-Instead of carrying a large sum of money as undivided profits, most banks set up a reserve fund for the payment of taxes, interest, bad debts and other necessary expenditures. As the payments are made, they are charged against this account. Thus the bank avoids creating a wrong impression in the published statements it is required by law to make. 

Circulation. This item represents the outstanding na tional bank notes issued by the bank. A definite promise to pay has been made, and the amount is therefore carried as a liability. 

39. Published Statements.-The law requires banks to submit statements to the proper authorities and to publish them regularly in local newspapers. This is in addition to the official examination to which all banks are subject by National or State Bank Examiners, Clearing House officials or Reserve Bank Examiners. The published statements, if fully understood, will give depositors an accurate idea of the standing of their bank. By learning to read between the lines you will soon discover that what at first appears to be only a formidable and uninteresting column of figures, is in reality a very simple and instructive picture of the progress and condition of your Bank. 

40. The Morris Plan.-During recent years there has grown up in the larger cities a chain of small banks whose business it is to take care of the needs of the small borrower. 

They are known as Morris Plan Banks. The founder, Mr.

Arthur J. Morris, realized that the extortion and usury practiced upon the small borrower was breeding discontent, socialism and anarchy and his first bank in Norfolk, Virginia, was successful both from a humanitarian and a financial standpoint. The essential features of these new banks are as follows: 

a. The Morris Plan bank will not make real estate or collateral loans, or loans based on pawn or chattel security. b. The basis of credit is character and earning power. c. The borrower must secure two signatures in addition to his own. d. All loans are made for a period of one year. e. All loans are amortized at the rate of 2% on the loan, or in other words, are paid back on a weeklydeposit basis. 

41. How the Plan Works.-Thus we will suppose a car penter has been ill and is owing his doctor, his grocer, his coal man and others a total of $250.00. He goes to a Morris 

Plan Bank and requests a loan to pay up his debts. He gets two friends to sign the note with him and the Bank gives him the money. At the same time he is required to open up a savings account and to make regular weekly deposits of $5.00. He goes out of the bank a happy man, proud of the bank's confidence in him, and able to give his best efforts to his job. Contrast his state of mind with that of the man who must patronize the loan shark, pay 15 to 20% interest, sacrifice his self respect, and put up his salary and his household furniture as security for a small loan. 

42. Character is Credit.-The Morris Plan Bank is simply another proof that in the last analysis character is the real basis of credit, and that character can be found in the ready cut cottage as well as in the gilded mansion.

HOW TO SAFEGUARD YOUR HEIRS 

1. Religion and Success.-History informs us that the world's most successful men have been those who carried their religious belief into their daily business experiences. 

In order to make good in life it has always been necessary to be good and to do good. 

2. After Death-What?-Volumes have been written on the immortality of the soul and the life beyond the grave, but little attention, if any, has been paid to the very practical problem of a man's property after his death. What is to become of your estate, Mr. Business Man? Have you taken every possible precaution? If you have you are one among hundreds. 

3. Unforseen Events.-A man may have an abiding faith in his ultimate destiny, but it does not always pay to display that same measure of faith in his fellow creatures. Experience teaches us that after death a man's best friends often turn against him and pay back his kind offices by attempting to defraud his widow and orphans. Even in the case of his most reliable associates in business, all relations and responsibilities undergo a radical change when he is gone. His wife or son, or daughter, lacking perhaps, prac-

tical experience and knowledge are often too hopefully confident as to their own ability to achieve superior results along new and untried lines. Unnecessary expense, litigation and loss naturally occur. 

4. Foresight. The successful business man too often fails to make adequate provision for the management and distribution of his estate, thus reducing its value, availability and safety. He may fail to make a will altogether.

He may attempt to draw a legal will without legal advice. 

Frequently he appoints as his executor or trustee a man who is incapable, unable, or unwilling to act in that capacity. 

5. Why You Should Make a Will.-For all these reasons and for many others a man who leaves any property whatever should exercise the greatest care and the keenest judgment in disposing of it. Any one inclined to leave his estate subject to the distribution provided by law should con sider the following:

a. Where there is no will, real estate is not controlled by the administrator, but passes to the heirs at law. Expensive partition proceedings are usually required before the property can be sold or mortgaged. b. Where there is no will, the rights of husband or wife depend on the unwieldy assertion of dower. 

It is sometimes impossible to determine which died first, and expensive litigation is necessary to properly dstribute the property. c. Where there is no will, it frequently happens that the estate is finally divided in a way which would be very unsatisfactory to the testator. d. Without a will it is impossible to preserve an interest for the family in a partnership or close corporation. e. Administration by the State is always impersonal, and inconsiderate. It involves immediate liquidation and distribution with the customary expensive and bitter litigation. f. Where there is no will the expense of the premium on an administration bond must come out of the value of the estate. (Foot note: For legal points and forms of wills see page 255).

6. Deeds of Trust.-There are many people who do not realize that there is another very satisfactory method of distributing and controlling property after death. A deed of 

Louis A Paeth-. 

trust is an instrument by which property is conveyed to a trustee with directions for its use and control. This transfer may be made either before or after death. It has many 

a. In the first place a deed of trust enables you to set aside a certain part of your property for some specific purpose, absolutely safe from any business reverses you may experience in the future. b. It takes effect immediately while you are able to observe its effects. If it is attacked you can see that it is enforced. Under a will you would be unable to do so. c. It saves the court costs and expenses of the probate and administration of your estate. d. Unlike a will it involves no inheritance taxes, which means a considerable saving. e. There is no uncertainty, delay, or interruption of business, after death. f. The control, income and management of the property may be retained under a deed of trust during the life of the maker.

g. And finally a deed of trust is revokable at any time just as a will may be destroyed or changed. 

7. A Will or a Trust Deed.-Notwithstanding all these advantages there are reasons why a will may be preferred in some cases. Perhaps the maker is unwilling or unable to impair the title, ownership or disposition of the property during his life. Again it may be that it is easier to include and dispose of all of his property at the time of his death. 

And in many cases probate proceedings are necessary to establish the fact that the real estate is not subject to the debts of the deceased owner. In certain instances of this nature, a will is advisable even if the bulk of the estate is disposed of through a deed of trust. 

8. The Choice of Executors and Trustees.-Whether a will or a deed of trust is decided upon, the question of the choice of executors and trustees, arises. Should a member of the family, or a trusted friend or business associate be chosen, or should a trust company be selected? Here is where many of us make our mistakes. Every day we read in the papers where individuals appear to have mismanaged estates and of the very large number of estates left open and unsettled. In addition to the much larger number of unreported cases where loss has resulted by reason of the failure of individuals in the management of estates, there are the following reasons why a trust company should be selected: a. An individual cannot always be depended upon.

At the last minute there may be a change in residence, failure of health, death, financial reverses, or a definite refusal to serve. b. Because a trust company is efficient, giving your estate the benefit of its years of experience, its knowledge of safe investment and the requirements of the law. e. 

Because a trust company is economical, cutting off every item of unnecessary expense, and employing every dollar of the trust as profitably as safety will permit. d. Because the fees are made lower than any competent individual could serve for. e. Because it is perpetual in that its management does not end with the death, disability, or absence of any individual.

f. Because it is safe. The Trust Company's sole duty is to provide safety for your estate. It will not drink, speculate, or use the funds for its own purposes. It is under the direct control and supervision of the State government. 

9. Life Insurance.-Many business men prefer to accumulate their estates in the form of life insurance. Any insurance man can tell you of huge policies running up as high as a half million dollars or more. No matter how large or how small your insurance may be, you should exercise the same care in the distribution of the money after your death. 

A certain amount of ready cash is necessary to pay funeral expenses, settle outstanding obligations, and to avoid the necessity of hasty liquidation. Instead of making the balance payable in a lump sum, why not put it in the form of a trust fund or have it paid in regular monthly payments during the life of the beneficiary. This method would do away with the possibility of loss through poor investments, and at the same time provide a steady, safe income to be depended upon no matter what happened. 

10. How to Save Court Costs.-There are many cases in which neither a will nor a deed of trust is necessary. For example, consider a man and wife without any material property other than the home they live in. Through a Joint 

Tenancy Deed, the title to this home may in most States, be made to pass to the survivor without a will or trust deed, and without any attorney's fees or court costs. An official entry in the county records of the death of one party is all that is necessary to establish a good title to the property in the other party. 

11. Joint Tenancy and Tenancy in Common.-Comparative ly few people seem to know about the advantages of a couple owning property in Joint Tenancy, as distinguished from tenancy in common, but there is a world of difference between the two. In the latter there is merely an undivided interest in the property which must be disposed of by will or intestate law after the decease of the owner. In a joint tenancy, on the other hand, the property is owned jointly, and at the death of one party, the ownership passes automatically to the survivor. Any well informed realtor or lawyer can draw up the necessary papers to convey the property to some third person, who will reconvey it to the husband and wife, in joint tenancy.
