HE FAILED TO BUDGET HOW TO SAVE MONEY IN THE HOME The Ten Commandments of Thrift. 

(Adopted by the American Bankers' Association.) 

1. Make a budget. 

2. Keep an intelligent record. 

3. Have a bank account. 

4. Carry life insurance. 

5. Make a will. 

6. Own your own home eventually. 

7. Pay your bills promptly. 

8. Invest in government securities. 

9. Spend less than you earn. 

10. Share with others. Thrift without benevolence is a doubtful blessing. 

1. Definitions.-Thrift may be defined as economical management. A budget is a comprehensive plan to limit future expenditures. An appropriation is one of the items of a budget, a sum of money set aside or reserved for a certain purpose. 

2. The Modern Business Man operates on the budget plan. 

Appropriations are made at the beginning of the year to cover manufacturing costs, selling expense, taxes, insur-

HOW TO SAVE MONEY IN THE HOME 

251 ance, advertising, development, and other expenditures.

Each transaction is carefully classified, charged to its proper appropriation and made a part of the permanent record. 

Thus a properly worked out budget is the very life blood of the organization. Without one, it is a matter of hit or miss. 

3. System at Home.-Take this same business man at home and we find an entirely different situation. There is an absolute lack of system. Supplies are purchased, obligations incurred, and help is hired without any reference to the income. There is no budget, no organized plan of living, and in most cases no records are kept. As a result the family income vanishes with nothing left to show for it, at the end of the year. 

4. It Pays to Plan Ahead.-Not only can you save more by systematic planning, but you can actually live better on less money.

This has been proven by the experience of thousands of people who have adopted a common sense budget and stuck to it. Banks all over the country are opening up special service departments where constructive advice and information is given in planning budgets on incomes both large and small and to those who are not depositors as well as those who are patrons of the bank. Your modern banker has recognized the need of such help. He is trying to encourage thrift. He wants you to manage your household affairs on the budget plan because he knows that you will thereby become a better citizen and a more valuable patron of his bank. His information, advice and assistance are free. 

5. The First Essential to a successful budget is the determination to keep accurate account of all expenditures.

Without such accounts your system is worthless. Ask the average man on the street what it costs him to run his automobile for a year and his guess will be anywhere from $200 to $1000. Ask the woman of the house what the family grocery bill is for a year and her answer will be equally vague. 

Guess work will not do. If you want to receive full value for every dollar, maintain a certain standard of living, and still put something aside, you must make a budget and see that your expenses do not exceed your appropriations. 

6. How to Make a Budget. Classify your future ex penditures under six general headings:-Savings, shelter, food, clothing, operating expense, and advancement. Each of these general headings should be fully subdivided to

253 SO avoid the necessity of a miscellaneous column which often proves the downfall of the budget. Next decide on a certain amount of saving each month, so much for shelter, food, clothing, operating and advancement, depending on the extent of your income. If there is a large bank in your neighborhood ask the cashier to help you make the appropriations. On the opposite page are shown some sample budgets as worked out by the Society for Savings in Cleveland, Ohio. They are based on living expenses in Cleveland and may require some variations in other places. It is hoped, however, that they will be of some assistance in meeting individual reqquirements. 

7. Keeping Within the Budget.-As stated above the important thing is to keep an accurate record of expenditures.

A multicolumar journal is the ideal arrangement with a separate column for each general and sub-head. If you pay by check it is a simple matter to enter the amounts from the check stub to the proper column in the journal. When all supplies are bought for cash, it is a good idea to enter each purchase in a small notebook to be transferred later. The next step, of course, is to compare the record month by month, to determine which items must be increased, to find out where savings may be made, and to keep the sum total of your disbursements within the limits set by your budget. 

You may fail dismally the first time, but you will succeed eventually. And in any event an accurate knowledge of your expenses will prove a revelation and an inspiration to you. 

8. Teaching Business to Wives and Children.-Women are frequently ridiculed because of their ignorance of business methods. How many widows are qualified by experience and training to manage the business affairs of the family? 

Responsibilities come quicker than we expect so why not be prepared? A budget system will supply the necessary preparation. It is like a new game or puzzle into which wife and children enter with unlimited enthusiasm, and from which they will derive a familiarity with financial and business transactions, and an ultimate understanding of the true meaning of thrift. They will learn to get full value for every dollar expended and they will learn that it is easy to save more than they ever saved before without in any way lowering their standard of living.

9. Success or Failure?-The millionaire railroad magnate, James J. Hill, once said: "If you want to know whether you are going to be a success or failure in life, you can easily find out. sure 

The test is simple and infallible. Are you able to save money? If not, drop out. You will lose. You may not think it but you will lose as as you live. The seed of success is not in you." Every man is the architect of his own fortune. Be sure that you take the first step to guard against failure. It

makes no difference whether you start a regular savings plan of $10.00 a month or $1,000, the results proportionately are worth any effort. Out of the acorn of thrift grows the oak of financial independence. The first syllable of TRIUMPH

HOW TO SAVE INSURANCE PREMIUMS 

1. Vast sums of money are lost every day in the United

States because of a general ignorance of the true meaning of an insurance contract. There is a tremendous waste of time, money, and security, wholly aside from the actual losses due to fire, lightning, wind, sickness, or accidents. 

2. Reasons for the Loss.-It is possible to classify all the contributing causes under two general heads, namely: ignorance and carelessness. Ignorance is responsible (1) for the fact that a policy holder does not know what his policy provides, (2) for the fact that an individual often pays an exhorbitant rate of insurance on his property, (3) for the fact that he seldom secures full protection, and (4) for the fact that after a serious loss the insured is often unable to es-

tablish a just claim. Carelessnes, on the other hand, (1) causes an annual loss of life and property which simply staggers the imagination, (2) lays waste and destroys thousands of buildings every day, (3) costs the country over 24 billion of dollars every year in accidents alone, and (4) keeps the rates on all kinds of insurance twice as high as they ought to be. 

3. Ignorance and Insurance Loss.-It is fitting, therefore, that we should ask ourselves a few pertinent questions. How much do we really know about insurance? How can we reduce this tremendous waste to a minimum? Let us see if we cannot profit by the unfortunate experiences of others. 

4. Do You Know Your Policy?—Your policy states in black and white just what the Insurance Company agrees to do and just what you as the insured agree to do. There are at least a dozen ways in which an ordinary insurance policy may become void on account of the policy holder's ignorance. 

5. Examples. Just to illustrate we will take the case of a partnership having purchased protection against fire for a five-year period. At the end of the first year let us suppose that the business increases, more capital is needed, and the partners decide to dissolve the partnership in order to form a corporation. All other necessary steps are taken, but no one thinks about the insurance, which still has four years to run. Shortly afterwards a fire occurs, and the adjusters refuse to pay the loss, pointing to a clause in the policy which reads:- "If any change, other than by the death of the insurer, take place in the interest, title or possession of the subject of insurance, this entire policy shall be void."

This identical clause appears in all standard fire insurance policies. It is put there to be read and understood, but nobody ever reads it or understands it until after the loss. As a matter of fact, there is a blank on the policy for assignment, and another for the company's consent, which is the vital thing.

Again suppose you are carrying an accident policy, pay ing the regular rate for your particular occupation. If you change your occupation, or enter upon more hazardous duties in your present line of work, you must secure the consent of the Insurance Company, and pay a higher premium. 

If you fail to do so your policy is void.

Suppose you own a building, fully covered by fire, tornado, explosion and all other forms of insurance, and make a contract to sell it to Jones. Now all the papers are drawn up and properly signed, but before the deed is delivered and before the purchase price is paid, the building is completely demolished by a cyclone. The Insurance Company could re, fuse to pay the loss, to you, because your ownership had ceased, and to the purchaser, because he had no contract of insurance, and the courts would sustain the Insurance Company. 

Here is one more example. "A" decides to build, borrows 

50% of the money on a mortgage from his banker "B" and hires a contractor "C" to build the house. Now "A" knows that "B" has taken out insurance on the new house to protect his loan, and consequently he feels perfectly safe. However, during the course of construction the house burns or blows down. "C" having prior lien on the property collects the insurance to pay him for services rendered, leaving "A" and "B" to adjust matters as best they may. 

6. The Result.-These are actual cases, which have been fought out in the courts, all because of the difference between what the purchaser of insurance thinks he is purchasing, and the protection which the policy actually provides. 

As a result most good Insurance Companies base adjustments on their established business policy, rather than on the terms of the policies issued. Settlements after the 

San Francisco earthquake demonstrated this fact in the strongest manner possible. Although practically every policy expressly exempted losses due to earthquakes, the Insurance Companies paid the whole bill in order to keep the good will of the insurance buying public. Nevertheless, it does not pay to risk a legal contest when the matter can be fully understood and adjusted before the loss occurs. 

7. Cheap Rates.-Many people allow the promise of low rates to influence them in buying insurance. This is natural but dangerous. Suppose for example that you want to insure your life and a glib tongued salesman bases his whole selling talk on the low premiums required by his company. 

Find out what his policy provides. What will its cash, loan or paid up insurance value be each year in comparison with similar policies offered by other companies? Is there a double indemnity feature? Is there any provision for cancelling of premiums in case of disability? Are there any 17

unreasonable restrictions, as to occupation, travel, liability in time of war, cancellation in case of fraud? Every one of these features has a direct bearing on the rate, and on the actual value of the policy to you. Frequently the highest priced insurance is the cheapest in the end, and this applies to every line of insurance. 

8. Mutual Companies.-The rates of fire insurance and automobile insurance are fixed; that is, they are the same in all standard companies. But strange as it may appear, the question of price is always important in writing up these two types of insurance. Why? Because of the fact that in almost every community there are local or semi, local mutual insurance companies selling fire and automobile insurance at nominal rates. In case of loss, the policy holders are assessed to make the payments. There are no high salaries to be paid, no unnecessary expenses, just the mere losses. The theory is beautiful. The danger lies in the limited resources of the companies, and in the purely local nature of the risks. If losses come too thick and fast, members drop out, the rates increase, assessments multiply and instead of the cheapest insurance in the world, the unfortunate policy holder finds it to be the most costly. The same thing is true of Fraternal Life Insurance Societies which are founded on the mutual theory. Experience has taught us that a successful insurance organization must be national in scope, and must distribute its risks and losses over an extended territory. 

9. What is Co-Insurance?-This form of insurance is a reduced rate insurance, and is sold with the understanding (many times not fully explained by the agent) that the insurance company is responsible and will pay for only a certain percent of the loss. More misunderstandings arise where this form is used than in "straight" insurance. In co-insurance, the insured agrees to always carry and pay premiums on a certain percent (usually 80%) of the insurable value. Where the insurance is 80% of the insurable value, it naturally follows that in the event of a total loss, or 100% loss, the insurance company pays 80% and the insured stands the balance. 

10. Explanation. This form of insurance is best explained by example, and the following suppositions will show how it works.

Suppose insurable value is. 

80% of insurable value... .$1,000.00 800.00

If loss is total, the face value of policy or.. 800.00 is paid. 

If loss is partial, say..

The full amount is paid, or 

Suppose insurable value is..

Insurance, on 80% basis, is only. 

Loss is...... 500.00 500.00 1,000.00 600.00 600.00 

The insurance company is liable for only three-fourths of the loss, as insurance is only three-fourths what it should be, so the amount paid would be threefourths of..... 600.00 or 450.00

It is, therefore, necessary where this form of insurance is used, to keep the amount of insurance at all times, up to 

80% of the insurable value. Where the insurable value varies at different seasons, several times a year, this feature is a disadvantage. 

11. Are You Fully Protected?-Is your house insured against fire, lightning, or windstorm? Have you life insurance to cover the mortgage on your home, to educate your children, and to provide for your family in case of your death or disability? Is your business properly insured? 

Are your employees insured for compensation? 

Are you insured against accident, disability, and illness? Is your automobile insured against fire, theft, collision, and personal liability? Does your life insurance cover inheritance taxes or have you an insurance estate which you can leave whole and free from inheritance taxes? If you are insured against all these contingencies, your mind is free from worry, you have equalized the chances, and you have made yourself and your family secure for the present and for the future. 

12. Alarming Facts for Auto Owners.-A blind-folded man trying to cross Michigan Avenue or Broadway during the rush hour isn't half as foolish as the automobile owner who neglects to carry full insurance against injuries to persons and property. And yet, the number of men and women who do not believe in this form of protection is astonishing. you are driving along a quiet street at a speed of ten miles an hour and a child deliberately runs under the wheels to be If

killed, the chances are a hundred to one that in a jury trial you will be held for damages from $5,000 up to $20,000 if not for murder. Most cars are insured against fire and theft only. Liability insurance may double your annual premium, but it may save you ten or twenty times the cash value of your machine. For proof of this statement consult the court records. 

13. The Small Town Ex cuse. The insurance records on liability bring out some interesting facts. In the first place the majority of the automobile accidents in the large cities occur outside of the congested districts. In other words, traffic supervision 1964 an in the downtown areas has reduced the number of accidents to a minimum. In the next place the automobile traffic in the average small town is now about on equal with that of the suburbs and outlying districts in the large cities. And finally, the opening up of good roads has made access to the cities so easy that a large percentage of outside machines are involved in city accidents.

For all these reasons the small town or rural car owner is no longer immune. He should buy full protection against personal liability and property damage. It is an investment that may pay back a thousand percent in dividends. To be without it is a risk no automobile owner can afford to take. 

14. Employer's Liability.-Practically all of the States now have laws known as Workmen's Compensation Laws which provide for compensation by the employer when workmen are killed or injured while performing their duties.

Ignorance and carelessness alone are responsible for the fact that many employers are not aware of their liability and fail to take out adequate insurance to protect themselves. Let the insurance Companies assume the

risk. The cost is a mere trifle when the unexpected happens, and an employee is killed or maimed for life. 

15. Life Insurance.-And finally, about your life insurance. 

This is not propaganda for the Insurance Companies. It is just a sincere attempt to bring out in a few words some of the reasons for insurance losses. You may not believe in life insurance. 

Perhaps you reason that by investing the same amount of money in safe securities you can double the returns over a period of twenty years. And you are right. But how many insurance buyers today would actually put away the amount of their prem- 000 iums? How many of them are qualified to select the proper investments? How many of them will be alive at the end of twenty years? There are just a few questions to ask yourself while we are on the subject of insurance. 

16. An Immediate Estate.-The day has come when it is no longer necessary to plead the case of life insurance. Its advantages are too well known. There are too many solicitors on the streets. The tendency, however, is to ignore the one big feature, the supreme selling talk for life insurance, namely, that it creates an immediate estate. It takes a succesful business man years and years to build up his fortune. The young man today who is earning a moderate salary can walk into an insurance office and by the mere stroke of a pen create an estate of $5,000, $10,000, $25,000, or $50,000 and up, depending upon his earning capacity and his ability to save. Of course, he must work and save to meet the premiums, but if he lives only an hour after the payment of the first premium, he has already done as much as the successful business man has accomplished in fifty years of active business. He has equalized the chances of life.

"His old horse died and his mule went lame, And he lost his cow in a poker game;

A cyclone came one summer day 

And blew his house and barn away;

Then an earthquake followed to make it good And swallowed the ground where his house had stood; 

And then the mortgage man came around 

And heartlessly claimed the hole in the ground;

This shock was so great that he up and died, And his wife and children wept and cried;

But something was left for the kids and wife, For he carried insurance on his life." 

-Selected. 

17. How Losses Are Paid.-A great many people have the idea that if the property is insured, and burns, the Insurance Company will without question pay the full amount of the policy. Unfortunately, this is not always the case. The policy is a contract in which both parties agree to do certain things, and we have just seen how easy it is to violate the terms of this contract through misunderstanding or ignorance. We now come to a matter of even greater importance, it being that of "proof of loss." 

18. Proof of Loss.-Whether your property is a residence with household goods, or a mercantile establishment with a stock of goods, the principle is the same. You must (a) present to the Insurance Company in writing a schedule of the loss, and (b) produce records or documents to prove your claim. This matter is so important, especially to the retail merchant or small manufacturer, that we give below our outline of the essential items for making up a satisfactory proof of loss: 

For the merchant:

Inventory as of a certain date, figured at replacement value.

Merchandise purchased since inventory, figured at replacement value.

Freight, drayage, and labor in handling the merchandise.

MINUS 

Sales since inventory, figured at cost.

Salvage.

For the manufacturer: 

Inventory as of a certain date, figured at replacement value.

Purchases of raw material. 

Manufacturing costs. 

Freight, drayage, etc., (In manufacturing costs figure only such overhead expenses as can be properly charged to manufacturing. Office overhead, that has to do with selling, etc., can not be included. Power, light, taxes, etc., can be figured as part of the manufacturing expense.)

MINUS 

Sales since inventory, figured at actual cost.

Salvage. 

19. The Necessity of Records.-The human memory can not be depended upon to keep track of transactions in business, therefore, written records are kept. The successful farmer, as well as the merchant and manufacturer must supplement his memory by written accounts. And these accounts are usually conspicuous by their absence when they are most needed to prove the accuracy of memory. Why?

Because in most cases they are not fully protected by fire. 

20. In Some States a clause appears in the fire insurance policy relieving the Insurance Company of all liability unless the policy holder can produce his last regular inventory and his record of sales and purchases since the date of the inventory. In every state settlements and payments are greatly delayed because of the distruction of vital records. 

21. A Loss of Millions.—Every year the loss of records means the loss of millions of dollars. Here we read of a big corporation carrying $100,000.00 in Fire Insurance, settling the loss for $75,000.00 because of its inability to prove the loss. Or take the average small town merchant whose store and records are entirely destroyed by fire. He collected his insurance money and ran an advertisement in the local paper informing his customers of his loss and requesting them to come in and pay their bills. About half of them came in and made settlement, but as only a few could remember the exact amount, he collected in only about $500.00. 

As a result he lost $2000.00 in accounts besides the loss of

future business from those who had refused to pay any attention to his advertisement. The value of most business houses rests on good will and so when a fire occurs, it is very important to start up business again promptly. If the essential records of a manufacturer or merchant should happen to be destroyed, it might take five or six months to secure duplicate invoices and records, before the loss could be satisfactorily proved. Such a delay would be the ruination of almost any business. 

22. The Reason for Record Loss.-There is just one reason for these losses. Business men in general are very particular about their employees, the quality of goods they produce, and the good will of their customers. They spend a great deal of time and money on their insurance problems and are careful to obtain full protection against every contingency. 

But here their precautions too often end. Instead of providing fire-proof safes to house their records they cut down the overhead expense by choosing an old out of date iron safe, or by using no safe at all. Consequently, where a loss occurs, the very devil is to pay. The Insurance Company won't. 

23. Two Ways of Protecting Records.-There are two ways of providing security for your valuable papers. One is by carrying them daily to a place sufficiently removed from the place of business to make it very unlikely that both places will be destroyed at one time. The other, better way, is to provide a proper receptacle for the records, so that no matter how severe the fire may be, they will not be destroyed. 

24. Fire Proof Safes. In recent years manufacturers of safes have devised means of determining just how much heat a safe will withstand and still protect its contents. In buying a safe do not be deceived. Find out the facts. 

25. What Your Policy Does Not Protect.—Here are a few of the valuable things an ordinary fire insurance policy does not protect:-Currency, accounts, bills, deeds, invoices, notes, securities, correspondence, manuscripts, card records, mortgages, formulae, contracts, heirlooms, and insurance policies. Make secure what you can't insure. 

26. Carelessness and Insurance Loss.-Coming now to the part that carelessness plays in the insurance world, we discover a serious state of affairs. Here again we must sub-

mit to a rigid self examination and be made to realize our individual responsibility. 

27. The Number of Fires.-Stand in front of your clock and watch the minute mark, say to yourself another fire has broken out, somebody's home, some child is being terribly burned-then add: It could have been prevented. That is the way it goes minute by minute, hour by hour, all through the year. 

There are 1,440 minutes in the twenty-four hours and there are 1,500 fires each day. There will be 1,500 tomorrow and 1,500 the day after, and these have not yet occurred and would not if people would be careful. 

Our per capita fire loss is four times as high as that of France and twenty times as bad as that of Holland. 

28. The Cost of Fires.-It is not merely the number of fires. It is the damage they do. The government reports state: "The loss by fire is greater than the combined value of the production of all our gold mines, silver mines, copper mines and oil wells each year." That was bad enough, but the report went on to say that the same fire tax is greater than the value of all the land and improvements of any of the following states: Maine, West Virginia, North Carolina, North Dakota, South Dakota, Alabama, Louisiana, or Montana. Like feeding one of these great states into a fire each year. Fires cost New York four and one-half times as much as they do London. 

29. They Can be Prevented. The National Board of Fire 

Underwriters makes a study of hundreds of thousands of fires. In one year they found that 28.9 per cent of all American fires came from a strictly preventable cause, while 47.8 per cent were partly preventable and 23.3 per cent came from unknown causes, which probably were largely preventable. These figures prove that the United States with all its advantages is a nation of careless people. We burn up our homes, risk our lives, and give away our most valued possessions all because of our carelessness. And in our business life this negligence increases the cost of our insurance, and increases taxes, so that the cost of this increased overhead is reflected in the cost of everything we buy. 

30. The Number of Accidents.-What has already been said about fire and theft prevention might also be said about the prevention of accidents. Every eighth man in the United States gets hurt in some way, and every tenth man dies in an accident.

31. Cause of Accidents.-Carelessness, of course, is the cause of nine-tenths of the accidents which occur. They could all be prevented. a. The automobile is the most dangerous place to be because more people are hurt in automobile accidents than in any other way. Properly handled, however, the motor car is by far the safest means of travel at our command. b. Next in number of accidents come those in the home, and there is very little difference between the two. Insurance Companies pay five times as much to people hurt in their own homes as they do to people hurt on trains or steamships. c. A good many people are hurt in games and recreations, most of which could be avoided by proper training and care. d. Travel on railroads and steamships is comparatively safe judging from the small number of accidents occurring there in proportion to others. The employees of the carriers are paid to protect the lives of the passengers and most of the accidents occur to people when they are violating the rules. e. The least number of accidents happen to people who are riding bicycles, motorcycles, and in horsedrawn vehicles, due no doubt, to the reduced speed and the fewer hazards. 

32. The Cost of Accidents.-Industrial accidents alone in the United States cost more than one billion dollars every year. Think of it! A loss of over a billion dollars in this enlightened day and age. This is the estimate of Sidney J. 

Williams, Secretary of the National Safety Council who investigated over three million industrial accidents in one year, causing an actual loss of 296,000,000 working days, not to mention hospital and doctor bills. Small wonder that the rate on accident insurance is growing higher year by year. 

Another authority puts the total cost of accidents in America for one year at $2,250,000,000.00 and adds the following facts: a. Nine out of every ten accidents could be prevented. b. Fifty-four automobile smash-ups every hour, threefourths of them happening at a rate of speed under 15 miles per hour.

C. 

The average automobile with brakes in perfect order cannot stop short of 20 feet if traveling 15 miles per hour. d. Every 108 minutes someone is killed in an automobile accident. e. Out of 10,555 deaths due to automobile smashups in New York State only 700 were due to careless driving and only 850 to defective mechanism. 

Over 9000 of these deaths were caused by careless pedestrians. 

33. Who Pays the Loss es?-Here are three men, Smith, Jones and Brown. 

Smith owns a beautiful home in the Jones possesses suburbs, many valuable family gems, and Brown drives a Twin 

Six. Because they believe in playing safe, Smith buys fire insurance on his house, Jones takes out a burglar policy and Brown has his automobile insured against theft. "Surely," they say, "we have done our duty as good citizens. Let the insurance company worry."

B&R 109350 

34. Playing Safe.-And because they know that the Insurance Company will shoulder the blame, Smith allows a lot of broken furniture, old newspapers, oily rags, worn out clothing and other junk to accumulate in his basement and attic; Jones frequently leaves his house unlocked, is careless about the servants he employs, and never notifies the mail man, milk man or paper boy when he goes on his vacation: and Brown never takes the trouble to lock his car or purchase an auxiliary lock. Consequently in the course of a few months the house burns down, the family jewels disappear, Brown is walking to work, and the Insurance Company pays the bill.

35. Who Really Pays.- 

But did you ever stop to think who really pays?

The rates charged by Insurance Companies are based on the total yearly losses they sustain. The more losses, the higher the rates for Smith,

Jones and Brown. The higher the rates for 

Smith, Jones and Brown, the higher these rates become for everybody-for you and me. And so in the end we all have to pay for the carelessness of others. 36. Crime Begets Crime.-Criminologists tell us that when personal carelessness makes crime easy, the number of criminals increase. Soon other cars are stolen, more homes are burglarized, the community gets a bad name and the insurance rates on theft and burglary advance by leaps and bounds. In addition the state is overburdened with the cost of punishing criminals, and taxes increase proportionately. 

37. Everybody Loses.-The results of carelessness are borne by all. Smith, Jones and Brown think they are good citizens. But are they? Ask yourself that question when you pay your next insurance or tax bill. 

38. Your Insurance Agent.-Turn your insurance problems over to a good agent. He can tell you which companies can best serve your particular interests. Find out what you have to insure, how much you ought to carry, and what conditions you must comply with. A real insurance counsellor will give you the following complete service:a. He will make a study of your problems and furnish you with the least possible number of policies that will safeguard your interest without overlapping or causing needless expense. b. He will place your insurance in companies of assured financial stability and with long standing reputations for prompt and fair settlements.

c. He will have experts inspect your property, calling attention to hazardous conditions, and suggesting ways for their improvement, thereby enabling you to secure the lowest possible rate on your insurance. d. He will watch the value of your property as it fluctuates from month to month and notify you whenever he finds that you are carrying more insurance than you need, or less than you would require in case of loss. e. In case of loss he will prepare the necessary papers and secure the quickest and best possible settlement of your claim. f. He will notify you well in advance of the expiration of your policy. g. Many accommodating agents will rewrite a policy and carry it at their own risk and expense for a few days in case you neglect to authorize a renewal. h. He will keep you informed of any changes in underwriting practices, policy changes, and any other insurance developments that may affect your interests. 

39. In Conclusion.-Let us re-emphasize the importance of full understanding the terms of an insurance agreement. 

You would not think of entering into an ordinary contract without reading it. Why should you do so with your insurance? You cannot afford to buy protection that does not protect, or insurance that does not insure.

HOW TO AVOID BAD INVESTMENTS 

1. Investment.-There is a successful doctor in a certain small town in Illinois whose investment experiences illustrate and emphasize the different points to be brought out in this chapter. Almost ten years ago he became interested in stocks for the investment of his surplus funds. He made a study of the automobile industry, saw its vast possibilities, watched its phenomenal growth, and finally purchased small blocks of stock in several well established automobile and tire manufacturing corporations. The results were success-

ALWAYS SEEK THE BEST INVESTMENT ADVICE. 

ful in a moderate way and he was able to double his capital in a very few years. After a similar investigation of the mining industry he put his money into copper and silver with equally gratifying results. 

2. Speculation.-And then the oil craze struck him. Along came an oily tongued orator from Louisiana who claimed to have a marvelous instrument for locating pools of oil thousands of feet under the ground. He pictured the millions of dollars in profits growing where but one had grown before, and the good doctor swallowed hook, sinker and line. He sold his other holdings, borrowed money from his local bank thereby securing a controlling interest in The Louisiana Mineral Corporation. Losses, taxes, interest, assessments and dry holes have been his portion ever since. 

3. Delusions. Now, it happened that the doctor had a host of friends among his patients, most of whom had that strange ambition to make a lot of easy money. Having unlimited confidence in the ability, judgment and integrity of their family physician, they, too, gathered together a hundred dollars here and a hundred there, so that practically the entire capital stock was held right there in that little town. 

When the break came and one loss or disappointment followed another, is it any wonder that in addition to his direct loss in dollars and cents the doctor lost not only the respect and confidence of his patients, but their patronage as well?

His was a three-fold loss-his capital, his reputation, and his business. 

4. The Result of Experience.-A prominent and influential banker in Chicago boasts that it cost him over one hundred thousand dollars to learn the value of money, and the principles of safe investment. Another admits that he has enough worthless oil and mining stock certificates to paper his office walls. These men have profited by their mistakes. 

They may have lost large sums but in doing so they gained the knowledge and experience necessary for their ultimate success. And in the present day and age their errors make it easy for us to avoid the common pitfalls, and to get from our investments a maximum return with a minimum risk. 

5. Reasons for Bad Investments.-It would be a superhuman task to describe all the reasons for investment losses. 

There are, however, certain fundamental reasons such as the lack of expert knowledge, lack of legal regulation, dishonesty, poor management, greed, salesmanship, and tips, all of which are considered below in the order of their importance. 

6. Lack of Expert Knowledge.-The story of the doctor illustrates this point better than any other. His original ventures were successful because he knew the facts about the different corporations, and could understand and appreciate the basic conditions in the industry. On the other hand his later experiences only served to show that it does not pay to plunge into the water until you know its depth and its temperature. Had he seen fit to make a study of the oil industry in Louisiana and a careful investigation of the character of his new associates, the story might have been different. 

7 The Lack of Legal Regulations is responsible for much of the investment loss. Some states have rigid corporation laws, others have practically none. Some states have adopted what is known as the blue sky law prescribing certain requirements with which stock promoters must comply.

The pity of it all is that even under the most rigid state laws, mistakes do occur, and even with a national blue sky law, it would be a physical impossibility to fully protect the investing public. Folks simply will not be legislated into making wise investments any more than they can be legislated into doing good or being good. But if we must have legal regulation, let us have a National law which will pro

tect the investor in every State and place all stock issues on an equal footing, regardless of location. 

8. Dishonesty and Poor Management.-Many a corporation with the most brilliant prospects for success falls by the wayside because of inefficient or dishonest management. 

Investors, both large and small, are inclined to overlook this important consideration or else to take the salesman's word for it. The common stock of many concerns represents not tangible assets but the good will and earning power of the organization. The hope of future profits, therefore, rests on the ability and integrity of the officers. 

9. Greed. The failure of many investors is due to their greed. Perhaps they have heard the story of the lawyer who helped organize the Ford Company, and whose annual income today runs up into the millions, or of the original stockholders in various corporations where $100.00 invested twenty years ago is worth a quarter of a million now. Their zeal for the unearned profit leads them to take all manner of chances with their hard earned dollars. Or perhaps they are anxious for profits but unwilling to run the risk of losses, and it often happens that even in the legitimate markets they drop out at the first sign of flurry or set back. They watch the temporary fluctuations rather than the long swings. 

10. Salesmanship.-Clever salesmanship is responsible for innumerable bad investments. Many a hard working individual is induced to draw out his savings by the apparent sincerity of the salesman, and the promise of fabulous profits in the future. Most wildcat propositions are promoted by men having no means of their own, and even if successful are so managed as to give the insiders all the profits. 

11. The Fallacy of Tips.-And finally we come to the question of "tips" or confidential scraps of information. A 

New York broker tells the story of a customer who ran wild one day on rumors. "A man gave me an order to buy a thousand shares of Erie at the market. The order was executed at 94. I had no sooner bought it than the stock went down. My customer returned and ordered the stock to be sold. It was then 922. In half an hour it was bought back again at 95. After consulting with other friends he ordered it sold again, this time at 90. Finally he came into the office and said 'I first saw one man who told me to buy,

and then another who told me to sell. I understand one is called a 'bull' and the other a 'bear.' I don't know much about these names but I do know, now, that I am a jackass.'"

This affords a good illustration of the way the average speculator is harassed and perplexed in Wall Street. A tip coming from the highest or from the lowest source should be taken for what it is worth, and that is usually nothing. 

12. Profitable Investments.-Having discussed the reasons for investment loss, let us look on the brighter side for a moment, and try to outline a plan for successful operation. 

First let us find out what the word finance really means. 

13. What Finance Does Not Mean.-The possession of wealth does not make a man a financier, any more than a kit of tools makes a mechanic. Finance does not mean speculation-although speculation has a legitimate place in the economic life of the country. It does not mean fleecing the public, nor parasitically fattening off the industry and commerce of the country. Neither can it be held responsible for the exploits of a man who, having made money in other ways comes into the market and goes on a financial spree. 

14. What Finance Does Mean.-Finance means construc tive work. It means mobilizing and organizing the wealth of the country. It means the promotion of trade, and the continuous study of world conditions. It creates new wealth and makes new jobs for workmen. 

15. The Evil Results of High Finance.-The popular idea of high finance is that it is a holdup, and it must be admitted that most of the notorious swindles in this country have been called high finance by the newspapers. For instance, when 

J. P. Morgan bought a street railway for five million and sold it for fourteen million to the New Haven which he controlled; or where The Standard Oil people paid $39,000,000 for a group of mines and unloaded $61,000,000 worth of water onto the public; or when Edward J. Addicks loaded a bonded indebtedness of $4,500,000 onto a $500,000 corporation; or when Mr. Ponzi sold stock and guaranteed 400 percent profit; or when Joseph Leiter's gambling in wheat caused a great rise in the price of bread in Europe and brought riots and bloodshed in Italy. Applied in these in stances, the term "High Finance" is a misnomer. In legitimate meaning it designates the most eminently respectable and trustworthy financial operations. 18

16. The Markets.-There are five principal markets in the United States, the New York Stock Exchange, the New York Curb Market, the Chicago Board of Trade, the New Orleans Cotton Exchange and the New York Cotton Exchange. The New York Stock Exchange is an unincorporated WHERE HANDS ARE ELOQUENT. 

voluntary asso- Iciation which has 

1100 members and has been in existence since 

May 17, 1792. 

One hundred million dollars worth of business is often transacted on the floor of the exchange in a sin- gle day. The New York Curb Market is an outside market where stocks are bought, and sold in companies whose stocks for some reason or other are not listed on the New York 

Exchange. The Chicago Board of Trade is the greatest grain market in the world. The cotton of the country is marketed almost entirely through the Cotton Exchanges of

New Orleans and New York. 

17. The Partial Payment Plan.-Small investors are able to buy odd lots of high grade investment securities on the payment plan. The purchaser makes an initial deposit, say 

20% of the total amount, and agrees to pay the balance in monthly installments. The broker advances the required balance on the securities, has the stock registered in his own name, and borrows what is necessary from his bank, depositing the stock as collateral. From the individual's standpoint this plan has many advantages, among them:a. It has all the advantages of a marginal transaction without the danger of being sold out. b. It enables the small investor to buy good stocks at favorable prices, and with a very small expenditure of capital. c. It enables the investor to so distribute his holdings that a loss in one investment may mean a corresponding gain in another.

Like all other good things the payment plan is likely to be abused. It may be used by the broker to secure needed funds, or he may disappear with the funds in his possession. 

The unreliable firm may give incorrect prices or "bucket" the order altogether, that is, not buy the stock at all. And finally the plan may also be used to induce reckless speculation on the part of those whose means would not permit speculation by the ordinary method. 

18. Buying on Margin.-In marginal transactions most of the necessary funds are borrowed. Suppose Mr. Henry 

Rennels desires to buy one hundred shares of Anaconda copper which is selling at a par of $100.00. The least margin any reputable broker will accept is $10.00 per share, so Mr. 

Rennels puts up his check for $1,000.00. The broker buys the 100 shares on the floor of the Exchange. At the close of Sorrow

the day he must be able to pay for the shares which means an expenditure of approximately $10,000.00 (100 shares at $100.00 each. In order to raise this amount the broker arranges with his bank to accept the shares after they are bought, as collateral for a loan which on standard stocks will be about 80 percent of the market value, or on this transaction, $8,000.00. This leaves a balance of $1,000.00 which the broker must pay out of his own funds.

If the stock within a short time goes up say 10 points, fortunate Mr. Rennels will perhaps give an order to sell, and the broker will secure about $11,000.00 for the block. With this he repays the bank loan of $8,000.00; reimburses himself for his loan of $1,000.00, and after deducting interest on the $9,000.00 supplied by the bank and by himself, and deducting his brokerage charges, he turns the rest over to Mr. Rennels. On the other hand if the stock goes down seven or eight points the broker calls for more margin or failing that he sells the stock, repays the bank loan, reimburses himself, deducts interest and brokerage charges as before and returns to Mr. Rennels anything that may happen to be left of his $1,000.00. 

19. Selling Short.-Now we will say that Mr. Rennels chooses to sell on margin, or "sell short," as they say in

Wall Street. He deposits his $1,000.00 as before and instructs his broker to sell short 100 shares of Anaconda copper. The broker sells the 100 shares on the floor of the ex change and is called upon to make delivery at the end of the day. As neither Mr. Rennels nor the broker owns the stock that has been sold, it is necessary for the broker to borrow from some owner. He does this in the "loan corner" of the Exchange where stocks are loaned to shorts on pay ment of the market price. THIS LOAN IS REALLY A 

SALE. It is provided, however, that on return of the stock the amount paid for the stock will be given back. This borrowed stock the broker uses to make delivery. If within a few days the stock goes down, Mr. Rennels orders his broker to buy a block at the lower price. This stock repays the lender of the stock with which delivery of the stock was originally made. The broker turns over to Mr. 

Rennels his $1,000.00 margin plus the difference between the price at which the block of stock was sold, and the price at which it was bought less the brokerage charges. Mr. 

Rennels will also get credit for whatever dividends may

have accrued on the borrowed block of stock while in the hands of the broker. On the other hand, if the stock goes up several points, the broker will call for more margin; failing that he will buy a block of stock with which to repay the stock he has borrowed, will deduct from the margin the difference between the price at which the stock was sold, and the price at which it was bought, together with interest and brokerage charges, crediting the stockholder with any dividends that may have accrued on the stock while in his hands, and will then return to poor Mr. Rennels anything that may be left of his original $1,000.00. 

20. Kinds of Investments.-There are three great classes of securities with which the investor should be familiar, investment securities, speculative securities, and wild cat securities. The purchaser of investment securities usually must content himself with a low rate of interest such as is paid on government bonds, real estate mortgages, properly secured corporation bonds, preferred stocks, and the like. 

The low rate of interest is acceptable because of the safety. 

Speculative securities include the common or unsecured stocks of reliable corporations with a good dividend record, or the prospect of future payments. Their market value often fluctuates violently but as a rule they yield a much higher rate of interest than do purely investment securities. 

And finally there is always a large class of wildcat investments being offered the public. Some are frauds, some partly fraudulent, and all are risky. They promise to pay big dividends but as their management is likely to fall down, and as they are not listed in any exchange, the careful business man does not regard them as satisfactory investments. 

The failures greatly outnumber the successes. 999 

21. How to Make Money in Wall Street.-To the question, 

"How can I make money in Wall Street?" there is probably no better answer than the one given by old Meyer Rothschild to a person who asked him a similar question. He said, "I buy 'sheep' and sells 'dear.' Those who follow this method always succeed. There has never been a year when there have not been two or three "set backs" in the markets when it was possible to purchase stocks, grains, or cotton at prices below their intrinsic value. The depression usually passes over in a few days and then the lucky or far-sighted buyer, as the case may be, comes in for his profits. The question of making money then becomes a mere matter of

calculation, the amount depending on the number and seriousness of the squalls. If young men had only the patience to watch the speculative signs of the times, to observe the old veterans of the Street in panic times coming out of their shells of security and purchasing good stocks to the extent of their bank balances, it would be possible for them to realize a net gain of 50% of their year's investments. 

22. When to Sell.-The great majority of occasional speculators select the buying side of the market. On the other hand the professional trader buys and sells with every turn of the market. The former makes money only on a rising market. The latter gets his profits on both rising and falling markets. If the public was educated to buy at the right time and to sell at the right time, the professionals in Wall Street would soon be forced out of business. 

23. How to Buy and Sell Grain.-Some years ago the estate of a wealthy old member of the Chicago Board of Trade was being settled up and among the papers found in his safety deposit box was a plain slip of paper with the following strange characters: Wheat 

Sell Jan. 10

Buy Feb. 21 

Sell May 10

Buy July 1 Sell Sept. 10 Buy Nov. 28 

Corn 

Sell May 10 

Sell Aug. 10

Buy Mar. 1 

Buy Jan. 25

An examination of his accounts showed that as nearly as it was possible to express it, this was his plan of buying and selling grain. And going back over the fluctuations in past years it developed that his formula was practically bullet proof. He had not always bought at the bottom and sold at the top but almost invariably he had realized a good profit on his transactions. 

24. What to look for in An Investment.-Every legitimate investment offering has been subjected and passed through the following test proceses:- 

a. Common sense judgment which includes a careful consideration of such questions as: 

1.-is the product a good one? 

2.-is there a market for it?

3.-is the location favorable for freights, labor, etc? 

4.-Is the management capable and honest? b. The audit which enters into 

1.-the cost of production 

2.-the selling costs 

3.-the assets 

4.-the earnings. c. The appraisal which is done by independent disinterested authorities, and places an unbiased valuation on 

1.-the real estate and buildings 

2. the machinery 

3.-the good will. d. The legal details covering question of 

1.-titles to properties owned 2.-incorporation 

3.-proper authorization of the issue by those in authority.

Not one man in ten is capable of conducting a thorough investigation of an investment offering. An analysis of any proposition based on the above formula will show up its short-comings if any exist, and prevent losses which might otherwise have resulted from too hasty action. 

25. The Value of the Broker's Knowledge.-The common delusion that expert advice is not required in speculation has wrecked many fortunes and reputations. When a man wants correct advice in law he hires a good lawyer. When he is sick and wants medical advice he consults a good doctor. When, therefore, a man wants expert advice on investments why does he take the word of a bar-room bum rather than that of a broker whose business it is to know all there is to know about investments, and whose success depends on his ability to give real service. Too many investors are like the man in an important case who acted as his own lawyer and finally admitted that he had a fool for his client. A reliable broker can tell you the inside information concerning corporations such as the outstanding stock, the bonded indebtednes, par value, dividend rate, volume of business, orders on hand, condition in the industry, character, standing and ability of the officers, prospects of future

disbursements, and countless other facts you would never dream of asking. A salesman offering an untested security acts in the capacity of a broker. His character, standing, and past experience should be carefully looked up. 

26. Statistical Organizations.—Then there are other com panies organized to serve the public solely in an advisory capacity. They plot out the fluctuations in commodity prices, stock exchange prices, and general business conditions over a long period of years. They call attention to the long swings and the short swings, and to the certainty of high prices following low prices. They offer at a stipulated price a complete investment service telling their subscribers when to buy, when to sell, and what particular stocks or bonds to buy or sell. While not aways correct, their forecasts are frequently of value. 

27. Warning. Every man who expects to invest in securities should be warned against bucket shops, and swindling brokerage concerns. Whatever money is turned over to them never gets out of their own pockets. It always pays to select an establishment having a reputation for giving sound advice, one with effective resources for supplying correct information, and one having a personal interest in making money for the client. 

28. The Reason for Markets.-The mere mention of the word "finance" brings to the average mind a scene of riotous gambling, and wild, unreasonable speculation. The stock exchanges, boards of trade, cotton exchanges and other general market facilities are in no sense gambling institutions. They are legitimate marts of trade where men in active business find an outlet for the investment of their surplus funds, and where they can realize on their holdings on short notice at a price quoted every day. For these two reasons if for no other, the markets claim a very important place in our economic life.
