HOW TO AVOID BUSINESS DEPRESSION 1. The Richest Country in the World.-The United States has been continually growing richer. The per capita wealth of this country is greater by far than that of any other country in the world. Formerly we owed vast sums of money to other countries while our railroads, mines and national resources were in a large measure owned by foreign capitalists. Today we are a great credit nation with all the rest of the world owing us millions of dollars. We have a new flexible banking system which releases sufficient funds

in the right place and at the right time. We have standardized our industries. A great merchant marine carries our products to the ends of the earth. Millions of dollars formerly spent for alcohol is now put into circulation in the pur- 

THE TRAGEDY OF THE SHUT-DOWN 

chase of homes, merchandise and better living conditions. 

And yet in spite of all these stabilizing factors, in spite of our unlimited wealth and vast national resources, our periods of great prosperity are inevitably followed by a corresponding depression. 

2.-History of the Ups and Downs.-The following figures prove the instability of our prosperity:

- 1893-1897 depression 1898-1902 

prosperity 

1903-1904 depression 1907 severe panic 1910-1912 

prosperity 

1913-1916 depression prosperity 1917-1920 1921-1923 depression 

3. The Cost of Changes.-These changes are uneconomical and they cause intense suffering. When business is good wages increase, the standard of living increases, manufacturing facilities are increased, and everybody is happy in an orgy of spending. Then quite suddenly the pendulum

HOW TO AVOID BUSINESS DEPRESSION 

283 swings back, business falls off, wages are reduced, the cost of living is supposed to come down, but doesn't, factories are idle, strikes break out, and everybody stops spending.

It is almost impossible to estimate the cost of these readjustment periods in dollars and cents. The American people paid dearly for the great prosperity which was theirs in 1917, 1918 and 1919. 

4. The Laboring Man, flushed with hitherto unheard of wages thought that at last he had come into his own. Every time the pay was raised the length of the working day was cut down. The shorter the working day the more time remained for recreation. The more time for recreation the greater became the demand for luxuries. Consequently the working man as a class made hay while the sun shone, but he made the wrong kind of hay. Instead of saving his surplus, he purchased silk shirts and expensive clothes, and rode to work in his own automobile. As a result when the break came he found himself invested with a lot of expensive tastes, and without either sufficient income to keep up the payments on the new victrola or the automobile, or a sufficient savings fund to tide him over the hard times. 

5. The Farmer had more to contend with than any other class. It is true that during the time of war prices he received good prices for his produce, but these prices were not out of proportion to the increase in the cost of production or in the cost of living. But when the drop came, the farmer was the first to suffer. While the cost of living remained practically the same the farmer's wheat dropped from $3.00 to $1.00 per bushel; his corn from $2.00 to 60 cents; his cotton from 43 cents to ten cents a pound; his wool from $1.00 to 30 cents and so on down the list. In other words, the farmer produced a crop under war time conditions of high rents, high wages and high overhead expenses, and had to accept pre-war prices for it. Farms which had been purchased at from $400.00 to $600.00 per acre would not pay interest on a $200.00 valuation. The renter who paid $15 to $20 per acre was forced to move. And to cap the climax, the farmer was obliged to pay 15 cents for an ordinary 5 cent loaf of wheat bread, $10.00 for a $5.00 pair of shoes or $50.00 for a $25.00 suit of clothes. His total loss simply staggers the imagination. 

6. The Manufacturers likewise failed to profit by the past. 

When war contracts were the order of the day and salesmen

got writer's cramp from writing out orders, manufacturers doubled and tripled their capacity. Apparently nothing could ever happen to the boom of prosperity. But something did happen and suddenly the farmer and the salaried man and the wage earner quit buying and many of these giant temples of industry are standing idle today or have been converted to other uses. 

7. The Stock Market. It is interesting to note that prices on the New York Stock Market have always been an indication of the trend of business conditions. Periods of inflation and depression have there been forecast with unfailing accuracy months in advance. Thus the high point in stock prices was reached in 1916 in spite of the great prosperity which reached its height in 1918 and 1919. The low point is always reached very early in the period of depression and the average price begins to go up when the depression seems to be at its lowest point. 

8. To End Business Depression. Thus we have seen that in spite of the sound basic condition of the country, we do have alternating periods of prosperity and depression, and that these periods of readjustment cost the people of the United States millions of dollars. The next question is how can these things be regulated or prevented? They can be regulated by a plan of action in which each of us has a definite part. 

9. The Wage Earner's Part.-Labor is the great conquer or, enriching and building up nations more surely than the proudest battles. Labor is the basis of all wealth for of what use were our most valuable natural resources if undeveloped by the hand of labor. But this very fact puts a great responsibility on those of us who are wage earners. 

We must give an honest day's work for an honest day's pay.

In our selfish ambitions we must not overlook the duty and the responsibility we owe to others. 

10. The Farmer's Part.-The farmer is already helping to stabilize the economic conditions of the country. He so diversifies his crops that the possibility of a complete crop failure is now altogether remote. His next great problem lies in the field of marketing. Under existing conditions the farmers of the U. S. sell 75% of their grain immediately after the harvest, so clogging the railroads and the markets that they are obliged to take the bottom price for the year, in fact, any price that the commission men and jobbers feel

HOW TO AVOID BUSINESS DEPRESSION 

285 inclined to pay. Could not this grain be stored in co-operatively owned elevators and released to the buying public at a fair and uniform rate and in accordance with the law of supply and demand? The fruit grower's association, the wool pool, the dairy marketing companies and the co-operative live stock commission houses are steps in the right direction. The farmer is making strides. His efficiency and his equipment have increased. The National and State 

Governments maintain large and effective experiment stations to guide him both in production and distribution. All these factors tend to provide the stability so greatly needed in our time. 

11. Manufacturer, Merchant and Jobber.-The employers of labor have a duty to perform not only to the laboring men themselves, but to the public. It is the duty of honesty. 

Is it honest for those of us who are manufacturers to refuse to accept orders unless they are on the expensive, unfair cost plus basis? or to close down our plants to avert a temporary loss? or to force prices up unfairly? or to wilfully cancel our contracts? Haven't we as merchants and jobbers forgotten that our aim in life is to serve the public, and not to selfishly extract the last full measure of illicit profit? 

12. The Government's Part.-Vast sums of money are expended annually by the government to improve the physical condition of the people. Bulletins are issued covering almost every conceivable phase of scientific and agricultural activity. But unfortunately, the powers above have overlooked the field of business endeavor. Famine and plague are things of the past, but hard times still follow inevitably in the wake of prosperity. Business must be taught to diversify its interests just as the farmer has been taught crop rotation. Business failures must be made as impossible as crop failures, panics as unheard of as yellow fever epidemics. Business men can be educated in the better methods of trade, just as the farmer has been taught better agricultural methods. 

13. The Consumer's Part.-And finally, we come to the individual. What can he do to promote economic stability?

In the first place we can develop the fidelity, industry, thrift and skill which are so essential for the foundation of permanent prosperity. Secondly, we must bear in mind the fact that over production simply means the production of the wrong thing in the wrong place or at the wrong time. And

in the last place we must realize that we, as ultimate purchasers have the power to determine the nation's production, and govern our purchases accordingly. 

14. United Action.-If each one of us could recognize and perform his duty, the time would soon come when hard times would be forgotten and we should enter upon such a period of permanent prosperity as has been the theme of all political parties since time immemorial. 

 1. Taxes, Definitions Of.-Taxes are assessments of money against persons or property, for public uses. A direct tax is levied directly on the people. An indirect tax is levied against goods for which the purchaser must pay. A poll tax is a tax levied against voters. An excise tax is an inland tax levied on commodities of home production and consumption. A customs duty is a tax on imported or exported goods. 

Internal revenue is a tax levied on tobacco, cigars, etc. Income tax is levied against persons whose income exceeds a certain amount. Property tax is levied against property, real or personal. 

2. Excessive Taxes.-Many people are paying more in taxes than their proportionate share, because of ignorance of the law. Accurate knowledge is necessary in order to properly file a personal property or an income tax return. 

A careful study of the following pages will supply the required information. 

3. Property Taxes.-In those states still using the old cumbersome and inefficient property tax, this is the usual form of procedure. 

a. All the property subject to tax is valued. b. The total amount of money to be raised is fixed. c. The total amount of money to be raised is then divided by the total valuation of the property, the result being the rate of taxation, or the sum to be raised on every dollar's worth of property.

Now, it makes no difference whether the valuation of the property is placed higher or lower than the actual value, because the rate of tax depends entirely on this valuation. It is of great importance to the individual tax payer, however,

that the valuation of his individual property is neither higher nor lower than that of others. 

In most States there is a County Board of Assessors, on Board of Review which is authorized to correct valuations. 

An individual believing himself overtaxed can and ought to apply to this Board for justice. 

4. Double Taxation.-This same property tax gives rise to a situation in which the same piece of property is taxed twice. Suppose a man buys a farm for $15,000.00 and gives back a mortgage for $10,000.00. He has an equity of but $5,000.00 in the farm and yet he pays a real estate tax on the whole $15,000.00 valuation. On the other hand, the holder of the mortgage is required to pay a personal property tax on the $10,000.00 mortgage. The $15,000.00 farm actually pays taxes on a $25,000.00 valuation. 

5. The Widow and Orphans are the chief sufferers under an unjust taxation system of this kind. When a man dies his estate usually goes through the courts. Its exact size and value become public knowledge and the taxes are assessed accordingly. Suppose among the assets there is a cash item of $1,000.00. This is taxed to the limit despite the fact that the total amount of cash listed in tax statements throughout the great State of Illinois, for example, is only a very few thousand dollars. In one year alone, there were less than five hundred watches listed and less than 100 diamonds in Illinois. It is an unjust system, one that makes liars out of otherwise perfectly respectable citizens. 

6. The Income Tax.-The United States Government adopted the Income Tax as a wartime measure, to raise funds necessary to the conduct of the war and other regular governmental expenses. It proved to be so just a method of raising revenue, and so popular that it is evidently with us to stay. And now the more progressive States are gradually abandoning the old Property Tax and are adopting a limited income tax plan of their own to take its place. 

7. Its Faults. However, there are certain faults which must be remedied. In the first place, the income tax return is rather a complicated affair. It requires no small degree of time and effort, and is likely to cause considerable confusion. Secondly, the tax payer must have a thorough understanding of the law itself, and of the numerous rulings pertaining thereto, in order to file a satisfactory return. And in the third place, the technical nature of the information

required, in nearly every case necessitates the hiring of paid assistants. Every banker, lawyer and accountant is drafted into the service for weeks and months before the returns must be filed. This is especially true among the big corporations whose accounting problems require the service of an expert. There are not half enough certified publia accountants in the country to fill the demand for them at this crucial time. 

8. How You Lose, Mr. Tax Payer.-It is not our desire or intention to criticize the Federal income tax law. It is the most equitable revenue producing method ever adopted by the American people. It takes the money from those who are best able to pay. But corporations, business men and individuals are paying more money for the preparation of their returns, and are actually paying more taxes than is really necessary, for the following reasons: a. Because they do not take time to master the fundamental principles of the law and its application to their particular problem. b. Because they do not make their books of account conform to the requirements and divisions of the income tax return. c. Because they probably are carrying on their books a lot of doubtful accounts and considerable merchandise which is obsolete or not readily salable. 

9. A Study of the Law and the instructions on the back of the blank will reveal sufficient information so that you can file a true and accurate return. If you neglect to learn, it will cost you money. For instance, one woman's income was derived chiefly from her husband's estate and she had paid an annual income tax amounting to about $100.00 for several years. The lawyer who had always assisted her in filing the return happened to be away one year so she decided to do the work herself. Now, it so happened that she had a few shares of stock in her local bank and upon inserting the figures she noticed that she paid no normal tax on dividends. Like a flash it came to her that at least half of her husband's income was derived from bank stock and dividends from corporations, and was therefore not subject to income tax. Had she taken the trouble to look into the matter sooner she could have saved one-half of her tax. 

10. Proper Books of Account are a valuable asset when the time comes for making out your income tax return. Many

merchants and business men keep but a haphazard record during the year and then expect some one to file an intelligent return for them in an hour or two. The first great care of business men should be to adopt a standard system of accounting, based on what experience tells is the most efficient in filing income tax returns. Accounts in your records should agree with and depend upon the various subdivisions of the income tax return. Then when the unpleasant but necessary duty of filing your return must be taken care of, your work will consist of a simple transfer from one account to another. Corporations quite generally have adopted this plan and there is no real reason why it cannot be carried out just as successfully by the partnership or individual. 

11. Inventory and Bad Debts.-Every time you pay a dollar of tax on a stock of obsolete or unsalable goods, or on a doubtful book account, you are needlessly taking a dollar out of your pocket and making a present of it to Uncle Sam. 

These are allowable deductions and should be charged off your books as such. Suppose you have $1500.00 on your books, $1000.00 of which you are sure to collect. Charge off the other $500.00 to loss and claim that amount as a deduction on your income tax. Do not abandon your efforts at collection for fear that you will defraud the government, because if you do collect in the money, it will show again as a profit on your books the succeeding year. The same rule applies to obsolete merchandise, patents, printing plates, dies, or to anything else which is really a loss, but still shows on your books as an asset. 

12. Tax Free Securities.-The issue of tax exempt securi ties has grown to such tremendous proportions that immense fortunes have been withdrawn from industry and invested in such a way that the incomes derived from them are almost entirely free from taxation. This works a double hardship on the average man in that it increases his tax burdens without giving him a chance to increase his earning power. 

13.-These are but a few examples of actual loss. The following complete income tax guide has been prepared by experts. It deals primarily with the preparation of personal income tax returns, and contains information and helps not ordinarily available to the layman. No attempt is made to assist in the filing of tax returns for corporations, who as a general rule hire their own tax experts. 19

It is hoped that this department will save readers of the Business Guide many hundreds of dollars in attorney's or accountants' fees.

For example, if you fail to find below the answers to your individual questions, you need not go to the trouble or expense of hiring an attorney or an accountant to assist you. 

In each Internal Revenue District, the government maintains an office with an expert in charge. There you may obtain, at no cost, any information you desire.

Or put your income tax problems up to the publishers of this book. Accurate and reliable information will be given absolutely free. Any reader of the Business Guide is entitled to this service. 

14. Where and When to File.-Income tax returns must be filed with the Collector of Internal Revenue for the district in which the taxpayer resides, or has his principal place of business on or before March 15 of each year or within two months and fifteen days following the close of the established fiscal year of taxpayer.

If the address of the collector is unknown, ask at your postoffice or bank. If you have no legal residence or place of business in the United States forward your return to the 

Collector of Internal Revenue, Baltimore, Md. 

15. Who Must File.-Every citizen of the United States, whether residing at home or abroad, and every person residing in the United States, though not a citizen, whose gross income for the taxable period amounted to $5000.00, or whose net income amounted to a. $1500.00 if single, or if married and not living with husband or wife. b. $3500.00 if married and living with husband or wife.

Husbands and wives may file singly or jointly. Form No. 

1040 (not 1040A) must be used for all single returns. The income of a minor or incompetent, if derived from a separate estate under control of a guardian, must be reported by the legal representative.

All corporations, partnerships and fiduciaries must file. 

16. Forms to Be Used.-Form 1040 is to be used where net income is more than $5000 (before deducting personal exemption and credits); where combined income of husband and wife making separate returns is more than $5000; in all cases where net income is derived from business or profession, including farming, regardless of amount.

Form 1040A is used where income is less than $5000 and is derived chiefly from salary or wages. 

Form 1040 F.Y. is used by individuals whose accounting period ends with a month other than December and by those reporting on a calendar year basis if any income is derived from a partnership, estate or trust using a fiscal year. 

Form 1120 is used for every domestic or resident corporation, joint stock company, association or insurance company not specifically exempted by the revenue act.

Form 1120A is used for corporations filing tax returns for a fiscal year.

Form 1065 is used by partnerships to report income paid by the partnership to the individual partners. 

Form 1041 is used by fiduciaries in reporting income distributed to beneficiaries. The above forms are all to be sent to the District Collector. 

17. Penalties.-For wilful failure to make and file a return on time not more than $10,000 or imprisonment for not more than one year, or both and in addition, 25 per cent of the amount of the tax. 

For wilfully making a false or fraudulent return not more than $10,000 or imprisonment for not more than 5 years, or both and in addition 50 per cent of the tax.

For deficiency in the tax, interest on the deficiency at 6% per annum to the date the deficiency is assessed and in addition 5% of the deficiency if due to negligence or intentional disregard of rules and regulations without intent to defraud, or 50% of deficiency if due to fraud. 

18. Returns of Information at Source.-All persons making payments to another of fixed or determinable income of $1500 or more, most render a return thereof on or before March 15 of each year on Form 1099, together with a letter of transmittal on form 1096. Full instructions are printed on these forms.

Form 1097 is used for reporting dividend payments of $500.00 or more to stockholders of domestic and resident corporations.

Form 1100 is used by a person doing business as a broker to show names and addresses of customers to whom payments were made or for whom business was transacted and other information called for on the form.

Forms 1099, 1096, 1097 and 1100 are all sent to Commis sioner of Internal Revenue, Sorting Section, Washington, D.C. 

When to Pay Income Taxes.-Income taxes may be paid in four installments, but if any installment is not paid on the date it is due, the whole amount of the unpaid tax must be paid upon notice and demand from the collector. 

Interest of 1% a month is also charged on past due installments. 

19. When to File Separate Returns.-A husband and wife each having a separate income may file either separate or joint return at their option. 

A joint return is advantageous: a. If either has sustained a net loss. b. If either has made contributions in excess of the limitation of 15 per cent of the net income. c. If either has credit for tax paid at source in excess of tax liability. d. If either has received dividends or other income exempt from normal tax but has sustained losses which reduce the taxable income to such an extent that a material part of the benefit of the credit against normal tax would be lost if separate returns were filed. 

20. Exemptions and Credits.-The following personal ex emptions and credits for dependents are allowed:

Citizens or Residents: 

a. Single person $1500 b. Married person living with spouse $3500. c. Head of a family $3500 d. Estates $1500 e. Corporations $2000-$3000 f. Non-resident aliens $1500. 

A credit of $400 for each dependent is allowed to citizens or residents of the United States and to non-resident aliens who are residents of Canada or Mexico. 

21. The Normal Tax applies at the same rate to all individuals. It is 2% on the first $4,000.00 in excess of exemptions and credits, 2% on the next $4,000.00 and 4% on the remainder of the net income. 

22. The Surtax rates begin with 1% at $10,000 and end with 20% on incomes of $100,000.00 or over, as follows:

INCOME-TAX

23. Corporation Tax.-Corporations now pay a straight tax of 11% on their net earnings with an exemption of $3,000.00 if such earnings are less than $25,330.00. 

24. Partnerships, Trusts and Fiduciaries pay no income taxes, although they are compelled to file returns showing the distribution of net income. The Beneficiaries include such income in their individual returns. 

25. Change of Status During the Year.-If an individual changes his status during the taxable year the exemption allowed must be pro rated. In other words if a tax payer marries on April 5th his exemption for the first three months of the year is 4 of $1500 ($375) and for the remainder of the year 4 of $3500 ($2625) or $3000 in all. The fractional part of the month is disregarded unless it amounts to more than half a month, in which case it is considered a whole month. 

If an individual dies during the taxable year, personal exemption and credits are determined by his status at time of death, but the surviving spouse, if any, is allowed full credit according to his or her status at the close of the taxable year. 

26. Division of Exemptions.-Personal exemption of $3500 

may be claimed by either spouse or divided in any proportions desired. It is usually taken by the one paying normal tax in the higher bracket. Credit for dependents cannot be divided. It must be taken by the one contributing chiefly to the support of the dependents. 

27. Head of a Family.—The treasury department has de fined the head of a family "to be an individual who actually supports and maintains in one household, one or more individuals who are closely connected with him by blood relationship, relationship by marriage or by adoption and whose right to exercise family control and provide for their dependents in based upon some moral or legal obligation.' 

28. A Dependent is one who is under 18 years of age or incapable of self-support because mentally or physically defective, dependent upon the tax payer and receiving from him the chief support on the last day of the taxable year. The credit for dependents is determined by the status of the tax payer on the last day of the taxable year.

37. To File or Not to File.-The government has recently sent out a warning to the effect that if you are a tax dodger, the chances are about ten thousand to one that you will be caught.

Nineteen thousand men and women in the government's revenue service join in the hunt for the wilful tax evader. 

It is a comparatively simple matter to discover the difference between a wilful fraud and an honest error.

Moral and financial wrecks lie in the wake of income tax wrong doing. Summary or financial punishment, loss of business standing or prestige, moral and money reverses, disgrace, disaster and even death is the result. 

Honesty with the government, in tax matters as in all others, is the best policy. 

38. Tax Pitfalls.-Aside from the results of fraudulent tax returns, there are serious pitfalls for the misinformed in the new revenue laws. For instance there are certain provisions which if ignored in the organization will strangle a new business in its infancy.

This is particularly true in respect to the sections that effect the purchase, exchange or sale of property, and the organization and reorganization of corporations. These statutes have been made necessary because of the fact that certain tax dodgers sought to avoid taxation by incorporating and reincorporating, transferring property to themselves at high prices and raising the basis of cost and reducing the taxable gain in event of a sale.

HOW TO AVOID BAD DEBTS 

303 

HOW TO AVOID LOSS IN BAD DEBTS 1. The Science of Credits is an important one. The im mense losses charged off by business men every year is shown by statistics based on the Federal Income Tax Returns. And yet it is difficult to apply exact rules at all times and for different lines of business. 

In 2. The Credit Man.-The aim of every business man should be to keep his losses as near the zero point as possible without needlessly limiting sales. In order to accomplish this result some one must be in charge of and responsible for credits. In large concerns there is a credit man. the vast majority of cases, however, this duty falls on the shoulders of the proprietor himself, or on one of the officers of the corporation. Slip-shod, haphazard methods of extending credit should never be permitted. They sap the very life blood of the business. the 

3. Knowledge Necessary to Credit Man.-Where trade is local the man in charge of credits needs to know all there is to know about the character, habits and financial condition of the purchasers. Theoretically the same thing ought to be true when a house sells its goods over an extended territory, but for practical purposes he must content himself with such general information as is available, coupled with an exact knowledge of the general financial situation in the territory covered. Every possible effort should be made to learn the particular hazards and peculiarities of the customer's business. On the other hand he must be thoroughly familiar with stock on hand, production costs and all the operative details of his own business. In addition to all these other considerations, a familiarity with the laws of finance, collection, exemption, bankruptcy and commercial paper is absolutely essential. 

4. Sources of Credit Information.—How is the credit man to obtain all this vital information? The fundamental facts of law are all clearly treated in another section of this book. 

Government market and crop reports show up the light and dark spots in the general financial condition of different parts of the country. And as for the reputation, habits and financial standing of individual customers, the credit man has four different sources of information open to him, namely: the Mercantile Agencies, local banks, trade reports and salesman's reports.

5. The Mercantile Agencies attempt to show in book form the net worth and the credit standing of every corporation, partnership or individual doing business in the United States and Canada. These books are issued quarterly by 

The Bradstreet Company and by R. G. Dun & Company. 

While their reports are not always accurate and must be qualified by past experience and other available information, they nevertheless are an invaluable source of credit information, and give business men a great inducement to keep their commercial records clean. It must always be remembered, however, that changes in personal, location, and credit standing, change in these listings at the rate of well over 50% every year. 

6. Local Information.—Many business houses prefer to get their credit information from local sources, such as the bankers or the attorneys in the customer's city. These are always valuable to verify the reports of the mercantile agencies, but as sources of original information they are not always reliable. Delay, partiality, enmity, inaccuracy or indifference in answering the requests for information, result far too frequently. Most banks refuse to give out credit ratings unless the individual happens to be one of its own customers. 

7. Trade Reports.-Credit men in the same or allied lines of business often exchange credit information. Manufacturers of certain products sometimes form an association to maintain prices, and to co-operate in the manufacture and sale of their goods. The members of such an organization are always glad to exchange credit information. Some of these even go so far as to maintain what is known as a black list containing the name and address of firms who are not reliable, and every credit man has a copy of that list. 

8. Salesmen's Reports.-Firms who employ salesmen to sell their products are in a position to get definite and reliable information on their customers. The salesman makes frequent visits, becomes acquainted with the customer, knows his reputation, observes his method of transacting business and is able to supply first hand reports not only on the customers, but on the general condition of the trade in the city and surrounding country. It does not pay to depend altogether on his reports, however, because his zeal for increased commissions might lead him to ignore the usual danger signals.

HOW TO AVOID BAD DEBTS 

305 

9. Kinds of Accounts.-Open Account is a term used where goods have been purchased by a debtor and charged to him on the books of the creditor. When an account has been agreed to by the debtor either written, by word of mouth, or by silence, it is called a stated account. 

10. Methods of Collecting Accounts.-Now let us suppose that you have made every effort to secure accurate credit ratings on the customers you are selling and that you have taken every known precaution to eliminate the undesirables. 

Even under the most favorable circumstances you will have some slow or doubtful accounts, and the question arises "How can you get the money?" The law is slow, tedious, and expensive. Do not resort to it unless all else fails. 

The following steps are to be taken in their order to bring about settlement, peacefully if possible, but by force if necessary. But remember that if you expect a friendly settlement, and continued business you must use diplomacy and tact. Make every possible concession to avoid litigation. 

11. Step Number One.-Send the statement when the ac count becomes due and payable, not on the 1st and 15th of the month. Enclose it with a friendly letter calling attention to the maturity of the bill and make it clear that a remittance is expected. Many customers must be educated to the fact that payments must be met promptly at maturity in order to maintain a good commercial rating. The following letters are suggested:

Collection Letter No. 1 

Dear Mr. 

Won't you sit down, open your heart, and tell me why you don't pay our invoice? 

This letter is not a dun—I dislike the word—but you have a REASON for not sending us that check which is due, according to our records. 

Please tell me now. 

Yours very truly, Allow ten days for a reply and in the absence of which send: 20

Collection Letter No. 2 

No answer to our note. 

You're there. 

We're here. 

A long way between.

Yet all distances are the same to this little red stamp. 

If you've broken a leg, had a fire, or got married, and cannot send our money, tell me the BIG REASON, and you will find us friends. 

How about it? 

Yours very truly, (A 2-cent stamp is pasted on the margin of the letter.) 

After another ten-day interval has elapsed send the following letter. It will bring in an astonishing number of replies:

Collection Letter No. 3 

Washington's picture didn't come back with REASON 

or CHECK. 

So far your friends have given us to understand that you paid your bills promptly, so we don't know whether you have died or gone out of business. 

Honestly, that sale wasn't all profit; so help us save what there was before interest eats it up. 

In other words

Hopefully, PLEASE REMIT NOW 

If there is still no reply, give him the other barrel and watch for results.

Collection Letter No. 4 

If you don't intend to pay us, stall us off, or give us a reason; why not be a frank American and say so? 

Be courteous enough to write a few blasphemous remarks, about how mean we have treated you and close. We sent you a stamp long ago.

Really, I'm tired of seeing this old account every morning. It makes me doubt my judgment. 

Come on now, be a sport. 

Yours in desperation, Please.

HOW TO AVOID BAD DEBTS 

307 These collection letters are short, friendly, and humorous, and yet they have the happy faculty of getting under the skin of the debtor, and convincing him of the writer's sincerity. They bring results and still maintain friendship for, and confidence in the firm. 

12. Step Number Two.-If collection letter No. 4 does not induce a reply, then you might just as well give up all idea of a friendly adjustment. It is at this point that a sight draft is valuable. Formerly when a merchant refused to honor a sight draft, he found that such action lowered his credit standing. This is not always true today because many firms make it a positive rule never to pay sight drafts. 

The presentation of such a draft, particularly in a small town, where everybody knows all about the affairs of everybody else, is likely to bring some results. If possible it is always more satisfactory to draw the draft through the debtor's own bank. 

13. Step Number Three.-After the sight draft has been drawn and refused it may be advisable to send the collection to a Justice of the Peace, or to the debtor's local bank either of whose charges will not exceed 10%. On the other hand an attorney may be able to effect a prompt settlement, his charge depending on the amount of the claim. Collection agencies using a series of letters threatening suit or attachment proceedings, or public advertisement, are often effective, but it must be understood that such a system does away with the last hope of future business. Any effort along this line is preferable to actual suit. 

14. Step Number 4.-In order to begin suit to enforce a civil debt a complaint is filed stating the facts upon which the action is founded. The court then summons the debtor to appear and answer the charges, and the case is tried upon its merits. If judgment is rendered in favor of the creditor, the sheriff attaches, seizes and sells enough of the debtor's property to satisfy the judgment. Either before or after the judgment is actually rendered, the creditor may cause to be issued a writ of garnishment or a writ of attachment. 

The former attaches money or property of the debtor in the possession of a third party while the latter authorizes the sheriff to seize the debtor's property in case he is about to leave the State, abscond, or is a non-resident. Bond is necessary in both cases to indemnify the debtor against loss caused by a wrongful suit.

15. Remember that suit is not advisable unless the account is a large one, and all other efforts have failed. Proper care in extending credit, and a good collection system will be worth more to your business than a hundred judgments. 

HOW TO AVOID LOSS IN SHIPPING 

And Information for Shippers

The carelessness and ignorance of the Shippers and Receivers of freight are responsible for another great annual loss of time and money. 

1. Instructions for Shippers.-When you receive an order to be shipped by freight you should comply with the following instructions: a. See that each item is carefully checked in packing. b. Use the utmost precaution to properly nail, seal or tie the shipping case. c. Mark the case plainly showing name and address of both shipper and consignee. d. Make out a uniform bill of lading in clear, legible form, and deliver to Railroad Company. 

2. Instructions for Receivers of Freight.-Great care must 

NEVER SHIP CARELESSLY PACKED GOODS.

HOW TO AVOID LOSS IN SHIPPING 

309 be used in accepting freight in order that there may be no misunderstanding. a. Remove freight promptly to avoid congestion and storage charges. b. Examine all freight before receipting the company. c. In case of any visible damage or loss, the agent should note same on the freight bill. d. In case of invisible loss or damage, notify Railroad agent immediately to come and verify your claim. e. Notify the freight agent in writing if you intend to store the cases without checking until some later date. f. If merchandise does not check with invoice, or if it is received in damaged condition, file a claim immediately. 

3. How to File a Freight Claim.-The law allows six months after date of delivery in which to file a claim on damaged merchandise and four months for non delivery of shipments after a reasonable time has elapsed. The documents required are: a. The original paid freight bill. b. The original invoice or certified copy. 

c. The original Bill of Lading or memo. 

On shipments damaged beyond repair or entirely lost you can claim full invoice value plus freight. Make an effort to dispose of the damaged merchandise and allow credit for same on your claim. This in no way invalidates the claim. 

Never file an excessive or unjust claim. Answer all correspondence promptly quoting file reference and furnish all available information. Be patient and trace claims every thirty days. The carrier's investigation takes anywhere from thirty to ninety days. 

4. Express and Parcels Post Claims.-In making claim against an express company, the procedure is practically the same.

The invoice or copy thereof, and copy of original express receipt are the necessary documents. The Postal 

Department has a standard form to be filled in and signed when making claim for lost or damaged parcels - post packages. 

5. The Published Rate.-It is very important for a shipper to consult the published rate. He cannot depend on the

HOW TO AVOID LOSS IN SHIPPING 

311 statement of the Railroad agents. If the agent quotes an incorrect rate, the shipper is liable for the published rate. 

According to law the published rates are common documents, and the Railroads cannot charge any other rate. Ignorance of this law leads to many losses. A manufacturer puts in his bid on a certain order and agrees to pay all transporta, tion charges. He gets the order but in making shipment discovers that he is compelled to pay a higher rate which wipes out his expected profit. On the other hand, he may figure cost too high and the order will go to his competitor who makes it his business to consult the legal published rate. 

Months or even years afterwards a shipper may learn to his sorrow that his merchandise has been moving under a wrong rate and be compelled to pay the difference. 

6. Correct Freight Classifications.—According to law a shipper must make it his business to know the correct freight classifications. He should do so for financial reasons as well. 

It is the duty of the traffic man to know the principal classifications, and the cheapest rate under each for his goods. He should describe the shipment in the exact language of the shipment, avoiding the use of trade names. Frequently there are chances to lower freight costs by finding the best designation in each classification. Thus the rates differ for goods crated and uncrated, in packages or in bulk, set up or shipped flat, the saving running as high as 50 or 75% in many instances. 

7. Errors in Billing. When goods are improperly routed or sent to a wrong destination owing to the shipper's error in making out the shipping ticket or bill of lading, the shipper must pay the excess freight. This is always true when the Bill of Lading is made out incorrectly and usually so when there is an error in shipping ticket, because of the fact that the carrier relies on the accuracy of the shipping ticket to expedite the shipment. Through mistakes, shipments are frequently billed to another town of the same name in another State or in an entirely different section of the country and the difference in the cost of the freight is a considerable item. 

8. Demurrage on Car Loads.-The Railroad allows forty eight hours after official notice of arrival of cars in which to unload. An unloaded car standing longer than this is subject to a demurrage charge, fixed by the tariffs. No charge is made for Sundays, Holidays, or days on which it

HOW TO AVOID POSTAGE LOSS 

1. Volume.-Through its 50,000 postoffices and 40,000 rural routes it is estimated that the U. S. Postal Department handles over five billion pieces of mail every year. 

2. Losses. With this immense volume of business it is hardly necessary to point out that losses do occur. Valuable letters and parcels disappear, occasional delays cause inconvenience and damage, but by far the greatest loss occurs as a direct result of carelessness and ignorance, on the part of the users of the mails. 

3. The Letters That Do Not Arrive.-Two hundred mil lion letters are mailed every year that require special examination and readdressing by postoffice clerks before they can be delivered. The Dead Letter Office receives over sixteen and a half million letters every year. It is impossible to compute the annual indirect loss of wrongly addressed parcels and letters reflected in business and money, failure to complete deals or keep appointments. Families are broken up, lovers separated, and countless human tragedies made possible, all because of the letters that did not reach their destination.

4. The Cost of Carelessness. It is estimated by the 

First Assistant Postmaster General, that approximately 140,000 letters bearing no address whatsoever are received every year in the Division of Dead Letters and its several 

COST CARELESSNESS CAUSES NINE-TENTHS OF POSTAGE LOSSES. 

branches. This represents an actual waste of at least $2800.00 in postage stamps alone, not to mention the value of their contents and it does not include the carloads of letters and parcels which never reach their destination on account of insufficient or incorrect addressing.

Again the receipt of postage stamps found loose in the mails would amount to about 200,000 yearly, with a nominal value of $5000.00. Carelessness in affixing the stamps is reponsible for most of this loss. 

And finally by reason of insecure wrapping more than 275,000 articles of merchandise are found loose in the mails every year, and sent to the postoffices at the respective division headquarters of the Railway Mail Service. These articles include everything from jewelry to automobile tires. 

The Dead Letter Office returns what it can, but the carelessness which misdirects letters is likely to record no return address with the result that millions of letters are destroyed and thousands of dollars worth of somebody's property is sold at auction.

5. Caution. To avoid losses of this kind it is well to keep in mind the following suggestions: a. Always write "Transient" or "General Delivery" on mail matter for persons not permanently located in the city addressed. b. Be sure that name and address is given in full with street and number, postoffice box, or R. F. D. address. c. Owing to the fact that in some states there is more than one town of the same or nearly the same name, it is always best to give the county. d. Do not abbreviate States. "Mo." and "Me." "N. Y." and "N. J." or "La." and "Ga." are often confused if carelessly written. e. It is essential that mail be properly prepared for mailing. See that letters are properly sealed and parcels securely wrapped. f. Always show the writer's specific postoffice address on the outside of outgoing mail. 

6. The Cost of Ignorance.-Sometimes an extensive ad vertising campaign is launched involving the expenditure of thousands of dollars, only to be held up as violating some one of the numerous postal regulations. It frequently happens that an advertising agency will ignore the postal requirements when preparing circulars and other matter for mailing with the result that a higher rate of postage must be paid than was originally intended. Postal authorities tell us that millions of letters and parcels pass thru their hands every year which could just a well go in another class at a lower rate. 

7. The Postal Guide.-A study of the rules, therefore, is the very first step in cutting down excessive mailing costs. 

This can best be done by the purchase and perusal of the Official Postal Guide, which will be sent postpaid by the Postoffice Department anywhere in the United States upon receipt of $1.00. It contains all rulings and information on postal subjects, complete lists of postoffices arranged alphabetically, by States and by Counties, together with all the latest changes. Supplements are published monthly. Some of the facts in the following pages are digested from the Postal Guide, and others are the result of practical experience in the mail order business. All will be found of value in avoiding waste and unnecessary expenditures.

THE RIGHT WAY. 

THE WRONG WAY. 

INDIANA OR MARYLAND?

A. First Class Mail 

8. Classification.-First class mail consists of letters, post cards, hand or typewritten communications and matter sealed against inspection. 

9. Rates of Postage.-Letters are carried thru the mails at the rate of 2 cents per ounce or fraction thereof; government postal cards at the rate of one cent each; private post cards, standard size, at the rate of 1 cent each; larger size at letter rates. 

10. Limit of Weight for first class matter is 70 pounds. 

11. Postage Prepaid. It is important that the proper amount of postage be prepaid. A piece of first class mail without enough postage is usually forwarded to destination and a postage due stamp affixed before delivery is made. In some cases, however, the addressee is notified to send the requird postage, which triples the expense and the time. A letter once removed from the regular channels of the mail is naturally subjected to more or less delay. 

12. Registry.-All classes of mail matter may be registered upon payment of regular postage and an additional fee of 15c for value not exceeding $50.00. The fee for a valuation between $50.00 and $100.00 is 20c, for $100.00 to $200.00, 30c and increasing by 10c for each valuation increase of $100.00.

The maximum indemnity is $1,000.00. The Post Office Department thereby assumes full responsibility for the safe delivery of the mail. The fee for a return receipt is 3c additional. It is always advisable to register valuable mail and to demand for a return receipt signed by the addressee. If fourth class matter is to be registered it must be sealed and prepaid at first class rates. 

13. Special Delivery.-Letters or parcels may be sent special delivery upon payment of an additional fee of ten cents up to two pounds in weight; from two pounds to ten pounds for 15c; over ten pounds, 20c. A combination of special delivery and special handling is now accorded to second, third and fourth class mail upon prepayment of a special fee of 15c up to two pounds, 25c up to ten pounds or 35c for parcels over ten pounds. 

14. Postal Money Orders.-The post office provides a safe

and economical means of sending money.

follows: 

The fees are as 

Not exceeding $ 2.505c 20.00 40.00-15c $2.50 5.007c 40.00 60.00-18c 5.00-10.00-10c 60.00 80.00-20c 10.00-20.00-12c 80.00-100.00-22c 

No single money order can be issued for an amount larger than $100.00. 

15. How to Avoid Excess Postage.-Business letters rare ly reach the weight limit and yet the full amount of postage must be paid on them. Circulars and other advertising matter can thus be included without extra cost. Postal cards and stamped return envelopes are frequently used when a permit for the use of a business reply card or envelope would serve the purpose admirably, the postage being payable only upon the return of the card or envelope. 

B. Second Class Matter 16. Classification.-Second class matter consists of news papers, magazines, and other periodical publications which have been entered at the postoffice as second class matter. 

17. Requirements.-Application for entry of a publication as second class matter must be made through the postmaster to the Third Assistant Postmaster General. The publications must be issued at regular intervals and sent only to persons who have paid for their subscriptions. Publications not desired may be refused by the postoffice. Copies must be complete. 

18. Limit of Weight.-There is no limit to the weight of second class matter. 

19. Rates of Postage.-The postage on second class mat ter is paid by the publisher in cash at pound rates. The advertising matter is pro-rated and goes at rates increasing from 12 c per pound in the first and second zones, to 7c per pound in the eighth zone, the zones being the same as for parcel post. All other matter in the publication is subject to a straight rate of 12c per pound regardless of the zone. 

Newspapers and magazines published not for profit and by or in the interests of religious, educational, scientific, philanthropic, agricultural, labor or fraternal societies, get a re-

duced rate of 14c per pound irrespective of destination. 

Higher rates are prescribed for light weight publications. 

Newspapers and magazines, when mailed by the public, may be sent at the rate of 1 cent for each two ounces or fraction thereof, regardless of weight or distance. 

20. Writing on Second Class Matter.-Writing on either the wrapper or the publication itself will subject the matter to the first class rate with the following exceptions: a. On the wrapper there may be written or printed (1) the name and address of the sender preceded by the word "from", (2) the name and address of the person to whom sent, and (3) the words "sample copy" or "marked copy," or both. b. On the matter itself the sender, (1) may place all the writing that is permitted on the wrapper, (2) may correct typographical errors, and (3) may designate by marks, not words, a word or passage in the text to which it is desired to call attention. 

C. Third Class Matter 21. Classification.-Third class matter consists of advertis ing cards, circulars, catalogs, and all printed matter excepting books. It includes proof sheets, corrected proof sheets, and manuscript accompanied by proof sheets. 

22. Requirements.-Third class matter must be sent unsealed, subject to postal inspection. Circulars or printed letters must be identical. They may bear a written, typewritten, or hand stamped date, the name and address of the person to whom sent and corrections of genuine typographical errors. Any other writing subjects them to first class rates. Letters obtained by means of the printing press, mimeograph, multigraph, or similar mechanical process are mailable third class provided they are mailed at the postoffice or other authorized depository in a minimum number of 20 identical unsealed copies. If mailed elsewhere or in smaller quantities they are subject to first class rates. A clear space of not less than 32 inches from top to bottom must be left at the right end of the address side of all mail matter for addressing, affixing stamps, post marking, and any words for forwarding or return.

23. Rates of Postage on unsealed third class matter is 1½ 

cents for each 2 ounces or fraction thereof up to and including 8 ounces in weight except that on books, catalogs, seeds, cuttings, bulbs, roots, scions, or plants (not exceeding 8 ounces) the rate is 1c for each 2 ounces or fraction thereof. 

Over 8 ounces parcel post rates apply. 

24. Under permit, identical pieces may be mailed in bulk at 12c a pound or not less than 1 cent per piece. 

25. Writing on Third Class Matter.-The same writing is permitted on and in third class matter as specified under second class mail. It is also permissible to include a simple dedication or inscription not in the nature of personal correspondence, such as Dear Sir, My Dear Friend, Merry 

Christmas, Yours truly, etc. A serial number does not affect the classification. 

26. Address. It is particularly important to see to it that all third class matter is carefully addressed. Directory ser- 

Ivice is not given this class of mail, so that if a specific address or box number is not given in the larger cities, the mail will be disposed of. 

27. The Use of Envelopes of unusual size or shape is objectionable, for the reasons that if they do not fit the sorting cases, and cannot be tied into packages with regular mail, their movement is greatly delayed. Postal clerks will naturally give other mail the preference. It costs money to mail, and the returns usually depend on the promptness of the delivery. 

28. Preparation of the Mail.-The importance of the careful preparation of mail matter has already been emphasized. 

In this connection attention should be called to the use of large display cards, photographs, calendars and similar matter. Cards and photographs measuring ten or twelves inches across are frequently delivered to the addressee with bent corners, because of insecure wrapping. Some business houses pay enormous prices for calendars and then mail them in tubes so frail that the string cuts through and ruins the enclosure. No matter how much money is spent or how expert the job of printing, the good impression on the customer is lost if the package does not come through in good condition. 

29. Metal Clips.-The use of metal clips on circulars or folders should be avoided. The clips prevent the mail going through the cancelling machine and neecssitate hand cancel-

ling. In addition the clips are apt to become detached with the result that loose enclosures may be lost. The use of a paper sticker, or of the postage stamp itself is a far better method, provided of course, that the matter is not thereby sealed against inspection. 

30. The Value of a Mailing Permit.-In mailing large quantities of third and fourth class mail, a permit is sometimes desirable. This method of mailing does away with the labor and expense of affixing the stamps. A permit of this kind may be obtained by applying at the postoffice. The number of the permit is printed on the outside of the mail matter, and the mailer pays the proper amount of postage in cash at the time of mailing. Another advantage of the permit plan is found in the fact that the mail receives less handling, reaches the addressee in better condition, and is not likely to be held up in the mails for any reason. It also removes temptation from the path of the dishonest employee. 

31. Precancelled Stamps.-The use of precancelled stamps is still more desirable. Before they are sold the stamps are cancelled at the postoffice by printing the name of the postoffice and State across their face. This obviates the necessity of running the letters through the cancelling machine, enables the user to separate the letters by cities and states, and thus assures speedy handling and prompt delivery. There is little chance for loss by theft. By actual tests it has been found that the precancelled stamps pull almost double the number of returns as against the mailing permit. The reason for this lies in the fact that the permit immediately stamps the matter as circular matter, which should be avoided at any cost. 

32. Club Mailings.-What has been said about getting the full benfit of postage under first class mail applies equally well to third class. The bulk rate being 12c per lb., advertisers may if they wish take advantage of the full weight. Some concerns have even conceived the idea of greatly reducing advertising costs by making up a club of ten or more mailers, inclosing a card or circular for each in the same envelope. A system of this kind has some advantage if the goods or services advertised are along widely divergent lines. Its disadvantage lies in the fact that the addressee's interest may be hopelessly divided. 

33. Mailing Lists.-The greatest mistake any mail ad- 21

vertiser can make is in the use of an out-of-date or inaccurate mailing list. Of the millions of third class letters mailed every month it is safe to say that at least a quarter of them never reach destination. Think of the loss that means in business, in dollars and cents, and in wasted effort. Even the most carefully compiled list is subject to constant change and should be tested regularly by guaranteeing return postage if the mail is undeliverable. This can best be done by printing or stamping on the envelope the words "Return Postage Guaranteed," directly under the sender's return address. In the case of a permanent mailing or subscription list postmasters are permitted to correct the lists when submitted for that purpose, by crossing off the names of those to whom mail cannot be delivered or forwarded, by adding the correct street or box numbers, and similar changes. This work is done at the expense of the owner of the list by substitute clerks in first and second class postoffices at the rate of 60 cents per hour. 

34. A Real Postage Saving.-Recent tests in direct mail advertising have developed some very interesting facts and information. For instance, it has been proven beyond all shadow of a doubt that for the average direct-by-mail advertising proposition, third class letters at lc each will bring as many replies and as high a class of returns as the same letter or folder sent first class at two cents each. In some cases, of course, individual tests should be made because of the many factors entering into the success or failure of a campaign. In the vast majority, however, advertisers can safely reduce their postage cost 25% by sending the letters third class. 

35. The Stamped Return Card.-Tests made in connection with the use of stamped return envelopes or cards have not established so definite a rule. A publisher seeking the renewal of subscriptions to his magazine found that with the unstamped cards his returns were 6.6% while with the stamped card they amounted to almost 17%. On the other hand a concern selling aluminum on approval made exhaustive test and finally came to the conclusion that their net returns were actually greater when they used the plain unstamped cards. This seems hard to believe and yet it proves the necessity of making accurat tests on each individual proposition. The stamped return card might easily double your

returns, but the extra expense should never be assumed until the results have been proven. A return card or envelope 

C.O.D. for the postage may solve your problem. 

36. Puzzle Contests.-The recent popularity of puzzle contests has led many business houses to adopt them as trade stimulators without fully understanding the statutes and the regulations of the Department. Two fundamental principles must be observed. In the first place, contests must be free and open to everybody. It is a lottery and a violation of statute if the contestant is required to purchase any article in order to qualify. And secondly, the rules governing the contest must provide that all contestants tying for any certain prize will receive the full prize. On the other hand, it is permissible to increase the size or value of the prizes to contestants who purchase certain articles. The advertiser who ignores these principles is sure to be involved in expensive litigation and likely to suffer severe financial loss. 

D. Fourth Class Mail 

37. Classification.-Parcel post or fourth class mail includes merchandise, farm and factory products, books, catalogs, miscellaneous printed matter weighing more than eight ounces, and all other mailable matter not embraced in the other three classes. This service reaches more places than any other transportation agency.

E. Miscellaneous Rules of Delivery 

45. Husband or Wife.-Neither husband nor wife can control the delivery of mail addressed the other, against the wishes of the one to whom it is addressed. In the absence of instruction to the contrary, the wife's letter will be delivered with the husband's mail unless they be known to live separately. 

46. Minors.-The delivery of mail addressed to a minor is subject to the order of the parent or guardian upon whom the minor is dependent. 

47. Prisoner's Mail.-A letter addressed to a person imprisoned to await trial, upon indictment, or pending indictment should be delivered in accordance with the order of the person addressed. In the absence of an order the mail may be delivered to the sheriff or officer in charge of the prisoner. 

48. Persons of the Same Name.-Where two or more per sons of the same name receive mail at the same postoffice, they should, if possible, adopt some form of address or other means by which their mail may be distinguished. 

49. Officials.--Mail addressed to a public official, or to an officer of a corporation, by his title, will be delivered to the person actually holding the title, the assumption being that the mail is intended for the officer as such. 

50. Advertised Mail.-The addressee of advertised mail of foreign origin is required to identify it and pay a fee of 1c before receiving it. 

51. Wrong Delivery.-A person receiving mail not intended for him should return it promptly to the postoffice. If opened by mistake it should be endorsed "Opened by mistake" with the signature of the person receiving it. 

52. Delivery to Sender.-When the sender of a letter desires to recall it, his application must be submitted to the postmaster at the office of mailing.
