EXPLANATION 

HERE is no such thing as the secret of success. Neither is it possible to lay down a definite plan or rule of conduct to assure the prosperity of an individual, or guarantee the success of a business venture. The experiences of others, the things they have learned, and the mistakes they have made are the only guide posts we have. 

The choice of occupation is of no consequence. 

In every line of human endeavor from the construction of mammoth engineering projects to the manufacture of chewing gum there is at least one man who is making millions. 

The spirit of service, as indicated by our attitude towards our work, our relationship with others, and our reaction to life itself, is, after all, the one thing that really counts.

-Loun A Parth- HOW SUCCESS IS WON 1. The Age of Miracles.-We are living in an age of miracles. Every once in a while some scientist, inventor, or executive discovers a new property, process or plan which revolutionizes modern industry, and opens up countless opportunities for still greater achievements. The wildest dreams of our forefathers have become matter-of-fact realities today. We fly through the air at terrific speed, the sound of the human voice carries around the world in an instant, and we cure the most loathsome disease through simple suggestion. Who is wise enough to fortell what tomorrow may bring? 

2. Opportunities Today and Yesterday. And yet there are folks who long for the good old days of boundless opportunity. They go about the streets bewailing the fact that once they could have purchased Sears Roebuck at par, or that they sold the home place just before oil was discovered, or that they were unlucky enough to have overlooked some other equally glorious opportunity. They plod hopelessly along, passing up chance after chance, overlooking unlimited possibilities, and vainly seeking thruout all the world the acres of diamonds which lie unsuspected at their own back door. Their unluckiness is nothing but shortsightedness.

3. One Thing Leads to Another.-Where would we be to day if the men who have gone before us had failed to visualize and take advantage of the possibilities of the future? 

The discovery of electricity, and the invention of the gasoline engine, wonderful as they seemed in the beginning, were nevertheless mere starting points. Think of the hundreds of thousands of men and the millions of dollars now employed in the business of the telephone, the telegraph and the radio, and the equally extensive development of the automotive industry in all its branches and accessories. 

The man who says that there is nothing left to invent or discover is a fool. His opportunities are broader than they have ever been before, in spite of what that unwise old philosopher said about opportunity knocking but once at every man's door. Some of us are so busy keeping the wolf from the door, that we haven't time to listen to opportunity's knock. 

4. The First Step.-Now that you are no longer discounting your prospects for the future, your first step is to look around you and to find out where your best chances lie. 

Parents, teachers, and friends will overwhelm you with advice. Salesmen and promoters will dog your footsteps, each one with the one and only big opportunity of your life. 

Ignore them. Remember that your opportunity lies not so much in some remote plan or possibility, as it does in your own development. Opportunity does not come with a blare of trumpets. It is ever present but it is hidden. Sometimes it is ready made. More often you must create it yourself. 

5. The Way to Success.-Success is another happy word for the modern American. Its appeal is common to all. 

And yet few of us are willing to pay the price. We do not like to forego our pleasures, or to make unreasonable sacrifices. Our most earnest plans for the future somehow seem never to materialize, with the result that before we realize it our opportunities are all in the past. History records us among the millions who wasted their opportunities. 

6. A Simple Success Formula.-Every successful man likes to select some peculiar trait, characteristic, talent or inspiration to which he can point with pride and say triumphantly: "There! That is the secret of my success.' "The popular magazines are filled with feature articles and interviews, many of which convey the impression that they are intended to be good advertising, paid for at exhorbitant

space rates. Take a hundred such articles, add to them the unpublished views of another thousand successful men; scramble, boil down and classify them; and the composite result of all their experiences might well be written in less than a dozen words, viz.:

I planned I worked hard 

I served faithfully.

There you have a simple formula, shorn of all its superfluities, easily remembered, and absolutely dependable in its results. Of course some men may be born with unusual talent or genius. Others may inherit vast wealth or power. 

But most men have neither genius nor inherited wealth. If they succeed it must be through their own efforts. Let us see how the right kind of a plan, honest work, and faithful service will bring about the desired result. 

A. The Value of a Plan 7. The Road Map.—A man who starts out to see America must have some definite route over which he expects to travel, or he will get nowhere. It is just so with the traveler on the road to success. There are certain sign posts and landmarks along the way, and you must know in advance what these guides are, where they are located, and just what each one means. 

8. How Will You Arrive?-The first of these signs on your road map ought to be your health. What will be your physical condition when you reach your destination? Will you be able to enjoy your victory, or will you find yourself but a jump or two ahead of the undertaker? You have known dozens of farmers, who after a lifetime of incessant toil, came to town, hoping against hope that they would live long enough to enjoy their dearly won leisure. Far too few of our successful business men ever live to enjoy the fruits of their labors. They keep their eyes glued so firmly on their ambition that they fail to see the danger signals all around them. If you would profit by their unfortunate experiences, plan a vigorous course of physical training and development. It can be accomplished right at home with a few minutes of your spare time, night and morning. It can begin today. So can a system of biologic living which requires plenty of fresh air and sunshine, and

moderation in all things, eating, drinking, sexual indulgence, and the use of stimulants. In other words you can start today to make good health the first and most important part in your success plan. 

9. Education.-The second distinguishing landmark along the way is labeled "education." Many people still hold to the belief that a business career can be taken up when all other attempts have failed. "Well," they say, "John has made a failure of the law, and everything else he has tried. 

Now I suppose he'll have to go into business." This attitude is responsible for a very large percentage of failures. 

If you and I knew all there is to know about human life, and science and industry, there would never be any more wars or famines, or strikes or fires, or failures. We would all be successful in everything we attempted. The trouble is that we need education, not necessarily of the book and college variety, but education in its broadest sense. We can learn something every day, and from every person we meet. And the thing to remember is that knowledge picked up on the streets or in the college of hard knocks is just as valuable and just as useful, as the same knowledge gained in the schools and colleges. 

10. How Busy Are You.-You have now determined, first to be careful of your health, and secondly to develop your success qualities through education. Both of these steps take time, and oddly enough "time" is the name of the third sign on our road map. A man can be exceptionally busy and still find time to do everything he ought to do, provided, of course, that he plans his daily work. To thousands of men such details as health and self education seem trivial and unimportant. They are like a certain merchant in a western city who insists that he hasn't time to study or read.

In reality he is so busy answering the phone, sweeping out the store, dusting the counters and doing the other work of his employees that when night comes he is all fagged out. Then there is the manager of the large manufacturing concern in the same city. This man has hundreds of employees and salespeople under him, and yet he appears to have time for every detail, and for a daily round of golf. The merchant is driven by his business. The manufacturer drives his business. One is nothing but an office boy. The other is an executive.

11. Waste Not, Want Not.-We come now to one of the most unpopular of markers. It is the easiest to see. It is the most talked of. It is one of the most important. And yet as far as most of us are concerned, it might just as well not be there. Far too many of us ignore the great big bold-face capital letters that spell SAVE. 

The reading of vital statistics makes us shudder. But the thought of being dependent on others at the age of sixty is even more distressing. The saving of money, therefore, is one of the first considerations in your success plan. 

Success is happiness, but happiness does not come from having everything you want. Happiness consists in having a little more than you need. Thus if a man, be he brick mason or banker, can spend a little less than he earns, he can soon build that saving into a nest egg, and a nest egg means independence, wealth, happiness. 

12. How Far Can You See?-There may be reasons why a man in good health, with a good education, and with a keen appreciation of the value of both time and money, may still fall short of his mark. In nine out of ten such cases the reason is simply the lack of vision, and this is the last terminal. To forge ahead you must have a broad vision.

You must be able to picture the future as you would like to have it, and then be willing to bend every ounce of your energy towards making that dream a living reality. Talk to the average man about a big salary, wealth or power, and he doesn't register. He lacks the vision. He must first be made to realize that his vision expands with his general growth. In other words, while a $10,000 job seems out of the question to a $1,500 clerk, yet to the $5,000 a year man it represents just another step forward. 

Here then is another rule that it will pay you to put into effect today: "Visualize the future." Decide what you want out of life, and then go after it, heart and soul. If your ultimate aim seems too far away, forget it for the present, and strive for something within your reach. Then when you have reached the intermediate goal you will look back and wonder why the position just ahead ever seemed so difficult.

So much for the value of a definite plan. The best plan in the world, however, is of no practical value unless it is backed up by honest effort.

SUCCESS HONEST EFFORT B. The Value of Hard Work 

13. Famous Alibis.-Alibis are counterfeit bills offered instead of the cold cash. 

They are reasons given for not doing a thing that could be done. The hall of Ill 

Fame and Failure is filled with the names of men who had good excuses for their failure. The Hall of Fame is made up of men who almost without exception achieved their success in spite of perfectly good alibis. Homer, Milton and Prescott were blind men.

Desmosthenes had a three-fold alibi. His lungs were weak, he had a harsh, grating voice, and he stuttered. 

Julius Caesar was an epileptic. Beethoven was stone deaf before he was forty. Charles Lamb spent his 21st year in an insane asylum and the rest of his life as a clerk. Lord

Byron, the poet, became a great boxer and swimmer in spite of the fact that he had a club foot. Pope was a hunchback. 

Carlyle had chronic indigestion and melancholia. Robert 

Louis Stevenson was a consumptive. Booker T. Washington was a Negro slave. Daniel Webster was too timid to recite in school. E. H. Harriman was a physical invalid. 

Hundreds of alibis, but never used, never thought. Compared to these circumstances our own excuses seem weak and unimportant. If hard work actually wrought such miracles in the lives of these men, think what wonders a little of the same medicine can accomplish in yours. 

14. Habit.—The things we do today are determined by the things we did yesterday, and will in turn determine our actions tomorrow. In other words we are all creatures of habit, rather than of circumstances. Almost without exception our actions are habitual, and yet we fail to realize the tremendous importance of that fact. A man bolts his food today, because he has been in the habit of eating that way. He may make the most solemn resolutions, but the chances are that when tomorrow comes he will find himself back again in the same old rut. "How can he break himself

of the habit?" you ask. It is useless to bewail a ruined digestion, and equally senseless to set a date in the future for the reformation. The time for action is not tomorrow or the next day, but today. RIGHT NOW. Let him force himself to eat slowly today. Tomorrow it will be infinitely easier. The same rule applies to all bad habits like the tobacco or drink habit, and it also applies to the formation of good habits, such as the work habit. If you are out of the habit of giving your best to your work, make a decided change for the better today. The future will take care of itself. 

15. Postponement.—This is a common fault. If you want to fail try putting off until tomorrow what you can just as well do today. On the other hand if you want to succeed, consider well the value of time. There is an inexhaustible market for it. Its worth ranges all the way from a dollar a day to a dollar a minute. Whenever you purchase an article of value you are buying mostly time. The manufacturer takes a few hundred dollars worth of materials and turns them into a $5,000 machine. The watchmaker buys a dollar's worth of steel and turns it into fine springs worth thousands of dollars. Tennyson took a plain sheet of paper and made it worth a fortune by writing a poem on it. Your individual success depends not only on the kind of time you have to sell, but on what you do with the kind you have.

The common laborer who pitches in and actually earns his four or five dollars a day is head and shoulders above the high salaried executive who postpones from time to time the execution of the very plans on which his high salary is based.

Learn to do it now. The road to ruin is paved with the good intentions of procrastinators. 

16. Concentration.-You must also learn concentration.

It is one of the most important elements of success. It is also one of the least understood. To most people concentration means an absorbing interest in some one thing to the exclusion of all others. This, however, is not the kind of concentration that a business man would use even though he had the ability. There are too many interruptions and counter interests demanding his attention from time to time. The real meaning of concentration in business is first, the ability to formulate a plan or policy, second to make suitable preparation for carrying out that plan or policy, 22

and third, to see that it is actually carried out. The nature of the work does not matter. Interruptions are sure to occur. Intelligent concentration recognizes and deals with them as they come up, without for one moment losing sight of the real problem in hand. 

17. Fight. All the world loves a man who with his back to the wall, and against heavy odds stands up four square and fights for his rights. The story is told of a world famous pugilist, that he was defeated in his first fight by a man scarcely half his own size. The derisive comments which followed him wherever he went so maddened him that he straightway went into training, followed the little fellow all over the country, fought all kinds of battles in all kinds of places, and finally in his supreme moment as a contender for the championship had the satisfaction of knocking the world's title holder out of the ring. In our every day business life success is won through the application of similar principles. There is always a fighting chance to come back. 

C. The Meaning of Service 

More and more material wealth is being mistaken for success. Greatness does not consist in the ability to pile up an immense fortune, or the power to sway vast empires. 

Greatness is to be found where a man is truly happy, and no man is truly happy unless he makes others happy with his happiness. 

18. Making a Name.-We have taught our American boys that they were cut out for Congressmen rather than carpenters, for bankers instead of blacksmiths, for a career, not a calling. Not more than one in a thousand ever preaches a great sermon, carves a great statue, or writes a poem that lives for centuries as a classic. nine hundred and ninety-nine to be failures? make a broom handle, a horseshoe, or a loaf world needs these vastly more than it does names. Find your place wherever it may be, and then seek to serve your fellow men as faithfully and as fully as you can. There is no other secret of success.

Better learn to of bread. The 

19. Fame and Wealth are magic words but look back thru history and down the list of noted men and women you have known and unless there was something substantial back of their dreams and ideals, unless their efforts were planned

for the benefit of others, what they really found at the end of the rainbow was only a pot of gold, an empty nothing.

What concerns us most is the future with its unlimited opportunities for development thru honest effort and faithful service. Elbert Hubbard once said: "To have worked is to have succeeded. We leave the results to time." 

20. The Spirit of Service.-Pick out any business house in the country and you will find that the measure of service rendered goes hand in hand with the measure of success attained. Examples are almost too numerous to mention. A salesman gives up a week end pleasure trip to help his customer install some new equipment. A merchant makes a special trip to the city to purchase a little low priced article just to help out a customer. A seed house refuses to sell plants to a would-be purchaser after the growing season has advanced too far. A publisher refuses to print clever vulgarity in his magazine, even though he knows that by so doing he could greatly increase his circulation. A tailor makes his clothes so strong that he rarely sees his customers oftener than one or twice a year. A bank cashier refuses to loan money to a wealthy and worthy client when he knows that the money is to be used in a highly speculative venture. It is true that some men may appear to succeed through the practice of different methods, but for lasting success, show me the business man whose first thought is not "How much will the traffic bear," but rather, "How much can we give our customers for the money." 

21. The Key to Success.-Thus there is no magic key or secret of success. Every man starting out on the journey can see if he will the sign posts that point out the direction.

Every man has within himself all these qualities which will ether make him or break him. And finally every man knows deep down in his heart that the principles of Jesus Christ, the brotherhood of man, or the golden rule of service, whichever you choose to call it, is the only true principle of success. Therefore, if you want to succeed wake up, go to work in earnest, and make the golden rule your one and only rule of action.

BOOKKEEPING 

1. Definition.-Bookkeeping is the art of recording pecuniary or business transactions in a regular and systematic manner. In a sense it is a branch of mathematics based on certain accepted rules and principles with which every one in this modern age should be familiar. 

2. Its Object.-The primary object of bookkeeping is to preserve a record of such exchanges and transactions as would otherwise be forgotten if trusted to memory. A set of books properly kept in time produces a business history that will prove of inestimable value to its owner in years to come. 

3. Ignorance and Neglect Dangerous.-It is surprising how many people buy and sell, settle accounts and transact various kinds of business without keeping any books themselves. They always depend upon somebody else's bookkeeping. 

4. Keeping Books Necessary to Success.-Show me a really successful business man and I will show you a man who keeps a careful and correct record of his transactions. Keep your own accounts; do your own figuring and never accept the figures of others without comparing them with your own. It is the only safe road to success. 

5. Compelling Forces of the Retail Merchant.-There are at least two main forces that compel the successful retail merchant to keep books. First, competition; second, credit.

BOOKKEEPING 

341 6. Competition.-In order to meet competition intelligently and without loss he must know exactly what the goods cost him, what his selling and overhead expenses are and what percentage to add to make the sale profitable. Goods not priced high enough to cover these items are actually sold at a loss. 

7. How to Arrive at the Proper Selling Price.-The most convenient way of arriving at the proper percentage to add to the first cost of goods for overhead is to use the average ratio of operating expenses to net sales covering a past period. For instance, if a merchant's annual sales for the last fiscal year were $25,000 and the expense of conducting his business was $5,000, his overhead was 20 per cent. By adding the desired percentage of profit on sales to the overhead percentage, and deducting from 100, gives the percentage of invoice cost to selling price. The invoice cost of an article divided by this percentage gives the selling price. Illustrating the above: 5000 25000.20 percentage of overhead. Figuring 10 per cent profit. 100 (20+10) =70 percentage of cost to selling price. An invoice cost of articles at $2.80.70 = $4.00 selling price. 

8. Rapidity of Turnover. The oftener goods are turned over the lower will be the required percentage for overhead expense and profit on each sale; besides quick turnovers warrant the buying of goods in larger quantities, thereby securing better prices. To ascertain the turnover divide the cost of goods sold during the year by the cost of the average stock carried. 

9. Credit. The second compelling force that requires the merchant to keep books is the obtaining and extending of credit. In order to obtain credit he is asked to furnish a correct statement of his financial condition either by his creditors, his bankers, or the commercial agencies. Likewise in extending credit the books of the business man should show who is entitled to credit, to what extent, what security, if any, how promptly obligations are met, the total of outstanding accounts and their realizable value. 

10. Depreciation. Furthermore, provisions should be made for depreciation on stock, buildings, fixtures, etc., age, obsolescence and wear and tear impair their value so that a certain percent of the original cost must be charged off annually as a loss in order to show the proper present worth.

11. Bookkeeping for the Farmer and Others.-What is true of the retail merchant is equally true of every other business man, farmer, mechanic and laborer. All need to keep books in order to know where they stand financially, what their resources and liabilities are, (3) whether they are making or losing money. Then if at any time they find it necessary to apply for a loan at the bank it will not be difficult for them to show by their books and a correctly prepared financial statement that they are entitled to it. 

A. How to Learn Bookkeeping 

12. Go to School.-There is no better way to learn bookkeeping than under the instruction of a competent teacher. 

High Schools, Business or Commercial Schools, Colleges and Universities include in their courses the study of bookkeeping and accounting. Night schools furnish instruction for those who are employed during the day. All who have an opportunity to attend school should take advantage of it. 

13. Home Study.-Where school instruction is not available some elementary work on bookkeeping should be secured and the evenings devoted to study. There is nothing very difficult or complicated about the subject. Sometimes a correspondence course is found helpful and satisfactory. 

14. Two Systems.-There are two systems of bookkeeping: 

Single Entry and Double Entry. 

15. Single Entry.-Single Entry is so called because only one entry is required for each transaction and only personal accounts or accounts with individuals are opened and kept in the Ledger. When we sell a person goods and he does not pay for them we debit or charge his account for the amount and when he pays the bill we credit his account. 

Likewise, when we buy merchandise and do not pay cash we credit the account of the seller for its value and when we pay him we debit his account. 

16. Books Necessary. The main books generally used are the Day Book, Cash Book and Ledger. Additional books of record such as Sales Books, Invoice Books, Bill Books and others are sometimes kept, depending upon the nature and extent of the information desired. 

17. How Gains and Losses Are Determined.-Since no accounts showing gains or losses are kept in Single Entry, an itemized statement of same cannot be obtained. However, the Net Gain or Net Loss of the business can be determined in the following manner: Ascertain the Present

BOOKKEEPING 

343 Worth by finding the difference between the Resources and Liabilities and compare it with the Investment. If the Present Worth is greater than the Investment the difference shows a net gain, if less, a net loss. 

18. Objection to Single Entry.-The chief objection is that there is no proof whatever against errors and omissions. 

If goods are sold on credit and posting is omitted to the person's account, the error may never be discovered. Or worse still, if the amount were posted to the credit instead of the debit side, the loss might be double; or if dollars were posted as so many cents the loss would be that many dollars less as many cents; or, if a creditor is paid and his account not charged, it might be forgotten and the same account paid twice. Such errors in single entry might never be discovered, whereas in Double Entry they would throw the books out of balance and cause an immediate search for the error. 

19. Double Entry.-Double Entry is so called because there are two or more entries for every transaction. Every time an account is debited for a certain amount, some other account or accounts are credited for a like amount. Furthermore, accounts are kept not only with persons, but with commodities as well. 

20. Books Used.-There are two kinds of books used in the Double Entry System: Principal and Auxiliary or Aid Books. Principal Books are books of original entry from which posting is made to the Ledger, such as the Day Book or Journal, Cash Book, Sales Book and the Ledger itself.

Auxiliary Books are used to classify business transactions. 

Among those used are the Blotter, Bill Book, Order Book, Invoice Book and a great many others. 

21. Day Book and Journal.-Formerly these two books were kept separately and entries made in the Day Book were arranged by debits and credits in the Journal before posting to the Ledger. Now the two books are consolidated into one, preferably called a "Journal," and the entries arranged for posting by debits and credits followed by a short explanation of the transaction. The ordinary two column Journal may be used, with the left hand column for the debit and the right hand column for the credit, but in order to save time and work in posting special Journals of four, six, eight and more columns are often prepared. The opening entry should contain an inventory of the Assets and Liabilities.

22. Cash Book.-This book is used for recording all cash transactions. The left hand or debit side is for recording receipts, and the right hand or credit side is for recording payments. The difference in the sums total of the two sides showing at any time the exact amount of cash on hand. The credit side of the cash book can never be the greater, because we cannot pay out more cash than we have received. The balance of cash on hand at the end of the month may be posted to an account in the Ledger. 

23. Sales Book.-This is a book in which all the merchandise Sales are recorded. The personal accounts charged therein should be posted daily and the total sales may be carried forward until the end of the month and then posted in one entry to the credit of a Sales Account in the Ledger. 

Where Sales and Credit Tickets are used instead of a Sales

Book, they may be sorted at the close of the day, charging the total cash receipts to cash, the credit sales to the accounts of their respective customers, and credit the total 

Sales to Sales Account. When goods are returned, Sales

Account must be charged with them and the customer's account credited. 

24. Ledger. The Ledger is the book of final results, collecting and classifying from the books of original entry, all debits and credits having the same name under the one heading called an account by a process termed posting. 

25. Ledger Divisions.-In a large business three Ledgers or Divisions of Ledgers are used, viz.: General Ledger, Purchase Ledger and Sales Ledger, the latter two carrying controlling accounts on the General Ledger. In a small business only one Ledger is used which may, however, be divided into three sections: (1) General Accounts, (2) Accounts Receivable, (3) Accounts Payable. With the present loose leaf ledger method this division can be easily made and by arranging the accounts under each division in alphabetical order a separate index is not necessary. 

26. The Fundamental Rule of Double Entry Bookkeeping. 

Debit what you receive; Credit what you give. This is bookkeeping in a nutshell. We debit what we receive because it costs us something; we credit what we give because it produces us something of value. Whenever we debit an item, it is always either to increase our resources or our losses, or to decrease the personal accounts or notes we owe known as liabilities. Whenever we credit an item, it is always

BOOKKEEPING 

345 either to increase our liabilities or our gains, or to decrease the personal accounts or notes owing us, known as resources. 

If this rule is fully understood, kept in mind and strictly adhered to, mistakes in bookkeeping will seldom be made. 

27. Another Rule.-For every amount entered on the debit side of an account or accounts, enter also a like amount to the credit side of some other account or accounts. 

28. The First Thing to Learn.-The law of debit and credit is the first thing to learn. Debit and credit are terms used to express the relation between persons or commodities that enter into any business transaction. The simplest meaning of debit is to charge and of credit to trust. Charges or debits are always entered to the left and credits to the right in the columns or sides of the books of entry. 

29. Resources or Assets.-A resource or asset is anything of value belonging to us such as cash, merchandise, buildings, real estate, store fixtures and furniture, notes receivable or any personal account owing to us. 

30. Liabilities.-A liability is an obligation that we owe such as notes payable or any personal account. 

B. Legal Points in Bookkeeping 

31. Entries as Evidence.-Only records of original entry are accepted as evidence in court. 

The Day Book, Journal as evidence of sale and delivery of goods or work done. 

32. When to Make Entry. 

-The time to make an entry or charge against the purchaser of goods or for work done is when the goods are ready for delivery or the work has been completed. 

33. Erasures. - Entries to be admissible as evidence, should be made by the proper person, and without erasure, alterations or interlineations. 

34. Correcting Mistakes.- 

Mistakes should be corrected by marking the wrong entry void, and then making a correct entry, or if there is suf- ficient room, make a brief explanation.

35. Itemized Accounts.-All accounts must be itemized and

no general charge can be considered as evidence without giving the items. 

36. Guaranteed Accounts.-If A. guarantees that he will see that B. will pay a certain bill of goods, then the goods must be charged to A. and not to B. in order to hold A. responsible; but if A. guarantees the account of B., if the account is for some date of the past, then such a guarantee must be in writing. 

37. Sworn Statements.-To collect a debt on the evidence of book accounts from a person in a distant place, a copy of the account should be made out and accompanied by an affidavit, setting forth that the above account is correctly taken from the book or records of original entries, and that the charges were made at or about the same time of their respective dates. That the goods were sold and delivered at or about the time the charges were made. That the charges are correct and the accounts just, and that the person named is not entitled to any credit or set-offs not mentioned in the account. This affidavit should be sworn to before a magistrate, commissioner or notary public and it will save the trouble of pro lucing or sending the books. 

C. Rules for Journalizing and Posting 

38. Personal Accounts.-Persons are debited when they get into our debit and when we get out of their debit. Persons are credited when we get into their debt, and when they get out of our debt. 

39. Property.-Property is debited under such titles as 

Merchandise, Real Estate, Cash, etc., when it comes into our possession. It is credited when it goes out of our possession. 

40. Allowances.-Discount, Interest, Commission, etc., are allowances debited when made by us, and credited when made to us. 

41. Losses and Gains.-An account shows a loss, if the thing it represents has cost more than it has produced; a gain if it has produced more than it cost. 

42. Resources and Liabilities.-An account shows a resource, if it represents property on hand or a debt owing to us; a liability if it represents a debt owing by us. The excess in an account showing either a resource or a loss will always be on the debit side and the excess showing either a liability or a gain on the credit side.

BOOKKEEPING 

347 

43. The Proprietor's Capital Account.-This account repre sents the proprietor's net capital. The title "Stock" is sometimes used instead of the proprietor's name. The account is debited for his liabilities assumed by the business, for all amounts drawn by him from the business for his private use, and for his net loss if any. It is credited for the amount of his investment on commencing business, for all later investments, and for his net gain if any. The balance of the account is his net capital at time of closing. 

44. Partnerships. In a partnership each partner's net capital would appear in the respective account bearing the partner's name and the net profit (or loss) carried to the credit (or debit) of these accounts in proportion agreed upon. 

45. Corporations. In the event of a Corporation this account is known as the "Capital Stock" account and represents the amount of capital stock issued. The profit or loss is carried to a separate account called "Surplus.' 

46. Proprietor's and Partner's Private Accounts.—With a single Proprietor or Partnership arrangement, it is advisable to open a private account under the proprietor's or partner's names to which all sums drawn by them from the business for private purposes are charged. At the close of the year the totals of these accounts are charged into the 

Proprietor's or Partner's Investment accounts. 

47. Cash. This is a title used to designate money. Under it we include Currency, Bank Drafts, Checks, Sight Drafts, Express and Postal Money Orders and usually all kinds of paper payable on demand. Cash is debited when received and credited when paid out. The difference shows the cash on hand which is a Resource. The debit side of Cash must always be equal to or exceed the credit side "because we cannot pay out more cash than we have received.” 

48. Merchandise. This is a general term for all goods and wares dealt in or carried in stock by an active business concern. A Merchandise account may be opened and debited with all goods bought and credited with all the proceeds from goods sold. The value of goods on hand unsold added to the proceeds from sales, less the cost, shows the profit on the goods sold. However, if the cost exceeds the other two items, the goods were sold at a loss. The Inventory of goods on hand is always a Resource. Sometimes for the purpose of showing profits and losses more in detail, separate accounts are opened with such commodities as "Flour,"

"Potatoes," "Apples," "Corn," etc., instead of including all under one general title as "Merchandise." 

49. Purchases Account.-Modern practice is introducing the Purchases Account in place of the debit to Merchandise. 

All merchandise purchased is debited or charged to Purchase 

Account. If Freight, Drayage, Expressage, etc., on same are kept separately, their totals should finally be charged into this account also. Credit the account with any merchandise returned to the seller or any discounts or allowances for defects, etc. The balance of the account is transferred to the debit of a "Trading Account." 

50. Sales Account.-This account is the credit of merchan dise. Credit it with the total sales of all merchandise as shown by the Sales Book, Sales Tickets or whatever method is used for recording same. Returned merchandise by customers, whether for cash or credit, should be charged or debted at selling price to this acocunt. The difference in the account will be the net sales which is transferred to the credit of "Trading Account." 

51. Bills or Notes Receivable.-These are other person's notes or written obligations which we hold for which we expect to receive a specific sum when due. Charge this account with all notes, time drafts, and trade acceptances held against others, and credit it when paid or otherwise disposed of. The balance will show the unpaid items which is a Resource. 

52. Bills or Notes Payable.-These are our notes or written obligations which others hold, for which we are to pay a certain amount when due. Credit this account with all notes given to trade creditors, or trade acceptances and time drafts accepted in their favor, and charge the account as the same are paid. Balance of account shows obligations outstanding, which is a Liability. 

53. Accounts Receivable.-These are accounts of persons or individuals owing us. Debit the General Ledger account under that heading with the total of all charges against these accounts during the month and credit it with all payments and allowances made on said accounts. The balance must agree with the sum of the balance of the individual accounts and represent a Resource. 

54. Accounts Payable.-These are accounts that we owe others. Credit the General Ledger account under that title with the total of all such accounts and debit or charge it with all that has been paid on them during the month. The

BOOKKEEPING 

349 balance must agree with the sum of the individual balances of the accounts that we owe. 

55. Expenses.-Under this title are generally included such items as Rent, Salaries, Office Supplies, Fuel, Light, Postage, etc. If it is desired to show these items in detail, separate accounts may be opened for each one in the Ledger. Expense 

Accounts finally close into Profit and Loss Account. 

56. Store, Office and Delivery Equipment. These are not 

Expense Accounts, but represent an investment. Charge 

Store Equipment with such items as Counters, Shelving, Scales, Measures, etc.; Office Equipment with such office furniture as Desks, Safes, Letter Files, etc.; Delivery Equipment with Trucks, Wagons, Horses, Harness, etc. Repairs for these should not be charged to any of these accounts; they are an Expense. A reasonable amount should be always charged off annually on Equipments for Depreciation. 

57. Depreciation. Property such as Buildings, Machinery, 

Tools, Store and Office Fixtures, depreciate from year to year by reason of wear and tear and obsolescence. In the course of time it becomes entirely worthless and must be replaced. Provisions are made for such replacement by setting up a certain percent of the original cost as a Reserve and charging off that much each year for depreciation to a 

Depreciation Account. Accounts and Bills receivable are also subject to shrinkage in value when some of them are found worthless and uncollectable, and a Reserve must be provided for Bad Debts. The percentage or amount to be charged off each year depends upon the estimated life or length of usefulness in the case of property, and the proportion of loss on notes and accounts that may be sustained. 

58. Reserves.-Part of the profits of a concern may be retained in the business to provide funds for certain future needs as for the payment of fixed debts or business extensions, depreciation, bad debts, income, taxes, etc. The sums set aside for such purposes are taken out of and charged to Surplus Account, and credited to the Reserve set up for that special purpose. 

59. Deferred Charges.-Insurance and other similar expense items paid ahead or beyond the date of closing the books are entitled to a credit for that portion of the premium on the unexpired time. This credit is entered on the credit side of Insurance accounts and the difference charged to Loss. 

After closing account this "Deferred Asset" will be brought forward to the debit side of Insurance as a Resource and

appears as such in the Financial Statement. Office Supplies, 

Packing Material on hand also come under this head. 

60. Accrued Interest Receivable.-Where interest has accrued but not yet paid on notes and other commercial paper, due from others, charge this account with the amount and credit Interest account. When the interest is received it is credited to "Accrued Interest Receivable." 

61. Accrued Expenses.-Accrued expenses such as Interest Payable, Salaries or Wages Payable, earned, but not yet paid, accrued Taxes Payable, etc., should be charged to these respective accounts at the end of the accounting period and credited when paid. 

62. Trading Account.—This account shows the inventory of merchandise at the opening of business, is charged with Purchases and Sales Allowances and credited with Sales. The

Inventory at closing is then credited and the balance will show the gross profit on trading. This gross profit is then transferred to the credit of Profit and Loss Account, and the inventory brought down for a new balance. 

63. Profit and Loss.-Charge this account with the balances of all expense accounts, and credit it with the gross profit from trading. The difference will be the net profit or loss, which is closed into the proprietor's account or to the 

Surplus Account. 

64. Trial Balance.-The Trial Balance is taken to ascer tain the equality of the debits and credits as posted into the Ledger. It is nothing more nor less than a copy of the accounts or their balances, and if the footings of the debits and credits do not agree there is an error in posting. In that case it becomes a "trial" in more than one sense. (See "How to locate errors in a trial balance.") The Trial Balance is not an absolute proof, of the correctness of the work, but if the footings are equal the work is generally regarded as correct. 

65. Monthly Summary of Business.-A monthly summary of purchases, sales, expenses and Ratios will be found useful for comparison. It may be arranged with columns for these various headings with the figures taken from the Ledger. Each month the figures for that month should be recorded so that the record will give the total for each month from the first of the year to date. The sum of these monthly totals will be the record of totals for the year. 

66. Profit and Loss Statement.-The amounts for making up this statement are best obtained from the Ledger.

It is

BOOKKEEPING 

351 made up periodically; usually annually or semi-annually when an inventory is taken. An actual inventory should be taken at least once a year. The basis should be "cost," or "cost or market price; whichever is lower," with conservative deduction for obsolete and shelfworn goods if figured at cost. 

When monthly profit and loss statements are desired and where the percentage of overhead and profit is known, the approximate cost of the goods sold can be arrived at as follows: Deduct the percentage of overhead and profit from 

100 and multiply by the amount of the net sales; the result will be the cost of the goods sold, which when deducted from the net sales will give the approximate gross profit on sales. 

67. Balance Sheet. This is a statement showing the financial condition of a business at a particular time. There are two forms of balance sheets in general use. One sometimes called a Financial Statement. This is the non-technical and more intelligible to the ordinary man; the other is the more technical form used mostly in statements drawn for publication. Both arrange the Assets or Resources in one group; and the Liabilities in another. The difference between the totals of the two groups gives the Present or Net worth of the business. The title of the statement should be in full and include the name of the business enterprise and the date. 

D. Locating Errors in a Trial Balance 

When Trial Balance totals do not agree it is certain that one or more errors have been made somewhere, but there is no single rule or combination of rules with which such errors can at once be located outside of a careful review of the entire work. However, the following hints and suggestions may be of service and help in locating them. 

68. Errors of Omission.-A large difference between the 

Debit and the Credit totals of a Trial Balance usually indicates an omission of some item or account. See if all the accounts or balances of accounts have been included in the 

Trial Balance. If an amount has been omitted in posting the

Trial Balance also will be out of balance that much. Look for such an unchecked amount in the books from which postings were made. 

69. Errors in Posting.-An amount posted to the wrong side of the Ledger will throw the Trial Balance just twice that amount out of balance. If the difference is divisible by 

2, look for half of that amount on the side with the smaller totals in the books from which postings were made and see

if such an amount was posted to the other side of the Ledger account. The Cash and Bills Receivable balance can never be on the credit side, nor the Bills Payable balance on the debit side of the account. 

70. Errors in Addition.-If the difference be 1, or in round numbers as 10, 100, or 1,000, the error very likely results from wrong addition or subtraction. Check the additions of the Trial Balance and if the error is not found there, check those of the Ledger also. Where Ledger Balances only are entered in the Trial Balance an error may have been made in finding the difference between the two sides of an account. 

If an error is in the cents column only, the columns to the left need not be re-added. 

71. Transposition of Figures.-If the difference is divisible by 9 the error may rest in a transposition of figures, as for instance 57 posted as 75 causing a difference of 18, or 735 posted as 537 causing a difference of 198, both of which are divisible by 9. Errors of transposition are difficult to find; however, if the difference consists of less than three figures such as 9, 18, 27, etc., a one-column transposition may have caused the error. Divide this difference by 9; if the quotient is 1, the difference between the two transposed figures is also 1; if 2 or 3 the difference between the transposed figures is likewise 2 or 3. When the difference lies between 99 and 1,000, the error may be due to a two-column transposition. Here the middle figure of the error is always a 9, as for instance 

981 written as 189 results in an error of 792. Dividing the two outside figures of the difference (72) by 9, the quotient 8 is also the difference between the two transposed figures (9 and 1). 

72. Slides or Transplacements.-Figures are transplaced when some or all of the digits of a number are moved one or more places to the right or left without any change in their order; for instance 32.7 written as 32.70 or 3.27 or as 300.27.

The first is a one-column, the others are two-column slides. 

The error caused by a one-column slide is always divisible by nine, a two-column by 99, a three-column by 999, etc. Such division disregarding decimals, always gives the figures whose transplacement has caused the error. The error caused by writing 327 as 32.70 is 294.30 which divided by 9 produces 

327; or 327 written as 3.27 causes a difference of 323.73 which divided by 99 produces 327; or 327 written as 300.27 results in an error of 26.73 which divided by 99 gives 27 the part transplaced.

SHORTHAND AND TYPEWRITING 

A few years ago this chapter would have been devoted to a study of penmanship, ornamental and otherwise. Today the typewriter is in universal use. In our schools and colleges an effort is made to produce neat, legible writers, but far more stress is laid on the subject of shorthand and 

1. Modern Inventions.-The modern efficiency expert often wonders how the old fashioned business man ever accomplished any results. Where letters were laboriously transcribed by hand and copied in antiquated letter presses, the whole operation is now done by the dictating machine and the typewriter in one-tenth of the time. Where book-keepers perched on high stools made detailed entries in huge bound volumes and spent hours in footing up long columns of figures, auditing and book-keeping machines now make the necessary entries, add, subtract, multiply, or divide the figures and take the place of ten men. Where rows of girls were formerly employed to address envelopes, a far neater looking address is assured through the use of any one of a dozen types of labor saving addressing machines. Of what use, then, is a beautiful handwriting in this machine age?

3. Typewriting. On the other hand it is possible to attain a fair degree of efficiency on the typewriter by the "sight" system without losing the time or going to the expense of mastering the elaborate "touch" system. In fact, any intelligent person in a few weeks can acquire such skill as would require many months by the "touch" system. With a typewriter in every office and one in nearly every home, there is a real need for the simple exercises included in the following paragraphs. 

4. The Choice of a Machine.-Select a machine with a standard keyboard such as the Royal, Remington, Woodstock, Underwood, L. C. Smith or Monarch. These machines may be rented by the month from any typewriter agency, with the privilege of applying the rent paid on the purchase price. 

Thus you may pay as you learn. 

5. "Sight Typewriting" is the system universally used by so-called one finger artists. In our system, however, we recommend right from the beginning the use of two fingers, the first and second on each hand. Later on as your skill increases you may bring into use the third and fourth digits. 

6. The Standard Keyboard.-The keyboard of all standard typewriters are identical and when you have mastered one you have mastered all. In the above illustration all the keys to the right of the imaginary line A.B. are struck with either the first or second fingers of the right hand; all the keys to the left of the line with the first and second finger of the left hand. The spacer bar should always be operated with the thumb, the shift keys, back spacer or tabulating keys by the little fingers, thus leaving the first two fingers free for the actual typing.

13. Capitals, Figures, Punctuation Marks, and Symbols.— 

Capital letters are made by pushing down the shift key with the little finger and then striking the letter required with one of the other fingers. The standard keyboard provides a special row of keys for all the figures except 1, which is formed by the small "1" or by the capital "I". Punctuation marks and symbols, with the exception of commas and periods, are also made on most machines by depressing the shift key. 

Care must be used to release the shift key before striking the next letter.

15. Speed. Now that you have mastered the keyboard it is time to try for speed. Although almost any will serve the purpose, the following practice sentence is suggested: "Now is the time for all men to come to the aid of the party." 

Copy this sentence at least 100 times every day until you are able to run off sixty words a minute with ease and accuracy. 

It is also good practice to write your personal letters on the typewriter, to copy interesting items from newspapers and magazines, always holding in your memory as many words as possible while copying them. You will be astonished to learn what rapid progress you can make in this way.

16. Sample Business Letters. In the chapter on letter writing (page 363) will be found any number of sample business letters.

Pick out one paragraph or one short letter every day and copy it twenty-five or thirty times, or at least until you can show three perfect copies. This will not only be good technical practice but it will make you familiar with the best forms of business English. In that same chapter you will learn how to dress up a business letter or a sales letter so that it looks its best. The form of a letter is almost as important as the message. 

17. Carbon Copies.-Duplicate copies may be had through the use of carbon sheets. To get the best results first lay the original sheet face downward on the desk; next lay the carbon paper on it face up, and on top of that the plain sheet of paper that is to receive the carbon copy; finally pick up the three sheets gently and insert into the typewriter in the usual way.

Again, every once in a while there is a need to address some public official. If there is a doubt in your mind as to the correct form just consult the following examples:

THE RIGHT LETTER IS A PRIVATE INTERVIEW BETTER BUSINESS LETTERS

How to Avoid Mistakes In Letters 1. The World as a Market.-The world is your market if you can write red blooded business letters. You can satisfy old customers, win new ones, adjust complaints, introduce new lines, sell more goods, and collect accounts. You can reach your trade in a single day, cover vast distances, and talk intimately with the millionaire or the laborer. Opportunity and success are in your grasp. 

2. The Volume of Mail.-Between four and five billion pieces of mail are handled yearly by the United States. If tomorrow, you might have a panoramic view of the thousands of fires being kindled by discarded mail matter you would get some idea of the tremendous waste in direct mail advertising. The sight of your own inspired copy going up in smoke might make your blood boil but it would make you sit up and take notice. You would get busy and find out the reason for your failure. 

3. Why Do Business Letters Fail?-There are five main reasons why business letters fail to accomplish the desired result. This failure is due either to their form, their word-

ing, their tone, their readers or their contents. Each cause will be discussed in the following paragraphs: 

4. The Form of a Letter.-A manufacturer would not think of dressing up his star salesmen in blue denims and sending them out to make sales and friends for the firm. 

And yet, that is exactly what many sales-managers are doing when they mail poorly clothed letters. The letter reproduced on page 374 is a very clever example of letter salesmanship, and yet when first tested it pulled only about 10

Three months later the same letter on good bond paper with carefully typed fill in was mailed to the identical list and brought over 6% returns. The difference between 2 of 1% and 6% is the difference between failure and success. 

5. The Effect.-"But," you say, "readers are not interested in examples of clever typewriting or artistic printing.

They want only the facts about the goods described." In a sense this is true, but if you want your letters read, if you want to sell goods, you must take every precaution to see that the first impression is a good one. Remember that every letter you write is a photograph of the individual or business behind it. 

6. What is Good Form.-Sometimes for the purpose of securing attention a correspondent may find it valuable to adopt an unusual form for his letter. Generally speaking, however, it is safer to stick to the standards which have been tried and proven. a. Use a standard size sheet of paper 8½x11 inches. b. Use a standard size envelope 32x6½ inches. c. Use business stationery with a business letterhead, printed or engraved, for all business letters. d. Adopt a uniform position for dates and addresses. 

See that the margins balance each other, the top and bottom, and left and right. e. f. Avoid saying too much, and thus making the whole letter appear cramped. g. Adopt some standard system of indentation and stick to it. 

7. Indicating the Paragraph.-There are two standard methods of indicating the beginning of a new paragraph in a letter, first by indenting the first line, and secondly by allowing double the space between the paragraphs. Some correspondents accomplish the same result by indenting every line in the paragraph except the first. Examples of the two preferred methods are shown in the accompanying illustration. 

8. The Address and "Fill In."-It has been argued that a filled in letter, no matter how cleverly executed, fools no one. Anyone accustomed to receiving large quantities of mail is able to tell at a glance whether a letter is individually typed or whether it is a filled in reproduction. There are,

however, certain sales schemes which bring satisfactory results if the letters are good imitations of real letters. In all cases where the "fill in" is used, the size and style of type and the color of the ribbon must be accurately matched. In an exhaustive series of direct mail tests a large Chicago concern found practically no difference in the percentage of replies between hand and machine addressed envelopes, or between filled in and unfilled in letters. On the other hand it is often claimed that returns are slightly increased through the use of a plain white, unprinted envelope. There is a decided air of mystery about such an envelope which leads a man to open it up and see what its all about. The increased return is not enough to figure on, but it makes possible a saving on the cost of envelopes. 

9. A Real Form Letter.-There are certain individuals who believe that the form letter of today is doomed to failure. It is at best, they argue, a makeshift, and an attempt to deceive that does not deceive. It must be admitted that form letters are getting too common and that in some respects they do not bring the proper results. For example, take the experience of the Automatic Lock Company. Their sales-manager wrote an unusual letter and had it multigraphed, filled in on a typewriter and mailed to a test list of dealers. It brought only 32% of inquiries. Not satisfied with the results he hired extra typists and had each letter individually typewritten, and individually signed with pen and ink. In one of the paragraphs he referred to the business of each individual dealer, by name. He used the same letter, mind you, with these few changes and the results simply staggered him. Instead of 32% returns the letter pulled an average of 68% on the entire list. This is not an imaginary case. It actually happened. 

10. The Necessity For Tests.-The method of addressing, the color of the ink, the color and grade of paper, all may enter into the success or failure of your form letters. The safe rule is to test first and save the plunge until you are sure of the result. 

11. The Wording of a Letter.-We come now to a discussion of improper wording as a cause of letter failures. A communication in which words are misspelled, grammatical errors occur, punctuation marks are misplaced, or meaningless words and phrases are used, cannot fail to create a bad impression on the mind of the reader. Spelling, grammar and

punctuation are elementary subjects and need not be discussed here. Study and practice, alone will bring proficiency in them. Let us merely point out how easy it is to change the entire meaning of a letter by the simplest error in spelling or the misuse of a punctuation mark. 

12. The Importance of Punctuation.—A young man writ ing to a friend says:-"I was married last Sunday night for the first time in five years; the church was full." He intended to say: "I was married last Sunday night; for the first time in five years the church was full." Here is a list of nine people: Mr. Smith, a merchant, his son, a lawyer, Mr. Jones, a clergyman, his wife, a milliner, and a little child. By changing the punctuation we have but five:- 

Mr. Smith, a merchant; his son, a lawyer; Mr. Jones, a clergyman; his wife, a milliner; and a little child. 

A clergyman, one Sunday morning received a note from a parishioner, which in his haste he read from the pulpit as written: "Captain John Smith, having gone to see his wife, desires the prayers of the Church for his safe return." The note should have been written thus:-"Captain John Smith, having gone to sea, his wife desires the prayers of the church for his safe return." These examples illustrate the importance of punctuation and spelling. In themselves they are simple and ridiculous, but in a business letter they might prove of grave importance. There is only one good rule for punctuation and that is to punctuate where the sense requires it. 

13. Useless Words and Phrases.-So many letters today are still cluttered up with a lot of meaningless and insincere phrases. Here is a fair example: 

Dear Sir:-We wish to acknowledge receipt of your esteemed favor of the 28th ultimo, and to advise you that same has been duly noted. As per your request we hand you herewith descriptive circular of the 

Hercules Hammer. We sincerely trust that you will favor us with an order.

Hoping to be advised of your decision, we are 

Yours truly,

Can you imagine a salesman walking into a man's office and trying to get business with a sales talk like that? The chances are that he wouldn't get a single order. And yet thousands of sales letters just as stilted and just as mean-

ingless are written and mailed every day at an approximate cost of 15 cents each. The salesman would say something like this:- 

Good Morning, Mr. Brown-If you will give me two minutes of your time I can show you a simple method of increasing your sales, or 

Good Morning, Mr. Brown:-Here is a sample of the 

Hercules Hammer you wrote about.

Why cannot the business letter start out just as naturally and give the man the information he wants, without using a lot of 18th Century stuff?

14. The Complimentary Close:-As indicated above there are many useless words and phrases commonly used in business letters. This fact, in the opinion of many correspondents, applies equally as well to the complimentary close. 

Why end up your letter with "Yours very truly," "Yours truly," or "Yours respectfully" when you can so easily make the last words mean something. “Earnestly," "Wholeheartedly," "Cheerfully," "Hopefully," "Desperately," "Good 

Luck," "Yours for Service," "Yours for Bigger Sales," "Always at your service," or "Until next time" are just a few unusual closes which do away with formality, and help make your letters intimate and personal.

Incorrect: According to instructions will cancel order 

Correct:

Incorrect: This party claims you have interfered with his territory. Correct: 

This person claims, etc.

We are inclosing these documents. Correct: c. Do not split infinitives.

Incorrect: We are trying to fully protect our sales- Correct: men.

Incorrect: I (we) will be glad to meet Mr. Jones. Correct: 

You (he, they) shall be glad to meet Mr. Jones. 

I (we) shall be glad to meet Mr. Jones. 

You (he, they) will be glad to meet Mr. Jones. 

The following are examples of the right and wrong use of shall and will when it is desired to express determination:

Incorrect: I (we) shall not submit to this outrage. 

You (he, they) will not submit to this outrage. 

Correct: 

I (we) will not submit to this outrage. 

You (he, they) shall not submit to this outrage.

15. The Tone of a Letter.-The tone of a letter may be the one big reason for its failure. Analyze every letter you send out. Is it original? plausible? clear? friendly? courteous? dignified? enthusiastic? forceful? If it lacks any one of these elements, you had better do a little revising. 

One correspondent found it payed to keep an extra carbon copy of every letter he wrote for a month. Several weeks afterwards he sat down and analyzed them carefully. He saw at a glance that some of the letters were carelessly or hurriedly written, that many of them were lacking in friendliness or tact, or enthusiasm, and that in practically every case he could suggest certain little improvements, to bring out certain interesting points, which in the enthusiasm of the writing he had overlooked. Read your letters over, then, when they are "cold." From them you will learn many valuable lessons. 

16. Business Letters Are Friendly Letters.-As a general rule the letters a man writes to his best friend are successful letters. The friend is made to feel that the letter is for him and for him alone. No one else matters. The salesman on the road talks straight to the prospect and not for the benefit of any one else in the office who happens to be listening. His success depends largely on his ability to make friends. A sales letter, or any other letter for that matter, must accomplish these two things. It must make friends with the reader and it must make him feel that the letter is written expressly to him and for his especial benefit. In other words, your letter must have a personal tone. 

17. How to Get the Personal Tone.-There is only one method of putting a personal note into your letter and that is to show a personal interest in the customer himself. If you are trying to sell him an article show him how it will benefit him. If you are adjusting a complaint, emphasize the fact that you value his good will and that you are not satisfied until he is. In collection letters, make him realize that you understand his position, and that you want only what is right and just. And in routine correspondence try

Mr. Physician:- 

Why is it that you—the friend of humanity—are compelled to lose more good hard cash than any other man in business?

Every month you have to charge up to loss scores of good fat accounts that dead beats refuse to pay. 

Mrs. Tom puts you off; Mr. Dick wants more time and 

Mr. Harry moves away; and so it goes season after season. You could take a month's vacation and buy a new car every year with the money you lose in this way.

Now suppose I could tell you how to stop all this; suppose I could tell you of a simple collection scheme used by one Doctor that enabled him to make thirty of his hardest and slowest customers pay up-penny for penny-the hundreds of dollars they owed him. 

Wouldn't you jump at the chance to get it?

Well here it is the simplest, most successful system ever devised; a system that does not require the assistance of an expensive collector; a system that you can operate without extra help—and the only expense is the cost of two or three two-cent stamps, and a few minutes of your secretary's time. 

Send no money. I am so sure that my system will collect in your accounts that I want to send it right along to you without any risk or obligation on your part. Just pay the postman $1.00 plus a few cents postage, give the system a fair and impartial trial for thirty days, and if at the end of that time you are not absolutely satisfied, you may return it at my expense and back comes every cent of your money. That's fair, isn't it? 

Don't bother to write a letter. Just sign your name on the enclosed stamped return card, and mail today. 

Until you try this system you will never know what it is costing you now to be without it. 

Expectantly yours,

A LETTER THAT MADE GOOD.

to make a friend of your customer, by showing real interest in his success and in his problems. 

18. The Difficulty.-"But," you say, "It is easy enough to use the personal touch in individual cases, but what am I to do with my form letters?" "Must I know each customer personally?" Certainly not. That would be impossible in a large business. But you must learn to consider each customer as an individual. You must learn to divide your prospects into certain broad groups, each member of which has certain likes or dislikes, and certain well defined problems. And finally you must be able to visualize some typical member of each group, and to write your sales letter directly "at" him, just as the successful orator singles out one individual in his audience.

One correspondent had the mistaken idea that he could make his reader believe he was getting a personal message merely by telling him so. He started out in this manner: 

Dear Sir: 

This is really a personal letter, but as I have a number of them to write, and as time is short, I have asked that they be printed and a copy sent to you.

In the following examples the reader doesn't need to be told that he is reading a personal message: 

Dear Sir: 

Believing you will want it, I have set aside a copy of a valuable directory, just off the press. 

Dear Sir:- 

If you could throw a golden ray of sunshine across the threshold of the bluest day your wife and babies will ever see-the day when you are called to the great Beyond-wouldn't it be worth while? 

Dear Sir:- 

If you should be visited tomorrow by an Internal 

Revenue man, investigating or checking up your income tax return, Dear Sir:- 

I want to talk to you a moment. 

I want to talk to you, and your wife, and your children.

I want to talk prosperity, the prosperity of your

home, your family, your business, your city, and your country. 

19. The "You" Element.-A great many correspondents fall down because they think and write in terms of "I" or "We" instead of in terms of "you." The average buyer is not particularly interested in you or in your business. He is more interested in himself and in his own business than he is in anyone or anything else in the world. For instance, a certain small town merchant sends out every month an appeal which reads something like this:- 

Dear Sir:- 

We are showing this season the most attractive line of men's furnishings we have ever handled. Our styles are correct and up to the minute in every respect. We have built up a reputation among the best dressed men in town and we assure you that we can supply just what you want in our line at prices which are right. Give us an opportunity to prove it. 

The words "we," "our," and "us" appear exactly eight times in this letter. The word “you” is used but twice. The writer evidently thinks four times as much about his own business as he does about the customer's. The same letter could be rewritten from the buyer's viewpoint to read thus:- 

Dear Sir:- 

If you could save $10.00 on every suit of clothes, $2.00 on your hats, $2.00 on every pair of shoes and 

50 cents on all your neckwear and handkerchiefs, you would have an extra $50.00 in the saving account at the end of the year. Drop into our store the next time you are down town. Compare our prices with those you have been paying elsewhere for the same quality of material and workmanship. You must be satisfied before we are.

Here the proportion is just reversed, there being seven "you's" to three “we's,” and the direct appeal to his pocketbook leads the reader into the store at the very first opportunity.

Again a manufacturer of printing machinery writes:- "If we cannot show you a great saving of time, if we cannot eliminate waste or spoilage-if we cannot fold more uniformly with a speed of 6000 to 9000 on

anything from onion skin to tag stock-then I give you my word you won't be bothered."

In this letter the printer sees the advantages of the machine in spite of the "we" attitude. At the same time the appeal would be far stronger if the identical thoughts were expressed in this manner:- 

You can save time. 

You can eliminate waste and spoilage. 

You can fold anything from onion skin to tag stock at the rate of from 6000-9000 an hour, and you can fold more uniformly than you have ever folded before. 

If the "Peerless" does not prove its worth in ten days you are under no obligation to keep it. 

20. Rules for Improving the Tone of Your Letter.-To summarize briefly, the right tone in a business letter can best be secured:a. By reading your letters over when they are cold. b. By writing as if you were talking to your best friend. c. By showing a personal interest in the person addressed. d. By grouping your prospects and making your appeal to a typical member of each group. e. By forgetting yourself and writing more about the other man's profits, savings, needs, or desires. 

21. The Mailing List.-Volumes might be written on the make up and checking of mailing lists. For our purposes it is only necessary to point out the fact that even though your letters are perfect as to form, wording, tone and contents, they cannot make sales unless they reach the right class of people. Many a writer of excellent letters has been considered a failure because his letters were never mailed to the right list, and on the other hand, many carelessly written letters do produce satisfactory results simply because they reach people who are in the buying mood. The mailing list, therefore, is of first importance. Names and addresses are constantly changing so that unless your lists are checked and revised regularly, you are losing money that might otherwise be yours. Frequently you receive friendly letters offering to send a free sample or a new booklet or some inexpensive premium if you will return the card. The chances are that the writer of that letter has

just one purpose in mind, namely, to correct his list. A plan of this kind is not always practical, but if the lists are worth addressing they are worth correcting. 

22. The Contents of a Letter.-As we have already seen, friendly letters and routine business letters will ordinarily be successful if their form is correct, if they are properly worded, and if they are friendly and personal in tone. Sales letters are more complicated because of the fact that they are expected to do just what a salesman would do if he were personally calling on the prospect. Therefore, every word in your sales letter is important. Every thought must have a definite purpose. You must lead your reader step by step through a description of your product and an explanation of your terms, just as the salesman does when he is talking face to face with the buyer. You must get attention, arouse interest, create desire, and bring about action. Analyze your proposition, decide what is vital, leave out the nonessentials, and go straight to the point. Let us now consider the sales letter.

Sales Letters 23. What a Sales Letter Must Contain.-A salesman does not go out on the road with just a general idea of the thing he wants to sell. He learns all he can about the article, studies the principles of salesmanship, and memorizes a model selling talk based on these principles. Just so with the successful writer of sales letters. He builds his letters on certain basic principles. Each one contains the following elements:- a. An opening paragraph which attracts attention or arouses interest. 

b. A description or explanation of the article. 

c. Arguments or testimonials proving its worth. d. Persuasion or inducement. e. A clincher.

Naturally, all of these elements are not always found in a successful letter. In many cases a mere description of the article and an explanation of its use will suffice to get the order without any special inducements. But bear in mind the fact that in the vast majority of cases, unless you create interest and desire, unless you prove your statements, unless you convince the customer that he is sure to benefit,

and unless you present some logical reason for buying now, you cannot expect a high percentage of sales. 

24. The Start of a Letter.-It is nine o'cock in the morning, and Mr. Average Man is reading his mail. Near by is the waste basket. He picks up each letter with a feeling of pleasure, rips it open eagerly, reads the opening paragraph, skims lightly over the balance, and tosses it regretfully into the already overcrowded waste basket. 

Now, Mr. Average Man has the average man's troubles, and the average man's ambitions. He is constantly on the watch for constructive suggestions, labor saving devices, plans for increasing business, and stopping losses. Many of the letters he opens contain valuable information-means for making more money and saving more money and yet he tosses them sadly into the discard. Why? Simply because the opening paragraph of the letter-the first few wordsfailed to get his attention or arouse his interest. 

25. Answering Inquiries. Suppose you are writing to a farmer who has answered your advertisement about drainage tile. He is already interested in your proposition and desires further explanation, and proof of its value. Is there any real reason why you should begin your letter in the way one concern did?- 

Dear Sir:

In reply to your favor of the 16th, I beg to state that I am enclosing herewith a descriptive circular showing prices and freight rates on "Sheppard Non 

Breakable Tile" in car load lots, etc.

Why should the writer "beg to state" something that you have taken the trouble to write him a letter about? If you were a farmer and wanted to drain out that bottom forty, wouldn't you think more favorably of a man who started his reply in this manner? 

Dear Mr. Jones:

Your letter shows that you want to find out all about tiling your farm in the cheapest and most lasting way. Am I right? Then I know just how you feel, and as drainage has been our main line for over thirty-five years, maybe we can give you some pointers that will save you both work and money.

The first letter is like a dash of cold water to the farmer. 

He feels that the writer is too far away to take any inter-
