SPECIMENS OF BUSINESS LETTERHEADS.

est in his farm problems. In the second letter he feels as though the writer had jumped on a train and come right out to the farm to help him lay his tile properly. The salesmanship of the man who writes the first letter is worth about 25 cents an hour. There is no limit to the earning power of a man who can write a letter like the second. 

Here are some other good ones:- 

Dear Sir: 

I am genuinely glad you wrote me about the "Iceless Refrigerator," and am more than delighted to tell you all about this new household necessity, which its thousands of friends declare to be the most economical refrigerator in the world. 

Dear Sir:

Here is the sample of "Kant Leak” you asked for. 

There's enough to patch up all the cuts and bruises in your oldest casing. Do it today, Mr. Smith, and convince yourself that this is the greatest selling opportunity you have ever discovered. 

Dear Sir: 

I am glad you answered my advertisement, and I am going to prove to your entire satisfaction that you can double your present salary. 

26. Writing Direct Sales Letters.—Suppose now that instead of answering inquiries you are writing a direct sales letter to people who never heard of you or your product.

The first few words of the letter must take the reader's mind from other subjects and focus it on the specific product or service you are offering. They must arouse his interest. 

They must change that interest into definite desire. 

27. The Display Head.-There are advantages to the display head or scare head with which some writers seek to compel attention. This consists of a short statement reproduced in capital letters, in red ink, underlined, or otherwise emphasized, having a tendency to make the reader sit up and take notice. Such a statement may be either in the form of a question, a command, or a declaration, thus:- 

EVER WATCH A CONTRACTOR MOVE A BUILD- 

ING?

ARE YOU ADMIRED IN YOUR COMMUNITY? 

WILL YOU COME WITH ME TO THE OTHER SIDE OF THE WORLD?

MAKE THE MOST OF YOURSELF! 

STOP PAYING RENT! 

SAVE ONE HUNDRED DOLLARS! 

FREE PROOF THAT I CAN RAISE YOUR PAY. 

FREE 10 VOLUMES OF EDGAR ALLEN POE. 

SOME NUTS TO CRACK. 

The advantage of the short opening lies in its power to arouse such interest or curiosity on the part of the reader that he will read the rest of the letter to find out what it's all about. Care should always be taken to be sure that the offer merits the interest aroused. If it does not, the whole effect is lost.

One disadvantage of the display head is that it immediately brands the letter as circular matter. It is rarely used in friendly or personally typewritten letters, and for this reason is often avoided in form letters. However, a modified form of the same idea can be used as an opening paragraph without any special emphasis, and still bring satisfactory results, as for example in these letters:- 

Dear Sir:- 

This letter is worth just ten times its weight in gold, if you will act promptly.

Dear Sir:- 

Jones discovered twenty-three different ways in which he was losing money in his business. 

28. Arousing Interest.-As already pointed out, it is not enough merely to attract the attention of the person addressed. You must interest him in your goods. This element may be worked into the body of the letter, or it may be included in the opening. The following paragraph gets attention and arouses interest at the same time: 

Dear Sir:- 

If you throw a $10.00 bill away you are out just ten dollars. If you toss this letter into the waste basket without reading it carefully, you may be out ten times ten dollars, because the offer it contains is worth at least that. 

29. Human Interest.-There are many ways in which interest may be aroused in a sales letter. Appeals to the pocketbook are perhaps the most common, although there are a thousand and one things in which the average man is interested. Your problem is simply to pick out the one

appeal most likely to lead him gently but firmly to the point where he is not only willing but anxious to part with his money. Be careful, however, that you write about his interests, not your own. Throw in a little human interest.

Tell him something new about the world in general or his business in particular and you have won his interest. A 

Publisher used the human interest story to good advantage, when he started his letter in this manner:- 

Dear Sir: 

By the light of a wood fire in an humble log cabin of the middle west, a lanky, ungainly boy spent his evenings pouring over the few dog eared books that came his way.

Again a letter broker seeking orders for mailing lists gives the reader a very interesting bit of news and some good advice besides, when he writes:- 

Dear Sir: 

In the 2,090,000 businesses listed in Dun's Commercial Agency last year, there were over 1,500,000 changes. This is just one more proof of the folly of using old names, one more reason why you should standardize on Smith's 100% guaranteed mailing lists. 

30. Rules for Starting a Sales Letter.-To summarize briefly, the following should be borne in mind when starting a sales letter:a. Be sure that the first few words attract attention. b. See that you arouse the interest of the reader. c. Be sure that your offer is worthy of the interest you arouse. d. Write about the reader's interests, not your own. 

31. Explanation and Description.-Having secured the attention and interest of the prospect, your next problem is to present a vivid word picture of the article or service you seek to sell. This is a real problem. Experts in the art of writing, authors, and instructors in Rhetoric all agree that the ability to write good description is the rarest of literary talents. Why? Simply because of the fact that before you can make the reader actually see the article, you must know all about it yourself—you must have a vivid picture of it in your own mind. The first step, therefore, in effective description is to analyze and study the article from every

standpoint. Here is an example of description which does not quite ring true:- 

"Presto Paste" is manufactured expressly for printers. Our old customers tell us we have the best paste on the market for the newspaper trade. Their re-orders prove it to us. 

The same material rewritten presents a vivid description in terms of the reader's needs:- 

Mix a little "Presto Paste" with cold water. It sets immediately. It does not sour. It cannot mold. You will find it the handiest, the most satisfactory and the least expensive "all purpose" paste you have ever used. 

32. Generalities.-The next step in effective description is to cut out the non-essentials and dwell on those details which are unknown, or can be presented, to the buyer from a new viewpoint. Do not generalize or use worn out expressions, and be prepared to back up your claims by facts. The following paragraph is not convincing because it deals in generalities:- 

"Reliable" Ribbons are absolutely the best typewriter ribbons that money can buy.

Now, there are hundreds of typewriter ribbons on the market and while the "Reliable" may be the best, your description should tell why. Emphasize the points of superiority in this manner:- "Reliable" Ribbons are real ribbons. They cannot fade, blur, smudge, or dry out. Their impression stands out clean and sharp, even after weeks of constant use. Economy plus efficiency plus durability equals reliability. 

33. Interest.-The real aim of description is to make the reader understand the goods and want the goods. Therefore, the next step in effective description is to use salesmanship in your description. Get the buyer's viewpoint and write with that sole idea in mind. 

A furniture dealer might have said that his furniture was manufactured from the finest quarter sawed oak. How much more convincing another sort of description would be:-

1 "Have you ever had the experience of coming suddenly from the cold, cheerless darkness of the night into a warm, soft hued room where every piece of furniture, every drape and every light seemed to say 'Come in. Here is happiness. Here is home?' Let us help you plan such a room with our furniture." 

A real estate dealer writes:- 

"I am offering for sale a substantially built, seven room house, on a lot 100x140 situated in the best residential section of the city."

Compare with:- 

The house faces South on a gently sloping lot, 100x140 feet. There are magnificent trees, and flowering shrubs, amid a beautiful lawn. 

The living 

There are seven rooms and a bath. room is large and homelike with a real old fashioned log fireplace. The dining room overlooks the spacious lawn, the kitchen is warm and sunny. Upstairs the bedrooms are light and airy; the bathroom fitted out with tile floor and modern plumbing. 

All this, mind you, in a neighborhood where everybody owns his own place, where there are no rented houses or apartments, where the word "home" means something.

There is a description that really describes. The picture it presents grips the interest of the reader and makes him 

Iwant that house. 

34. Explaining a Service.-About the same laws and rules hold good when the thing to be sold is a service rather than a definite article. Suppose, for example, that you are seeking to sell your knowledge and experience as an income tax expert. Which of the two descriptions below is more likely to drive home the point or get the order? "My Income tax service is complete in every respect.

I have filed tax returns for hundreds of corporations, partnerships, and individuals. There is no problem too big or too little for my organziation to handle in a prompt, accurate, businesslike and effective manner. A trial will convince you."

This expert appears to be patting himself on the back, an attitude to be avoided in the good letter. Note how clever- 25

ly another writer brought out the same facts without creating a wrong impression:- "Look here, Mr. Business Man, let me banish your 

Income Tax problems. Let me free your mind from doubts and fears. Let me save money for you just as I have saved thousands of dollars in taxes for other business concerns. In other words, let my service prove to you that March 15 is just like any other day in the year. The fee is comparatively small and is not payable unless the work has been completed to your entire satisfaction.” 

35. Enclosures.-Some description may be necessary in the letter even though an actual sample is enclosed. It is always well to point out distinguishing or superior features. 

The same is true when catalogs, descriptive circulars or other printed matter are sent in the same envelopes. These are valuable because they permit of more detailed description than would be suitable in the letter. A single sentence may by the assistance of the enclosures, tell the whole story simply and clearly:- "There is as much difference between the old fashioned pantry and the Kitchen Kabinet as there is between the ox team and the aeroplane." 

But, remember, that no matter how attractive the sales literature may be, the sale itself must be made in the letter. 

Do not depend for success upon your enclosures alone. 

36. Rules for Description.-To summarize there are five distinct rules for describing goods or service in a sales letter:

a. Analyze and study the article from every conceivable angle. b. Avoid non-essentials and the commonplace details. c. Be specific. d. Get the buyer's point of view and write in relation to his needs. e. Use attractive enclosures, but do not rely on them alone. 

37. Proof.-A successful sales letter must contain some convincing proof of your claims. You must satisfy the customer that your goods or your services will be of some benefit to him. You may know their value, but the custom-

er doesn't until you have proved it, by one of the following methods. 

38. Proof by Trial.-A free trial is one of the simplest and most convenient forms of proof. Here is a straightforward offer which at once convinces the reader that the manufacturer means business: "Remember, there is no sale, no obligation until you are satisfied. Use the “sharpener" for ten days. If you are not fully satisfied, simply ship it back at my expense, and I will refund every cent of your money."

Here is still more convincing proof:- "Don't take my word for the value of these cigars.

Don't take as final the judgment of the thousands of discriminating smokers who have used my brand for years. Let me lend you a box for a week-AT MY

EXPENSE so you can judge for yourself how good they are. If they do not compare favorably with cigars, selling for twice the price, send them back to me collect, and you will owe me nothing."

Surely, I reason, a concern would not dare make so liberal an offer unless there is real value in their goods. 

39. Proof By Tests.—If your product is such that you can conveniently send a sample through the mail you can describe certain tests to prove its merit. A manufacturer of varnish makes use of an illustration in all his advertisements, showing a woman pouring boiling water on a varnished table, and this is a convincing proof of quality. A certain paper house sent out a sample of enameled stock with the following letter: "When you fold a piece of ordinary enameled stock, you know that the surface of the paper is broken. 

Apply the same test to this sample of Buckeye Enamel enclosed. Here at last is an enamel sheet that will fold as perfectly as a high grade bond."

A prominent life insurance company solicits business by sending out a miniature policy in which they call attention to certain new and important features. They ask the reader to compare these features with those found in his own or other policies. A paint manufacturer tells how to test the quality of paint, a tailor how to know an all wool grament from a

substitute, or a shirt maker how to test silks. In all these instances the reader learns something new and is given an opportunity to satisfy himself of the value of the thing offered for sale. 

40. Proof By Testimonials.-Bona fide testimonials are a great help in sales letters, just as they are in personal salesmanship. If you can prove through direct and complete statements that your goods are used and liked by great men and leading corporations your chances of making sales are improved. Fake testimonials and unsigned statements, however, will do more harm than good. A sentence like the following offers no conclusive proof: 

A prominent railroad official has just placed his order for his winter's supply. 

Whereas this means something: 

The Oliver Typewriter is standard equipment in the offices of Montgomery Ward & Company. 

Give the complete name, title and address when quoting the letter:- 

Mrs. John Jones, 2345 Riverside Drive, President of your local Woman's Club, is a user of the Standard Encyclopedia and has this to say of it:— 

Sometimes it is necessary to refer the reader of the letter to the complete testimonials or to a list of prominent users in a circular enclosed, thus:- 

Mr. Farrell says the Guide is worth a million dollars. Read his letter on the enclosed circular, etc. or,

The enclosed circular contains a list of the many influential corporations using the Multigraph to reduce printing bills. 

41. Indirect Proof.-Frequently some indirect proof will answer the same purpose. Statements like "Ask any banker," "Consult your local physician" or "Your lawyer will verify the statement" are convincing because of their apparent sincerity. You do not follow up such leads because you feel sure that the statements will be verified. Proof of the salability of an article is also contained in this frank sentence:- "I just wish you could be here this morning to see the reports and orders which are pouring in from all over the country."

And finally cultivate sincerity. Your letter may contain a dozen other proofs, but it will fail unless its tone from beginning to end breathes frank, straight-forward honesty. On the other hand, sincerity alone may be eonugh to get the confidence of the buyer. In a letter sent out by a retailer there was not one word of direct proof, but it contained this unusual paragraph:- 

Many men come in who simply say: "Pick me out a nice suit-I'll leave it to you. You know my size."

It is that kind of confidence in this store and its merchandise which makes business life worth while. 

There are no names mentioned, no dates given. There is nothing to prove the statement and yet you are somehow convinced that it is true. 

42. Sincerity.—Thus to summarize, a sales letter must be sincere. To be successful it must offer convincing proof of your sincerity and this result may be accomplished either:a. By the offer of a free trial. b. By convincing tests. c. By bona fide testimonials. d. Or by some indirect method. 

43. Persuasion.—Many sales letters fail because they lack the all important element of persuasion. Suppose, for example, that your line is radio, and that in your letter you have aroused the attention and interest of the reader, explained the advantages of your outfit, and proven its real merit. Now if you bring your remarks abruptly to a close and sign your name you will probably get some orders. Suppose, however, that instead, you proceed to show the reader how your machine will be of practical value to him by adding this paragraph:- "Aside from its countless entertainment features, a Radio Set may save you many times its price in marketing your produce. Only last week an Indiana farmer had a car load of hogs on the way to the Railroad when he received via wireless the news of a sharp break in the market. He held up the shipment for a few days until the flurry was over and sold at a decided increase. You, too, can 'tune in' every morning and get quotations on grain, cattle, hogs, or produce direct from the great central markets."

Perhaps the farmer has never thought of the matter in just that way. The letter persuades him that a radio outfit will put dollars and cents into his pocket. He is made to see the profit rather than the expense. 

An investment broker accomplishes the same result when he summarizes his claims in this one brief sentence:- "Until you have our service, you will never know what it is costing you now, not to use it." 

44. The High Pitched Voice.-Many correspondents try to emphasize their sincerity and to make a favorable impression by capitalizing or underlining words and phrases in their letters. In some cases this plan is valuable but it is easily overdone. Too much emphasis on non-essentials destroys the reader's interest in the really important matters. 

The following paragraph is taken from a letter sent out by a Publisher advertising a new book: 

"THE CHARMINGLY GRACEFUL AND COURT- EOUS SOCIAL LETTER which STRIKES EX- ACTLY THE RIGHT CHORD justly creates an EX- TREMELY FAVORABLE IMPRESSION of the writ er, who, if able also to converse and to speak 

READILY AND INTELLIGENTLY, to use EX- PRESSIVE and EXACT ENGLISH, has an ASSUR- ED POSITION among CULTIVATED and SUC- CESSFUL people. THIS NEW BOOK is a WON- DERFUL AID to the READY USE of English in LETTER-WRITING or in CONVERSATION. There is no other book like it. To the NOVICE as well as to the SCHOLAR, its value will be IMMEDIATELY

APPARENT.” 

Here is effective persuasion and yet when you receive such a letter you cannot fail to feel the writer's determination to sell you something. It's just exactly as though an enthusiastic young salesman dashed into your office and in a high pitched voice demanded that you give him your order. Nine times out of ten he wouldn't get the business even if you recognized a real need for his product. 

45. Persuasion By Exhortation.-Lead the prospect to do willingly what you want him to do. Do not make a strained effort to get action at the end of the letter. "Do it now," “Don't delay another minute," "Can you afford to be without this time saver," and similar exhortations accomplish

very little unless the way has been properly paved for them, or unless you are on friendly terms with your reader. 

Weave your persuasive arguments into the body of the letter. Present every fact from the buyer's viewpoint and let his common sense judgment do the rest. You cannot command him to do something that he doesn't want to do. One correspondent is successful when he sums up the whole letter in this way:- "These are the facts. The decision is in your hands. Your order will be filled the same day it reaches us." 

46. Other Forms of Persuasion.-No matter what form of persuasion you decide to use, be sure that your appeal will strike a responsive chord in the reader's mind. If you are advertising a correspondence course, you appeal to ambition, if you are selling a luxury you appeal to pride or love of pleasure; and so on down the list. A book publisher made this unusual appeal when he wrote a letter to 

Fathers and Mothers:- "What a wonderful thing it is to feel yourself responsible for a human life. But, oh, how much more exalting is the knowledge and power to meet decisively the first fundamental questions in the life of your own flesh and blood. The 'PARENT'S GUIDE' 

will give you both the knowledge and the power." 

47. Special Inducements.-Persuasion may take the form of some special inducement such as a marked reduction in price, a special introductory offer, a limited supply, a free sample, or an extra package if you send your dealer's name. 

For example a publisher writes:- "There are only 73 sets offered at this special price. Use the enclosed postal promptly as these few sets will be snapped up at once."

A magazine publisher offers a specific inducement when he says:- “As our gift we will give you free a large sized reproduction in full color, all ready for framing, of 

VanDyck's beautiful Baby Stuart, the most popular of this great artist's many paintings, if your card is received in two weeks."

There is hardly a sales plan which does not permit of some special inducement to get prompt action. You may offer

Dear Friend:- NO MORE "COLDS" IN HEAD OR THROAT

There are sure to be damp days; wet, slushy days; days when the chill, raw winds go through you like a knife.

Now is the time to protect yourself against "colds" and other menacing kindred diseases resulting from exposure to inclement weather. "Cold" in the head or throat is a GERM DISEASE.

"Cold Insurance" Blank on its way right now.

Note the display head, the news interest, the persuasive element, and the simplicity of ordering.

premiums of all kinds, agree to accept small monthly payments, allow long time or future billing, warn customers of an approaching advance in price, or agree to furnish special services. Under ideal circumstances the inducement will gather up and emphasize all the advantages of your offer, and thus turn desire into action: "We will not only ship the machine by express prepaid for a week's examination, but we will send you 

Professor Hertz' 500 page volume entitled 'Pleasure and Profit In Radio.' This is free if you act promptly.' 

48. The Danger of an attractively presented inducement lies in the tendency to overdo the thing. An interesting beginning may fool a reader into finishing the letter, but it won't bring any business unless the proposition is a worthy one. Similarly it does not pay to play up in big type an inducement which in reality is scarcely worthy of mention. 

The one rule to be followed in this respect as in all others, is to adopt the golden rule in business, and to show your customers that you are on the square. 

49. The Clincher.-The final test of a successful sales letter is the clincher. You may have aroused the interest of your reader; perhaps you have explained your proposition to his entire satisfaction and proved every statement; you may have convinced him of a real need and offered him an extra inducement which has created real desire in his mind. 

What are you going to do about it? Are you going to rest your case there, or will you clinch the order now? 

50. The Salesman as a Model.-What does the salesman do under similar circumstances? If he is a real salesman he summarizes his selling points and lays before the prospect a convenient order blank, lacking only the name on the dotted line. He gives you something to sign and makes it hard for you to refuse. On the other hand the inexperieneed salesman may have been just as clever in his sales talk and your own desire may be just as urgent, but if instead of asking for the order then and there he promises to see you next week, the whole effect of his argument may be hopelessly lost. In your sales letters you can profit by the example of the star salesman, and by the mistakes of the order taker. 

51. The Failures.-Thousands of letters are put into the mail every day lacking this one vital clinching element. How

many times have you received letters which worked you up to the point where you were anxious to buy, and then closed with some superficial statement like this: "I would be glad to give you any further information you desire" or "Hoping to hear from you by return mail?" The waste basket claims them one by one. The same letter would fairly shake the money from your savings account if it ended up with a real clincher such as: "Simply wrap a $2.00 bill in this letter and mail it at my risk, today," or "The card brings everything without risk or obligation on your part." 

52. Coupons and Cards.-The nature of your product will determine the best form of clincher to use. 

The little para graph above is just one example. Every sales proposition can be improved by the use of a similar device. Make it easy to order. Include a return postal card requiring nothing more than a signature. The coupon or application blank printed at the bottom of the letter or on the descriptive circular is sometimes effective. Here are a few examples: "But this is for prompt orders. the handy card at once.' 

So sign and mail "Let us send you this lamp for a week's examination. The card brings it. Merely drop it in the mail." "Just sign the coupon below-that's all. Place it in the enclosed addressed envelope-and mail it right now." "Don't send any money. Just check the style wanted on the enclosed card and mail today." "The enclosed card is signed, addressed, and stamped, ready for mailing. It will bring our representative to give you an accurate estimate without any risk or obligation on your part." "Pick up the telephone now, while the matter is before you, and let us do the worrying. Ring Drexel 2858."

You have noticed the similarity in all these closing paragraphs. The reader is given something to sign or some simple little act to perform. He doesn't have to sit down and write or dictate a letter or order. All that is taken care of. The writer has made it so easy to order that he just can't find a good excuse for not acting. That is the main idea of the clincher, to get action, and unless you know

and understand its possibilities you are going to write a lot of letters without getting very much action. 

53. Rules For Clinching Sales.-Briefly then, the duty of the clincher is to get immediate action. Remember the following rules: a. Make it easy to order or reply. b. Give some real reason for prompt action. c. Make your coupon or return card simple and easily understood. d. Don't try to bully or force your prospect against his will. e. Never write a sales letter which does not demand a reply of some kind.

If you will follow these few simple fundamentals you will soon find that the increased returns will pay you a thousand per cent on the extra time and thought expended. 

Routine Business Letters 

It is not only in the realm of sales letters that losses occur. Ordinary routine letters when carelessly or thoughtlessly written may be the chief reason for a falling off of business or loss of good will. If you are acknowledging orders, adjusting complaints or collecting accounts, cultivate the friendly tone. Make your letters clear, neat, courteous, and as brief as the circumstances will allow. 

54. Classifying Routine Correspondence.-The first step in solving this particular problem is to recognize the essential differences between the several types of routine letters and to classify your correspondence accordingly. There are four broad groups of routine business letters, namely, inquiries, orders, complaints, and credits, each of which must be written from a different viewpoint. The forms suggested below are simple and effective, and may be varied to fit any particular need. 

55. Writing Inquiries.-Although inquiries may lead to sales, to adjustments or to the granting of credit, they must be considered in a class by themselves. Fundamentally, they are requests either for information or for favors. Great care should be used, therefore, to avoid asking for information that you might easily obtain yourself, or for favors that can only be granted at the cost of great personal sacri-

fice or inconvenience. As a general rule business ethics require a stamped return envelope and a letter of thanks in all unsolicited inquiries. 

Request for Information 

A friend has recommended your Safety Razor Sharpener. 

Please give me information on the following points: 

Will your Sharpener take all blades or is a special model required for the Durham Duplex Razor?

What is the retail price and what will be the cost to me in dozen lots? 

Yours very truly,

The Hon. Frank Reid, Washington, D. C. 

Dear Mr. Reid:- 

Asking a Favor 

For some unknown reason the Superintendent of Documents has removed our name from the list of those entitled to receive the government crop reports. 

As these bulletins are vital to the success of our business, we want you to investigate the matter and see what can be done about it. 

Your assistance will be deeply appreciated. 

Sincerely yours, 56. Answering Inquiries. All inquiries should be answered promptly, fully and courteously. Tell your correspondent what he wants to know. Suppose, for example, you are manufacturing automobile parts and you get an inquiry for a radio receiving set. There are three courses open to you. 

If you ignore the letter entirely, you are ignoring the rules of common decency. If you write a curt letter denying your interest in radio sets you are still lacking in courtesy. If, however, you write a pleasant, friendly reply telling the applicant where the sets may be secured, you are doing the decent, courteous thing. Such a letter may take up your time and energy, but it nevertheless creates a favorable impression and may open the way to future sales.

Printed order blanks are usually provided with spaces for all necessary data and information. However, when a letter is necessary be sure that it covers all the details, such as catalog or list number, description of the goods, method of shipment, date of shipment, consignee, destination, and amount of remittance or other enclosure. When requesting that a missing order be duplicated or when reordering do not fail to repeat the order in full. It is far safer to say too much than not enough. Here is a safe model to use:-

Ordering a Bill of Goods

58. Acknowledging Orders.-Your own experience will prove the statement that it pays to reply to an order immediately. If you have sent money away in payment for a bill of goods you want to know that it has been received and that it is having prompt attention. If you fail to receive an acknowledgment within a day or two, your opinion of the firm is lowered even though you find out later that the goods were forwarded the very moment your order was received. Promptness, therefore, is the first essential in replying to orders. Some firms use brief form letters of acknowledgment, others, printed cards. Whenever possible, however, it is good business practice to write personal letters and thus take advantage of every opportunity to create good will and stimulate business. For example a Knitting 

Company writes:- Acknowledging An Order

59. Writing Complaints.—Mistakes occur in every business, from the most efficiently managed trust to the smallest cross roads store. When you send an order any number of things may happen to make it necessary for you to write a complaint. There may be a delay in shipment; you may receive more or less merchandise than you ordered; you may receive a bill of goods that is defective; that has been misrepresented, or that you did not order at all. Frequently you are billed at prices higher than you expected to pay. When mistakes of this kind occur you are often tempted to sit down and write a hot letter of criticism. Don't do it. Your common sense will lead you to make allowances for human errors, and your better judgment will tell you that your claim will receive more consideration if it is written calmly and courteously. Remember, that as a general rule the other fellow has no desire or intention of cheating you, and that he feels worse than you do about the error. 

Make your complaint within a reasonable time, but before doing so be sure that the mistake is not your own.

Goods Failed to Arrive 

Please look up our order No. 186 for 3 dozen Keller- Koats.

The main shipment arrived promptly, but the 2 dozen Jerseys No. R33 which you promised to mail on the 25th have not reached us.

As our customer has waited long and patiently for these sweaters, we ask you to duplicate the order and get them here as soon as possible. In the meantime, if the first lot comes in we will notify you.

60. Adjusting Complaints.-Every complaint, no matter how trivial or how unjust, deserves a courteous reply. The ability to bring a dissatisfied customer back into the buying mood is another one of those rare literary talents. It is the easiest thing in the world to lose the confidence of your trade by ignoring their claims. The customer is not always right, but for all practical purposes it pays to adopt that attitude and to give him the benefit of the doubt, whenever he complains about your merchandise or your service. On the other hand if you can not allow the claim, say so. Do not try to evade the issue. 

Error in Shipping

These might be divided into four classes, first, those asking for credit, second, those replying to applications for credit, third, letters asking for credit information, and fourth, collection letters. Examples of the first three groups are shown below. For collection letters proper, see page 351.

Limiting Credit

Remarks: 

62. Application for a Position.-Here is a type of personal letter which must not only follow the outward form of a business letter, but must be governed by the principles of the successful sales letter. When you write an application for a position you are in reality selling yourself or your services. Forget yourself. Write not so much about your own interests or your own accomplishments as you do about the needs and desires of the employer. Your problem is to arouse his interest and desire; you must persuade him that your qualifications will be an asset to him in his business; you must prove your ability to his entire satisfacton; and as a final climax or clincher you should make it easy for him to buy by your readiness to come for an interview at his convenience. The question of salary can best be left to the per-

sonar interview. Notice the way these points are brought out in the following letters: 

In Answer to an Advertisement

Dear Sir: 

Your advertisement shows that you want someone who knows how to write good letters. He must be able to:- 

1. develop new business, 2. keep old customers satisfied, 3. adjust complaints in a friendly way, 4. collect your accounts when due. 

My experience includes six years of correspondence work in the advertising and sales departments of the National Bag Company, to whom I respectfully refer you. My age is 25. My education consists of a High

1. A Real Problem.-Here is a problem which confronts every man in business. Every year unbelievable sums are tossed haphazard into the insatiable maw of advertising, without any real plan, without the slightest idea of the expected results, without any definite checkup of the actual return in dollars and cents. One advertiser has adopted the rule of using a full page in the leading newspapers in his territory, both daily and Sunday. Another uses only such space as he will never be forced to decrease. A third advertises only when business is slack. And still another follows the simple rule of making the space suit the copy. 

In this chapter we shall endeavor to point out some of the common mistakes in advertising, and to outline a plan of action which will reduce these errors to a minimum. 

2. What is Advertising?-Webster defines advertising as the science of turning the attention of others to a certain thing. In other words, advertising is telling the other fel-

low what you have to offer. This is not confined to the printed page of a newspaper or magazine, nor to catalogs, folders, booklets or circular letters. There are many other ways in which a firm's products are advertised. An effective window display, a sign board, or a personal call by a salesman may be the best available means of bringing the goods to the attention of the public. Besides all these recognized methods, however, there is always present a certain amount of indirect advertising without which any campaign will fail. For example, the firm which makes a practice of giving real service and real satisfaction earns a reputation for fair dealing which is passed around by word of mouth. Advertising thus founded on the rock of public confidence is advertising of the very highest type. It is the cheapest and best in the long run. He 

3. The Man Who Does Not Believe in Advertising.-You have all met him, the man who thinks advertising does not pay. There is one in our town. His name is Jones. has run a men's furnishing store here for five years, or rather the store has run him, because today he is a bankrupt. His argument was that everybody in town knew him and knew what he had in the store. "They've got to wear clothes, and when they need anything, they'll come in," he used to say. Smith, a competitor, moved in next door about a year ago. He ran something special every week, and told people about it in the local papers and in special form letters. His windows were a revelation to the community. And on top of it all, he soon established a reputation for having good goods at good prices. As a result Smith's business shows a big increase every month, while Jones has made an assignment for the benefit of creditors. 

4. Does Advertising Pay?-That question can best be answered by an analysis of the habits of this man Jones who openly declared his lack of confidence in modern advertising methods. "Big Ben" wakened him every morning. He washed with "Pears" soap and shaved with a "Gillette." He wore "B. V. D's," "Not-a-Seam" Hose, "Paris" garters, "Cluett" shirts, "Arrow" collars, "Cheney" cravats, "Society Brand" clothes, "Douglas" shoes, and "Knox” hats. 

For breakfast he ate "Sunkist" fruit, "Kellogg's" breakfast food, “Blue Valley" creamery butter, "Premium" bacon, and drank a cup of "Yuban" coffee. Before he ever started down to the store in the morning he had made use of not less than

seventeen different nationally advertised articles. You will find a similar condition in the life of every individual who is foolish enough to doubt the value of advertising. 

5. The Value of Expert Advice.-Probably the greatest mistake that any business man can make is to plunge recklessly into an advertising campaign without a thorough knowledge of the fundamental principles of advertising. 

Such knowledge is rarely the possession of the average business man. In large concerns an expert is a necessary part of the organization, whereas the small merchant usually considers the publicity work as his own duty. But the real specialist in the form of the advertising agency is available to one and all. Here are gathered together a group of advertising experts with a broad knowledge of the business itself, with an intimate acquaintance with the pulling power of various mediums and with a fund of invaluable experience. Just as the doctor knows medicine and the lawyer knows law, so it is the business of the advertising man to know advertising. 

6. The Cost of Expert Advice.-Contrary to the ordinary belief the cost of agency help is not exhorbitant. Naturally a reasonable fee is charged for the writing of circular letters, folders, booklets and other literature to be used in a mail campaign, but this fee must be in proportion to the service rendered. On the other hand the advertiser is asked nothing for the preparation of copy to be used in newspaper or magazine advertising. This expense is borne by the papers and magazines themselves and is paid in the form of a commission on the price of the space used. Consequently the inexperienced publicity seeker who does not avail himself of the best advice and assistance is making a grave mistake. 

7. An Advertising Plan.-Before starting out to spend any money for advertising, a business man should analyze his problem. He should ask himself these five questions:a. What does the buyer want? b. How does my product fit that want? c. What tone should dominate my advertising? d. What are my principal appeals for trade? e. What is the best method of advertising to adopt?

In attempting to answer these questions the advertiser must realize that there are four principal classes of buyers, first, those who are neither familiar with nor interested in the product; second, those who are not familiar with the product

but will recognize a need for it; third, those who are known users of similar products, and fourth, those who use similar products but are accustomed to buy them in a different way. 

Let us consider each classification: 

8. Buyers in Class 1.-If you want to sell to a man who knows nothing about you and has no immediate use for your product, the problem is a difficult one. He thinks he is getting along very nicely without it. You must make him feel that he does want your product. You must utilize all the persuasive powers at your command. Show him the possibility of more profit thru the use of the article. Make him feel the loss of being without it. 

9. Buyers in Class II.-Here we find a buyer who is unfamiliar with the article you offer for sale. At the same time he is quick to recognize its value when it is brought to his attention. "Just the thing I have always wanted," he exclaims, and his order is almost a foregone conclusion.

Your task is merely one of explanation and description. 

Once you have made him see the product in relation to his own needs, he is ready to act. 

10. Buyers in Class III.-Suppose that you are selling an article that everybody buys, such as food or clothing. Your task here is primarily one of publicity. You must make your brand better known that that of the other firms who are selling the same kind of goods at the same prices. You cannot appeal to the buyer's desire for financial gain. Instead you should emphasize the quality of your own article and its superiority over the offerings of your rivals. The promise of service and satisfaction should be the dominant note in your advertising. 

11. Buyers in Class IV.-When you ask a man to change his method of buying food or clothing or anything else that he is accustomed to buying, you must give him a logical reason for making the change. The saving in dollars and cents is the real reason why thousands of people stopped buying supplies from the local retailers and sent their orders to the large mail order houses or direct to the factory. 

If your plan of merchandising is different or unusual in any way, you cannot expect to change the buyer's habits unless your advertisements convince him that it will be worth his while to make the change. 

12. Planning the Campaign.-Analyze your proposition, group your prospects according to the above classification,

and plan your campaign accordingly. You can then turn to your own advantage the points on which the prospect is already sold, and overcome one by one the objections and the difficulties which might prevent the sale. 

13. Methods of Distribution.-The question of distribution must always be considered in connection with the advertising problems. There are really just five methods open to the manufacturer, namely: a. Direct sale by mail from factory to consumer. b. Canvassers selling to the consumer. c. Manufacturer's agents selling to jobber or retailer. d. Wholesalers selling to retailers. e. Direct sale to the retailer.

The advertising must conform to the particular method selected. 

14. The Fundamentals of Advertising.—What are the fundamental principles which govern a successful advertisement? Authorities have gone into the psychology of the sale from every conceivable angle. They have evolved countless theories, formulae and plans. But after all is said and done there are just four essentials to a successful ad vertisement: 

It must be seen. 

It must be read. 

It must be understood. 

It must produce action.

If it is not seen, read, or understood it cannot hope to accomplish its purpose. If it does not ultimately produce that action which is its real purpose, it represents wasted effort. 

15. Seeing the Advertisement.-The first purpose of the advertisement, then, is to be seen-to attract attention. 

The choice of the medium is perhaps the most important consideration in bringing the advertisement to the attention of the largest possible number of people. Then come the words themselves, the arrangement of the copy, the size and style of type, the color and the spacing, in the order of their importance. 

16. Modern Advertisers have discovered certain interesting facts about the art of attracting attention. They know, in the first place, that the impression created must be favorable to the goods advertised. Common sense warns of the

danger in going too far off the subject in order to get attention. Secondly, they know that fundamentally all people act in the same way under similar circumstances. And finally, they have given us a list of the various elements that can always be relied upon to attract attention in an advertisement. Briefly, these are a. Motion, suggested by the artist in the illustration or by some unusual arrangement of type is one of the best means of attracting attention. b. Headlines, set in large type, attract the eye of the reader. c. Contrast, between the old and the new, the good and the bad, or the desirable and the undesirable is a device which turns the reader's attention in the right direction. d. Arrows to point out in the text or illustration some distinguishing feature, or some decided advantage, are used to a large extent in advertising machines. e. Favorable Position is very important in getting the copy seen. Experienced newspaper and magazine advertisers usually select the top of the column on the right hand side as near to the reading matter as possible. The back page of a magazine is the most desirable, with the inside front and inside back covers coming next. f. Pictures tell their story where the printed words might be entirely overlooked. As attention getters they are invaluable. g. Color is often used to attract attention. It can also be made use of to picture the product as it actually appears and thus serve as an identification mark at the time of purchase. h. Curiosity is a wonderful force in advertising. To see the words "Who is a Frog?" or similar meaningless phrases staring at you from newspapers and bill boards at once excites your interest. Anything that is novel or out of the ordinary serves the same purpose. 

17. Reading the Advertisement. It is easy enough to get attention; the difficulty comes when you try to change that attention into personal interest. A cry for help will attract

the attention of everyone within hearing distance, but unless there is some real danger, the attention is immediately lost. 

Thus, the second step in successful advertising is to change attention into interest. 

18. Mechanical Makeup.-If interest is to be held thruout the advertisement, it is very important that the type be clear, legible, and pleasing to the eye. People simply will not read anything that is tiring. In the same way much of your effect will be lost if the selection and arrangement of illustrations and type does not harmonize with the written message. Different sizes and styles of type are made use of to emphasize the important points. Short paragraphs, short sentences and simple words also help to sustian the reader's interest. 

19. The Human Interest Story is universally used to arouse interest. It deals with fundamentals. It affects all classes. The appeal may be to pride, fear, comfort, style, health, appetite, or any one of a thousand other things in which the reader is interesed. Man is selfish, and if you can show him how to solve some difficult problem that he meets in his business or home life, if you picture the article in terms of his own needs and desires, you have won his undivided interest. If you talk about your own aims and ambitions, you will lose it. 

20. Mental Images.-A successful advertisement will call up in the reader's mind a series of pleasing mental pictures, closely connected, and following each other in logical order. 

Involuntary interest is sustained to the very end. The reader is led step by step to do the very thing the writer intended him to do. An advertisement that does not lead to some definite conclusion, cannot be expected to bring about decision and action. 

21. Rules for Arousing Interest.-If you want your advertisement read, therefore, remember first, that you must make it pleasing to the eye and easily read; second, that you must forget yourself and appeal to the interests of the people who will see the advertisement, and finally that you must reach some logical conclusion. 

22. Understanding the Advertisement.-You have attracted attention, you have won interest; now to explain your proposition. Of what use is a clever heading, an attractive illustration, or an interesting lay-out if the reader cannot figure what it's all about. As the author of the advertise-

ment your third problem, therefore, is to make the reader understand exactly what you are advertising for sale, how it affects him, and what you want him to do about it. 

23. Unmistakeable Clearness is, therefore, absolutely essential. It saves time, energy and space, each one of which means a saving of money. It stimulates decision and action. 

Sentences should be concise, and to the point. Each paragraph should have some connection with the one before it. 

Thoughts should be presented clearly and logically. 

24. Description and Explanations.-Your advertisement must be so worded that the reader will get a vivid mental picture of the article or service offered. This sounds easy, but as a matter of fact, there is nothing more difficult to write than interesting and effective description. The picture must be complete in your own mind before it can be successfully conveyed to others. Non-essentials must be eliminated, and emphasis placed on those details which show the article in relation to the reader's interests. 

25.-Proof as an Aid to Understanding.—The real mean ing of an advertisement can sometimes be explained by telling what the article or service has done for others. In other words, the reader often demands proof not only of the value of the thing advertised, but of its usefulness. You must prove your words either by the sincerity of your offer, by the breadth of your guarantee, or by first hand convincing testimonials from satisfied purchasers. 

26. The Story is a simple yet effective means of making the reader see the light. This may take the form of the anecdote, a single episode, a complete narrative, a dialogue, news item, or historical incident. Public speakers know the value of the story in driving home an argument, and make use of it on every occasion. In advertising, as in public speaking, the great danger lies in the tendency to pay too much attention to the story and to overlook its direct application. 

27. Reason Why Copy.-Fundamentally, all advertising is educational. If it is educational in fact as well as in theory, that is, if it tells how, when, where, and why, it is readily understood. In all your efforts toward making your advertisements understood, therefore, strive for simplicity, interesting and accurate description, convincing proof, apt illustration, and the education of the reader.

28. Action.-The mere fact that your advertisement is placed where it will be seen by millions of people does not mean that it will accomplish its purpose. This brings us to the fourth fundamental-action. Hundreds of thousands may read and understand every word of it, but if they fail to act, your efforts have been wasted. Formerly many advertisers beiieved in the influence of an advertisement irrespective of its direct results. Today such publicity is far too expensive, and experts agree that it is the direct tangible results that count. 

29. Methods of Producing Action.-A successful adver tisement will pluck the reader by the arm and induce him to ask for a certain brand, to send in an order direct, to ask for further information, or otherwise decide to part with some of his hard earned money. This decision is brought about by one of two processes, reasoning or suggestion, or by a combination of the two. 

30. Reasoning or Suggestion.-Although cold, hard logic is very useful in advertising, experience teaches us that action is produced far more frequently by suggestion. In other words, a man who would ignore the most logical arguments, might be led to act thru gentle suggestion. For example, let us suppose that you are selling an automobile. 

If you choose the process of reasoning you will talk about the value, strength, simplicity, speed and economy of the machine. You will emphasize some important point of superiority. You will forestall all possible objections. You will strive to bring about favorable decision and action by the very force and sincerity of your arguments. If, however, you adopt the other method you would probably ignore many of the economic considerations, and dwell on some of the more appealing advantages. Your copy would suggest the pride, pleasure and prestige of ownership, the health and happiness of outdoor life, or the satisfaction of being able to outdistance your neighbor. An apt illustration and a few words of suggestion will frequently bring greater results than a whole page of logical arguments. Usually, however, a combination of both processes is desirable. 

31. Confidence. People buy advertised articles because they feel confident that such articles would not be so strongly advertised unless they possessed real merit. Confidence, therefore, is the basis of all action. If you have something new and unheard of, considerable money must be spent in

advertising in order to establish the confidence of the public. 

The newer the product, the greater the need of advertising becomes. Strong testimonials from important people will help. Many advertisers print a list of prominent users, some rely on the strength of their money back guarantee, while others inspire the same feeling of confidence by their simple sincerity. A statement such as "Fifty years in business" or a picture of a large manufacturing plant convinces the reader that there is something worth while, something tangible, back of the advertisement. Without that feeling, no matter how inspired, the campaign will fail. 

32. Inducement.-Every advertisement should contain some definite reason for immediate action. Your own experience is proof of this. How often you have seen a description of something you wanted, and determined to send for it at some future date, only to forget all about it the next day. As an advertiser you must remember this very human trait. Be sure that all your advertisements include something to stimulate action. This may take the form of a "special limited time offer," "an introductory offer, good for 30 days only," "a special price," "a free offer," or any one of a hundred others, in which personal gain is the real inducement. 

33. Making it Easy to Order.-The more you can reduce the number and the difficulty of the things you want the reader to do, the better your chances are of having them done. Make your instructions or suggestions simple, definite, and easy to carry out. Avoid the necessity of letter writing. "Call Main 700 and let us deliver one today" induces action by the very simplicity of the suggestion. "Don't bother to write a letter. Just indicate your size on the coupon below, put it in an envelope and mail today" sounds so easy that action follows quite naturally. This mechanical ease of response is after all the real factor in producing action. 

34. Display vs. Classified Advertising. The display ad vertisement is like a salesman. It tries to create a desire where none existed before. On the other hand the want ad is merely an order taker. The sale is made before the classified column is ever consulted. In planning and writing advertisements many business men make the mistake of ignoring this essential difference. They use display space when the classified would bring the best results. And even in the

use of the want ad columns the tendency is usually to use general statements, thus failing to give sufficient information to complete the sale. In classified advertising the aim should be to keep out the curiosity seeker, and limit your replies to actual prospects. Suppose for example you have a used car for sale. Thousand of ads appear every day worded just like this one:- 

BUICK ROADSTER, latest model, looks like new; must sell; Bargain.-Oscar Lamp, 1636 W. Madison. 

No price. No specific information. Just a jumble of meaningless words. How much better it would be to give the facts, thus:- 

BUICK ROADSTER 6A, driven 2500 miles; good tires; $500 cash. Oscar Lamp, 1636 W. Madison.

This advertisement is not a bit longer than the other, but it is certain that the people who reply have $500.00 that they would be willing to pay for such a car. One reply to this ad is worth a dozen of the others. 

35. In Conclusion.-We have now discussed briefly the underlying principles of successful advertising, and pointed out some of the more common mistakes. In bringing this chapter to a close it might be well to call attention to the unlimited possibilities in this field. Seemingly impossible feats are daily being accomplished thru the right kind of advertising. As M. Coue says, “Ca passe, it is passing,” all your troubles disappear if you will face them. One merchant wanted to get away from the cold inhumanity of the monthly statements of his customer's accounts. Every month he printed a small advertisement right on the statement and found to his delight that it not only improved his collections, but increased his sales. The supreme example of getting the most for your money is found in the automobile industry. Every year an immense exhibition is staged in every large city. Its one object is to sell automobiles. 

And yet so subtle is the propaganda that hundreds of thousands actually spend their hard earned cash to gain admission-just for the privilege of seeing the display and giving their orders to the various manufacturers. Advertising has done this for the automobile business. Are you using it to the best advantage in yours?

A DOZEN DO'S AND DON'TS FOR SALESMEN 1. Begin by Talking His Language.-Learn your prospect's likes and dislikes. Find out what his hobbies are, and base your approach on these. Then show your goods. 

2. Be a Good Listener.-Use more ear and less tongue. 

Give your customer a chance to sell himself. Remember that it's selling, not talking, that counts. 

3. Put Quality Before Price.—You must know your goods, what they are, and what they will do. Show your customer how good merchandise always builds good will and increases profits in the long run. Learn to dramatize a sale. 

4. Service.-Dig into your prospect's problems and study his needs. Help him to move his goods and orders will follow. 

Service of this kind means more than high sounding phrases. 

5. Talk Business.-Get down to business quickly. Watch for chances to mention the details of delivery, the good service you give others and the liberal terms of your firm. 

6. Building Good Will.-You should sell your company as well as your goods. There's no surer way of increasing your sales, and earning rapid promotion. 

7. Don't Take "No" for an Answer.-Resourcefulness will often enable you to turn a flat refusal into a real order. 

There's a difference between making a sale and taking an order. 

8. New Markets.-Be on the watch for new ways of using your goods, and new methods of distribution. Make several missionary calls every week. Don't be a bell ringer. 

9. Make Every Hour Count.-Learn to classify the differ ent hours of the day. There is a "best" time to make a sale and there is also a "worst" time. Use the unlikely hours of the day for missionary work and for planning your campaign in the "best" hours. 

10. Make Friends.-Make your customers your friends and there will always be a welcome for you. Keep your selling on a personal basis. No other factor means half as much to you. 

11. Keep Fit.-A successful salesman must keep mentally and physically fit. It's up to you to create new buiness. Your first duty therefore is to keep yourself in such good physical condition and your mind so free of worries that you can give your best every day. 

12. Be Courageous. A good salesman is usually somewhat of a philosopher. His own courage and convictions are reflected in the mind of the customer. It's human nature to covet a seat on the band wagon. Courage is the key that unlocks the secret of dealing with all sorts and conditions of men.

WEIGHTS AND MEASURES 

1. How Obtained.-Weight is the measure of the force of gravity, or the earth's attraction for a body or substance, and varies with the mass of the body, or the quantity of matter that it contains. The weight of an article, therefore, can be obtained by comparing its measure of attraction to the earth with that of a fixed standard unit, as for example, an ounce or a pound. This process of comparison is generally accomplished by a mechanical device known as a scale or a balance.

A Measure is a standard unit established by law or custom, by which quantity is measured or estimated. Thus, length is ascertained by applying the foot or yard measure; capacity by the use of the quart, the gallon, or the bushel; time by the use of the second, minute or hour. 

2. Fundamental Quantities and Units.-There are three fundamentally different kinds of quantities that can be measured, viz., length, mass, and time; all other measurements may be reduced to these three. The basis of all measurements is some standard primary unit from which all other units are derived. Accordingly, the yard, the pound, and the second are the respective accepted fundamental units of length, weight, and time, in our common system of measurement.

3. Two Systems.-There are two systems of units of weight and measurement in general use, the English and the Metric system. While the latter system has been legalized in the United States, the former is the one more commonly in use here. 

4. Units of Length.-The yard which is the standard unit of length for the United States is defined as the distance between the 27th and 63rd divisions of a brass bar deposited in the Bureau of Weights and Measures at Washington, D. C., at a temperature of 16 2/3 C. One-third of this distance constitutes the foot, and one-thirty-sixth the inch. Nearly all civilized nations have at some time employed a unit of length the name of which bore the same significance as does foot in English. There can scarcely be any doubt therefore, that in each Country this unit has been derived from the length of the human foot. It is probable that in England after the yard, a unit which is supposed to have represented the length of the arm of King Henry I, became established as a standard, the foot was arbitrarily chosen as one-third of this standard yard. In view of such an origin it is quite evident that no agreement existed among the units in use in different countries and even now we find such conventional measures as the Barleycorn used by shoemakers; the 

Palm and the Hand used to measure the height of horses; the Span, the Fathom, the Cable Length, and the Knot used by sailors to measure depths and distances at sea; and the 

Pace for distances in walking. 

5. Units of Weight.—The standard unit of weight is the 

Troy Pound adopted by the Mint at Philadelphia and elsewhere, and contains 5760 grains. It is equal to the weight of 22.794377 cubic inches of distilled water and is less than the pound avoirdupois. The unit of weight for all ordinary purposes adopted in this country and in England is the Avoirdupois Pound which is equivalent to 7000 grains. It is the weight of 27.7015 cubic inches of distilled water. 

6. Units of Time.-Time is a part of duration and the second is taken among all civilized nations as the standard unit of time. It is the 1/86400 part of the time from noon to noon. A true year is the time of one revolution of the earth around the sun, which is 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 46.75 seconds. Figuring 365 days as a common year, the time lost in the calendar in 4 years will lack only

44 minutes, 55.4 seconds of a day; hence, we add 1 day to 

February every fourth year, calling it Leap Year which contains 366 days. 

In 100 years this difference of 44 minutes, 55.4 seconds amounts to 18 hours, 43 minutes, 5 seconds; hence, at the end of 100 years we omit to add 1 day, thus losing 5 hours, 12 minutes, 55 seconds, which is corrected by adding 1 day at the end of 400 years. Therefore, every year devisible by 4 (except Century years) and every Century year divisible by 400 is Leap Year. 

7. Derived Units.-From the measure length are also obtained the measurements of Area and Volume; for an area is expressed as the product of two lengths, and a volume as the product of three lengths. For these reasons the units of area and volume are looked upon as derived units, depending on one fundamental unit, the unit of length. 

8. Tables. To facilitate calculations, tables of all the important measures and weights have been arranged in a systematic and orderly way, and printed on the following pages for your help and guidance.

The Metric System 9. The Origin and Nature of the System.-The Metric 

System originated in France. It is a system of weights and measures based upon the meter as the fundamental unit; hence the term, metric. From the meter which is also the basic unit of length, three other units are derived, viz: the are, the unit of surface; the liter, the unit of volume or capacity; and the gram, the unit of weight. These four constitute the primary units of the system. In its multiples and submultiples a decimal system is adopted. Ascending in value from each primary unit the measure is multiplied by ten, and bears a Greek prefix indicating its value, as deca-which signifies 10; hecto-which signifies 100; kilowhich signifies 1000; and myra-which signifies 10,000.

Similarly descending in value, the terms bear a Latin prefix indicating their relation to the unit, as deci-which denotes 

10th; centi-which denotes 100th; and milli-which denotes 

1000th. The prefix mega-when employed, denotes a multiple by 1,000,000; the prefix micro-the 1,000,000th part.

Thus with the primary units indicating the weight or measure, and the prefixes designating the number of units or fractional units clearly and definitely fixed in mind, the system is simple and self-explanatory. 

10. Demand for a Uniform System.-Formerly every country or nation had its own units of weights and meas-

ures. When commerce spread and trading increased this lack of uniformity in measures and weights greatly complicated business transactions everywhere. A uniform system seemed desirable in commerce as well as in science. Men of affairs urged that such a system be devised and efforts were made to perfect it, but the task was not an easy one. 

To be of value, such a system must be scientific and practical; it must be adapted to measure and weigh anything; it must be suited to all people, for all purposes and for all times. Finally at the time of the French Revolution the extreme inconvenience of existing weights and measures, together with the confusion arising from the use of different standards in different localities led the National Assembly of France to appoint a commission to devise a more logical system. The result of the labors of this commission was the present Metric System. 

11. The Development and Basis of the System.-Prior to the actual proposal in the French National Assembly which resulted in the Metric System, many features desirable in a universal system had been independently submitted. Decimals introduced into Europe by Stevenius became part of the new system. Abbe Mouton suggested self-defining terms which with some improvement were embodied. James Watt held that all units of weight and measure should be derived from the single unit of length, since every system of Weights and Measures must have an invariable unit for its base; and every other unit of its entire system should be derived from it, according to a fixed law. This was made a basic principle of the Metric System. Several others further proposed that this unit of length be taken from an invariable dimension found in nature. The French Government in order to obtain such an invariable unit, measured a degree of the arc of a meridian on the earth's surface for a basis; and from this computed the length of the meridional arc from the equator to the pole on the meridian of Paris. This length they divided into ten million equal parts and then took one of these parts for the unit of length, and called it a meter. Thus the meter, equal to one ten-millionth of the quadrant of the earth, or 1 yard, 3 inches and 37 hundredths of an inch, very nearly, became the basic unit of the Metric System as well as the primary unit of length. 

The International Standard Meter is recorded and preserved

by the distance between two transverse parallel lines ruled on a platinum-iridium bar, kept at the freezing temperature or 0° Centigrade, at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, near Paris, France.

For the sake of convenience great numbers of rods of the same length as this standard meter bar have been made and scattered all over the world. They are the common meter sticks and are divided into 10, 100 or 1000 equal parts, great care being taken to have all the parts of exactly the same length. While the meter originated as a fraction of the earth's quadrant or distance between the equator and the North pole it is not now thought of in that way but rather as the distance between the two lines on the bar mentioned above. 

12. Other Primary Metric Units.-Using the Meter as a basis, the units of surface, volume and weight were also fixed. The are became the unit of surface or land measure and consists of a square whose side is 10 meters. The Liter was made the unit of volume or capacity for both liquid and dry measures and equals 1 cubic decimeter, or 61.026 cubic inches. It is the volume of a cube which is one-tenth of a meter (about 4 inches) on a side and represents a quantity of distilled water which at its maximum density will counterpoise the standard kilogram in a vacuum. It is equivalent to 1.057 quarts. A liter and a quart are therefore, roughly equivalent measures.

In order to establish a connection between the unit of length and the unit of mass or weight, the commission directed a committee of the French Academy to prepare a cylinder of platinum which should have the same weight as a liter of water at its temperature of greatest density, namely, 4° 

Centigrade (39° Fahrenheit). An exact equivalent of this cylinder, made of platinum-iridium and kept at Sevres with the standard meter, now represents the standard of mass in the metric system. It is called the standard kilogram and is equivalent to about 2.2 pounds. One one-thousandth of this was adopted as the fundamental unit of weight and named the gram. For practical purposes, therefore, the gram is equal to the weight of one cubic centimeter of distilled water at its maximum density, equal to 15.432 grains or .03527 ounces avoirdupois. The kilogram, or kilo, is the unit of common weight in trade and is a trifle greater than

21/5 pounds avoirdupois. The National prototype standard apportioned to the United States under the direction of the International Committee was received in 1890, and with the meter standard, also of platinum-iridium are in the custody of the Bureau of Standards of the Department of Commerce, Washington, D. C. 

13. The Scale of Tens.-The denominations of the Metric 

System correspond to the orders of the Arabic Notation and are written like decimals, or U. S. Money on a scale of tens, each order of units occupying one place; the lowest denomination at the right. The names mill, cent, and dime, used in 

U. S. money, correspond to milli—, centi—, and deci— in the 

Metric system. Applying the system to our U. S. money we might call the eagle a deca-dollar, since it is ten dollars, the dime a deci-dollar, since it is one-tenth of a dollar, etc. 

14. Square and Cubic Measures.-Units of square meas ures form a scale of hundreds; hence two places must be allowed for each order, and units of cubic or solid measures form a scale of thousands; hence three places must be allowed to each order. It is simply a squaring and cubing of the scale of tens. 

15. Approval and Adoption.-The metric system was introduced in 1793 and definitely adopted by France in 1799. 

It spread rapidly from nation to nation. The United States legalized it on July 26, 1866, and in 1893 adopted the Meter and Kilogram, as the fundamental standards from which the yard and the pound are to be derived. Great Britain also has legalized it. In 1875 the leading Nations signed the treaty of Paris establishing the International Bureau of Weights and Measures providing for new standards of the meter and kilogram and for their international custody. 

John Quincy Adams, years before suggested that a council of nations be called to fix a single invariable and international system for all peoples and all times. This suggestion was realized in the treaty of Paris, the results of which assured the permanency and final success of the metric system, which is in actual use practically in every civilized nation on the globe. For scientific measurements it has become the universal language of the world.

Measurements of Irrigation Water 

The measurement of irrigation water in the Western States has brought about an entirely different and somewhat complicated system of measurement. This system varies in different localities, on account of the variation in the method of payment for water. 

Space does not permit us to give a description of the methods of measurement, or of the devices which have been adopted. We present merely a definition of the various units in use.

Acre Inch. This is one-twelfth of an an acre-foot or the equivalent of a sheet of water one acre in area and one inch deep. One cubic foot per second running continuously for one hour will supply about one acre inch.

Acre Foot. This is equivalent to a body of water one acre in area and one foot deep, or, 43,560 cu. ft. One cubic foot per second (50 So. California inches or forty California

Statute inches) running continuously for 24 hours will supply about 2 acre feet (1.9834 acre ft.) This unit is also used in estimating coal in place.

Cubic Foot Per Second. The equivalent of a stream of water one foot wide and one foot deep flowing at the rate of one foot per second.

Gallon. When the water is pumped the quantity is usually estimated in gallons per minute (G. P. M). One cubic foot per second is about the same as 450 gallons per minute. 

Miner's Inch.-The miner's inch of water does not represent a fixed quantity, being measured generally by the arbitrary standards of the various ditch companies. Generally, however, it is considered to mean the quantity of water that will escape from an opening one inch square through a two inch plank with a steady flow of water standing 6 "in" above the top of the escape aperture, the quantity so discharged amounting to 2274 cubic feet in 24 hours. Locally, miner's inch represents a flow of 1½ cubic feet of water per minute and the statute miner's inch in California is so defined. It is equivalent to a flow of 114 gallons per minute. The old miner's inch in California is equivalent to a flow of nine gallons per minute.

Twenty-Four Hour Inch.-This unit represents one inch 

(the exact amount of which varies with locality and local custom) running for twenty-four hours.

Mensuration or Geometry 1. Any one who has occasion to determine the length of lines, the area of surfaces, or the volume of solids may find in the following definition, rules and examples just the information he needs. 

2. Definition of Terms.-Geometry is that science which treats of the powers and properties of magnitudes in general, where length, breadth and thickness are considered. A Point (.) is a position without dimensions. A line ( -) is a figure of one capacity, namely, length. A superficies (surface) is a figure of two dimensions, length and breadth. 

A solid is a figure of three dimensions, length, breadth and thickness. Parallel means extended in its same direction and equidistant at all points (===). Horizontal means parallel with the water line. Vertical or Perpendicular means parallel with a plumb line. Diagonal means obliquely across a polygon (figure 4).

1.7205 of a five sided frustum; by 2.5981 of a six sided frustum; by 4.8284 of an eight sided frustum. (c) Multiply the average area by the perpendicular height.

Example: Find the cubic feet in a six sided frustum, the two ends of one side being 4 feet by 6 feet and 10 feet high. 

Solution: 

(a) 72+4²+(7X4)=93. (b) 93÷3×2.5981-80.54 sq. ft., area of average base. (c) 80.54X10-805.4 cubic feet, Answer. 

27. A Spheroid is an elongated globe having a fixed and revolving axis. 

To find its area: Multiply the revolving axis by the fixed axis and that by 3.1416.

To find its volume: Multiply the square of the revolving axis by the fixed axis and that by .5236. 

Examples: Find the area and volume of a spheroid, re volving axis 10 inches, fixed axis 20 inches. 

10×20×3.1416-628.32 square inches, Area. 

102×20.5236=1047.2 cubic inches, Volume.
