Land Measure 

1. How to Locate Land.-A tract of land one mile square containing 640 acres is called a section. The public domain of the United States is divided by north and south lines, six miles apart, into strips called ranges. These are again divided by east and west lines, six miles apart, into squares of 36 square miles, called townships. 

2. Designated by Numbers.-The ranges are numbered both east and west from some principal meridian, and the townships in each range are numbered both north and south from a certain base line, for the purpose of easy reference by the land offices. The 36 sections in each township are numbered from the north east corner west, and back on the second tier, east, etc. 

3. School Land.-Section 16 in each township is reserved for school purpose; also Section 26 in some of the newer states. 

4. How to Read and Write Descriptions.-The accompany ing cut will explain how legal descriptions are written. 

A, B, C and D are described as the N.W.4 of Sec. 25. 

A is the N.W.4 of the N.W. 

of Section 25. 

C, D is the S.½ of N.W. of

Section 25. 

X, Y is the N.2 of S.E.4 of

Section 25. 

Z is the N.E.4 of S.W.¼ of 

640 ACRES. 

SEC. 25. 

Section 25. 

Where the government surveys cannot be used a full description must be written out by the county surveyor. 

5. To Find the Number of Acres in a Tract of Land.-Di vide the number of square roads by 160, or the number of square chains by 10. A field 80 rods long and 40 rods wide contains 3200 square roads. 3200-160=20 acres, Ans. 

A tract of land 27 chains 34 links (27.34 ch.) by 12 chains 

84 links (12.84 ch.) contains 27.34×12.84-351.03 sq. ch.; 

351.03-10=35.1 acres, Ans.

How to Locate a Mine 1. Who May Locate a Mine.-Any person of lawful age who is a citizen of the United States or shall have legally declared his intention to become such may locate a mine. 

2. Must Be Actually Discovered.-A mineral bearing ledge, lode or vein must be actually discovered on the claim it is proposed to locate. 

3. The Ground Entitled To.-Unless the width is modified by a law of a local mining district, the ground entitled to with a mining claim is 1,500 feet along the ledge by 300 feet each side of the ledge, or 600 feet wide. 

4. Point of Discovery.-The point of discovery may be within any part of the 1,500 feet. 

5. Boundary Description. In the boundary description of a mine use the terms easterly and westerly, northerly and southerly instead of the more positive terms east, west, etc. 

Make the general description as short as possible, and mention adjacent or neighboring mines, distance and direction, well-known natural objects, or permanent monuments. 

6. Location Notice.-The location notice must be posted at the point of discovery. The corners of claims must be marked by blazed trees, stakes or monuments. 

About five days are allowed to post up location notice, and from ten to thirty days to have the same recorded. Record with the district recorder, or if an unorganized mining district, record with the county recorder. If not in actual personal possession of the proposed location, post location notice and have it recorded as soon as possible. 

7. Assessment Work.-To hold a mine $100 worth of assessment work in labor or improvement must be done on it annually, and the calendar year in which to commence the assessment work begins with the January following the fractional year in which the location is made. Two or more locators on the same ledge may consolidate and do the amount of their combined assessment work on one claim of the group. 

The affidavits of assessment work by two credible witnesses should annually be filed with the district or county recorder. 

When $500 worth of assessment work has been done on a mine a patent to it may be obtained from the Government.

SHORT METHODS OF ARITHMETIC 

Modern business demands practical and concise laborsaving rules and methods. In a great many instances the ordinary methods of calculation prove too slow and cumbersome for the present age and consequently quicker and shorter computations have been devised. In the following short methods of computation we have endeavored to show in a clear and comprehensible manner how calculations may be shortened and accurate results obtained at a great saving of time and labor over the ordinary procedure. Our aim has been to show the "how" rather than the "why" of the operation, and merchants, mechanics, farmers, in fact everybody who uses figures should find valuable information in these pages. 

The Grouping or Lightning Method of Addition. 

The following example will explain the process together with a unique method of disposing of the carrying figures: "Lightning Addition" simply is the ability to see and take in the result of two, three or more figures at a time without stopping to add each figure separately. 

PROCESS: Commencing at the bottom of the right hand column, sum up and add as indicated by the brackets, thus: 10+18=28+18=46. 44 689 274 925 657 542 759 461 632 547 5486 Write the tens or carrying figure 4 over the next column and the unit figure 6 under the column added. Now add the next column in the same way: 13+14=27+17=44+4=48. Again write the carrying figure 

4 over the next column and the right-hand figure 8 directly below the added column. Proceed with the last column as before, viz: 15+18=33+ 

17 50+4 54 which place below the column and the answer 5486 is complete.

To avoid the possibility of mistaking the carrying figure for an entry or sum, a light line may be drawn below the carrying figures, or they may be written smaller than the others and with a lead pencil. 

THE BEST COMBINATIONS.-Group the figures, as conveniently as possible. Sometimes the grouping of only two figures will make better combinations than three or more. Groups of 5, 10, or 15 are always easy to add. When several numbers of the same denomination occur in a column combinations can be made faster by mentally multiplying the like figures and adding to them the unlike ones, as for instance in a column where there are four 5's and one 3, group 4X5+3-23. After a little practise the mind readily grasps the groups of figures in the quickest and most convenient way. Two or more columns can be added at a time in the same manner. 

Never add up a column thus: 7 and 2 are 9 and 1 are 10 and 9 are 19 and 2 are 21 and 7 are 29 and 5 are 33 and 4 are 37 and 9 are 46.

Adding by "Casting Out the Tens." 

This method is sometimes used to relieve the mind when adding long columns of figures. 

EXAMPLE.-Begin at the bottom and add the first column until a sum of 10 or more is reached, thus: 

7+5=12. Cast out or disregard the 10 for the time being by placing a dot or dash over the 5, and continue adding 2+3+4+6=15. Place a dot or dash above the 6 and disregard the 10 and keep on adding 

5+1+2=8. Place the 8 under the column added. Now count up the number of tens dropped (2) and add them to the next column thus: 2+5+1+8=16. Mark the 8, then 6+3+5=14. Mark the 5 and continue 

4+9=13. Mark 9 and conclude with 3+4=7, placing the 7 under the column added. Count up the number of tens dropped which is 3 and add them to the next column which completes the sum 378.

EXAMPLE: 

249227 963685 325436 892705 162231 40010 432170 504360 24 30 25 27 34 32 3569824 

The Civil Service Method of Addition. 

OPERATION 

42 91 56 34 88 15 57 378 

Commence at the right and add each column of figures by itself. Group figures wherever possible. 

For instance the first column equals 24; put down the entire number 24; the next column equals 30; put that down as shown; the next column equals 

25, the next 27, and so on. When all the columns are added and their sums placed as shown, add these sums for the final result.

The advantage of this method is that a person's attention may be drawn to other things while figuring, and then be able to resume work again where he left off. The work is always complete as far as the columns are added. In places of business where there is much talking or other disturbance this method commends itself.

Adding and Subtracting Fractions. 

RULE 1. To find the sum of two fractions with 1 for numerator, add the denominators for the numerator of the answer and multiply them for the denominator.

EXAMPLE: 1/4+ 1/5= 

(4+5=9 4 X 5 20 answer.

RULE 2. To subtract them, subtract the denominators for the numera tor of the answer and multiply them for the denominator.

EXAMPLE: 1/7-1/10= 

7 X 10-70 

Methods of Proving Addition. 

answer Although there are numerous ways of verifying the results of addition there is really no royal road or "short-cut" to absolute proof of the accuracy of the operation. However, the following methods may be of value:

1st. 

After adding the columns upward, add the same downward. 

With different combinations of figures each way, if both sums agree the answer may be assumed as correct. With the Civil 

Service Method of Addition each column can be proved separately by this method. 

2nd. After adding long columns of figures in the usual way, split them in the middle and add each half separately and then combine the results. If the two operations agree the answer is invariably correct. 3rd. 

The sum of the digits of the answer will, when the answer obtained is correct, be found to equal the sum of the units obtained from each line in the example.

Operation: 743-7+4+3=14=1+4=5 235=2+3+5=10=1+0=1 981-9+8+1=18=1+8=9 15=1+5=6 1959-1+9+5+9=24=2+4=6

How to Find the Perpendicular Height of a Right-Angled Triangle When Base and Sum of Perpendicular and 

Hypothenuse Are Known.

PERPENDICULAR HYPOTHENUSE BASE RULE:-From the square of the sum of Perpen dicular and Hypothenuse take the square of the base and divide the difference by twice the sum of Perpendicular and Hypothenuse.

Or, divide the square of the base by the combined length of Perpendicular and Hypothenuse; one-half of the difference between the quotient and the combined length is the Perpendicular. 

EXAMPLE:-A flagpole 90 feet high is broken by the storm in such a manner tha its top reaches the ground 30 feet from the stump, forming a rightangled triangle. How high up is the flagpole broken? 30X30 90 10 

SOLUTION:-90X90-30X30=7200 

7200 2X90=40 Ans. or 90-10 2=40 Ans. 

How to Measure the Distance Across a River, or to Some Other Inaccessible Point. 

The approximate distance across a river or to some other inaccessible point, where the ground is level, may be determined by means of the brim of a hat. Stand on the river bank, close to the water and look across to the other shore. Lower the brim of your hat till its edge just cuts the other bank. In this position and steadying yourself by placing the hand under the chin, turn around carefully until you face level ground on your side of the river, and observe where the edge of your hat again cuts the ground. The distance between that point and where you stand is the breadth of the river.

7 

Another Method to Find the Distance From A to B Across the River.

Measure any distance, AD along the shore. Then measure half the distance between A and D planting a stake at C. At D run a line as far as F and perpendicular to line AD. Then measure along line DF until you reach a point that falls in line with points B and C. Call this point E. Now the triangles ABC and CDE are similar and distance DE equals distance AB across the river.

Lightning Method of Multiplication and Division 

To multiply by 125, divide by 8, and call it thousands, because 125 is % of a thousand. 

To multiply by 122, divide by 8; call it hundreds. 

To multiply by 14, divide by 8; call it tens. 

To multiply by 622, divide by 16, call it thousands. 

To multiply by 64, divide by 16, and call it hundreds. 

To multiply by 314, divide by 32, and call it thousands. 

To multiply by 333 1-3, divide by 3, and call it thousands. 

To multiply by 33 1-3, divide by 3, and call it hundreds. 

To multiply by 3 1-3, divide by 3, and call it tens. 

To multiply by 50, divide by 2, and call it hundreds. 

To multiply by 66 2-3, divide by 15, and call it thousands. 

To multiply by 833 1-3, divide by 15, and call it ten thousands, by annexing four ciphers. 

To multiply by 83 1-3, divide by 12, and call it thousands. 

To multiply by 8 1-3, divide by 12, and call it hundreds because 8 1-3 is 1-12 of a hundred. The reason is similar in each case. 

To multiply by 166 2-3, divide by 6, and call it thousands. 29

To multiply by 16 2-3, divide by 6, and call it hundreds.

To multiply by 12-3, divide by 6, and call it tens. 

To mutiply by 37½, take % of the number, and call it hundreds; 872, % of the number, and call it hundreds, etc.

We simply reverse these methods to divide. To divide by 

10,100, 1,000, etc, we remove the point one, two and three places to the left.

To divide by 25, remove the decimal point two places to the left, and multiply by 4.

Removing the point two places divides by one hundred; hence the quotient is four times too small; hence we remove the point two places, and multiply by four. 

To divide by 2½, remove the point one place to the left, and multiply by 4.

To divide by 125, remove the point three places to the left, and multiply by 8.

To divide by 122, remove the point two places to the left, and multiply by 8. 

To divide by 14, and multiply by 8. remove the point one point to the left, There are about 14 cubic feet in one bushel. hence dividing the number of cubic feet by 14 gives the number of bushels nearly. 

To divide by 133 1-3, remove the point three places to the left, then multipy by 3 and divide by 4. 

To divide by 8 1-3, remove the point two places to the left, and multiply by 12.

The Complement Rule. 

The complement of a number added to the number makes it 10, or 100, or 1000, etc. The complement of 98 is 2, of 91 is 9. To find the product of these two numbers multiply the complements together; and for the other two figures subtract across, either the two from the 91, or the 9 from the 98.

How to Figure up the Plastering of a Room by Cancellation. 

Rule.-Multiply the distance around the room in feet by the height of the room in feet, and this result by the price per square yard, and divide the product by 9, because there are 9 square feet in a square yard. 

For the ceiling, multiply the length of the room by the width of the room in feet, and this by the price per square yard, and divide the product by 9. Add the two results, and you have the cost of plastering the room. 

EXAMPLE:-What would it cost to plaster a room 18 feet wide, 22 feet long, and 9 feet high, at 20 cents per square yard?

The Curious Figure 9. 

Multiply 9 by any figure you like, and the sum of the digits of the product will be 9. Thus, 4X9-36; add the digits, 3+6=9. So it goes up to 11 times 9=99; add these, 9+9=18, add again 8+1=9. You will never be able to get away from the figure nine. 9X454-4086, add the digits and the result is 18, and 8 and 1=9.

Again: Take a row of figures. 

Reverse the order of the figures. 487,632 236,784 Subtract, 250,848 

Add the digits and the result is 27, and 2+7=9. 

If You Don't Believe It-Try It! "Put down the number of your living brothers. Multiply it by two. Add three. Multiply the result by five. Add the number of living sisters. 

Multiply the result by ten. Add the number of dead brothers and sisters. 

Subtract one hundred and fifty from the result." "The right-hand figure will be the number of deaths, the middle figure the number of living sisters, and the left-hand figure the number of living brothers."

The Possibilities of Compound Interest 

There was a mortgage issued out in Idaho, way back in 1861, amounting to $170.00 with interest at the rate of 10% per month.

The conditions were not fulfilled, and at the end of some fifty years, the mortgage was still unsatisfied. With interest at the rate of 10% per month, compounded semiannually, the debt at that time amounted to $45,972,003,182,- 826.50, nearly forty-six trillions of dollars. Let us take an every day case of the man who smokes 2 or 3 10-cent cigars every day. The same money put out at 6% compound interest would grow with startling rapidity as shown in the following table:

Bankers' 60 Day Interest Method 

In banking a great many loans are made and interest figured on 30, 60, and 90 days time. The following is a simple method: 

RULE 1. To find the interest on any amount for 60 days, move the decimal point two places to the left in the principal and the result will be the interest at 6%. 

2. For 30 days divide by 2; for 15 days divide by 4; for 90 days increase by 2; for 120 days multiply by 2. 

3. For any other rate than 6% increase or decrease result as shown in previous table.

EXAMPLE: 

What is the interest on $350 for 90 days at 7%?

SOLUTION: 

$350 at 6% for 60 days.. 

For 90 days increased by 2... $3.50 1.75 5.25 .88 $6.13 

Interest for 90 days at 6%.. 

For 7% increase by 1/6.. 

Interest at 7%.......

NOTE: The above rules are based on 360 days to the year, whereas it actually contains 365 days. To find the exact or accurate interest decrease the result obtained by 1/73 of itself and the answer will be as though the interest had been originally figured on the basis of 365 days to the year.

But in sums of $500 or less or with times of 30 days or less, the difference between the 360 and 365 days basis is too small to make appreciable difference. Besides, 360 days are now generally accepted as a basis.

How to Use the Interest Tables 

1. The interest on any sum of money, and for any length of time, may be obtained, by adding to or doubling any certain sum, or length of time in the tables, viz: If the interest on a certain sum of money at 

8 per cent for a given time should be $28, one-half of $28 or $14 would equal the interest at 4 per cent, etc. 

2. If the interest at 6 per cent should amount to $26 on a certain sum of money for a given time, twice that amount or $52 would equal the interest at 12 per cent, and half that amount would equal the interest at 

3 per cent. 

3. The tables are computed on the principle of 360 days in a year, the rule adopted by bankers and merchants throughout the entire country. 

4. When the fraction of interest is a half. cent or more, a whole cent is taken, but when less than a half cent, nothing is charged.

WHAT A BUSINESS MAN OUGHT TO KNOW ABOUT PRINTING* 

1. Every business man resorts to some form of printing in order to carry on his business. When the average man orders stationery, or plans an advertising campaign the conversation with the printer or the written quotation strikes him as being a meaningless jumble of picas, ems, points, layouts, zincs, screens, reams, and equally unintelligible terms. The following pages have been prepared with special reference to the needs of the beginner, athough even the skilled craftsman will find them a source of convenient reference. 

2. Type Measurement.-The pica is 12 points long or 1/6 

of an inch. The em is a unit of measurement based on the square of the size of the individual type. It is a unit of area to determine the amount of matter set in a page of type. The point is measured up and down, not by width. An inch of type space measured up and down contains 72 points. 

Dividing 72 by the size of any type in points gives us the number of lines of that type which can be set solid, to an inch. For example, by dividing 72 by 8 we find that 9 lines of 8 point can be set, solid, in a single inch. 

3. Copy and Layout.-By copy is meant such matter as is to be arranged in type form. The layout consists of a dummy indicating the position of the headings, text and illustrations, which the finished product shall contain. 

4. Illustrations.-A half-tone is a reproduction of a photograph or wash drawing, on copper plates, to be used in printing. The design is first photographed thru a screen of fine lines, and the negative then printed on a copper plate and etched in acid. Rough paper requires coarse screen; highly finished stock takes a fine screen. Zinc etchings are reproduced from pen drawings, wood engravings, and printed pages, by exactly the same process as half tones except that no screen is used in making the negative. The Ben 

Dey process is one by which zinc plates are shaded and tinted for printing purposes. By the color process plates can be *Much of the material used in this chapter is by special permission of the W. B. Conkey Company from their book "What a Business Man should 

Know about Printing and Bookmaking."

PRINTING INFORMATION 

475 made to reproduce in several different colors. An electrotype is not an engraving. It is a metal reproduction of a half tone, etching, cut or type page for printing purposes. 

5. How to Determine the Dimensions of a Cut.-Suppose you have a photograph to be reduced to a certain width and you want to know how high the cut will be. Draw a figure having the same dimensions as the photograph in this manner: B E

Now draw the diagonal line A C. Next mark off on the bottom line the width A E of the cut you desire made. The point at which the perpendicular F E touches the diagonal A C will give you the height of your cut when reduced. If the height is known the width can be determined in the same way.

NAMES, SIZES, AND WEIGHTS OF PAPER.-Antique finished paper is practically unfinished. Laid has a low finish but is watermarked. 

Eggshell is antique finished paper which has been ironed. Machine finish is smoother than antique having been calendered or ironed. English finish gives a smooth surface without gloss. S & SC means that the paper has been sized to make it glossy, and super-calendered to make it smooth. 

Enameled paper is coated to fill up the pores. Dull Coated is made in the same way but is dull instead of glossy. The following tables give detailed information as to names, sizes, and weights:

USEFUL  Roof Elevations 

The Gable is a space in the form of a triangle on the end of a building, with a common double roof. 

The Pitch of the roof is the relation which the height of the ridge above the level of the roof-plates bears to the span, or the distance between the studs on which the roof rests. 

Quarter Pitch is a roof that is one-fourth, a third pitch one that is one-third, and a half pitch one that is one-half as high as the width of the building.

The Span is the width of the building. 

To Find the Area of the Gable End 24 FEET 

RULE: Multiply the width of the building by the height of the roof and take one-half of the result for the number of square feet. If the roof is "quarter pitch" find the area in square feet by multiplying width of the roof by % of itself. 

Length of Rafters

The pitch and span should be figured so as to result in the length of a rafter that cuts with the least waste in material. A few inches may often result in a great saving. 

The length of rafters for the common pitches can be determined by the following table of ratios. To the lengths thus obtained, however, must be added the extension of the rafters at the caves.

How to Find the Length and Bevel of Rafters With Steel Square 

1. 20 Place your steel square on a board (say the building is 40 feet long), 20 inches from the corner one way, and 7 inches the other, and mark it as shown in the above figure. Now the angle at c will be the bevel of the upper end, and the angle at d the bevel at the lower end of the rafter. 

2. Length of Rafter. -The length will be from a to b on the outer edge of the board. The 20 inches shows the 20 feet, or half of the width of the building; the 7 inches the 7 foot rise. Now the distance from a to b, on the edge of the board, is 21 inches, two-twelfths and one-quarter of a twelfth (always use a square with inches on one side divided into twelfths), therefore this rafter will be 21 feet and 24 inches long. Roofing 

How to Find the Number of Shingles Required For a Roof. 

RULE: Multiply the length of the ridge pole by twice the length of one rafter and if the shingles are to be exposed four inches to the weather multiply by 9; if exposed 4½ inches multiply by 

8; if exposed 5 inches multiply by 

71/5 and the result will be the number of shingles required for the roof.

NOTE: Shingles are 16 inches long and average about 4 inches wide. They are put up in bundles of 250 each. 900 shingles laid 4 inches or 800 shingles laid 4½ inches, or 720 shingles laid 5 inches to the weather, will cover 

100 square feet.

EXAMPLE: How many shingles 

I will it take to cover a roof 30 feet long with the rafters on each side 14 feet; shingles exposed 4 inches?

SOLUTION: 30X14X2X8=6720 

shingles.

Stone Work 

A cord of stone like a cord of wood is 8 feet long, 4 feet wide and 4 feet high and contains 128 cubic feet. 

A perch of stone work is 162 feet long, 1½ feet high and 1 foot thick and contains 244 cubic feet.

Usually 24 cubic feet of mortar and filling are contained in each perch of stone-work.

How to Find the Number of Perches in a Wall 

RULE: Multiply together length, height and thickness in feet, and divide this product by 244 (or multiply by .0404) and the result will be the number of perches in the wall. 

EXAMPLE: A wall is 40 feet long, 15 feet high and 2 feet thick. 

How many perches?

SOLUTION: 40X15X2÷244-48 12/25 perches, or 

40X15X2X.0404-48.48.

How to Find the Number of Cords of Stone in a Pile 

RULE: Multiply together the length, width and height in feet and divide by 128.

EXAMPLE: How many cord of stone in a pile 24 feet long, 8 feet wide, and 4 feet high?

SOLUTION: 24X8X4÷128-6 cord. 

Brick-Work 

Bricks are of different sizes, varying according to custom of State or locality. The Baltimore Brick is 84 x 4% x 2% inches; the Maine brick 

7½ x 3% x 2% inches; the Michigan brick 8½ x 4% x 2% inches; the New 

York brick 8 x 32 x 24 inches, and the Fire brick 9% x 45% x 2% inches.

They are estimated and sold by the thousand. A common brick is 8 inches long, 4 inches wide and 2 inches thick, and contains 64 cubic inches. Twenty-seven bricks make one cubic foot of wall without mortar, or 22½ bricks one cubic foot with mortar, the mortar filling about 

1/6 of the space.

Five courses of common brick with mortar equal one foot in height on a chimney.

Laid flat it takes 42 bricks to a square foot; on edge it requires 9. 

One cubic foot of brick work with common mortar weighs from 100 to 

110 pounds.

A bricklayers hod will hold 20 common bricks; the ordinary load, however, is 16 walling or 12 facing bricks.

One cask or barrel of lime mixed with 5% yards of sand will make sufficient mortar to lay 1,000 bricks.

How to Find the Number of Common Bricks in a Wall or Building 

RULE: Multiply together the length, height and thickness of the wall in feet and the result again by 22½ and the product will be the number of bricks in the wall.

For a wall 8 inches thick, multiply the length and height in feet together and that result by 14 and the product will equal the number of bricks.

When doors and windows occur in the wall, multiply their height, width and thickness together, and deduct the result from the solid contents of the wall before multiplying by 22% or 14 as the case may be. 

EXAMPLE: How many bricks in a wall 60 feet long, 15 feet high and 2 feet thick? 

SOLUTION: 60 x 15 x 2 x 22½ 40,500 bricks.

EXAMPLE: 

8 inches thick?

SOLUTION: 

How many bricks in a wall 40 feet long, 10 feet high, and 

40 x 10 x 145,600 bricks.

Lathing the 

Lathing is estimated by square yard. One-half the surface of openings is usually deducted. 

Laths are 4 feet long 1½ inches wide and are put up in bundles of 50 each. Placed about % of an inch apart 16 are estimated to the square yard or a bundle to 

3 square yards.

How to Find the Number of Laths to Cover a Room

RULE: Find the number of square yards in the room and multiply by 16; the result will equal the number of laths necessary to cover the room. 

EXAMPLE: How many laths required for a room 12 x 10 feet and 9 feet high? 

12 x 2 plus 10 x 2 equals 44 feet distance around room. 

44 x 99 equals 44 square yards for walls. 12 x 10 9 equals 13 1/3 square yards for ceiling. 44 plus 13 1/3 x16 equals 917 laths or 18 1/3 bundles. 

Plastering 

Plastering is usually figured by the square yard. 

Six bushels of lime, 40 cubic feet of sand and 12 bushels of hair will plaster 100 square yards with two coats of mortar.

One-third of a barrel of stucco will hard-finish 100 square yards of plastering. 'In plastering, deductions for openings such as doors, and windows are usually not allowed, because the extra work of finishing around them balances the material saved. However, some deduct one-half the surface of the openings.

How to Figure the Cost of Plastering a Room RULE: Multiply the sum of the length and width of the room in feet by 2 for the distance around it and this product by the height dividin the result by 9 for the number of square yards in the walls. Then multiply the length and width of the room in feet together, and divide by 9 for the number of square yards in the ceiling. 

Add the two results and multiply by the price per square yard and you have the cost of plastering the room. 

EXAMPLE: What would it cost to plaster a room 22 feet long, 18 feet wide and 9 feet high at 50 cents per square yard? 

SOLUTION: 22 plus 18 x 2 equals 80 distance around room. 

80 x 9 9 80 No. of square yards in walls. 

22 x 18 9 44 No. of square yards in ceiling. 

80 plus 44X50 equals $62.00.

How to Make the Curves for Brick and Stone Arches 

Measure the width, and draw the figure as above. If the points in 

1, 2, 3, 4, etc., are equal on both sides, the curve will be an exact part of a circle.

Definitions for Mechanics 

An angle is the opening between two lines that direction. have a different

When two straight lines cross each other so as to form four equal angles, each angle is called a right angle. 

An acute angle is less than a right angle. An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle.

A triangle is a figure having three sides. 

A surface having four straight lines and four right angles is called a rectangle.

A rectangle whose sides are equal is called a square. 

The perimeter of a figure is the distance around it. 

An arc is any part of the circumference of a circle. 

A chord is a line drawn through the circle and ending on the circumference. 

A quadrant is a quarter circle.

A tangent is a line that touches a circle but does not cut it. 

A polygon is a figure bounded by straight lines. 

The following figures show the principal polygons used with numbers of sides of each:

Pentagon. Hexagon. Heptagon. Octagon. 

Nonagon. 

Decagon.

Concentric circles are circles that have the same center and the space included between their circumference is called a ring. 

Useful and Practical Rules for Mechanics To Find the Diagonal of a Square. 

Multiply the side of the square by 1.41421.

To Find the Circumference of a Circle. 

Multiply the diameter by 31/7 or multiply the area by 12.566 and extract the square root of the product. 

To Find the Area of a Circle. 

Multiply the square of the radius by 31/7.

The radius is one-half the diameter. 

To Find the Diameter of a Circle. 

Divide the circumference by 31/7.

To Draw a Circle Through Three Points. 

Let the three points be A, B and C. Join A and B and B and C by straight lines. At the middle points of these lines draw lines perpendicular to them. This can easily be done by using a square. Produce these lines and let them meet at O. O is the center of the circle. With 

O as center and OA as radius construct the circle. 

To Find the Area of any Polygon. 

Find the center of the figure and multiply distance around the figure (perimeter) by one-half of the diameter and the result will equal the area. B 

Inscribed and Circumscribed Squares.

The square described within the circle is exactly half as large as the square described outside of the circle, that is the described one is one half the area of the circumscribed square.

The square C D NK contains exactly one-half the area of the square A C M B. 

It is thus easily seen that the area of the crcumscribed square (that is the square AC M B) is equal to the square of the diameter of the circle.

How to Lay Off Small Lots of Land. 

Farmers and gardners often find it necessary to lay off small portions of land for the purpose of experimenting with different crops, fertilizers, etc. To such the following rules will be helpful: 

One acre contains 160 sq. rods, or 4,840 sq. yards, or 43,560 sq. feet. 

One acre it will take 208 7/10 feet each way. 

One-half acre it will take 1472 feet each way. 

One-third acre it will take 1201½ feet each way. 

One-fourth acre it will take 104% feet each way. 

One-eighth acre it will take 734 feet each way.

How to Make an Ice Chest. 

Take two dry goods boxes, one enough smaller than the other to leave a space of three or four inches all around when placed inside the larger box. Pack this space between the two boxes closely with sawdust and make a heavy cover to fit neatly inside the top of the larger box. A small pipe inserted in the bottom of the chest will carry off the waste water. For family use and all ordinary purposes it will be as serviceable as refrigerators costing twenty-five times as much. 1. 

Rules for Measuring Lumber 

A FOOT OF LUMBER is one foot long, one foot wide and one inch thick. This is called a Board Foot. 

2. PIECE STUFF OR DIMENSION STUFF is lumber that is two or more inches thick and of uniform width and length.

3. 

SCANTLING is usually from three to four inches wide and from two to four inches thick. 4. 

JOIST is two-inch lumber of any width. 

5. PLANK is two inches in thickness and wider than a scantling. 

Rule for 12-foot Boards: Find the width of the boards in inches and add together, and the sum obtained will be equal to the number of feet in the pile. (Each inch in width equals one foot of lumber.)

Note: Use no fractions. If a board is between 9 and 10 inches wide, but nearer 9 than 10, call it 9; if nearer 10 than 9, call it 10. If it is 

92, call it either 9 or 10.

For 14-foot boards add the width of the boards in inches, and to the sum add 1/6 of itself, and the result will equal the number of feet in the pile.

For 16-foot lumber, add the width of the boards in inches and to that sum add 1/3 of itself, and you will have the number of feet in the pile. 

Example: How many feet of lumber in ten boards, 9 inches wide and 

16 feet long?

SOLUTION: 

10X9 90. 1/3 of 90 30. 

30+90=120, the number of feet. 

30 FEET 10 FEET 20 FEET 

10 FEET How to Find the Height of a Tree. 

Suppose you desire a log 30 feet long-measure off from the base of the tree 30 feet (allow for the height of the stump), then measure 10 feet back, and put your 10-foot pole at B; let some one hold it the height of the stump from the ground, then put your eye at E, looking over the top of the pole at C, and where the eye strikes the tree at D, will be 

30 feet from A.

N. B. This rule will apply to any tree, or any height. The principles hold true in any case. 

How to Find the Height by Measuring the Shadow. 

RULE: Measure a pole, and hold it perpendicular in the sun, and measure its shadow, then measure the shadow of the tree whose height is desired. Then multiply the length of the pole by the length of the tree's shadow, and divide the product by the length of the shadow of the pole, and the result will be the height of the tree. 

EXAMPLE: If a pole 3 feet long casts a shadow 42 feet long, what is the height of a tree whose shadow measures 180 feet? 

SOLUTION: 180x3÷42=120 feet, the height of the tree.

How to Find Number of Feet (Board Measure) in a Log 

RULE: Subtract from the diameter of the log in inches, 4 inches (for slabs); one-fourth of this result squared and multiplied by the length in feet will give the correct amount of lumber made from any log. 

EXAMPLE: How many feet of lumber can be made from a log which is 36 inches in diameter and 10 feet long?

SOLUTION: From 36 (diameter) subtract 4 (for slabs)=32. Take 

4 of 32=8, which multiplied by itself equals 64. Then multiply 64 by 

10 (length)=640. Ans.

ROPP'S RULE: Square the diameter in inches and subtract 60 from the result, then multiply this result by the length and divide by 2, and cut off the right hand figure.

How to Use the Log Table 

First find the average diameter of the log by adding together the two ends of the log, in inches; then divide by two, and the result will equal the average diameter, and then apply the above table. 

EXAMPLE: How many feet of lumber are there in a log 15 inches at one end and 21 inches at the other, and 22 feet long? 

SOLUTION: 15+21=36; one-half of 36=18 inches, the average diameter.

Then refer to the column under 18 inches opposite to 22 and you will find the answer-269 feet.

CEMENT AND HOW TO USE IT 

The word "Concrete" itself is of Latin origin, meaning "grown together" and implies a body formed by separate particles of different materials combined into a solid mass. 

Kinds of Cement.- 

There are two general kinds, Natural and Portland Cement. The raw material from which natural cement is made is found in a natural state and is made by calcining (burning) cement rock, but the temperature required is considerably lower than that needed for making Portland Cement. 

Portland Cement, however, is the kind used almost exclusively in this country and is manufactured in about 25 different states. 

The raw materials used by different plants vary greatly, nor is the chemical composition the same, so that it cannot be reduced to a formula. 

What Portland Cement is.-So far, then, as it is possible to give an accurate definition, Portland cement may be defined as any cement which, on being tested, will manifest the characteristic properties that engineers have agreed to associate with the name "Portland" and which will meet the requirements that have been accepted as standard. 

Raw Materials.-As a matter of fact, however, the raw materials are limestone (also chalk and marl, which are really forms of limestone), clay, shale and slate, also blast-furnace slag. These in proper proportion are heated to a temperature at which melting begins (2000° to 4000°F). 

The resulting cement clinker is then ground to an impalpable powder to which a very small percentage of gypsum is added.

How to Use Cement.-In using cement for concrete work it is necessary to mix it with water and aggregates-these aggregates consist of sand, cruched stone or gravel. That is to say, you must use either cement, sand and gravel or cement, sand and crushed stone, or any material that can take the place of gravel or crushed stone. These must be thoroughly mixed and the proper amount of water added. 

The Proportions required for different kinds of cement or concrete construction are shown on the preceding page. 

For example for a rich mixture 1:2:4 means one part cement, 2 parts sand and 4 parts gravel or crushed stone.

By Consistency is meant the relative wetness of the mixture. VERY WET is mushy enough to run readily off the shovel. MEDIUM WET is wet enough to make it jelly-like. 

DRY MIXTURE is about like damp earth used generally for foundations, etc. 

Cisterns, Tanks and Barrels

In measuring cisterns, tanks, reservoirs, barrels, etc., the barrel is figured at 31½ gallons and the hogshead at 63 gallons. 

A gallon of water weighs about 8 pounds avoirdupois, and contains 231 cubic inches.

A pint is generally estimated as weighing a pound. 

How to Find the Capacity of Round Cisterns and Tanks. 

RULE: Multiply the square of the diameter in feet by the depth in feet and this result by .1865 for the capacity in barrels, or by 5.875 (5%) for the capacity in gallons. 

EXAMPLE: How many barrels will a round cistern, 5 feet in diameter and 8 feet deep hold? How many gallons?

SOLUTION: 5 x 5 x 8 200, 200 x .1865 37.3 barrels. 

200 x 5.875=1175 gallons.

How to Find the Capacity of Square Cisterns, Tanks and Watering Troughs. 

RULE: Multiply the length, width and depth in feet together and this product by 7% (or for exact results by 7.48) and the result will be the number of gallons. 

For capacity in barrels multiply by .2375.

For small tanks and troughs reduce feet to inches then multiply the dimensions together and divide result by 231 for gallons. 

EXAMPLE: How many gallons will a square cistern 6 x 6 and 8 feet deep hold? How many barrels?

SOLUTION: 6 x 6 x 9=288x7=2160 gallons. 

EXAMPLE: 

288 x .2375 68.4 barrels.

What is the capacity of a small watering trough 6 feet long 2 feet wide and 10 inches deep? 

SOLUTION: 6 x 12 x 2 x 12 x 10=17280 square inches. 

17280231 75 gallons nearly.

How to Find the Capacity of a Tapering Round or Square Cistern or Tank. 

RULE: Square both the upper and lower diameter and to the sum of their squares add the product of one diameter multiplied by the other. 

Divide the result by 3 and multiply by .7854 for the average base of a 32

round tapering tank. Then multiply this product by the depth in feet and the result by 7.48 for the number of gallons. 

Divide this product by 31% for the number of barrels. 

NOTE: For tapering square tanks, and cisterns proceed in the same manner except that the multiplication by .7854 should be omitted. 

EXAMPLE: How many gallons will a tapering round tank hold whose lower diameter is 12, upper diameter 8, and depth 10 feet? 12x12=144 8x8 64 8x12 96 3)304 

101 1/3 x .7854-79.5872 

79.5872 x 10 =795.872 

795.872 x 7.485953.12 gallons.

SOLUTION: 

10x10=100 14x14-196 10x14-140 3)436 145 1/3 145 1/3 x 12= 1744

How to Find Contents of Barrels and Casks. 

RULE: Add together the diameters of the bung and head in inches and divide by 2 for the mean or average diameter. Then multiply the square of the mean diameter by the length of barrel or cask in inches and this result by 34. Cut off the four right hand figures and it will equal the number of gallons. 

EXAMPLE: How many gallons in a barrel whose bung diameter is 

22 inches, head diameter 18 inches, and length 30 inches. 

SOLUTION: 22+18÷2-20 average diameter. 

20x20x30x34=40.8000 or 40 4/5 gallons.

Papering 

Wall paper is sold by the roll: border by the yard. Single rolls are 

24 feet long and 1% feet or 18 inches wide and contain 36 square feet or 

4 square yards.

Double rolls are 48 feet or 16 yards long. Mostly all paper is made up in double rolls.

When a room has many doors and windows their width should be deducted from the total distance around the room before finding the number of strips, but where there are only a few such openings no allowance is made, because there is always waste in cutting the paper. 

How to Find the Required Amount of Paper for a Room 

RULE: Measure the distance around the room in feet; deduct the width of doors and windows: 2/3 of the remainder will equal the number of strips required for the walls. Divide this number by the number of strips that can be cut from one roll and it will give the number of rolls required for the walls. 

For the ceiling take 2/3 of the width of the room in feet for the number of strips required. Then find how many strips the length of the room can be cut from a roll and divide the number of strips required by the number of strips from one roll which gives the number of rolls necessary for the ceiling. If a fraction is over always add another roll. 

When the room is very long it may be a saving to run the strips crosswise. For border divide the distance around the room in feet by 3 for the number of yards.

EXAMPLE: How many rolls of paper and yards of border are necessary to paper a room 12 feet long 11 feet wide and 8 feet high? 

SOLUTION: 

12 x 2 plus 11 x 2 equals 46 feet, distance around room. 46 x 2/3 equals 30 2/3 or 31 strips. 

24 feet equals length of 1 roll 8 height of room equals 3 strips from roll. 

31 strips 3 strips from roll equals 10 1/3 or 11 rolls for walls. 

11 X 2/3 equals 71/3 or 8 strips for ceiling. 

24 12 equals 2 strips from 1 roll. 

82 equals 4 rolls for ceiling. 

463 equals 15 1/3 or 16 yards border. Distance

Carpets 

Ingrain Carpet is 36 inches or one yard wide. Brussels and 

Velvet Carpets are 27 inches or 

34-yard wide.

How to Find the Number of 

Yards of Carnet to Cover a

Floor: 

RULE: Divide the width of the room by the width of the carpet in feet. This will give the number of strips necessary. If there is a fraction over in the division add another strip. Then multiply the number of strips by the length of the room in feet and divide by 3; the result will equal the number of yards of carpeting to cover the floor. If there is any waste in matching figures, add this to the length of the room before multiplying by the number of strips. 

For Brussels Carpet it is best to reduce the width of the room to inches and divide by 27, the width of Brussels in inches, for the number of strips. Then multi- ply the length of the room in feet by the number of strips and divide by 3 for the number of yards necessary to cover the floor. 

It is sometimes more economical or desirable to run the strips crosswise. In that case divide the length of the room by the width of the carpet and multiply this, the number of strips, by the width of the room before dividing by 3. 

EXAMPLE: A room is 12 feet 9 inches by 14 feet 6 inches. How many yards Ingrain Carpet are required to cover the floor?

SOLUTION: 124÷3-44 or 5 strips. 

142X5÷3 24 1/6 yards.

EXAMPLE: How many yards of Brussels Carpet will it take to cover a floor 15 feet 9 inches by 10 feet 2 inches in the most economical way when there is no waste in matching?

SOLUTION: 

10 feet 2 inches equals 122 inches. 

122 27 4 14/27 or 5 strips. 

15X5÷3-264 yards lengthwise.

How to Write Your Name on Iron Tools 

1. Melt a little beeswax or hard tallow and pour it on the iron at the place intended to be marked. After the wax or tallow cools take an awi or sharp piece of iron and write your name on it. 

2. Pour a little nitric acid on the wax. where you have written your 

Then wipe off the wax, name, and allow it to remain a few moments. and your name remains indelibly marked as written in the wax. 

3. Be careful and allow none of the acid to come in contact with your clothes or hands.

How to Write Your Name on Glass 

1. Apply beeswax and write your name as in the above. 

2. Then instead of nitric acid, apply hydrofluoric acid and your name will remain permanently written on the clear surface of the glass. 

How to Make a Hole in Glass 

Place a piece of stiff clay or putty on the part where you wish to make the hole. Make a hole in the putty reaching to the glass and just the size you want the hole in the glass. Pour a little molten lead into this hole and the piece of glass will drop out. This will not fail unless the glass is very thick.

One coat, or priming will take, per 100 yards of painting, 40 pounds of lead, 2 gallons of oil, and 1 quart of spirits of turpentine. Two-coat work, 40 pounds of lead and 2 gallons of oil. Three-coat, the same quantity as two-coat; so that a fair estimate for 100 yards of three-coat work would be 120 pounds of Itad and 6 gallons of oil. 

One gallon priming color will cover 50 superficial yards; white zinc, 50 yards; white paint, 44 yards; lead color, 50 yards; black paint, 50 yards; stone color, 4 yards; yellow paint, 44 yards; blue color, 45 yards; green paint, 45 yards; bright emerald green, 25 yards; bronze green, 75 yards.

One pound of paint will cover about 4 superficial yards the first coat, and about 6 each additional coat. One pound of putty, for stopping, every 20 yards. One gallon of tar and one pound of pitch will cover 12 yards, interchange the first coat, and 17 yards each additional coat. A square yard of new brick wall requires, for the first coat of paint in oil, 4 pound; for the second, 3 pounds; for the third, 4 pounds.

A day's work on the outside of a building is 100 yards of the first coat, and 80 yards of either second or third coat. An ordinary door, including casings, will, on both sides, make 8 to 10 yards of painting, or about 5 yards to a door without the casings. An ordinary window makes about 

22 or 3 yards.

The first named color is always the principal ingredient, and the others follow in the order of their importance. 

Thus in mixing a limestone tint, white is the principal ingredient, and the red the color of which the least is needed. The exact proportions of each color must be determined by experiment with a smaller quantity. It is best to have the principal ingredient thick, and add to it the other paints thinner.

1. The Business of Farming.-A successful farmer must know many things and be able to perform numerous duties outside of the things he knows and does in connection with the tilling of the soil and the raising of live-stock. He must be something of a mechanic, a carpenter, a painter, mason, and general jack of all trades. He is the executive, advertising, sales, purchasing and accounting departments of a big business, all in one. This being the case every page of the BUSINESS GUIDE contains something of value to him, and even though this particular chapter is intended expressly for him, it nevertheless includes information and tables which will be found valuable in any other line of business.

2. Estimates.-Every farmer has his own method of figuring. He can tell at a glance the weight of an animal. 

He figures this bin will hold so many bushels of grain, and that corn crib so much corn. Usually his estimates are י י near enough to the truth for all practical purposes, but there are times when it is dangerous and costly to guess. 

At sales, and on other special occasions when any inaccuracy may mean a loss in dollars and cents the farmer needs a reliable source of information. All the following short methods of figuring, the rules for estimating, and the ready reference tables have been assembled in one chapter to meet this very real need. They are accurate, time tested, and absolutely reliable.

How Much Advantage is Given in Changing the Evener 

53 Caution.-In moving the center pin of an evener one inch toward one of the end pins it changes the draft twice as much as it does to move one of the end pins one inch toward the center pin. Or in other words, moving the center pin changes the draft twice as much as changing one of the end pins or clevises.

An average evener is 42 inches in length. 

Now if the center pin is moved one inch from the center to the right or left, the horse drawing on the short end will pull about 2/40 more than the horse drawing on the opposite end. 

If one of the end pins is moved one inch the difference will be about 1/40. 

EXAMPLE:-If a team of horses draws 2000 pounds, and the center pin is moved one inch from the center, what part of the whole load will each draw? 

2000X2/40=100 pounds, the difference. 

50+1000-1050 pounds. 1000-50 950 pounds.

Hence the horse at the short end of the evener draws 1050 lbs., and the other horse draws 950 lbs.

The draft on a 14-inch plow, plowing 4 inches deep, is about 1000 lbs.; 

5 inches deep, 1250 lbs. ; 6 inches deep, 1500 lbs.

How to Measure Hay, Straw and Grain 

*A ton of dry hay is variously estimated from 400 to 500 cubic feet to the ton.

To be on the safe side it is best to estimate about 500 cubic feet to the ton. 

Hay in a Mow

RULE:-Multiply the length in feet by the height in feet and this by the breadth in feet; and divide the result by 500 and you have the number of tons.

EXAMPLE:-How many tons of hay in a mow 20 feet long, 10 feet high, and 15 feet wide?

SOLUTION:-20X10X15÷500=6. 

Ans.

How to Estimate the Number of Tons in a Stack 

RULE:-Multiply the length in feet by the width in feet, and this by one-half the height, and divide the product by 300. 

EXAMPLE:-How many tons of hay in a stack 20 feet long, 12 feet high, and 15 feet wide?

SOLUTION:-20X6X15÷300-6 tons. Ans. 

How to Estimate the Contents of a Round Stack 

RULE:-Multiply the square of the distance around the stack in yards by 4 times the height in yards, and point off two places from the right, and this will be the number of cubic yards in the stack, which divided by 20 will equal the number of tons.

507. EXAMPLE:-How many tons of hay in a stack, distance around the bulge, 25 yards, and height, 9 yards? 

SOLUTION:-25X25-625, then 625X36=22,500, pointing off two places makes 225, then 225÷20=114 tons. Ans. *Some authorities allow only 350 cubic feet for a ton of timothy hay when thoroughly settled. Others allow 343 to 420. For millet allow only 

216 cubic feet to the ton. The fact is, hay in stack or mow can only be approximately ascertained by measurement. 

How to Find the Number of Bushels in a Bin or Box 

RULE:-Multiply together the length, breadth and depth in feet and this product again by 8 and cut off the right hand figure. The result will be the number of bushels. 

For more exact results multiply by 80357 and cut off the five right hand figures or, multiply together the length, breadth and depth in inches and divide the result by 2150.4 the number of cubic inches in a bushel. 

EXAMPLE:-How many bushels in a bin 12 feet long, 10 feet wide and 

6 feet deep?

SOLUTION:-12X10X6X8=576 bushels or 

12X10X6X80357-578 bushels. 

12X12=144 length in inches. 

10X12=120 width in inches. 

6X12 72 depth in inches. 

144X120X72=1244160 Sq. inches. 

12441602150.4-578.57 bushels.

How to Find the Contents of a Wagon Box 

A common wagon box 10 feet long and 3 feet wide will hold 2 bushels for every inch in depth. 

RULE: Multiply the depth of the wagon box in inches by 2 and the result will be the number of bushels.

If the wagon box is 11 feet long add one-tenth of the number of bushels to itself. 

EXAMPLE:-How many bushels of grain will a wagon box hold 10 feet long, 3 feet wide and 22 inches deep?

SOLUTION:-22X2-44 bushel. 

11 ft. long: 44÷10 4.4. 

44+4.4 48.4 bushel. 

Shrinkage of Grain

In deciding to keep their grain farmers should take into account the shrinkage. Wheat will shrink two quarts to the bushel in six months from the time it is threshed. Corn shrinks much more, the shrinkage being nearly one-fifth of the whole amount. So that for corn forty cents from the field is as much as fifty cents in March. In the case of potatoes, the loss from October to May is about thirty-three per cent. 

Bushels 

The dimensions of the bushel are 18½ inches inner diameter; 19% inches outer diameter. and 8 inches deep: and when heaped the cone is not to be less than 6 inches high, which makes a heaped bushel equal to 

14 struck ones.

All methods of estimating the contents of silos are approximate. The variety of corn, how rank the growth, how mature when put up, whether light or heavy eared, how short it was cut up, how fast the silo was filled, how well it was tramped, how much water was added, and many other factors affect the weight of the ensilage. They should be borne in mind when using the accompanying table.

Rule: For a more accurate estimate find the true diameter in feet. 

Multiply the square of the diameter by 0.7854 to give the square feet of area, and this multiplied by the depth in feet will give the capacity in cubic feet.

Now multiply each cubic foot by 33.4 lbs. for the first five feet of depth, 36.7 lbs. for the second five, 39.2 lbs. for the third five, 40.8 lbs. for the fourth five, 41.6 lbs. for the fifth five, 42.6 lbs. for the sixth five, and 43 lbs. for all below the thirty foot depth. This gives you the weight in pounds. The weights for each five feet may be averaged and the whole silo estimated in one operation. 

Example: How many tons of silage in a silo 12 feet in diameter and 

36 feet high, when it is three-quarters full? 

Solution: 12X12=144X0.7854-113.09X27=3053.43 cu. ft. 

Average weight for each 5 feet-38.3X3053.43=116946.36 lbs. or 58.47 tons. Ans. 미래 

​Parth How to Measure Ear Corn in the Crib. 

Measuring corn in the crib is at best an estimate. Much depends upon the condition of the corn. A bushel of corn means either a bushel of shelled corn or ear corn enough to make a bushel of shelled corn. 

RULE:-Multiply the length in feet by the height in feet and that again by the width in feet, multiply the result by 4 and cut off the right hand figure and you have the contents in bushels of shelled corn. 

EXAMPLE:-How many bushels of shelled corn in a crib of corn in the ear, 20 feet long, 10 feet high and 8 feet wide?

SOLUTION:-20X10X8X4=640.0 bushels. Ans. 

This is the result when 22 cubic feet or 4320 cubic inches are taken for a bushel.

Counting 4200 cubic inches in a bushel multiply by. 4100 46 66 66 66 66 4000 66 66 66 66 66 46 66 3900 66 "6 66 06 66 66 46 3800 46 66 66 66 66 66 411 421 432 448 455

In each of these cases cut off the three right hand figures after multiplying. The result will be the number of bushels. There is often a disagreement in measuring ear corn in the crib. As will be seen from the above, the differences result from taking a different number of cubic inches to the bushel. 

Here is another very simple rule:

Multiply the cubic feet by 4 and divide the product by 9. 

EXAMPLE:-A crib of corn is 15 feet long, 8 feet wide and 9 feet high. 

How many bushels of corn does it contain? 

SOLUTION:-15X8X9-1080X4=4320÷9-480 bushels. 

This allows 24 cubic feet. or about 3900 cubic inches for a bushel. 

This rule is not only very simple but is very frequently used. It will hold out in good dry corn. 

When the crib is flared at the side multiply half the sum of the top and bottom widths in feet by the perpendicular height in feet, and then again by the length in feet. This gives the number of cubic feet. as above.

How to Estimate the Contents of a Pile of Grain, Potatoes, Etc. 

RULE:-Put the commodity in the form of a heap. Then multiply the diameter in feet by itself, and then again by the height in feet, and divide the result by 4, and you have the approximate contents in bushels. 

EXAMPLE:-How many bushels in a heap of grain 6 feet in diameter and 3 feet high?

SOLUTION:-6X6X3÷4-27 bushels. Ans. 

How to Figure Up a Load of Grain. 

RULE:-Find the total number of pounds and divide that by the number of pounds in one bushel and it will equal the number of bushels. 

EXAMPLE:-How many bushels in 2840 pounds of wheat, and what will it cost at 90 cents per bushel? 

SOLUTION:-2840÷60-47 bushels and 20 pounds or 47 1/3 bushels. 

47 1/3X90c. $42.60. Ans.

How to Calculate the Weight of Coal in a Bin or Box. 

A solid cubic foot of anthracite coal weighs about 93 pounds. When broken for use it weighs about 54 pounds. Bituminous coal when broken up for use weighs about 50 pounds. 

RULE:-Multiply the length in feet by the height in feet, and again by the breadth in feet, and this result by 54 for anthracite coal, or by 50 for bituminous coal, and the result will equal the number of pounds. 

To find the number of tons. divide by 2,000. 

EXAMPLE:-A coal bin is ten feet long, 8 feet wide, and 5 feet high. 

How many tons of anthracite coal will it hold? SOLUTION-10X8X5X54-21,600. 

21,600 2,000=10 tons and 1,600 pounds. 

Amount of Charcoal in a Bin.

Multiply length, breadth, and height (all in inches) together, and divide by 2571, the number of cubic inches in a bushel of charcoal. 

How to Find the Number of Cords in a Pile of Wood. 

A cord of wood is a pile 8 feet long, 4 feet wide and 4 feet high and contains 128 cubic feet.

RULE:-Multiply the length in feet by the width in feet and that result by the height in feet and divide the product by 128 and you have the number of cords.

Example:-How many cords in a pile of wood 4 feet wide, 7 feet high, 24 feet long. 

SOLUTION:-4X7X24-672 cubic feet. 

672÷128 54 cords. Ans.

A cord of wood contains 128 cubic feet when the wood is cut 4 feet long. It is an error to suppose that a cord should always contain 128 cubic feet, as, for instance, cooking stove wood is seldom over 20 inches in width when corded, but the width is counted the same as if it was four feet. As for instance in the following example:

RULE: Multiply the length of the pile by the height, and divide by 32. 

EXAMPLE:-How many cords are contained in a pile of stove wood 

17 feet long, 6 feet high and 19 inches in width? 

SOLUTION:-17 length X 6 height=102; 102÷32=3% cords. Ans.

How to Find the Weight of Cattle By Measurement. 

To find the approximate weight, measure as follows: 1. The girth be hind the shoulders. 2. The length from the forepart of the shoulderblade along the back to the bone at the tail, in a vertical line with the buttocks. Then multiply the square of the girth in feet by five times the length in feet. Divide the product by 1.5 for average cattle (if cattle be very fat, by 1.425; if very lean, by 1.575) and the quotient will be the dressed weight of the quarters. Thus: The girth of a steer is 6.5 feet, and the length from the shoulder-blade to the tail bone is 5.25. The square of 6.5 is 42.25, and 5 times 5.25 is 26.25. Multiplying these together gives 1109.0625, which, when divided by 1.5, produces 739.375 lbs., the approximate net weight of the steer after being dressed. 

The Short Method. 

Multiply the distance around the animal (back of the fore-shoulder) by itself, and then multiply that result by 17.5 and you have the weight of the animal (nearly.)

Railway Signals. 

One whistle signifies "down brakes." 

Two whistles signify "off brakes." 

Three whistles signify "back up." 

Continued whistles signify "danger." 

Rapid short whistles "a cattle alarm."

A sweeping parting of the hands on a level with the eyes signifies "go ahead."

Downward motion of the hands with extended arms signifies "stop." 

Beckoning motion of one hand signifies "back."

Red flag waved up the track signifies "danger. 

Red flag stuck up by the roadside signifies "danger ahead."

Red flag carried on a locomotive signifies "an engine following." 

Red flag hoisted at a station is a signal "to stop." 

Lantern at night raised and lowered vertically is a signal "to start." 

Lantern swung at right angles across the track means "stop." 

Lanterns swung in a circle signify "back the train."

Thermometers Compared. 

There are three kinds of thermometers in general use thruout the world, the Centigrade, the 

Reaumer, and the Fahrenheit. The freezing and boiling points on their scales compare as follows: 

Freezing Pt Boiling Pt 

Centigrade Zero 100 degrees Reaumer 

Zero 80 66 66 

Fahrenheit 32 degrees 212

The accompanying illustration shows at a glance how the scales compare.

Formulae For Equivalents. 

To find the same temperature on different scales the following rules may be used: 

Centigrade to Reaumer-multiply by 4/5ths. 

Centigrade to Fahrenheit-multiply by 9/5ths and add 32. 

Reaumer to Centigrade-multiply by 5/4ths. 

Reaumer to Fahrenheit-multiply by 

9/4ths and add 32. 

Fahrenheit to Centigrade-subtract 

32 and multiply by 5/9ths. 

Fahrenheit to Reaumer-subtract 

32 and multiply by 4/9ths.

The Mechanical Powers 

There are six simple mechanical elements which overcome resistance. 

They are: 1, the Lever; 2, the Wheel and Axle; 3, the Pulley; 4, the 

Inclined Plane; 5, the Screw, and 6, the Wedge. In their operation the applied force is called the power and the resisting force is called the weight. 

1. The Lever is a long bar turning on a prop called the fulcrum. The arms of the lever are the parts on each side of the fulcrum.

RULE. The power applied to a lever is increased as many times as the power arm is longer than the weight arm.

EXAMPLE: What weight can a man weighing 160 lbs. raise with a lever 

10 feet long, the fulcrum being 9 feet from the power and 1 foot from the weight?

SOLUTION: 

91-9; 9X160-1440 lbs., or by proportion 

160:1440 lbs. Ans. 1:9= 

2. The Wheel and Axle is a modifica tion of the lever and acts on the same principle. 

3. The Pulley is a grooved wheel turning on a pin in a frame called a block. A single pulley affords no mechanical advantage but in system of pulleys called the Block and Tackle the power applied to the hauling line is increased as many times as there are pulleys in both blocks.

EXAMPLE: Find the number of pounds that can be raised by applying a power of 50 lbs. to a block and tackle having three pulleys in each block. 

SOLUTION: 50X6 = 300 lbs. Ans. མི་ཅ་ 

RULE: The power is increased as many times as the diameter of the wheel is greater than the diameter of the axle.

EXAMPLE: How much weight can be raised by a wheel 60 inches in diameter and an axle 3 inches in diameter by applying a pull of 50 lbs.?

SOLUTION: 60÷3=20; 20 X 50= 

1000 lbs. or by proportion 3: 60= 

50:1000 lbs. Ans. 

4. The Inclined Plane is, as its name indicates, an even surface sloping at an angle between the horizontal and the vertical. It is used for moving heavy merchandise from one level to another.

RULE: The power applied is in creased as many times as the length of the inclined plane is greater than the elevation.

EXAMPLE: If it requires all of a man's strength to lift a barrel weighing 100 lbs. into a wagon 3 feet from the ground, how heavy a barrel could he roll into the wagon by means of a 9-foot plank?

SOLUTION: 9÷3=3; 100X3=300.

5. The Screw is a modification of the inclined plane. The distance between the threads is called the pitch of the screw. The power is applied to a wheel or lever attached to the screw. Thus to raise the weight the distance between the threads, the wheel must make one complete revolution, which is 62/7 times the length of the lever. 

BALER AND RULE: The power applied is in creased as many times as 6 2/7 times the length of the lever is greater than the pitch of the screw. 

EXAMPLE: What pressure can be exerted by a screw with 2-inch pitch by applying a power of 50 

ĺbs. to the end of a 14-inch lever? SOLUTION: 14X6 2/7 X 50÷2=8800 

lbs. Ans. 

6. The Wedge is also an adaptation of the inclined plane. In fact, it may be considered as a double inclined plane. It is used for splitting wood or stone but the friction encountered is SO great that it is almost impossible to compute its mechanical advantage.

RULE: Apart from friction the power applied is increased as many times as the length of one of its slant sides is greater than ½ the thickness of its head. 

EXAMPLE: Thus a wedge, one of whose slant sides is 10 inches long and head 2 inches thick would exert a force (10% of 2) or 10 times greater than the power applied without considering the friction involved. 

To Extract the Square Root 

RULES. 1. Beginning with units, point off the given number into periods of two figures each (the last period may have but one figure). 2. Find the greatest square in the left-hand period and place its root on the right as in division. 3. Subtract the square from the left-hand period, and to the remainder, bring down the next period for a dividend. 4. Take twice the root figure for a trial divisor and find how often it is contained in the dividend excepting the right-hand figure; write the quotient as the second root figure; and also annex it to the trial divisor. 5. Multiply the completed divisor by the last root figure, subtract the product from the dividend, and bring down another period for a dividend. 6. Add the last root figure to the complete divisor for the next trial divisor, and proceed as before until the last root of each period is found. 7. If the trial divisor is not contained in the dividend, write a zero in the root and on the right of the trial divisor, and bring down another period. 8. If the number is not a square, the root may be extracted to any number of decimal places by adding periods or ciphers to the remainder. 9. In pointing out decimals begin at the tenths place. 10. To extract the square root of a common fraction reduce it to a decimal. 

EXAMPLE: Find the square root of 5317636. 

There being four periods, the root will consist of 4 figures. The greatest square of the first period is 4 and its root is 2. The first dividend is 131 and the first complete divisor 43. The second trial divisor (46) not going into 27 (6) write a zero in the root and in the trial divisor (46), then bring down the next period; and the complete divisor is contained 6 times. 5317636 (2306 4 

Sq. Root Ans. 43) 131 129 4606 27636 27636

To Extract the Cube Root RULES. 1. Separate the numbers into periods of three figures each by placing a lot over units, thousands, etc. (The left-hand period may have but one or two figures.) Find the greatest cube in the left-hand period and place its root on the right as in division. Subtract the cube from its period and bring down the next period as a dividend. 2. To three times the square of the root figure add two ciphers for first trial divisor. In a separate column, "A," write three times the root figure. Find the second root figure by trial and write it in the root, also annex it to the number in "A." 3. 

Then multiply the number in column "A" by the second root figure, and add the product to the trial divisor, thus forming the complete divisor. 

4. Multiply this divisor by the second root figure, subtract the product from the dividend and to the remainder bring down another period for the new dividend. 5. To find the 2nd trial divisor add together the complete divisor, the number just above it and the square of the last root figure and annex two ciphers, and thus proceed as before. 6. When the trial divisor is not contained in its dividend, write a zero in the root, annex two zeros to the trial divisor and one zero to the last number in "A" and then bring down another period to the dividend.
